q: What is Apex and where does it run?
alt: Can you explain what Apex is?
Tell me about the Apex programming language
what is apex in salesforce
Why do we need Apex when we have Flow?
a: Apex is Salesforce's own programming language. It's strongly typed and object-oriented, the syntax looks a lot like Java, and it runs entirely on Salesforce servers. Because the platform is multitenant, every Apex transaction is controlled by governor limits, so one customer's code can't hog shared resources. Apex is compiled and stored as metadata, it has DML and SOQL built in, and code needs test coverage before it can be deployed to production. I reach for it when declarative tools handle the logic poorly: complex bulk processing, integrations with REST or SOAP callouts, custom controllers for LWC, batch and asynchronous jobs, and reusable services. For example, if an order has to be sent to an external system over REST and the response written back to the record, that's Apex work. My rule on the team is Flow first for simple automation, and Apex when I need control, performance or testability, and in design reviews I ask people to say which side of that line a requirement falls on.
points: Strongly typed, object-oriented, Java-like syntax
Runs on Salesforce servers in a multitenant model
Governed by per-transaction limits
Native SOQL, SOSL and DML
Needs test coverage before production deploy

q: What data types are available in Apex?
alt: Explain primitive data types in Apex
Which data type should I use for currency in Apex?
what are the different data types in apex
Integer vs Long vs Decimal in Apex
a: Apex has primitives, sObjects, collections, enums, and user-defined or system classes. The primitives are Integer, which is 32-bit, Long, which is 64-bit, Double, Decimal, String, Boolean, Date, Datetime, Time, Id, Blob, and the generic Object. sObjects like Account or a custom object represent records, and the generic SObject type lets me write reusable code. The collections are List, Set and Map. For money I always use Decimal, because currency fields map to Decimal and it avoids floating-point rounding. Say I'm adding up Opportunity amounts for a discount calculation: with Decimal the totals come out exact, with no rounding surprises. The tricky one is nulls. Every uninitialized variable is null, even a Boolean. So if I declare Boolean isVip and never set it, using it can throw a NullPointerException. I either initialize my variables or null-check them. In code review, a Double on a money calculation is one of the first things I flag.
points: Primitives: Integer, Long, Double, Decimal, String, Boolean, Date, Datetime, Time, Id, Blob
Decimal for currency values
sObject and generic SObject types
Collections: List, Set, Map
Uninitialized variables are null, even Boolean

q: What is the difference between List, Set and Map in Apex?
alt: List vs Set vs Map, when do you use each?
Explain Apex collections
list set map difference in apex
Which collection allows duplicates in Apex?
a: All three are collections, but each solves a different problem. A List is ordered, indexed from zero, and allows duplicates, so I use it for query results and for bulk DML. A Set holds only unique values, so it's mainly for lookups and building filters. A Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys, and it's the backbone of bulkified code. Here's a typical case. In a Contact trigger, I collect the AccountIds from Trigger.new into a Set and use it in a WHERE Id IN clause. I pass that query straight into the Map constructor, which gives me a Map of Id to Account. Then inside the loop I just call get with the AccountId, with no extra query. One gotcha: String keys in Sets and Maps are case-sensitive, so 'ABC' and 'abc' count as two different keys. When I review trigger code, a query inside a loop where a Map should be is the first thing I look for.
points: List: ordered, indexed, duplicates allowed
Set: unique values, fast contains()
Map: unique keys to values, used for lookups
new Map<Id, Account>(query) builds an Id map
String keys in Set/Map are case-sensitive

q: How do you group child records by parent using a Map in Apex?
alt: Write code to build a Map of AccountId to list of Contacts
Map<Id, List<Contact>> example
how to create map of account id and contacts
Show a common Map pattern used in triggers
a: I use the Map of Id to List pattern. Say 200 Accounts come in and I need each one's Contacts. First I get the Accounts into a Map keyed by Id, using the Map constructor on a query. Then I run one query for the Contacts, filtered with that map's keySet. I loop through the Contacts, and for each one I check containsKey on a Map of Id to List of Contact. If there's no list for that AccountId yet, I put a new empty list, then I add the Contact to it. After that, inside any loop I can call get with the Account Id and get all its children, with no extra SOQL. The nice part is it stays at two queries whether 5 records come in or 200. That's exactly what bulkification means. I expect this pattern to be second nature on my teams, because it's the difference between code that passes a unit test and code that survives a data load.
points: Map constructor on a query gives Id to record
One query for children using keySet()
containsKey check, then put an empty list
Constant number of queries regardless of volume

q: What is the difference between static and instance variables and methods in Apex?
alt: Static vs instance in Apex
When would you use a static method?
what does static keyword mean in apex
Do static variables keep their value across transactions?
a: A static member belongs to the class itself, and an instance member belongs to each object I create with new. I call a static method straight on the class, like Utils.formatPhone, without creating an object, so I use static for stateless utility logic and service methods. Instance variables hold state for one particular object. The Apex-specific part is that a static variable only lives for one transaction. Everything in that transaction shares it, which is why it's used for recursion guards and caching query results. For example, if my Account trigger's logic ends up updating the same Accounts again, a static Set of already-processed Ids stops it from running twice. But that static is reset for the next transaction, and it's never shared between users. Also, a static method can't directly use instance variables. In reviews I watch for static state used carelessly, because it's an easy source of order-dependent bugs in tests.
points: Static: belongs to the class, called without new
Instance: one copy per object
Static variables persist only for one transaction
Used for recursion control and caching

q: How do constructors work in Apex?
alt: What is a constructor in Apex?
Can you overload constructors in Apex?
explain default constructor apex
What is constructor chaining with this()?
a: A constructor is a special method with the same name as the class and no return type, and it runs when I create an object with new. If I don't write any constructor, Apex gives me a default no-argument one. But as soon as I write a constructor with parameters, that default no longer exists unless I add it myself. That one catches people out. Say I add InvoiceBuilder(Id accountId), and some older code still calls new InvoiceBuilder() with nothing. That call breaks until I add the no-argument constructor back. I can overload constructors with different parameter lists and chain them with this(...) as the first statement, so I don't duplicate initialization code. A child class calls the parent constructor with super(...). And I use a private constructor when I want to stop people instantiating a class, like a singleton or a pure utility class. So when someone adds a parameterized constructor to a shared class, I ask them to search for existing callers first.
points: Same name as class, no return type
Default no-arg constructor only if none is defined
Overloading and this(...) chaining
super(...) calls the parent constructor
Private constructor for singleton or utility classes

q: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class in Apex?
alt: Interface vs abstract class
When would you use an abstract class over an interface?
can an apex class implement multiple interfaces
difference between interface and abstract in apex
a: An interface is a pure contract. It only declares method signatures, with no implementation, and a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class can have abstract methods that children must implement, plus normal methods with shared logic, member variables and constructors. But a class can extend only one class, and an abstract class can't be instantiated. I choose an interface when unrelated classes need the same capability. The platform's own Queueable, Schedulable, Database.Batchable and Comparable are good examples of that. I choose an abstract class when several related classes share common code. For example, I'd write a base trigger handler that holds the dispatch logic, and then an AccountTriggerHandler and a CaseTriggerHandler extend it and only fill in their own specific handler methods. The trade-off I explain to the team is flexibility versus shared code: interfaces keep things loosely coupled, while an abstract class cuts duplication but ties every child to one parent.
points: Interface: signatures only, multiple allowed
Abstract class: shared code plus abstract methods
Single inheritance for classes
Neither can be instantiated directly
Platform examples: Queueable, Batchable, Comparable

q: Explain virtual, abstract and override keywords and how inheritance works in Apex.
alt: How does inheritance work in Apex?
Why do I need the virtual keyword to extend a class?
what is the override keyword in apex
Are Apex classes final by default?
a: In Apex, classes and methods are final by default, which is different from Java. If I want another class to extend mine, I have to declare it virtual or abstract. A virtual method has a default implementation that a child may override. An abstract method has no body, so the child must implement it. In the child class I write extends ParentClass and mark the method with the override keyword, otherwise it won't compile. Inside the child I can call super.methodName() to reuse the parent logic, and protected members are visible to subclasses. For example, a virtual BaseNotifier class with a virtual send method, and an EmailNotifier that overrides send, calls super.send() for the shared part, then adds its own email logic. Apex supports only single inheritance of classes, but a class can extend one class and implement several interfaces at the same time. On my teams I keep inheritance shallow, usually one base class, because deep hierarchies get hard to debug and review.
points: Classes and methods are final by default
virtual: optional override; abstract: mandatory
Child must use override keyword
super calls the parent version
Single class inheritance

q: How would you use polymorphism in Apex to avoid long if-else chains?
alt: Give an example of polymorphism in Apex
How do you implement the strategy pattern in Apex?
Type.forName dynamic class instantiation example
how to make apex logic configurable without code changes
a: I'd go with an interface for the behaviour and one class per variation, then pick the class at runtime. For example, a DiscountStrategy interface with GoldDiscount and StandardDiscount implementations. The calling code only knows the interface, so adding a new tier means adding a new class, not editing a growing if-else block. To make it configurable I store the class name in custom metadata and use Type.forName to create the instance, then cast it to the interface. This is the strategy pattern plus a simple factory, and it is also easier to test because I can pass a fake implementation. I always handle the case where Type.forName returns null because the class name is wrong. The trade-off is more classes to navigate, so I only push this pattern when a chain has several branches that keep changing, not for a simple two-way check.
points: Program to an interface, not a concrete class
One class per variation (strategy pattern)
Type.forName + newInstance for runtime selection
Class names can live in custom metadata
Null-check the Type returned by forName

q: What is the difference between with sharing, without sharing and inherited sharing?
alt: Explain sharing keywords in Apex
What happens if I don't declare any sharing keyword on a class?
with sharing vs without sharing
what is inherited sharing in apex
a: These keywords decide whether Apex respects record-level sharing for the running user. With sharing enforces the user's sharing rules, so queries only return records the user can see. Without sharing ignores record sharing and sees everything, and I only use that for deliberate system operations. Inherited sharing runs in the sharing mode of whatever class called it, and if it's the entry point, like an LWC controller, it runs as with sharing. Say a sales rep can only see their own Opportunities. A with sharing query gives them just theirs; a without sharing query gives them everyone's. If there's no keyword at all, it depends on the API version. From API version 67.0 the class runs with sharing. In older versions it follows the caller, and as an entry point it runs without sharing, except Aura controllers and @AuraEnabled methods called from LWC, which run with sharing. That's easy to get wrong, so on my teams every class declares a keyword, with sharing by default, and a missing keyword is a review comment.
points: with sharing: respects the user's record access
without sharing: ignores record sharing
inherited sharing: follows the caller, with sharing at entry point
No keyword: with sharing from API 67.0; older versions follow the caller
Sharing keywords do not enforce CRUD or FLS

q: A user complains that your LWC shows records they should not be able to see. How do you investigate and fix it?
alt: Users are seeing other people's records in a Lightning component
LWC is exposing data beyond the user's access, what went wrong?
component shows records that the user doesn't have access to
How do you secure an Apex controller used by LWC?
a: I treat this as a security issue first, so I check the sharing declaration on the controller and on every helper class it calls. The usual cause is that the controller, or the service class running the query, is declared without sharing, so the query ignores the user's sharing rules. To confirm, I log in as that user and compare what the component returns with what a list view shows. Say the list view shows 40 accounts and the component shows 300. That gap is the sharing problem. The fix is to declare the controller with sharing and, better, run the queries in user mode with WITH USER_MODE, which also enforces object and field permissions. If a helper class genuinely needs elevated access, I keep it separate, mark it without sharing on purpose, and only expose the minimum fields. Then I add a System.runAs test for a restricted user so it can't regress. I'd also tell the stakeholder plainly what was exposed and to whom, because that's a data-access incident, not just a bug.
points: Check the controller's sharing keyword first
Reproduce by logging in as the user
Use with sharing plus WITH USER_MODE
Isolate intentional system-mode code
Add a runAs test for a restricted user

q: How does exception handling work in Apex?
alt: Explain try catch finally in Apex
What are common exceptions in Apex?
can we catch limit exception in apex
How do you handle errors in Apex code?
a: Apex uses try, catch and finally, just like Java. I wrap risky code in try, catch specific exception types first and the generic Exception last, and use finally for cleanup that must always run. The common ones are DmlException, QueryException when a single-record query returns no rows, NullPointerException, ListException for a bad index, SObjectException when I read a field I didn't query, CalloutException and JSONException. Every exception gives me getMessage, getTypeName, getLineNumber and getStackTraceString for logging. For example, around a callout I'd catch CalloutException first to log the failed request, then generic Exception as the safety net. The key gotcha: System.LimitException can't be caught, so governor limits have to be avoided, not handled. For LWC I throw an AuraHandledException with a friendly message, and in triggers I use addError on the record. My standard for the team is no empty catch blocks: every catch either logs, rethrows or shows the user something useful.
points: Catch specific exceptions before generic Exception
Common: DmlException, QueryException, NullPointerException
LimitException cannot be caught
AuraHandledException for LWC errors
addError to block a record in triggers

q: How do you create and use a custom exception in Apex?
alt: Write a custom exception class
What are the rules for naming a custom exception?
how to throw custom exception in apex
Why create custom exceptions?
a: I create a class that extends Exception, and its name has to end with the word Exception, otherwise it won't compile. I don't have to write constructors, because Apex automatically gives me ones that take no argument, a message, a cause exception, or both. Then I throw it with the throw keyword when a business rule is broken, and callers can catch that specific type separately from system errors. For example, if someone orders 10 units and only 4 are in stock, I throw new InsufficientStockException('Only 4 units left'). The UI can show that clear message, and in the logs those failures are easy to filter. If the caller needs more detail, I can also add my own properties, like an error code. I like the team to keep a small set of named exceptions per domain, so error handling stays consistent instead of everyone inventing their own.
points: Extend Exception; name must end with Exception
Built-in constructors: (), (msg), (cause), (msg, cause)
Throw with throw new ...
Catch the specific type separately

q: What is the difference between DML statements and Database class methods?
alt: insert vs Database.insert
What does allOrNone false do?
dml statement versus database methods
When would you use Database.update instead of update?
a: A DML statement like insert accounts is all-or-nothing. If one record fails, the whole operation rolls back and a DmlException is thrown. The Database class methods, like Database.insert(records, false), let me set allOrNone to false, so the valid records are saved and the failed ones are reported. They return result objects, like SaveResult for insert and update, UpsertResult and DeleteResult, and I check isSuccess and getErrors for each record. For example, if I'm loading 1,000 contacts and 3 have a bad value, a plain insert saves none of them. Database.insert with false saves the other 997 and tells me which 3 failed. Database methods also accept DMLOptions, for example to run assignment rules or allow field truncation, and an AccessLevel for user mode. Both cost the same against governor limits. I use Database methods for data loads and integrations where partial success is acceptable. The real question I ask is whether the business can live with partial data. If they can't, it stays all-or-nothing.
points: DML statements: all-or-none, throw DmlException
Database methods: allOrNone flag
Return SaveResult, UpsertResult, DeleteResult
Support DMLOptions and AccessLevel
Same governor limit cost

q: Write code to insert records with partial success and log the failures.
alt: How do you process Database.SaveResult?
Partial insert in Apex with error handling
database dot insert all or none false example
How do you know which record failed in a bulk insert?
a: I call Database.insert with allOrNone set to false and loop through the SaveResult list. The results come back in the same order as the input list, so index i in the results matches index i in my records. That's how I tie each error back to the source record. Say an integration sends 500 contacts and two of them fail validation. Those two fail, the other 498 save. For each failure I read the status code, the message and the fields involved, and collect them into a log list or a custom log object. At the end I insert all the log records in one DML, or publish an error event. That way one bad row in an integration batch doesn't block the good rows, and support can see exactly what failed. The guardrail I set is that a partial-success call without error handling doesn't get past review, because silently dropped rows are worse than a visible failure.
points: allOrNone = false allows partial success
Results are in the same order as input
Read getStatusCode, getMessage, getFields
Log failures in bulk, not per record

q: How do savepoints and rollback work in Apex, and what are the gotchas?
alt: Explain Database.setSavepoint and Database.rollback
What are the limitations of savepoints?
transaction control in apex
Does rollback reset static variables?
a: Database.setSavepoint marks a point in the transaction, and Database.rollback(sp) undoes every DML done after that point while the transaction carries on. I use it when I catch an exception and want to return gracefully without leaving half-created data. For example, I insert an Order, then its line items fail. I roll back to the savepoint so I'm not left with an empty Order. The gotchas matter here. Both setSavepoint and rollback count against the DML statement limit. Rollback doesn't reset static variables or the in-memory sObjects, so records inserted after the savepoint still carry their Ids, and inserting them again fails unless I clear the Id or clone them. If I roll back to an earlier savepoint, any later savepoints become invalid. And savepoints can't be shared across separate trigger invocations. In review I check that anyone using rollback also handles those stale Ids, because that's where the subtle bugs come from.
points: Rollback undoes DML after the savepoint
Both calls count as DML statements
Static variables and in-memory Ids are not reset
Rolling back to an earlier savepoint invalidates later ones
Cannot cross trigger invocations

q: You need to create an Account, Contact and Opportunity together, and if any fails nothing should be saved. How do you do it?
alt: How do you make multiple DML operations atomic?
All-or-nothing save across objects in Apex
rollback all records if one insert fails
Undo the account insert if the contact insert fails
a: I'd handle this with a savepoint and an explicit rollback. By default, if an exception isn't caught, the whole transaction rolls back anyway. The problem starts when I catch the exception to show a friendly message, because then the earlier DML would stay committed. Say the Account and Contact insert fine, but the Opportunity fails. If I've caught that error, I'm left with an Account and a Contact and no Opportunity. So I set a savepoint before the first insert and do the three inserts in order inside try. In catch, I call Database.rollback to that savepoint, then throw an AuraHandledException or return an error response. That gives me one atomic unit of work across objects. In a larger codebase I'd put this in a service method, or use a Unit of Work pattern that registers the records and commits them together, with the savepoint handled centrally. It's a bit more ceremony, but I'd rather standardise it once than have each developer hand-roll their own rollback logic.
points: Uncaught exceptions already roll back everything
Catching means you must roll back yourself
Savepoint before first DML, rollback in catch
Unit of Work pattern for larger codebases

q: What is dynamic Apex and when would you use Schema describe?
alt: Explain dynamic Apex
What is Schema.getGlobalDescribe used for?
schema describe methods in apex
How do you get object and field information at runtime?
a: Dynamic Apex means writing code that works with objects and fields decided at runtime instead of hard-coded at compile time. It has three parts: Schema describe to read metadata, dynamic SOQL and SOSL with Database.query or Search.query, and dynamic DML using SObjectType.newSObject plus put and get on generic sObjects. A good example is a generic related-list LWC. You pass it an object name like Case or Invoice__c, and the same Apex builds the query and reads the fields for whichever object it gets. I also use it for field sets, checking field permissions, and reading picklist values. A performance tip: Schema.getGlobalDescribe is expensive, so I prefer direct tokens like Account.SObjectType, or Schema.describeSObjects for specific objects, and I cache describe results in static variables. I'm careful about where the team uses it, though, because the compiler won't catch a typo in a field name, so I keep dynamic code to genuinely generic components.
points: Describe: object and field metadata at runtime
Dynamic SOQL/SOSL with Database.query and Search.query
Dynamic DML with newSObject, put and get
Avoid getGlobalDescribe in loops; cache results

q: Write Apex to read field details and active picklist values dynamically.
alt: How do you get picklist values in Apex?
Get all fields of an object using describe
fetch picklist values apex code
How do you check if a field is updateable in Apex?
a: I use the fields map from the object's describe to loop through every field and read its label, type and permissions, which is handy when I'm building a dynamic form. For picklists, I call getDescribe on the field token, loop through getPicklistValues, and keep only the active entries. For example, if Lead Source still has an old value that an admin deactivated, the active check keeps it out of my dropdown. These describe calls respect the running user, so isAccessible and isUpdateable tell me what that user can actually do. If the object name comes in as a string, I use Schema.describeSObjects with that name instead of the global describe. In an LWC I usually prefer the UI API wire adapters for picklists, but in Apex this is the standard approach. I'd ask the team to keep this in one shared utility so describe logic isn't copied across classes.
points: fields.getMap() returns all field tokens
DescribeFieldResult gives label, type, permissions
getPicklistValues + isActive filter
Use describeSObjects when the name is a string

q: How do you write dynamic SOQL safely and prevent SOQL injection?
alt: What is SOQL injection and how do you prevent it?
Database.query vs Database.queryWithBinds
safe dynamic soql example
Is String.escapeSingleQuotes enough?
a: SOQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a query string, so someone can change the WHERE clause and read data they shouldn't. Say a search box glues whatever the user types straight into WHERE Name equals that text. If they type a quote followed by an OR condition, they've rewritten the filter and can pull back records they were never meant to see. My first choice is bind variables, which keep input as data, never as query text. With Database.queryWithBinds I pass a map of bind names to values plus an AccessLevel, so the query also runs in user mode. For parts that can't be bound, like field or object names, I validate them against the schema describe or an allow-list. String.escapeSingleQuotes is a fallback for string literals, but it doesn't protect field names or numeric input, so I don't rely on it alone. In code review, dynamic SOQL built from raw user input is a hard stop for me.
points: Never concatenate raw user input
Bind variables keep input as data
queryWithBinds with a bind map and AccessLevel
Allow-list field/object names via describe
escapeSingleQuotes is only a fallback

q: How do you use SOQL inside Apex, and what errors are common?
alt: Explain inline SOQL in Apex
What is a bind variable in SOQL?
list has no rows for assignment to sobject error
How do you query parent and child records in Apex?
a: In Apex I write SOQL inside square brackets, and it returns a List of sObjects. I pass Apex values in with bind variables using a colon, like WHERE Id IN :accountIds. For parent fields I use dot notation, like Account.Name on Contact, and for children I use a subquery on the relationship name, like Contacts. The most common error is assigning a query directly to a single sObject. If nothing comes back, you get 'List has no rows for assignment', and if more than one row comes back, that errors too. For example, assigning a query on Account by name to one Account variable breaks the day there's no match, or two. So I query into a list and check isEmpty. Reading a field I didn't select throws an SObjectException. And aggregate queries return AggregateResult, which I read with get and an alias. In review, a query assigned straight to a single record with no handling is something I always flag.
points: Inline SOQL in brackets returns a List
Bind variables with colon
Parent dot notation, child subqueries
Query into a List to avoid no-rows errors
Unqueried field access throws SObjectException

q: What is a SOQL for loop and why would you use it?
alt: Difference between a normal for loop on a list and a SOQL for loop
How does SOQL for loop help with heap size?
soql for loop chunks of 200
When should I use the list version of a SOQL for loop?
a: A SOQL for loop puts the query directly in the for statement, like for (Account a : [SELECT ...]). Behind the scenes, Salesforce fetches the records in chunks of 200 instead of loading the whole result into memory at once, so it greatly reduces heap usage on large queries. There's also a list form, for (List<Account> chunk : [SELECT ...]), which gives me 200 records at a time so I can do one DML per chunk. Say a query returns 10,000 contacts. With the list form that's 50 chunks of 200, so 50 DML statements, not one per record. But it doesn't bypass the 50,000 query-row limit, because every row still counts. I use it when a query may return thousands of records in one transaction, and I never put DML or another query inside the single-record form. It's one of the patterns I point the team to when a job starts hitting heap limits, before anyone reaches for Batch Apex.
points: Query placed directly in the for statement
Records fetched in chunks of 200
Reduces heap usage
List form allows DML per chunk
Still counts toward 50,000 query rows

q: What is a wrapper class and why do we use it?
alt: Explain wrapper class with an example
Why use a wrapper class in LWC?
what is wrapper class in salesforce apex
How do you show a checkbox with records in a table?
a: A wrapper class is a custom Apex class that bundles data from different sources into one object, so I can work with it or send it to the UI. The classic example is a table where each row needs a record plus a selected checkbox. So the wrapper holds, say, an Opportunity and a Boolean isSelected, and the user ticks the rows they want to process. I also use wrappers to combine fields from multiple objects, add calculated values, or represent JSON from an external API. For LWC, every property I want on the client must be annotated with @AuraEnabled, and the method returns a list of wrappers. Wrappers keep the UI simple, because the component receives exactly the shape it needs. When I review LWC controllers, I prefer a clear wrapper over a raw sObject with extra values bolted on, because the contract between Apex and the component stays obvious.
points: Custom class combining records and extra fields
Classic use: checkbox + record row
Combine multiple objects or calculated values
@AuraEnabled on properties for LWC
Also used to model JSON

q: Write a wrapper class for an LWC table and sort it with Comparable.
alt: How do you sort a list of wrapper objects?
Comparable interface example in Apex
wrapper class with aura enabled properties
How do I sort custom objects by a field in Apex?
a: I create an inner class with @AuraEnabled properties so LWC can read them, and a constructor that maps an Opportunity into the row shape, including a derived flag. Here that's isLarge, for amounts over 100,000. To sort the rows, I implement the Comparable interface and its compareTo method, returning a negative number, zero or a positive number. Then calling sort on the list uses my logic. I sort by amount descending and treat a null amount as zero, so an Opportunity with no amount still sorts cleanly, as zero. Newer API versions also have a Comparator interface, which lets me pass different sort orders to the sort method without changing the wrapper class. The controller uses with sharing and a user-mode query. I keep the sort logic inside the wrapper so it can be unit-tested on its own, and that's what I look for in review.
points: @AuraEnabled properties for LWC
Constructor maps sObject to row
Comparable.compareTo controls sort()
Handle nulls in comparison
Comparator allows multiple sort orders

q: How do you serialize and deserialize JSON in Apex?
alt: JSON.serialize and JSON.deserialize example
How do you convert a JSON response into an Apex object?
parse json in apex
Convert Apex object to JSON string
a: I create Apex classes that mirror the JSON structure, then call JSON.deserialize with the JSON string and the class type, and cast the result. Property names must match the JSON keys, and extra keys in the JSON are ignored by default. Say an API returns a customer with name, email and a dozen other fields. If my class only has name and email, I get those two and the rest is skipped. To go the other way, I call JSON.serialize on any object or list, or serializePretty for readable output in logs. Serialize also has an option to suppress null values, which is handy for clean API payloads. For very large or streaming responses there's JSONParser, and JSONGenerator if I need to build JSON piece by piece. Typed classes are my default, and the team standard, because they give compile-time safety and anyone reading the code can see the payload shape.
points: Model the JSON with Apex classes
JSON.deserialize(json, Type) then cast
JSON.serialize / serializePretty
Option to suppress nulls when serializing
JSONParser and JSONGenerator for advanced cases

q: An API returns JSON with dynamic keys and a field named like an Apex reserved word. How do you parse it?
alt: How do you parse JSON when the structure is not fixed?
JSON key is a reserved keyword in Apex, how to handle?
json deserialize untyped example
What if the JSON keys change per response?
a: I'd go with JSON.deserializeUntyped whenever the keys aren't fixed, or a key is a reserved word like limit or class that I can't use as a property name. It returns an Object that I cast to Map<String, Object>, and nested arrays come back as List<Object>, so I navigate the structure by key and cast each value. For example, if the response has a key called limit, I just read it with get('limit') on the map, no Apex property needed. Numbers can come back as Integer or Decimal, so I convert through String.valueOf to be safe. Another option for a reserved word is to replace the key in the raw string before typed deserialization, but that's fragile. If most of the payload is stable, I mix both: typed classes for the stable part and untyped maps for the dynamic part. I'd also ask the API owner for a sample payload and a documented contract, because untyped parsing breaks quietly when the shape changes.
points: deserializeUntyped returns Map<String, Object>
Arrays come back as List<Object>
Cast values carefully; numbers may be Integer or Decimal
Useful for reserved words and dynamic keys

q: What is the difference between custom settings and custom metadata types?
alt: Custom settings vs custom metadata
When do you use hierarchy custom settings?
custom metadata type vs custom setting which is better
Can custom metadata records be deployed?
a: Both store configuration, but the big difference is this. Custom metadata records are metadata, so they deploy with change sets, packages or the Metadata API along with the code. Custom setting records are data, so they must be loaded separately in each org. Custom settings come in list and hierarchy types. Hierarchy settings can hold different values at org, profile and user level, which is perfect for something like a trigger bypass. For example, I can switch a bypass flag on only for the integration user, and everyone else keeps it off. Custom metadata supports relationships, for example to other metadata or to object and field definitions, and its getAll and getInstance methods don't use SOQL queries. One more difference: Apex can update custom settings with normal DML, but custom metadata needs the Metadata API from Apex. The question I ask the team is simple: should this value move with a deployment, or be changed per org at runtime?
points: Custom metadata records deploy as metadata
Custom setting records are data per org
Hierarchy settings vary by org, profile, user
CMT getAll/getInstance avoid SOQL
CMT not editable with normal DML

q: You need configuration for an integration endpoint, feature toggles and a trigger bypass for data migration. Where would you store each?
alt: How do you design configuration in a Salesforce org?
Where should I store API endpoints and credentials?
custom metadata or custom setting for feature flags
How do you bypass triggers during a data load?
a: I'd split it by purpose. The endpoint and authentication go in a Named Credential with an External Credential, never in custom metadata or code, so secrets are managed securely and the URL can differ per environment. Feature toggles and business mapping rules go in custom metadata because they should be version-controlled and deployed with the code, and reading them costs no SOQL. The trigger bypass goes in a hierarchy custom setting, because I can switch it on just for the migration user or profile without a deployment and switch it off afterwards. My trigger handler checks that setting first. This keeps secrets, deployable config and runtime switches cleanly separated. I write that split into our team guidelines so nobody has to guess, and an endpoint URL or token in code is an automatic rejection in review.
points: Endpoints and auth: Named Credentials
Feature flags and mappings: custom metadata
Per-user trigger bypass: hierarchy custom setting
Trigger handler checks bypass first

q: How do you read custom metadata records in Apex without using SOQL?
alt: Custom metadata getInstance example
Write a feature flag utility in Apex
get all custom metadata records apex
Does querying custom metadata count against SOQL limits?
a: Every custom metadata type has static methods. getAll returns a map of all records keyed by DeveloperName, and getInstance returns one record by DeveloperName or Id. These don't consume SOQL queries, so they're ideal inside triggers that run in bulk. I usually wrap them in a small utility class so the rest of the code just asks a question like isOn. For example, my trigger calls FeatureFlags.isOn('Auto_Assign_Cases'), and inside, that's just a getInstance call returning a checkbox value. Because the platform caches the records, these reads are fast. SOQL against custom metadata is still possible when I need filtering or relationship fields. And in tests I can inject fake records into a test-visible variable, so the test doesn't depend on whatever's configured in the org. I make that wrapper the team standard, so nobody scatters raw getInstance calls with hard-coded names across the codebase.
points: getAll(): map keyed by DeveloperName
getInstance(): single record
No SOQL consumed
Wrap in a small utility class
SOQL still available for filtering

q: What are the Apex best practices you always follow?
alt: Tell me some Apex coding best practices
How do you write good quality Apex code?
apex best practices interview question
What should you avoid when writing Apex?
a: My non-negotiable is bulkification. Every trigger and method should handle 200 or more records, with no SOQL or DML inside loops, using Sets and Maps instead. For example, if a data load updates 200 Accounts and the trigger queries Contacts inside the loop, that's 200 queries for one save. One query outside the loop fixes it. I keep one trigger per object with the logic in a handler class. I avoid hard-coded Ids by using custom metadata, custom labels, or querying by DeveloperName. I enforce security with with sharing and user-mode queries. I handle exceptions properly and never swallow them silently. I query only the fields I need, use selective filters, and move heavy work to asynchronous Apex. For tests, I create my own test data, write meaningful asserts, and test bulk, positive and negative cases, not just the coverage number. These are also the items on my team's code review checklist, so they're standards, not just personal habits.
points: Bulkify: no SOQL/DML in loops
One trigger per object, logic in handler
No hard-coded Ids
Enforce sharing, CRUD and FLS
Meaningful tests with bulk and negative cases

q: How do you enforce CRUD and field-level security in Apex?
alt: Does Apex respect field level security?
How do you check object and field permissions in Apex?
crud and fls enforcement apex
What is user mode in Apex?
a: By default Apex runs in system mode, which ignores the user's object and field permissions, so I enforce them explicitly. My first choice is user mode: WITH USER_MODE on SOQL, AccessLevel.USER_MODE on Database methods, or insert as user and update as user on DML statements. User mode enforces CRUD, FLS and sharing together. Say a support agent has no access to a Salary field. In system mode my query would happily return it to their screen. In user mode, that field is checked against their permissions. When I'd rather quietly remove the fields they can't access instead of failing, I use Security.stripInaccessible, which returns cleaned records and tells me which fields were removed. In older code you'll see describe checks like isAccessible or isUpdateable, or WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED, but Salesforce now recommends user mode. And remember, with sharing alone only handles record access, not CRUD or FLS. For new code on my teams, user mode is the default, and system mode needs a written reason.
points: Apex runs in system mode by default
WITH USER_MODE and AccessLevel.USER_MODE
insert as user / update as user
Security.stripInaccessible to remove fields
with sharing does not cover CRUD/FLS

q: What is the difference between WITH USER_MODE and WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED?
alt: with user mode versus with security enforced
Why does Salesforce recommend USER_MODE?
Does WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED check sharing?
user mode vs security enforced in soql
a: I'd standardise on USER_MODE. Both make a SOQL query respect the user's permissions, but USER_MODE is broader, and it's what Salesforce now recommends. WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks object and field read access only for fields in the SELECT and FROM clauses. It doesn't enforce sharing, and it throws on the first inaccessible field. WITH USER_MODE enforces sharing as well as CRUD and FLS, and it checks fields used anywhere in the query, including WHERE and ORDER BY. For example, if a user can't see Annual Revenue and I only use it in the WHERE clause, SECURITY_ENFORCED doesn't check it, but USER_MODE does. USER_MODE also handles more cases like polymorphic fields, and its QueryException can list all the inaccessible fields through getInaccessibleFields. And user mode is available for DML and Database methods too, so I get one consistent approach for reads and writes. When we touch older classes, I have the team migrate SECURITY_ENFORCED to USER_MODE as part of that change, rather than as a separate big-bang project.
points: SECURITY_ENFORCED: SELECT/FROM fields only, no sharing
USER_MODE: sharing + CRUD + FLS
USER_MODE checks WHERE and ORDER BY fields too
getInaccessibleFields lists all failures
USER_MODE also works for DML

q: How do you use Security.stripInaccessible?
alt: Write code using stripInaccessible
How do you remove fields a user can't access before DML?
strip inaccessible fields apex example
What does SObjectAccessDecision return?
a: Security.stripInaccessible takes an access type, like READABLE, CREATABLE, UPDATABLE or UPSERTABLE, and a list of records, and returns an SObjectAccessDecision. Calling getRecords gives me copies of the records with the inaccessible fields removed, and getRemovedFields tells me which fields were stripped for each object. I use it when I want graceful degradation instead of an exception. For example, an LWC edit form sends back five fields, but the user is only allowed to edit four of them. With UPDATABLE, the fifth field is stripped and the other four save. The gotcha is to always use the returned records for the DML, or for returning to the client, never the original list. It handles relationship fields and subqueries as well. That original-list mistake is exactly what I check for in review.
points: AccessType: READABLE, CREATABLE, UPDATABLE, UPSERTABLE
getRecords() returns sanitized copies
getRemovedFields() for logging
Use the returned list, not the original

q: A security review or code scan flags CRUD/FLS and sharing violations across many Apex controllers. How do you remediate?
alt: How would you fix security scanner findings in Apex?
AppExchange security review failed on FLS, what now?
code analyzer flagged crud violations in apex
How do you make an existing codebase secure for user access?
a: I'd treat this as a prioritised remediation, not a big-bang rewrite, so I start by triaging. I list every entry point exposed to users, meaning @AuraEnabled methods, REST resources, Visualforce controllers and invocable methods, because those matter most. Say the scan flags 60 classes and 15 of them are LWC controllers. Those 15 get fixed first. For each one I make the sharing explicit, with sharing or inherited sharing, and keep any genuine system-mode helper small and documented. Then I convert queries to WITH USER_MODE and DML to user mode, or use stripInaccessible where partial data is acceptable. I avoid returning raw sObjects with extra fields. I run Salesforce Code Analyzer in the CI pipeline so new violations fail the build, and I add runAs tests with a limited permission set user to prove access is enforced. False positives get documented, not ignored. For stakeholders, I'd report progress as user-facing entry points fixed versus remaining, which is clearer than a raw violation count.
points: Prioritize user-facing entry points
Explicit sharing keyword on every class
User-mode queries and DML, or stripInaccessible
Code Analyzer in CI to block regressions
runAs tests with a restricted user

q: How do you structure Apex code in a large org with many developers?
alt: What architecture do you follow for Apex?
Explain service layer, selector layer and domain layer
apex enterprise patterns fflib
How do you organize triggers and business logic at scale?
a: I'd go with a layered approach, inspired by Apex Enterprise Patterns. Triggers stay thin: one trigger per object that calls a handler through a small framework with bypass support. Business logic lives in service classes that are bulk-safe and reusable from triggers, LWC, batch or APIs. Queries live in selector classes, so field lists and security are consistent and easy to mock. Domain classes hold object-specific validation and defaults. For DML across objects I use a Unit of Work, so commits happen once and in the right order. Configuration goes in custom metadata. For example, a discount calculation is written once in an OpportunityService, and the trigger, an LWC button and a nightly batch all call that same method. This makes code testable with mocks, reduces merge conflicts and keeps governor limit usage predictable. The trade-off is more classes and some ceremony, so I scale it to the org. A small team may only need triggers, services and selectors, and I'd agree that up front rather than enforce every layer by habit.
points: Thin triggers with a handler framework
Service layer for business logic
Selector layer for queries
Domain layer for object rules
Unit of Work for DML ordering

q: Does a class declared with sharing enforce field-level security?
alt: Is with sharing enough for security?
What is system mode vs user mode in Apex?
with sharing enforce fls or not
Does Apex respect profile permissions automatically?
a: No, and that's a common misunderstanding. With sharing only enforces record-level access: sharing rules, role hierarchy, org-wide defaults and manual shares. It doesn't enforce object permissions or field-level security. Apex runs in system mode for CRUD and FLS by default. So a with sharing class can still read a salary field the user can't see on the page layout, or update an object the user has no edit permission on. Picture an HR component. The manager only sees their own team's records, which is sharing doing its job, but the salary column still shows up because nothing checked field-level security. To enforce those, I need user mode on queries and DML, or Security.stripInaccessible, or explicit describe checks. So a secure controller needs both: an explicit sharing keyword and user-mode data access. That's why my review checklist has sharing and CRUD/FLS as two separate items, because one doesn't imply the other.
points: with sharing = record access only
CRUD and FLS ignored in system mode
Use user mode or stripInaccessible for CRUD/FLS
Secure code needs both layers

q: Your trigger works for 200 records but skips logic for records beyond the first 200 in a single insert. What is wrong?
alt: Static Boolean recursion flag is skipping records
Why does my trigger only process the first chunk?
recursion guard bug with more than 200 records
Trigger logic not running for second batch of records
a: This is the classic static Boolean recursion guard bug. When Apex inserts more than 200 records in one DML, the trigger fires once per chunk of 200, but all in the same transaction, so static variables are shared. If the handler sets a static hasRun flag to true on the first chunk, every later chunk sees it and skips. The fix is to track processed record Ids in a static Set and only skip records already handled, or better, design the logic so it is safe to run again by checking whether the relevant field actually changed against Trigger.oldMap. I then add a test that inserts more than 200 records to prove it. For exactly this reason, a plain static Boolean guard isn't allowed in our trigger framework.
points: Triggers run in chunks of 200 within one transaction
Static variables are shared across chunks
Static Boolean flag skips later chunks
Use a static Set<Id> or compare old vs new values
Test with more than 200 records

q: Is string comparison in Apex case-sensitive?
alt: Difference between == and equals for Strings in Apex
Are Map keys case-sensitive in Apex?
string equals vs double equals apex
Why does my Set contains check fail for different case?
a: It depends on how I compare. The == operator on Strings is case-insensitive in Apex, so 'Hot' == 'hot' is true. The equals method is case-sensitive, and equalsIgnoreCase is the explicit case-insensitive version. Collections are different again. Set<String> contains and Map<String, ...> keys are case-sensitive, so a lookup with different casing returns false or null. That's a common source of bugs when keys come from user input or an external system. Say I build a map of country codes with 'IN' as the key, and the integration sends 'in'. The get comes back null and my lookup fails, even though the value looks the same to a person. So my habit is to normalize keys, for example with toLowerCase, both when I put them into a Map or Set and when I read them back. It's a small thing, but I call it out when reviewing integration code, because the bug only shows up with real data.
points: == on Strings is case-insensitive
equals() is case-sensitive
equalsIgnoreCase() for explicit intent
Set and Map String keys are case-sensitive
Normalize keys with toLowerCase

q: How would you design an error logging framework in Apex that survives transaction rollback?
alt: How do you log errors if the transaction rolls back?
Design an Apex logging framework
platform event for error logging apex
Why are my error log records not saved after an exception?
a: I'd build it on platform events. If I insert a log record and then the transaction fails, the log is rolled back with everything else. So I publish a platform event for each error, with the event's publish behaviour set to publish immediately. Those events are published even if the transaction later rolls back. A platform event trigger or flow subscribes and inserts the log records in a separate transaction. For example, if an order save fails halfway and the whole thing rolls back, the error log is still there the next morning, because it came through the event. My Logger class collects entries in memory during the transaction and publishes them in bulk. It captures class, method, message, stack trace, user and a correlation Id, and respects a log-level setting in custom metadata. I also add a scheduled purge so the log object doesn't grow forever. I'd also make that Logger the one approved way to log on the team, so we don't end up with three half-finished logging approaches.
points: Normal log inserts roll back with the transaction
Platform event with publish immediately survives rollback
Subscriber inserts logs in a separate transaction
Buffer and publish in bulk
Configurable log level and retention purge

q: What are governor limits and why does Salesforce enforce them?
alt: Explain governor limits
Why do governor limits exist?
what is governor limit in salesforce
What happens when you exceed a governor limit?
a: Governor limits are runtime limits Salesforce enforces on every Apex transaction, like how many SOQL queries, DML statements, CPU time or heap memory one transaction can use. They exist because Salesforce is multitenant. Many customers share the same servers and database, so the platform makes sure one org's inefficient code can't slow everyone else down. Think of an apartment building sharing one water tank: every flat gets a fair quota. When a limit is exceeded, Salesforce throws a System.LimitException, which can't be caught, and the whole transaction is rolled back. So if my trigger hits a limit partway through a 200-record load, none of the 200 records are saved. That's why I design for limits from the start: bulkify the code, write efficient queries, and move heavy work to asynchronous processing. When a stakeholder asks why we can't just process everything in one click, this is the explanation I give.
points: Per-transaction runtime limits
Protect shared multitenant resources
LimitException cannot be caught
The whole transaction rolls back
Design for limits up front

q: What are the most important governor limits you should know?
alt: List common governor limits with numbers
How many SOQL queries can you run in a transaction?
governor limits list soql dml cpu heap
What is the DML limit in Salesforce?
a: The ones I keep in mind: 100 SOQL queries in a synchronous transaction and 200 in asynchronous. 150 DML statements. 50,000 rows retrieved by SOQL, and 10,000 rows processed by DML. CPU time of 10 seconds synchronous and 60 seconds asynchronous. Heap size of 6 MB synchronous and 12 MB asynchronous. 100 callouts per transaction, and 50 future method calls per transaction. With System.enqueueJob, you can add 50 Queueable jobs in a synchronous transaction, but only one from an executing Queueable. For Batch Apex, the default scope is 200 and the maximum is 2,000. Five batch jobs can be active at once, and the flex queue holds up to 100 more. To make it real: if a trigger runs one query per record, a 200-record data load blows through the 100-query limit about halfway in. I expect everyone on the team to know these roughly by heart, because design decisions depend on them.
points: SOQL: 100 sync / 200 async
DML statements: 150; DML rows: 10,000
Query rows: 50,000
CPU: 10 s sync / 60 s async; Heap: 6 MB / 12 MB
Callouts 100; future 50; enqueueJob 50 (1 from a Queueable)

q: How do you avoid hitting governor limits in Apex?
alt: What techniques prevent governor limit errors?
How do you write limit-safe code?
how to avoid governor limits in salesforce
Tips to stay within governor limits
a: The core technique is bulkification. Never put SOQL or DML inside a loop. Collect Ids into Sets, query once into Maps, and do one DML per object on a List. For example, instead of updating each Contact inside the loop, I add them to a List and run one update at the end, so 200 records cost one DML statement, not 200. I query only the fields and rows I need, with selective, indexed filters, and use SOQL for loops for large result sets. I avoid recursion with proper guards, keep one trigger per object, and watch for flows on the same object, because they share the same limits. Heavy or long work goes to Queueable, Batch or future methods, which also get higher limits. I cache repeated lookups in static variables within the transaction, and during development I use the Limits class to see how close I am. On my teams, a test with 200 records is the proof I ask for.
points: No SOQL/DML in loops; use Sets and Maps
Selective queries, only needed fields
Recursion guards and one trigger per object
Move heavy work to async
Cache lookups; monitor with Limits class

q: Show how you would bulkify a trigger that has a SOQL query inside a loop.
alt: Fix this trigger that queries inside a for loop
Write a bulkified trigger example
soql inside for loop fix
How do you rewrite non-bulkified trigger code?
a: The broken version runs a query for each record in Trigger.new, so 101 records means a too many SOQL queries error. To fix it, I loop once to collect the parent Ids into a Set, run a single query with WHERE Id IN that Set and load the results into a Map, then loop again and read each parent from the Map. That turns N queries into one, no matter whether 1 or 200 records come in. Because this is a before trigger, I just set the field on the record and need no DML at all. In a real project the logic would sit in a handler class rather than the trigger body. In review I reject a trigger that queries inside a loop even if its test passes, because a single-record test hides the problem.
points: Collect Ids in a Set first
One query into a Map
Second loop reads from the Map
Before trigger: modify fields without DML
Move logic to a handler in real code

q: What is the Limits class and how do you use it?
alt: How do you check how many SOQL queries have been used?
Limits.getQueries example
limits class methods apex
How can code check governor limit usage at runtime?
a: The Limits class tells me how much of each governor limit the current transaction has used and what the maximum is. The methods come in pairs, like getQueries and getLimitQueries, getDmlStatements and getLimitDmlStatements, plus getCpuTime, getHeapSize, getQueryRows and getCallouts. I use it in two ways. During development I log the values at key points to find which part of the code consumes the most. In production code that processes variable volumes, I check the remaining headroom. For example, inside a loop I compare getQueries with getLimitQueries, and if I'm getting close, I hand the rest of the records to a Queueable instead of failing. That matters because a LimitException itself can't be caught. I use that headroom check selectively, though. Sprinkled everywhere it makes code hard to follow, so it belongs in the few paths where volume really varies.
points: Paired methods: getX and getLimitX
Debug which code consumes limits
Check headroom and defer to async
Proactive because LimitException cannot be caught

q: What is a mixed DML error?
alt: Explain MIXED_DML_OPERATION
What are setup and non-setup objects?
mixed dml operation error salesforce
Why can't I insert a User and an Account in the same transaction?
a: A mixed DML error happens when one transaction does DML on a setup object and on a non-setup object. Setup objects affect access, like User, UserRole, Group, GroupMember, PermissionSetAssignment and queue configuration. Non-setup objects are normal business records like Account, Contact or custom objects. Salesforce blocks mixing them because sharing recalculation for setup changes has to be handled separately. A typical case: an onboarding process updates an Account and, in the same transaction, inserts a PermissionSetAssignment for a user. That throws the error. The fix is to split the work into separate transactions, usually by moving the setup object DML into a future method or a Queueable. In test classes, I wrap the setup DML inside System.runAs, which gives it its own context and avoids the error. I warn new developers about it early, because it usually appears when someone adds user provisioning to an existing process.
points: Setup objects: User, Role, Group, PermissionSetAssignment
Non-setup: business records
Cannot mix both in one transaction
Fix: future or Queueable for setup DML
In tests: use System.runAs

q: When a Contact is created you must also assign a permission set to a related user. You get MIXED_DML_OPERATION. How do you fix it?
alt: Mixed DML when assigning permission set from a trigger
Create a User from a Contact trigger without mixed DML
how to fix mixed dml error in trigger
Permission set assignment fails after inserting a record
a: This needs two transactions. The Contact insert is non-setup DML and PermissionSetAssignment is setup DML, so they cannot happen in the same transaction. So I'd move the permission set assignment into a Queueable that runs in its own transaction. The trigger handler collects the user Ids in bulk, queries the permission set by its API name rather than a hard-coded Id, and enqueues one job with all of them. Queueable is better than future here because I can pass collections, get a job Id and add a Finalizer for failure handling. In the test I wrap the setup records in System.runAs and use startTest and stopTest so the job runs. I'd also confirm with the business that a short delay before the user gets access is acceptable, since that's the trade-off.
points: Contact is non-setup, PermissionSetAssignment is setup
Move setup DML to a Queueable
Bulk-collect user Ids; query permission set by Name
Test with runAs and startTest/stopTest

q: You get 'Too many SOQL queries: 101'. How do you troubleshoot and fix it?
alt: How do you debug System.LimitException too many SOQL queries
Too many soql queries 101 error fix
what causes too many soql queries
My trigger throws 101 SOQL error, what do I check?
a: First I reproduce it and open the debug log. I look at the cumulative limit usage section and the SOQL_EXECUTE lines to see which class and line runs the queries over and over. The usual causes are a query inside a loop, including one hidden inside a helper method that's called per record; trigger recursion, where an update re-fires the trigger; or several triggers and record-triggered flows on the same object all adding queries in one transaction. For example, a getAccountTier helper can look harmless, but if it runs a query and gets called once per Opportunity, a 200-record update means 200 queries. The fix is to bulkify: collect Ids, query once into a Map, cache reference data in static variables, and add a recursion guard. Then I write a test with 200 records to confirm it stays well under the limit. If it keeps recurring on one object, I treat it as a design problem, too much automation on one save, and review that object with the team.
points: Use debug log limit usage and SOQL_EXECUTE lines
Look for queries in loops or in helpers called per record
Check recursion and other automation on the object
Bulkify, cache, and guard recursion
Prove with a 200-record test

q: Code works fine when a user edits one record in the UI but fails with governor limit errors during a data load or integration. Why, and how do you fix it?
alt: Works for single record but fails in bulk
Integration fails with too many SOQL but UI works
data loader causing governor limit errors
Why does bulk API load hit limits but UI save does not?
a: A UI save processes one record, but a data load or integration sends up to 200 records per trigger execution, so any per-record query, DML or callout multiplies. Say my trigger does one query per record. In the UI that's one query, no problem. In a 200-record load it's 200 queries, and the save fails. Loads expose non-bulkified code, a flow with Get Records or Update Records elements inside a loop, or a chain where an after-update trigger updates related records that fire their own triggers and flows, all sharing one set of limits. So I review the full order of execution for that object, not just my trigger, and bulkify every piece. I make the logic skip unchanged records, add a bypass setting for large migrations, and move very heavy work to a Queueable or Batch. And my tests always insert 200 or more records. I also ask for a realistic data-volume test before go-live, because single-record UAT simply won't find this.
points: UI = 1 record; loads = up to 200 per chunk
Per-record logic multiplies
Flows and cascades share the same limits
Review the full order of execution
Skip unchanged records, add bypass, move to async

q: A transaction fails with 'Apex CPU time limit exceeded'. How do you handle it?
alt: How do you fix CPU timeout in Apex?
Apex CPU time limit exceeded error
what counts toward cpu time in salesforce
My trigger is hitting the 10 second CPU limit
a: CPU time counts the time spent executing Apex and declarative automation like flows in the transaction. It doesn't count time waiting for the database to run a query or for a callout response. The limit is 10 seconds synchronous and 60 asynchronous. Common causes are nested loops over large lists, describe calls or heavy string and JSON processing inside loops, too many automations firing on the same save, and recursion. For example, matching 2,000 Contacts against 2,000 Accounts with a loop inside a loop is four million comparisons. Put the Accounts in a Map and it's 2,000 lookups. I find the hotspot with debug logs and Limits.getCpuTime checkpoints. Then I optimize the algorithm, skip records that didn't change, consolidate automation, and move non-urgent work to asynchronous Apex, which gets the higher limit. I'd also challenge whether every automation on that save is still needed, because removing one is often cheaper than optimising it.
points: 10 s sync / 60 s async
Counts Apex and automation, not database or callout wait time
Replace nested loops with Maps
Find hotspots with logs and getCpuTime
Move non-urgent work to async

q: An object has triggers, several flows and managed package automation, and saves randomly hit the CPU limit. How do you find the culprit?
alt: How do you profile CPU usage across triggers and flows?
Intermittent CPU limit errors on save
find which automation is using the most cpu
Apex log analyzer for performance
a: I'd measure before changing anything. I capture a debug log of a failing save with Apex profiling set to a fine level and analyze it with a tool like the Apex Log Analyzer extension in VS Code, which shows a timeline of how much time each trigger, flow and package method takes. I compare a slow save against a fast one, because random failures usually come from data variations, like an account with thousands of children or an expensive branch. I also map the order of execution to spot cascades where one update re-fires another object's automation. To confirm, I temporarily bypass components with a custom setting in a sandbox and remeasure. Then I fix the worst offender first, and raise managed package issues with the vendor. I'd share that timeline with stakeholders too, because it turns 'the system is slow' into a specific list of what we fix first.
points: Debug log with profiling + Apex Log Analyzer
Compare slow vs fast saves for data patterns
Map the order of execution for cascades
Bypass components one by one in a sandbox
Fix the biggest consumer first

q: Your code throws 'Apex heap size too large'. What do you do?
alt: How do you reduce heap size in Apex?
Heap size limit exceeded fix
what is heap size in salesforce apex
Processing large files causes heap error
a: Heap is the memory my transaction holds: 6 MB synchronous and 12 MB asynchronous. The error usually comes from loading large query results into a List, selecting fields I don't need, especially long text and rich text, holding file or attachment bodies as Blobs or Base64 strings, or building big JSON payloads. A classic one is code that pulls every file on a record, bodies included, into one list so it can send them somewhere. A few large PDFs and you're over. To fix it, I use a SOQL for loop so records are processed in chunks, select only the fields I need, clear or null out collections when I'm done with them, and avoid keeping everything in a static variable. For large volumes I move to Batch Apex, where each execute gets its own heap, and I monitor with Limits.getHeapSize. In review, I flag any query that pulls body or long-text fields without a clear need.
points: 6 MB sync / 12 MB async
Causes: large lists, wide queries, file bodies, big JSON
SOQL for loops and fewer fields
Clear collections when finished
Batch Apex for large volumes

q: You get 'Too many query rows: 50001'. How do you resolve it?
alt: Query returns more than 50,000 rows
How do you process more than 50k records in Apex?
too many query rows 50001 error
Trigger fails because a rollup query returns too many rows
a: The 50,000 limit is cumulative across all SOQL queries in the transaction, not per query. So three queries that each return 20,000 rows will fail, even though none of them is over 50,000 on its own. First I find which queries return the most rows. Often it's an unfiltered query, or a rollup on a parent with huge numbers of children. Then I make the queries selective with indexed filters, fetch only what the logic truly needs, add a LIMIT where it makes sense, and avoid re-querying the same data. If the business really needs to touch more than 50,000 records, that work doesn't belong in a synchronous transaction. I move it to Batch Apex with a QueryLocator, which can process up to 50 million records, with each execute having its own limits. If a synchronous process genuinely seems to need that much data, I push back on the requirement, because usually the design should change, not just the query.
points: Limit is cumulative across all queries
Find and filter the biggest queries
Selective, indexed filters and LIMIT
Batch Apex QueryLocator for large volumes

q: How do governor limits differ between synchronous and asynchronous Apex?
alt: Which limits are higher in async Apex?
Sync vs async governor limits
why move logic to queueable for limits
Does batch apex get fresh limits per execute?
a: Asynchronous Apex, meaning future, Queueable, Batch and Scheduled jobs, gets higher limits on a few key resources: 200 SOQL queries instead of 100, 60 seconds of CPU instead of 10, and 12 MB of heap instead of 6 MB. Many limits stay the same, like 150 DML statements, 50,000 query rows, 10,000 DML rows and 100 callouts. In Batch Apex, each execute call is its own transaction with a fresh set of limits, which is why batch is the right tool for large data volumes. For example, if a manager clicks a button to recalculate commission for one rep, I keep it synchronous so they see the answer right away. Recalculating for every rep at month end goes to batch. The trade-off is that async work doesn't run immediately, so I only move work there when the user doesn't need the result instantly. That's usually a conversation with the business about how fresh the result really needs to be.
points: Async: 200 SOQL, 60 s CPU, 12 MB heap
Same: 150 DML, 50,000 rows, 10,000 DML rows, 100 callouts
Each batch execute has fresh limits
Trade-off: no immediate result

q: What causes 'Too many DML statements: 151' and 'Too many DML rows: 10001'?
alt: How do you fix too many DML statements error
What is the DML rows limit?
dml inside for loop error
too many dml rows 10001
a: The 151 error means the transaction ran more than 150 DML statements, almost always because an insert, update or delete is sitting inside a loop. Database class methods count the same, and so do savepoint and rollback calls. The fix is to add records to a List inside the loop and do a single DML after it, ideally one per object. The 10,001 rows error is different. It means more than 10,000 records were processed by DML in one transaction, even if it was just a few statements. For example, one update on a list of 12,000 records is a single statement, but it still fails. That's a volume problem, not a coding style problem, so I move that work to Batch Apex, where each execute gets its own 10,000-row allowance. In review, DML inside a loop is an automatic change request from me.
points: 151: more than 150 DML statements, usually DML in a loop
Collect records and do one DML per object
Savepoints and rollbacks also count
10,001: more than 10,000 DML rows
Use Batch Apex for high volume

q: You need to process around two million records every night. How do you design it within governor limits?
alt: Design a nightly job for millions of records
How would you process large data volumes in Apex?
batch apex design for large data
How do you choose batch size for a large job?
a: I'd use Batch Apex with a QueryLocator in start, since it can return up to 50 million records, and schedule it with a Schedulable class. The start query must be selective on indexed fields so it doesn't time out. Each execute gets fresh limits, so I keep the logic bulkified inside it. Then I tune the scope size. The default of 200 is fine for simple updates, and for two million records that works out to about 10,000 chunks. If each record needs complex logic or callouts, I go smaller. I use Database methods with allOrNone false and log the failures, Database.Stateful only for small counters, and the finish method for a summary email or to chain the next job. I also keep in mind that only five batch jobs run concurrently. I'd also agree the failure process with the business up front: who gets the summary, what counts as a partial failure, and how we rerun just the failed records.
points: Batch Apex with QueryLocator (up to 50M records)
Selective indexed start query
Tune scope size to the per-record cost
Partial success with logging; Stateful for counters
Schedule it; mind the 5 concurrent batch limit

q: Which limits are per transaction and which are org-wide, and how do you monitor org-wide limits?
alt: What are the org-level limits in Salesforce?
Daily async Apex execution limit
how many scheduled jobs can you have
How do you check API usage and org limits?
a: Most Apex limits, like SOQL, DML, CPU and heap, reset with every transaction. Others are shared across the whole org over time. One is the daily limit on asynchronous Apex executions, which is 250,000 or 200 times the number of user licenses, whichever is greater. So an org with 2,000 licenses gets 400,000 a day, while a small org gets the 250,000 floor. Others are the 24-hour API request allocation, a cap on concurrent long-running requests, 100 scheduled Apex jobs at a time, and platform event and storage allocations. I monitor them in Setup on the System Overview and Company Information pages, through the REST limits resource, or in Apex with the OrgLimits class. For integrations, I alert before API usage gets close to the allocation. On integration-heavy orgs I'd make those alerts someone's named responsibility, because an API allocation running out at month end is a business outage, not just a developer issue.
points: Transaction limits reset every transaction
Daily async Apex executions: 250,000 or 200 per license
API requests per 24 hours
100 scheduled Apex jobs at once
Monitor via System Overview, REST limits, OrgLimits

q: A callout fails with 'You have uncommitted work pending. Please commit or rollback before calling out'. How do you fix it?
alt: Callout after DML error
uncommitted work pending error in Apex
can I make a callout after insert in the same transaction
How do you do DML and a callout together?
a: Salesforce does not allow a callout after DML in the same transaction, because it cannot hold a database transaction open while waiting on an external system. I'd pick one of three fixes, in this order. If possible I reorder the code so all callouts happen first and the DML happens after. If the DML must come first, for example a trigger that saves a record and then syncs it, I move the callout into a Queueable that implements Database.AllowsCallouts, or a future method with callout set to true, so it runs in a new transaction. For decoupled designs I publish a platform event and let the subscriber make the call. I also remember the callout limits: 100 per transaction and 120 seconds total time. In review I look at where callouts sit relative to DML, because this error often only appears once someone adds a new automation to the object.
points: No callout after DML in the same transaction
Do callouts first, then DML
Or move the callout to a Queueable/future
Platform event for decoupling
100 callouts, 120 s total timeout

q: Since you can't catch a LimitException, how do you make long-running Apex fail gracefully?
alt: Can you catch System.LimitException?
How to handle governor limit failures gracefully
transaction finalizer queueable example
What happens to my Queueable if it hits a limit?
a: Right, a LimitException can't be caught, so my strategy is prevention and recovery. For prevention, inside loops that process variable volume, I check headroom with the Limits class. When I get close, I stop and enqueue a Queueable with the remaining records. Say I'm working through 5,000 records and I'm getting near the CPU limit at record 3,000. The last 2,000 go to a new job instead of the whole thing crashing. For recovery, I attach a Transaction Finalizer to Queueable jobs. The finalizer runs after the job finishes, even if it failed on an uncaught limit exception, and it can check the result, log the error and re-enqueue the job a limited number of times. For batch jobs, I make execute idempotent so a failed chunk can be retried, and I monitor AsyncApexJob for failures. I'd also agree a retry limit and an alert path with the support team, so a stuck job gets noticed rather than silently retried.
points: LimitException is not catchable
Check headroom and hand off to a Queueable
Transaction Finalizer runs even after limit failure
Retry with a cap; make work idempotent
Monitor AsyncApexJob

q: Why do we write test classes, and what is the 75 percent code coverage rule?
alt: What is the minimum code coverage for deployment?
Explain code coverage in Salesforce
75 percent code coverage rule
Do test classes count toward code coverage?
a: Test classes prove the code works, and they protect it from breaking when someone changes it later. They're also mandatory. To deploy Apex to production, all tests must pass, org-wide coverage must be at least 75 percent, and every trigger needs some coverage. Test classes themselves aren't counted in the coverage calculation. If I deploy with specified tests, each class and trigger in the package must reach 75 percent on its own. So if the org is at 90 percent but the one class I'm deploying is at 60, that deployment still fails. But coverage is just the minimum. A test that runs every line and asserts nothing can hit 100 percent and prove nothing. So I aim for meaningful tests with real asserts that cover bulk, positive, negative and permission scenarios.
