On my teams, coverage is the floor, and the asserts are what I actually review.
points: Required for production deployment
75% org-wide; every trigger needs coverage
Test code not counted in coverage
RunSpecifiedTests: 75% per class/trigger in the package
Asserts matter more than the number

q: How do you write a basic test class in Apex?
alt: What is the @isTest annotation?
Structure of an Apex test class
at is test annotation
Is the testMethod keyword still used?
a: I annotate the class with @isTest and usually make it private, since nothing else calls it. Each test method is static, returns void, takes no parameters, and is annotated with @isTest. The older testMethod keyword is deprecated. Inside a method I follow arrange, act, assert. For example, to test a discount rule, I create an Account and an Opportunity, call my discount method between Test.startTest and Test.stopTest, then query the Opportunity back and check the discount with an Assert method. That test data is never committed to the database; it's rolled back automatically. By default, tests can't see existing org data either, which keeps them independent. And classes annotated with @isTest don't count against the org's Apex code size limit. Arrange, act, assert is the structure I ask everyone on the team to follow, so any test reads the same way.
points: @isTest on class and methods
Methods are static void with no parameters
Arrange, act, assert
Data is rolled back automatically
No org data visible by default

q: What is @testSetup and how does it work?
alt: Explain the testSetup annotation
How is testSetup different from creating data in each method?
test setup method apex
Do changes in one test method affect another when using testSetup?
a: A method annotated with @testSetup runs once before the test methods in that class and creates common test data. Each test method then sees a fresh copy of that data, because any changes a test method makes are rolled back before the next one runs. Say five test methods all need an Account with three Contacts. I create them once in testSetup instead of five times. And if the first test deletes a Contact, the second test still sees all three. Test methods get the records by querying them, since static variables set in the setup method aren't carried over. A class can have only one testSetup method, and it can't be used in a class annotated with seeAllData true. Also, if setup throws an error, every test in the class fails. I steer the team towards testSetup plus a data factory, so setup stays in one predictable place.
points: Runs once per class before test methods
Each test gets a clean copy of the data
Query records in tests; statics are not kept
One per class; not with seeAllData=true

q: What do Test.startTest and Test.stopTest do?
alt: Why use startTest and stopTest?
How do I make an async job finish in a test?
test dot start test stop test
Does startTest reset governor limits?
a: Test.startTest and Test.stopTest mark the part of the test that exercises the code under test. Code between them gets a fresh set of governor limits, separate from the limits used to create test data, so setup doesn't distort the results. The second key behaviour is asynchronous code. Any future method, Queueable, Batch or Scheduled job started after startTest runs synchronously when stopTest is called, so I can assert on its results right after. For example, if my trigger enqueues a Queueable that updates the Account, I do the insert inside startTest and stopTest, and right after stopTest the Account is already updated. Each test method can call startTest only once. So my pattern is data creation before startTest, the method call inside, and asserts after stopTest. It's the first thing I check when someone tells me an async test randomly doesn't see its results.
points: Fresh governor limits between them
Async jobs complete at stopTest
Only once per test method
Setup before, act inside, assert after

q: What is System.runAs and what does it enforce?
alt: How do you test code as a different user?
Does runAs enforce field level security?
system dot run as in test class
When would you use runAs?
a: System.runAs runs a block of test code as a specific user, so I can test behaviour for different profiles, roles or permission sets. It enforces the user's record sharing, so a with sharing class will only return records that user can see. On its own it doesn't enforce the user's object and field permissions. But if the code uses user mode or stripInaccessible, those checks run against the runAs user. For example, I create a sales rep user, run my controller as them, and assert they get only the Opportunities they're allowed to see, not a colleague's. I also use runAs to avoid mixed DML errors when creating users and business records in the same test. And it can only be used inside test methods. For any controller that exposes data, I expect at least one runAs test with a restricted user before I approve it.
points: Runs a block as another user
Enforces record sharing
Not CRUD/FLS by itself; user-mode code will check them
Also avoids mixed DML in tests
Test methods only

q: What is seeAllData and why should you avoid it?
alt: Explain @isTest(seeAllData=true)
Can test classes see org data?
see all data true disadvantages
How do you get the standard price book in a test?
a: By default, since API version 24.0, test methods can't see existing data in the org, which keeps tests isolated and repeatable. Setting @isTest(seeAllData=true) lets tests read real org data, but I avoid it. Tests then depend on records that may differ, or not exist, in another sandbox or in production, so deployments fail unpredictably. For example, a test that expects an Account called Test Customer to already exist passes in my sandbox, then fails in production because nobody ever created it there. Some setup data is visible anyway without seeAllData, like users, profiles, record types and organization details. For the standard price book I use Test.getStandardPricebookId instead of seeAllData. The few remaining cases are rare legacy objects that can't be created in tests. On my teams, seeAllData needs a written justification in the pull request.
points: Default false since API 24.0
seeAllData=true creates environment dependence
Users, profiles, record types visible anyway
Test.getStandardPricebookId for pricebooks

q: Write a test data factory class.
alt: What is a TestDataFactory and why use it?
How do you create reusable test data?
test data factory example apex
How do you create a test user in Apex?
a: A test data factory is a public @isTest class with static methods that build valid records for tests. That way every test class doesn't repeat the same setup, and a new required field only needs one fix. Say an admin makes Industry required on Account. Without a factory, every test class that inserts an Account breaks. With one, I add Industry in the factory and they all pass again. I usually give the methods a count and a doInsert flag, so a test can tweak fields before inserting. The factory fills required fields and sensible defaults, and builds users with a unique username, because usernames are unique across all Salesforce orgs. Since it's annotated with @isTest, it doesn't count toward code size, and it can only be called from tests. I make the factory the single standard for test data on a project, and new test classes that build records by hand get sent back in review.
points: Public @isTest class with static builders
count and doInsert parameters for flexibility
One place to fix new required fields
Unique usernames for test users

q: Write a test class for a trigger, including bulk and negative cases.
alt: How do you test an Apex trigger?
Test class for before insert trigger
trigger test class with 200 records
What scenarios should a trigger test cover?
a: For a trigger I insist on three things: the positive path, the negative path where the logic should not apply, and bulk, by inserting 200 records in one DML to prove it is bulkified. This example tests the trigger that sets Priority to High on opportunities under Hot accounts. Common data goes in @testSetup, the DML is wrapped in startTest and stopTest, and I assert on records queried back from the database, not on the in-memory list, because before-trigger changes are only visible after a re-query. Each assert has a message so a failure explains itself. For update triggers I also test the case where the relevant field changes and where it does not. That trio is my minimum bar before a trigger change gets approved.
points: Positive, negative and bulk (200) cases
Common data in @testSetup
Re-query records before asserting
Assert messages explain failures

q: How do you test that code throws an exception or that a validation rule blocks a record?
alt: Testing negative scenarios in Apex
Assert that an exception was thrown
how to test addError in trigger
test class for validation rule error
a: I call the code inside a try block and put Assert.fail right after the call, so the test fails if no exception happens. In the catch block I catch the specific exception type and assert on the message. Assert.fail throws an AssertException, which my specific catch doesn't swallow, so the test still fails correctly. For validation rules or addError in triggers, I prefer Database.insert with allOrNone false. Then I assert that isSuccess is false and check the status code or message, which avoids a try-catch entirely. For example, if a validation rule blocks Opportunities with a negative Amount, I insert one with minus 100 and assert the save failed with my rule's message. That proves the business rule is enforced, which coverage alone never shows. On my teams, every validation rule or addError the business cares about gets a negative test like this.
points: try + Assert.fail after the call
Catch the specific exception, assert message
Database methods with allOrNone false for validation rules
Check status code or message

q: How do you test an HTTP callout using HttpCalloutMock?
alt: Write a mock class for a REST callout
Callouts are not allowed in tests, what do you do?
http callout mock example
How does Test.setMock work?
a: Tests can't make real callouts, so I implement the HttpCalloutMock interface. Its respond method receives the HttpRequest and returns a fake HttpResponse with the status code, headers and body I choose. In the test I register it with Test.setMock before calling the code, and the platform routes every callout to my mock. I make the mock configurable, for example by passing in the status code, so I can test both success and error handling. Say my code calls a shipping API. One test gives the mock a 200 with a tracking number, another gives it a 500, and I check my error handling kicks in. Inside respond I can also assert on the request, like the method or endpoint, to check that my code builds it correctly. For SOAP callouts the equivalent is the WebServiceMock interface. I ask for at least one failure-path mock per integration, because the error handling is what runs in production at the worst moment.
points: Implement HttpCalloutMock.respond
Register with Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mock)
Configurable status to test success and failure
Assert on the request inside respond
WebServiceMock for SOAP

q: When would you use StaticResourceCalloutMock or MultiStaticResourceCalloutMock?
alt: Mock a callout with a static resource
How do you test code that calls multiple endpoints?
static resource callout mock example
Store sample JSON response for tests
a: StaticResourceCalloutMock is a built-in mock that returns the body of a static resource. So I can store a realistic, large sample JSON response as a file instead of writing it inside the test. I set the resource name, status code and headers, then pass it to Test.setMock. For example, I take a full sample response from the vendor's API docs, save it as a static resource, and the test uses it exactly as is. When the code under test calls several different endpoints in one transaction, I use MultiStaticResourceCalloutMock and map each endpoint URL to its own static resource. These are quick and keep tests readable, but they always return the same response. So for dynamic behaviour, or for asserting on the request, I write a custom HttpCalloutMock instead. My rule of thumb for the team: static resources for realistic payloads, custom mocks when the logic depends on what was sent.
points: StaticResourceCalloutMock: body from a static resource
Set resource, status and headers
MultiStaticResourceCalloutMock: endpoint to resource map
Custom HttpCalloutMock for dynamic responses

q: How do you test a future method?
alt: Test class for @future method
Future method is not executing in my test
how to test asynchronous future method
Why do I need stopTest for a future call?
a: A future method runs asynchronously, so in a test it wouldn't finish before my asserts unless I wrap the call in Test.startTest and Test.stopTest. When stopTest runs, all queued asynchronous work, including future calls, executes synchronously. Then I query the database and assert the result. I create the data before startTest. If the future method makes a callout, I also set an HttpCalloutMock before calling it. The same pattern works when the future is called indirectly, for example from a trigger, as long as the DML that fires the trigger happens between startTest and stopTest. Say an Account trigger calls a future method that updates a related record. I insert the Account inside startTest and stopTest, and after stopTest I query that related record and assert on it. I'd steer new code towards Queueable over future anyway, but the testing pattern is the same.
points: Wrap the call in startTest/stopTest
Future runs at stopTest
Query and assert after stopTest
Set a mock if the future makes callouts

q: How do you test a Queueable class, especially one that chains another job?
alt: Test class for Queueable Apex
Chaining queueable in test class gives error
how to test queueable chaining
Check AsyncApexJob status in a test
a: I enqueue the job between Test.startTest and Test.stopTest. At stopTest it runs synchronously, so I can assert on the data, and on the AsyncApexJob status using the returned job Id. The catch is chaining. Older documentation said chaining Queueable jobs in an Apex test throws an error, and the current docs only support testing chains with an appropriate stack depth. So I still guard the chain. The simplest guard is checking Test.isRunningTest before enqueueing the next job, but a cleaner design is to make the chaining decision a separate, testable method, or inject a flag. Say job A processes invoices and then enqueues job B to send emails. I test A on its own, test B by enqueueing it directly with the right input, and test the chaining logic itself as plain unit logic. When I review chained jobs, I also check that the chain has a clear stopping condition, because an unbounded chain is a bigger risk than a missing test.
points: Enqueue inside startTest/stopTest
Assert data and AsyncApexJob status
Chaining in tests is restricted
Guard the chain; test each link separately

q: How do you test a Batch Apex class?
alt: Test class for batch apex
Why does my batch test process only 200 records?
how to test database.executebatch
Batch apex test with startTest and stopTest
a: I create test data, call Database.executeBatch between Test.startTest and Test.stopTest, and at stopTest the start, execute and finish methods all run synchronously. Then I query and assert. The important rule is that a test can only run one execute chunk, so the number of test records must fit in a single scope. With the default scope, that means 200 or fewer records. So 150 test records is fine, but 250 is not. If I need to test the logic on more data, I test the execute method's helper directly. I also cover the finish method's behaviour, like a summary email or a chained job, and the error handling, using some records that are set up to fail. In review I check the test data count against the scope size, because that's a common reason batch tests fail for no obvious reason.
points: executeBatch inside startTest/stopTest
start, execute and finish run at stopTest
Only one execute chunk in a test; keep records within scope
Test finish and failure paths

q: How do you test a Schedulable class?
alt: Test class for scheduled Apex
How to test System.schedule
schedulable apex test class example
Verify a CRON expression in a test
a: I call System.schedule with a job name, a CRON expression and an instance of my class, inside Test.startTest and Test.stopTest. It returns the CronTrigger Id, so I query CronTrigger and assert that the expression and next fire time were stored correctly. The scheduled job runs as part of stopTest. A scheduler usually just launches a batch or a Queueable, so I keep it very thin. For example, my nightly cleanup scheduler only has one line that calls executeBatch on the cleanup batch. The real business logic is tested in the batch's own test class, so the scheduler test only proves the scheduling and wiring work. I also make sure the job name is unique, or the schedule call fails. Thin schedulers are a team standard for me, because logic buried in a scheduler is hard to rerun manually when something goes wrong.
points: System.schedule inside startTest/stopTest
Query CronTrigger by the returned Id
Keep the scheduler thin
Test business logic in the batch test
Job names must be unique

q: What is the Assert class and how is it different from System.assertEquals?
alt: Assert.areEqual vs System.assertEquals
What assert methods are available in Apex?
new assert class in apex
Why should test methods have asserts?
a: The Assert class is the newer, more readable way to write assertions in Apex tests. It has Assert.areEqual and areNotEqual, isTrue and isFalse, isNull and isNotNull, isInstanceOfType, and Assert.fail to fail a test on purpose. The older System.assert, assertEquals and assertNotEquals still work, but the Assert names make the intent clearer, and it adds checks like type checks and an explicit fail. For example, Assert.areEqual with expected 'High', the actual priority, and the message 'Hot accounts should get High priority' tells you exactly what broke when it fails. Either way, I always pass a message as the last argument. A test without assertions only produces coverage and proves nothing, so every test method should verify the expected outcome. Messages on asserts are something I ask for in every review.
points: Assert.areEqual, isTrue, isNull, isInstanceOfType, fail
System.assert methods still supported
Assert class is clearer and richer
Always add a failure message
No asserts = coverage only

q: How do you mock dependencies in Apex tests using the Stub API?
alt: Explain StubProvider and Test.createStub
Mocking in Apex without DML
apex stub api example
How do you unit test a service without querying the database?
a: The Stub API lets me create a fake version of a class at runtime. I implement System.StubProvider, whose handleMethodCall method receives the method name and arguments and returns whatever I want, then call Test.createStub with the class type and my provider. For it to be useful, the code under test must accept the dependency, for example through its constructor, so I can pass the stub instead of the real selector. Say my service gets overdue invoices from an InvoiceSelector. Instead of inserting invoices, the stub just returns three in-memory ones. No DML, no SOQL, so the test runs fast, and I can simulate cases that are hard to set up. The limitations: it can't stub static methods, private methods or system classes, and it only works in test context. The trade-off is extra design work up front, so I use stubs where they speed up the suite and keep a few real-DML tests for the full flow.
points: Implement System.StubProvider.handleMethodCall
Test.createStub(Type, provider)
Requires dependency injection in the code
No DML/SOQL: fast, isolated tests
Cannot stub static or private methods

q: How do you design Apex code so that it is easy to test?
alt: What makes Apex code testable?
Dependency injection in Apex
how to write testable apex code
Unit tests vs integration tests in Salesforce
a: I'd design for testability from day one rather than retrofit it. I separate concerns so each piece can be tested alone. Triggers only delegate to handlers, business logic sits in services, and queries sit in selector classes. Dependencies like selectors, callout clients or the current date are passed in through constructors or exposed as @TestVisible variables, so a test can swap in a stub or a fixed value. For example, if renewal logic depends on today's date, I pass the date in, so the test can say 'pretend it's 31 March' and check the result. I program to interfaces for things like external services, so I can provide a fake. That lets most tests be fast unit tests using the Stub API or a mocking library like ApexMocks, while a smaller set of integration tests do real DML to prove the full flow, including triggers and validation rules. I explain that balance to the team as a pyramid: lots of fast unit tests, fewer slow end-to-end ones.

Inject dependencies via constructor or @TestVisible
Interfaces for external services
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests
Stub API or ApexMocks for mocking

q: Your production deployment fails because code coverage is 74 percent. What do you do?
alt: Deployment failed due to insufficient code coverage
How do you increase code coverage quickly but properly?
code coverage below 75 deployment error
Which classes are pulling the coverage down?
a: I'd fix it with real tests, not filler. First I find where the coverage is missing. I run all tests in a sandbox that matches production and check the coverage per class in the Developer Console, Setup, or the Salesforce CLI with code coverage output, sorting by uncovered lines. Usually a few big classes or old unused code pull it down. For example, one large class sitting at 30 percent can be the whole reason the org is at 74. I write proper tests for the uncovered branches, especially error handling and else paths, using a data factory and real asserts. I also delete dead code, because removing unused classes raises the percentage honestly. If I deploy with specified tests, I remember that each class and trigger in the package must reach 75 percent individually. And I avoid tests that only exist to touch lines. Then I'd add a coverage check to the pipeline, so we find out at pull request time, not on deployment day.

Test uncovered branches with real asserts
Remove dead code

No assert-free coverage tests

q: Tests pass in the sandbox but fail during production deployment. What could be wrong?
alt: Test classes fail only in production
Why do my tests behave differently in prod?
test failing in production deployment but passing in sandbox
How do you make tests environment independent?
a: Almost always, the tests depend on the environment. Typical causes are seeAllData, or queries that expect existing records; hard-coded Ids, or record type and profile names that differ in production; validation rules, required fields, duplicate rules or flows that exist in production but not in the sandbox, so my test data no longer saves; custom settings or metadata values that differ; and date-dependent logic. For example, production has a validation rule requiring Phone on Account and the sandbox doesn't. Every test that inserts an Account without a phone passes in the sandbox and fails in production. The fix is making tests self-contained. Create all data through a factory, look up record types by DeveloperName, avoid seeAllData, and set required configuration inside the test. I validate the deployment first and run all local tests in a recently refreshed full or partial copy sandbox. I'd also keep sandboxes refreshed on a regular cadence, because configuration drift between sandbox and production is usually the root cause.

Hard-coded Ids or names
Extra validation rules or flows in prod
Different custom settings/metadata; date logic
Self-contained tests; validate before deploy

q: Your test fails with MIXED_DML_OPERATION when you create a User and an Account. How do you fix the test?
alt: Mixed DML error in test class
How to insert user and account in the same test method
runAs to avoid mixed dml in test
Setup object and non-setup object in test class error
a: In tests the fix is System.runAs. I insert the User, or other setup records like a group member or permission set assignment, inside a runAs block. The runAs block starts a separate context, so the setup DML and the business DML no longer collide. A common pattern is to run as the current user, by creating a User sObject with UserInfo.getUserId, just to get that separate context. Then I create the Account and test data outside the block, or inside another runAs block for the new user if I want to test their access. This only applies to tests; in production code I use async processing instead. I keep a small helper for this in the test data factory, so nobody on the team has to rediscover the pattern.
points: Wrap setup DML in System.runAs
runAs with the current user just for the context
Business data outside or in another runAs
Production code uses async instead

q: Your callout test fails with 'You have uncommitted work pending'. How do you fix the test?
alt: Callout test fails after inserting test data
uncommitted work pending in test class
DML before mock callout in test
How to insert test data and test a callout in the same method
a: In a test, creating records and then calling code that makes a callout looks like DML followed by a callout in one transaction, which is not allowed. The fix is to do all the test data DML before Test.startTest, then call Test.startTest, set the mock with Test.setMock, and call the callout code before stopTest; the docs say startTest must come before setMock in this case. The platform treats the part inside startTest and stopTest separately, so the callout is allowed. If the code itself does DML and then a callout, that is a real bug, not just a test problem, and the code should be refactored to call out first or move the callout to a Queueable. When a test hits this, I ask the developer to check whether the production path has the same problem, because it often does.
points: DML first, before Test.startTest
startTest first, then setMock, then the callout
If the production code does DML then callout, fix the code

q: Your Apex test suite is slow and has random failures in CI. How do you stabilize it?
alt: Flaky Apex tests in the pipeline
UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW in test runs
how to speed up apex test execution
Tests fail randomly when run in parallel
a: Random failures usually come from parallel test runs touching the same rows, which shows up as UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW, often on shared records like custom settings or the standard price book. Or they come from tests that depend on dates, record order or existing data. For example, a test that queries with LIMIT 1 and no ORDER BY, and expects a particular record back, can pass one run and fail the next. So I make every test create its own data, avoid seeAllData, never rely on query order without ORDER BY, and use fixed dates where logic is date-sensitive. For speed I use @testSetup, reduce data volumes to what each test needs, and replace database-heavy unit tests with stubs. If a few tests genuinely conflict, I isolate them or disable parallel testing for that suite. In CI I run targeted tests per change and the full local suite nightly. I'd also track flaky tests as real defects with an owner, because a suite people don't trust stops protecting anything.
points: Lock errors from parallel tests on shared rows
Self-contained data; no reliance on order or dates
@testSetup and smaller data volumes
Stubs instead of DML for unit tests
Targeted tests per change, full suite nightly

q: How do you test Apex logic that depends on custom metadata records?
alt: Can you insert custom metadata in a test class?
Mock custom metadata in Apex tests
custom metadata type in test class
My test depends on a specific mdt record
a: I can't insert custom metadata records with DML in a test. Tests can read the deployed records without seeAllData, but relying on them is fragile, because an admin can change the values and break the tests. So I design the code to read metadata through one place, for example a @TestVisible static variable or a small selector, and in the test I inject in-memory records. A reliable way to build them with field values is JSON.deserialize into the metadata type. For example, say a discount rule record gives Gold customers 10 percent. My test injects its own Gold rule at 10 percent, so if an admin changes the real one to 12, the test still passes. That way the test controls exactly which configuration exists, covers each branch, and keeps passing whatever is configured in the org. I'd make that injection point a standard in our selector layer, so every metadata-driven feature is testable the same way.

Deployed records are visible but fragile to depend on
Read metadata through one injectable place
Build in-memory records with JSON.deserialize

q: What are the best practices for writing Apex test classes?
alt: How do you write good test classes?
Test class best practices in Salesforce
what should a good apex test cover
Common mistakes in test classes
a: I create all my own test data, ideally through a test data factory, and avoid seeAllData so tests run the same in every org. I use @testSetup for shared data and wrap the code under test in Test.startTest and Test.stopTest. I test positive, negative and bulk scenarios, with at least 200 records for triggers, and use System.runAs to test different users and permissions. Every test has meaningful asserts with messages, not just coverage. I mock callouts with HttpCalloutMock, never hard-code Ids, and keep each test method focused on one behaviour with a descriptive name. For example, a method called discountNotAppliedForInactiveAccount tells you what broke before you even open the code. Finally, I aim well above 75 percent, but I care more about covering the important logic paths. These are also the points I check when I review someone's test class.

@testSetup and startTest/stopTest
Positive, negative, bulk and user-based tests
Meaningful asserts with messages
Mock callouts; no hard-coded Ids

q: How do you test that sharing rules are respected by your Apex code?
alt: Test with sharing in a test class
Verify a user cannot see another user's records
runas test for record visibility
How do you test org-wide defaults in Apex tests?
a: I create a user with a limited profile, create records owned by someone else, then call my code inside System.runAs for that user and assert they only get records they should see. Because runAs enforces record sharing, this proves that my class is declared with sharing and that the queries do not leak data. It depends on the org-wide default for the object being private, so I note that in the test. I also add the positive case, where the user owns a record or has it shared, and assert it is returned. If the code uses user mode, the same test also checks object and field permissions. For anything that returns customer or financial data, I treat a sharing test like this as required, not optional.

Call the code inside System.runAs

Add the positive case too

q: Is using Test.isRunningTest in production code a good practice?
alt: When is Test.isRunningTest acceptable?
Why is Test.isRunningTest considered a code smell?
test is running test in apex class
Alternatives to Test.isRunningTest
a: No, I'd avoid it. In general it's a code smell, because the code then behaves differently in tests than in production, so the test isn't really verifying the real path. Say a method checks Test.isRunningTest and skips a step when it's true. The test passes, but that step was never exercised. I accept it only in narrow cases where the platform gives no other option, for example avoiding Queueable chaining, which tests have historically not allowed, or skipping something that can't run in test context. Even then, I prefer to wrap it in a @TestVisible flag or setting so the test controls it explicitly. The better alternatives are dependency injection, the Stub API, HttpCalloutMock for callouts, and @TestVisible variables to override configuration. Those keep the production logic identical in both contexts. In review, a new Test.isRunningTest check gets questioned every time.
points: Usually a smell: tests skip the real path
Acceptable narrowly, e.g. Queueable chaining
Prefer a @TestVisible flag the test controls
Use DI, Stub API and mocks instead

q: What is an Apex trigger?
alt: Can you explain what a trigger is in Salesforce?
what is a trigger in apex
Why do we use triggers in Salesforce?
Tell me about Apex triggers in simple words
a: An Apex trigger is Apex code that runs automatically before or after records are inserted, updated, deleted or undeleted on an object. A trigger is defined on one object, lists the events it listens to, and receives the affected records through context variables like Trigger.new. For example, a trigger on Opportunity can listen for after update, and when a deal moves to Closed Won, it creates an onboarding Case for that account. We use triggers when declarative tools like Flow can't handle the logic cleanly, for example complex cross-object validation, heavy bulk processing with maps, or logic that needs tight control over errors and recursion. As a best practice, I keep the trigger itself very thin and put the real logic in a handler class.
points: Runs automatically on DML: insert, update, delete, undelete
Before or after the record is saved
Records come in through context variables like Trigger.new
Keep the trigger thin, logic in a handler class
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: What are the different trigger events in Salesforce?
alt: How many trigger events are there?
List the events a trigger can run on
Is there a before undelete trigger?
what are trigger events before insert after insert etc
a: There are seven trigger events: before insert, before update, before delete, after insert, after update, after delete and after undelete. There's no before undelete. Before events are for validating or changing the records being saved, without any extra DML. After events are for when you need the record Id or you're working with other records, like creating children or updating a parent. For example, defaulting a Lead's Rating as it's saved is before insert. Creating a follow-up Task for a new Contact needs the Contact's Id, so that's after insert. One trigger can list several events, and I normally list all the events an object needs in a single trigger and route them to a handler.
points: 7 events: before/after insert, update, delete, plus after undelete
No before undelete event
Before: change or validate same records; after: related records, Ids
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: What are trigger context variables?
alt: Explain Trigger.new, Trigger.old, newMap and oldMap
What context variables are available in a trigger?
what is trigger dot new and trigger dot old
What does Trigger.isExecuting mean?
a: Context variables tell the trigger what's happening and give it the records. Trigger.new is the list of new versions of the records, and Trigger.old is the list of old versions. Trigger.newMap and Trigger.oldMap hold the same records keyed by Id. Boolean flags like isInsert, isUpdate, isDelete, isUndelete, isBefore and isAfter tell you the event and timing. Trigger.operationType gives the event as a single enum value, Trigger.size gives the number of records in this invocation, and Trigger.isExecuting is true when the current code was called from a trigger. The combination I use most is in an update: I take a record from Trigger.new, look up the same Id in Trigger.oldMap, and compare them to see whether, say, the Stage actually changed.
points: Trigger.new / Trigger.old: lists of records
Trigger.newMap / Trigger.oldMap: maps keyed by Id
isInsert, isUpdate, isDelete, isUndelete, isBefore, isAfter
operationType, size, isExecuting

q: What is the difference between a before trigger and an after trigger?
alt: Before vs after trigger, when do you use which?
When should I write a before trigger instead of an after trigger?
before trigger versus after trigger difference
Why can't I update Trigger.new in an after trigger?
a: I use a before trigger when I want to validate or change the same records that are being saved, because I just set fields on Trigger.new and Salesforce saves them, with no extra DML. For example, filling in a default region on a new Account is a before insert job. I use an after trigger when I need the record Id or the saved values, or when I'm working on other records, like creating child records, updating a parent, or enqueuing a Queueable. In an after trigger, Trigger.new is read-only. So changing the same record there would need another update statement, which wastes limits and can cause recursion. That's why same-record changes belong in before.
points: Before: same-record field updates and validation, no DML needed
After: record Ids available, related records, async jobs
Trigger.new is read-only in after triggers
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Which trigger context variables are available in which events?
alt: Is Trigger.newMap available in before insert?
Why is Trigger.new null in a delete trigger?
In which events can I use Trigger.oldMap?
when is trigger new map not available
a: Trigger.new is available in insert, update and undelete triggers, and you can only modify it in before triggers. Trigger.old is available in update and delete triggers. Trigger.newMap is available in before update, after insert, after update and after undelete, but not in before insert, because new records don't have Ids yet. Trigger.oldMap is available in update and delete triggers. So in a delete trigger I work with Trigger.old or oldMap. For example, to stop someone deleting an Account that still has open Cases, my before delete logic loops over Trigger.old, because Trigger.new isn't available there. And in before insert, I only have Trigger.new as a list.
points: Trigger.new: insert, update, undelete (editable only in before)
Trigger.old and oldMap: update and delete
Trigger.newMap: not in before insert (no Ids yet)
Delete triggers: use Trigger.old
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Why do you get a 'Record is read-only' error in an after trigger, and how do you fix it?
alt: I'm getting FinalException record is read-only in my trigger
Can we update Trigger.new in after insert?
how to fix record is read only error apex trigger
Why can't I set a field on Trigger.new in after update?
a: That error appears when you try to change a field on a record in Trigger.new inside an after trigger. In after context the records are already saved, so Trigger.new is read-only. Say an after insert trigger on Case tries to set a Status on the same Case. That line throws the error. The fix is to move that field assignment into the before trigger, where you set the value directly and it's saved with no extra DML. If you really need the after context, for example because the value depends on the record Id, then build new sObject instances with just the Id and the changed field, and update those, with a guard so the update doesn't loop.
points: After trigger records are read-only
Move same-record changes to before trigger
If after context is needed, update new instances by Id with a guard
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: What is bulkification in triggers and why is it important?
alt: How do you make a trigger bulk safe?
What does it mean to bulkify a trigger?
Why should a trigger handle 200 records at a time?
bulkify apex trigger example
a: Bulkification means writing the trigger so it works correctly and efficiently when it receives up to 200 records at once, not just one. Data Loader, integrations and batch jobs send records in bulk, and governor limits apply to the whole transaction. So a query or DML per record quickly hits the 100 SOQL or 150 DML limit. For example, if someone loads 200 Contacts and my trigger queries the parent Account once per Contact, that's 200 queries, and the load fails. The pattern I follow is: loop once to collect Ids into a Set, run one query into a Map, loop again to apply the logic, collect the changes into a List, and do a single DML at the end.
points: Trigger can receive up to 200 records per invocation
Collect Ids in a Set, query once into a Map
No SOQL or DML inside loops
One DML on a list at the end
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: How do you avoid SOQL and DML inside a for loop in a trigger?
alt: Show me a trigger with SOQL in a loop and fix it
How do you remove queries from inside loops?
my trigger has update inside for loop how to fix
Rewrite this trigger so it doesn't hit too many SOQL queries
a: I move every query and DML out of the loop. First I loop through the trigger records and collect the Ids I need into a Set. Then I run one query with WHERE Id IN :set, or a parent-to-child query, and store the results in a Map or list. Then I loop again, make the changes in memory, add the records to a List, and do one update at the end. In this example, when an account owner changes, all open opportunities move to the new owner with one query and one DML, no matter how many accounts are in the batch.
points: Bad: query or update per record
Good: collect Ids, one query, one DML
Only process records whose field actually changed
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Why should you have only one trigger per object?
alt: What is the one trigger per object pattern?
What happens if there are two triggers on the same object?
why one trigger per object best practice
Should I create a new trigger for every requirement?
a: Because if there are multiple triggers on the same object for the same event, Salesforce doesn't guarantee which one runs first, so the behaviour is unpredictable and hard to debug. Say one trigger sets an Account's region, and a second trigger assigns the owner based on that region. If the second one happens to run first, it reads a blank region and assigns the wrong owner. With one trigger per object, I control the order of logic explicitly inside the handler. I can apply a single recursion strategy and a single bypass switch, and every developer knows exactly where to look. The trigger just delegates to a handler class, and the logic is split into well-named methods or service classes that are easy to unit test.
points: Order of multiple triggers on the same event isn't guaranteed
Single entry point controls order explicitly
One place for bypass and recursion logic
Thin trigger, logic in handler and service classes
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Can you write a trigger handler framework?
alt: How do you structure a trigger with a handler class?
Show me your trigger framework
explain trigger handler pattern with code
What does a base trigger handler class look like?
a: Sure. I keep the trigger to one line that calls the handler's run method. A base class does the routing with a switch on Trigger.operationType, checks a bypass list, and has an empty virtual method for each event. Each object handler extends the base class and only overrides the events it needs, calling service classes for the real logic. For example, my AccountTriggerHandler only overrides beforeInsert, to default the Rating, and afterUpdate, to move open opportunities when the owner changes. The other events just do nothing. This gives one trigger per object, a predictable order, one place for bypass logic, and handler methods I can unit test. Teams can also bypass a handler from code through a static bypass set, for example during a data fix.
points: Trigger calls handler.run() only
Base class routes events with switch on Trigger.operationType
Object handler overrides only needed events
Static bypass set to switch handlers off in code

q: How do you use Trigger.operationType in a trigger?
alt: What is System.TriggerOperation?
Use switch on in a trigger instead of if else
how does trigger operation type switch work
What values does Trigger.operationType return?
a: Trigger.operationType returns a System.TriggerOperation enum, like BEFORE_INSERT or AFTER_UPDATE, which combines timing and event in one value. I use it with a switch on statement instead of nested if conditions on isBefore and isInsert. It reads cleanly, every event is routed in one place, and one when branch can cover several events. For example, if before insert and before update both need to default the same field, I write one when branch listing BEFORE_INSERT and BEFORE_UPDATE and call the method once. The values are BEFORE_INSERT, BEFORE_UPDATE, BEFORE_DELETE, AFTER_INSERT, AFTER_UPDATE, AFTER_DELETE and AFTER_UNDELETE.
points: Returns System.TriggerOperation enum
Use with switch on for clean routing
One when branch can list several values

q: How do you prevent recursion in a trigger?
alt: How do you stop a trigger from firing again and again?
What is the best way to handle recursive triggers?
trigger recursion static set of ids
My trigger is calling itself, how do I stop it?
a: I use a static Set of Ids in the handler to remember which records have already been processed in this transaction. Static variables live for the whole transaction, so when my after update logic does a DML that fires the same trigger again, the records already in the set are skipped. For example, an after update on Account updates a field on those same Accounts. That update fires the trigger again, but those Ids are already in the set, so the logic doesn't run twice. I prefer this over a static Boolean, because a Boolean blocks every later chunk of 200 records and any legitimate second update. I also check that the relevant field actually changed using oldMap, which on its own stops most recursion.
points: Static Set<Id> of processed records, not a static Boolean
Statics live for the whole transaction
Also check real field changes with oldMap
Boolean guard skips later 200-record chunks
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Your recursion check uses a static Boolean, and when 1,000 records are inserted in one Apex DML only the first 200 get processed. Why?
alt: Why is a static boolean a bad way to stop recursion?
Trigger logic only ran for the first 200 records, what is wrong?
static boolean run once trigger problem
Records after the first chunk were skipped by my trigger
a: Because a static Boolean is shared across the whole transaction, and a single DML of 1,000 records fires the trigger in chunks of 200 within that same transaction. The first chunk sets the flag to true, so the next four chunks see it and skip the logic. The same thing happens when another automation legitimately updates the record again in the same transaction. The fix is to track processed record Ids in a static Set, so each record is handled once but new records are still processed, and to only run logic when the relevant fields changed.
points: Trigger runs per 200-record chunk in the same transaction
Boolean set by chunk 1 blocks chunks 2 onwards
Use static Set<Id> plus field-change checks
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: How do you decide between a trigger and a record-triggered flow?
alt: Flow vs trigger, which one would you use?
When would you choose Apex trigger over Flow?
trigger or flow how to decide
Should all automation move to Flow?
a: My default is Flow for simple same-record updates and straightforward automation, because admins can maintain it, and before-save flows are very fast for field updates. For example, setting a Case's priority from its type is a perfect before-save flow. I choose a trigger when the logic is complex or needs heavy bulk processing with maps, precise error handling, reusable Apex services, async callouts, or events Flow doesn't support, like undelete. I also follow a per-object rule. Mixing many flows and triggers on one object makes the order of execution hard to reason about, so a team should agree which tool owns which object.
points: Flow: simple, admin-maintainable, before-save is fast
Trigger: complex logic, large volumes, fine error control
Record-triggered flows have no undelete event
Agree a per-object standard to avoid mixing

q: How do you use addError in a trigger?
alt: How do you show a validation error from a trigger?
What is the difference between record addError and field addError?
how to stop a record from saving in trigger
Throw a custom error message on a field from Apex
a: addError stops the record from being saved and shows a message to the user. If I call it on the record, the message appears at the top of the page. If I call it on a field, like contact.Email.addError, it shows next to that field. For example, if the business wants only work email addresses on Contacts and someone enters a personal one, I put the error right on the Email field so the user sees exactly what to fix. In an all-or-none DML the whole operation fails, while with partial success only the records with errors fail. I mostly call it in before triggers for validation, and I keep it bulk-safe by checking all records in one loop, without querying per record.
points: record.addError: message at top of page
record.Field.addError: message next to the field
Use in before triggers for validation
All-or-none DML fails all; partial success fails only bad records

q: Can you use addError in an after trigger, and what happens?
alt: Does addError work in after insert?
Can I block a save from an after trigger?
adderror after trigger rollback
What happens to DML done in a trigger when addError is called?
a: Yes. addError works on Trigger.new records in after insert and after update, and on Trigger.old in delete triggers. The record is saved but not yet committed, so calling addError makes that record's save fail. In an all-or-none operation the whole transaction rolls back, including any DML the trigger already did. With partial success, Salesforce rolls back and retries the save with only the good records. I use it in after triggers when the check depends on data that only exists after save. For example, if the rule counts records with a SOQL query and that count has to include the records being saved right now, the check has to run after save, because only then can the query see them. But for simple checks I prefer before triggers, because failing early avoids wasted work.
points: Works on Trigger.new in after insert/update and Trigger.old in delete
Record isn't committed yet, so it rolls back
Partial success: Salesforce retries with the good records
Prefer before triggers for simple validation

q: Write a trigger that handles undelete, and explain when it fires.
alt: When does an after undelete trigger run?
How do you handle records restored from the recycle bin in a trigger?
trigger after undelete example
Is Trigger.old available in undelete?
a: After undelete fires when records are restored from the Recycle Bin, either from the UI or with Database.undelete in Apex. There is only an after undelete event, and Trigger.new and Trigger.newMap hold the restored records, while Trigger.old is not available. A common use is recalculating a custom roll-up on the parent, because the restored child should count again. Here, when contacts are restored, I recount the contacts on their accounts with one aggregate query and one update.

Trigger.new and newMap hold restored records
Typical use: recalculate custom roll-ups

q: How do you disable or bypass a trigger without deploying code?
alt: How do you switch off triggers during a data migration?
Trigger bypass using custom metadata or custom permission
how to bypass trigger for integration user
Can admins turn off a trigger in production without a deployment?
a: I give every trigger a kill switch. A custom metadata type, say Trigger_Setting__mdt, holds one record per object with an Is_Active__c checkbox, so an admin can switch an object's trigger logic off org-wide during a migration, and because it's metadata it can be deployed and is the same across environments. On top of that, a custom permission like Bypass_Triggers, given through a permission set to an integration or migration user, lets just that user skip the logic. The trigger checks both first, using getInstance and FeatureManagement.checkPermission, and getInstance doesn't use a SOQL query.

Custom permission via permission set for per-user bypass
FeatureManagement.checkPermission + Trigger_Setting__mdt.getInstance
No deployment needed to flip either switch

q: Can you write triggers on both standard and custom objects? Are there objects that don't support triggers?
alt: Can I write a trigger on a standard object like Account?
Which objects support Apex triggers?
trigger on custom object vs standard object
Can you write a trigger on a platform event?
a: Yes. Triggers work on custom objects and on most standard objects like Account, Contact, Opportunity, Case and Lead. They also work on some standard child objects, such as OpportunityLineItem, CaseComment and ContentVersion. A few standard objects don't support triggers, so I check the object reference before I plan the design. You can also write triggers on platform events and Change Data Capture change events, but those only support after insert. The syntax is the same; you just use the API name. For example, a trigger on Invoice__c for a custom object, or on Order_Event__e for a platform event. For Change Data Capture, the name ends in ChangeEvent, like AccountChangeEvent.

Some standard objects don't, check the object reference
Platform event and CDC triggers: after insert only
Use API names: __c, __e, ChangeEvent

q: If an Apex DML inserts 1,000 records, how many times does the trigger fire, and how do limits apply?
alt: What is the trigger batch size?
Does a trigger process records in chunks of 200?
1000 records inserted how many times trigger executes
Are governor limits reset between trigger chunks?
a: The trigger fires five times, once for each chunk of 200 records, and all five runs are in the same transaction. That means governor limits are shared, so if each run uses 30 queries, the fourth chunk will break the 100 SOQL limit. Static variables also carry over between chunks. With Data Loader it's different: each batch it sends, 200 records by default, is a separate API call and transaction, so limits apply per batch. This is why I keep the number of queries per trigger run constant and small, regardless of record count.
points: Trigger runs per chunk of 200 records
All chunks share one transaction and its limits
Static variables persist across chunks
Each Data Loader batch is its own transaction

q: Can you make a callout directly from a trigger?
alt: Why can't I call an external API from a trigger?
How do I make an HTTP callout from a trigger?
callout from triggers are currently not supported error
trigger callout future method or queueable
a: No. A synchronous callout isn't allowed from a trigger, because the trigger runs while the database transaction is open, and Salesforce won't hold it open while waiting on an external system. You get the error 'Callout from triggers are currently not supported'. The solution is to hand the work to asynchronous Apex: a future method marked callout=true, or preferably a Queueable that implements Database.AllowsCallouts. Say every new Account has to be sent to an ERP. The trigger collects the new Account Ids and enqueues one Queueable for the whole batch, not one per record, and that job makes the callout. The async job starts only after the transaction commits, so the external system only hears about data that was really saved.
points: Synchronous callouts are blocked in triggers
Use @future(callout=true) or Queueable with Database.AllowsCallouts
Async job runs after commit
Enqueue once per trigger run, not per record

q: How do you write a test class for a trigger?
alt: How do you test an Apex trigger?
Write a bulk test for a trigger
test class for trigger with 200 records
How do you get code coverage for a trigger?
a: I test the trigger through DML, because that's what fires it. I create my own test data with @TestSetup, never relying on org data, and I use 200 records to prove the trigger is bulk-safe. I put the DML between Test.startTest and Test.stopTest, so I get fresh limits and any async work finishes. Then I query the results and assert the actual outcome with the Assert class. For example, if the trigger defaults a Region on Accounts, I insert 200 Accounts, query them back, and assert all 200 got the right Region. I also cover negative paths, like asserting that addError blocks a bad record, and every event the trigger handles, not just insert.
points: Fire the trigger with DML on test data
Use 200 records to prove bulk safety
Test.startTest / stopTest, then assert results
Cover negative paths and all handled events

q: What happens to triggers when records are merged?
alt: Is there a merge trigger event?
How do you detect a merge in a delete trigger?
merge account trigger masterrecordid
Which triggers fire on a lead or contact merge?
a: A merge doesn't have its own trigger event; it fires delete and update events instead. The losing records fire before delete and after delete, and the winning record fires before update and after update. In the after delete trigger, the losing records in Trigger.old have MasterRecordId set to the winner's Id, so I check that field to tell a merge apart from a normal delete. Say two duplicate Accounts are merged. The duplicate shows up in after delete with MasterRecordId pointing at the survivor, so my code knows it's a merge, not someone really deleting a customer. Child records that get reparented to the winner during the merge don't fire their own triggers. That matters for custom roll-ups, so I recalculate for the master record myself.
points: No merge event: delete for losers, update for winner
MasterRecordId set on deleted losers in after delete
Reparented children don't fire triggers
Recalculate custom roll-ups for the winner

q: Your trigger fails with MIXED_DML_OPERATION. Why does it happen and how do you fix it?
alt: What is mixed DML error in Salesforce?
I update User and Account in the same trigger and get an error
mixed dml operation setup and non setup object
How do you avoid mixed DML in a test class?
a: MIXED_DML_OPERATION means the transaction did DML on a setup object, like User, Group, GroupMember or PermissionSetAssignment, and on a non-setup object like Account, in the same transaction. Salesforce blocks it because setup changes affect sharing and access calculations. A common case is a User trigger that fires when someone is deactivated and tries to reassign that person's Accounts in the same transaction. In a trigger, the fix is to move one side into a separate transaction, usually a Queueable or future method for the non-setup DML. In tests, I wrap the setup DML in System.runAs. Not every User update triggers it; it mostly appears when fields like role, profile, username or active status change.
points: Setup (User, Group, PermissionSetAssignment) + non-setup DML in one transaction
Fix: move one side to Queueable or future
Tests: use System.runAs around setup DML
Common trigger: user deactivation or role change

q: Are there operations that don't fire triggers?
alt: Which operations skip Apex triggers?
Does a cascade delete fire triggers on child records?
when do triggers not execute in salesforce
My trigger didn't run when records were deleted with the parent, why?
a: Yes, some system and mass operations skip triggers. Examples are cascading deletes of child records when a master record is deleted, child records reparented as part of a merge, mass campaign status changes, mass division transfers, mass address updates, renaming or replacing picklist values, changing a custom field's data type, and managing price books. So if my design depends on a trigger, I check whether one of these paths can bypass it. For example, say I keep a custom count of Contacts on Account using a Contact trigger. When two Accounts are merged, the Contacts moved to the winner don't fire that trigger, so the count goes stale. That's why I plan a recalculation, like a scheduled batch that reconciles the values.
points: Cascade deletes of children don't fire child triggers
Merge reparenting, mass updates, picklist renames skip triggers
Plan a reconciliation batch for critical roll-ups

q: How do triggers behave with partial-success DML like Database.insert with allOrNone set to false?
alt: Do triggers fire again when some records fail?
Database insert false trigger runs twice
What happens to static variables when Salesforce retries a partial save?
allornone false trigger retry behaviour
a: When some records fail, Salesforce rolls back that attempt and retries the save with only the records that succeeded, so the trigger fires again for them in the same transaction. Because it's the same transaction, static variables are not reset. That's a real trap. Say I update 100 records with allOrNone false and 5 fail. My trigger runs for all 100 and a recursion guard stores their Ids. The attempt is rolled back, the retry runs for the 95 good ones, and the guard says they're already done, so it skips them. The DML from the first attempt was rolled back, so the logic silently never happens. I keep guards tied to real field changes where possible, and I make sure counters and side effects can't be doubled or lost on a retry.
points: Failed attempt is rolled back, good records are retried
Trigger fires again in the same transaction
Static variables are NOT reset between attempts
Id-based guards can wrongly skip the retry
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: How would you design the trigger architecture for a large org with several teams working on the same objects?
alt: How do you organise triggers when many teams touch Account?
Design a scalable trigger framework for an enterprise org
metadata driven trigger framework
How do you stop teams overwriting each other's trigger logic?
a: I'd standardise on one trigger per object and a shared handler framework, so everyone plugs into the same entry point. Handlers stay thin and call service classes split by business domain. I'd use custom metadata to register and order handler classes, so a team adds logic without editing another team's code. For example, the sales team and the service team both need logic on Account. Each writes its own handler class and adds a metadata record with its run order, and nobody touches the other team's file. The framework provides one recursion approach, per-object and per-user bypass through custom metadata and custom permissions, and consistent error logging. I'd also agree when to use Flow versus Apex per object, require bulk tests with 200 records, and push heavy or callout work to Queueables.
points: One trigger per object, shared framework
Custom metadata registers and orders handlers per team
Common bypass, recursion and logging
Per-object Flow vs Apex standard, bulk tests mandatory

q: What is the scope of a static variable in a trigger?
alt: How long does a static variable live in Apex?
Are static variables shared between transactions?
static variable lifetime trigger context
Why do we use static variables in trigger handlers?
a: A static variable lives for the whole transaction, not just one trigger call. So if the same trigger runs several times in one transaction, because of 200-record chunks, a re-save from other automation, or a DML that fires it again, the static value is still there. That's why we use static variables for recursion guards and to cache query results within a transaction. For example, if my handler loads a map of region settings into a static variable during the first chunk, the next four chunks of a 1,000-record Apex insert reuse it instead of querying again. When the transaction ends, the value is gone and the next transaction starts fresh. Static variables are never shared between different users or different transactions.
points: Lives for one transaction
Persists across trigger chunks and re-fires
Used for recursion guards and caching
Not shared across transactions or users

q: How do you write a trigger on a platform event?
alt: Write a platform event subscriber trigger
Which events does a platform event trigger support?
platform event trigger after insert example
Which user does a platform event trigger run as?
a: A platform event trigger only supports after insert, because publishing an event is like inserting it. It runs asynchronously in its own transaction, and by default as the Automated Process user rather than the publisher, so I set owner fields explicitly if they matter. It can receive large batches, so I keep it bulk-safe. For resilience, I can use EventBus.TriggerContext setResumeCheckpoint, or throw EventBus.RetryableException, so events are retried instead of lost. For example, in my trigger on Order_Event__e, each event becomes an order log record. I build all the log records in one list and insert them once, however many events arrive in the batch.
points: Only after insert
Runs async, by default as Automated Process user
Bulk-safe: batches can be large
setResumeCheckpoint / RetryableException for resilience

q: What are the best practices for writing Apex triggers?
alt: Tell me trigger best practices
What rules do you follow when writing a trigger?
apex trigger best practices list
How do you write a good trigger?
a: The main ones: one trigger per object, with a thin trigger that calls a handler class. Bulkify everything, with no SOQL or DML inside loops, using Sets and Maps. Use before triggers for same-record updates and validation, and after triggers for related records. Only process records whose relevant fields changed, by comparing with oldMap. For example, if my logic reacts to an Opportunity's Stage, I skip records where someone only edited the Description. Prevent recursion with a static Set of Ids, not a Boolean. Never hard-code Ids. Move callouts and heavy work to Queueables. Add a bypass switch, and write bulk tests with 200 records.
points: One thin trigger per object + handler
Bulkify: no SOQL/DML in loops
Before for same record, after for related records
Check field changes, Id-based recursion guard, no hard-coded Ids
Async for callouts, bypass switch, bulk tests

q: How do you handle errors when your trigger updates related records?
alt: How do you show a friendly error when a related update fails in a trigger?
Database update with allOrNone false inside a trigger
trigger error handling save result adderror
What if one child record fails to update in my trigger?
a: I use Database.update with allOrNone set to false, then loop through the SaveResults. The results come back in the same order as the list I passed in, so for each failure I can find the related record and map it back to the record that triggered it. Then I either call addError on that triggering record, so the user sees a clear message instead of a generic exception, or I log it to a custom error object if the main save should still succeed. For example, an Account update pushes a change down to its Contacts. If one Contact fails, I trace it back to its Account and block just that Account with a clear message, while the other Accounts in the batch save normally.
points: Database.update(list, false) returns SaveResults
Results are in the same order as the input list
Map failure back to triggering record and addError
Or log to a custom object if the main save should continue

q: Explain the order of execution in Salesforce when a record is saved.
alt: What is the order of execution?
What happens step by step when I click Save on a record?
order of execution triggers validation rules flows
Walk me through the save order in Salesforce
salesforce order of execution in short
a: When a record is saved, Salesforce loads the record and runs system validation, then runs before-save record-triggered flows, then before triggers. Next it re-runs system validation and custom validation rules, then duplicate rules. The record is saved to the database but not committed, and after triggers run. Then come assignment rules, auto-response rules, any remaining workflow rules, escalation rules, processes, and after-save record-triggered flows. After that, entitlement rules, roll-up summary updates on the parent and grandparent, and criteria-based sharing. Finally everything commits, and post-commit work runs, like sending emails and starting queued async jobs. Here's why it matters. If my before trigger sets a Case field and a validation rule checks that field, the rule sees my value, because validation runs after before triggers. But an email from that save only goes out once everything commits.
points: System validation -> before-save flows -> before triggers
Validation rules -> duplicate rules -> save (not committed) -> after triggers
Assignment, auto-response, workflow, escalation, after-save flows
Entitlements, roll-ups, sharing -> commit -> post-commit (email, async)
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Which runs first, a before-save flow or a before trigger?
alt: Does a before-save flow run before the Apex trigger?
flow vs trigger which executes first
If a flow and a trigger update the same field, which value wins?
Do after triggers run before after-save flows?
a: The before-save record-triggered flow runs first, then the before trigger. So if both set the same field, the trigger's value wins because it runs later. On the after side, after triggers run before after-save flows. Say a before-save flow sets an Opportunity's discount to 5 percent and a before trigger sets it to 10. The record saves with 10, and the admin looking at the flow can't work out why. That's exactly the kind of thing you run into when debugging an unexpected value. In practice, I avoid having a flow and a trigger update the same field on the same object, because whoever maintains it next will struggle to work out which one is in control.
points: Before-save flow -> before trigger
After trigger -> after-save flow
Last writer wins on the same field
Don't let two automations own one field
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: If a before trigger sets a field, will validation rules see the new value?
alt: Do validation rules run before or after triggers?
Can a before trigger fix data so the validation rule passes?
validation rule fires after before trigger
Why does my validation rule fail because of a value my trigger set?
a: Yes. Custom validation rules run after before triggers, so they evaluate the values the trigger set. That means a before trigger can fill in or correct a field so the record passes validation. For example, if a rule requires a Region on Lead and my trigger fills in Region from the country, the rule sees the filled value and the save goes through. It also means a trigger can accidentally cause a validation error the user doesn't understand. Some system checks, like layout-level required fields on a standard UI save, run before the trigger, so a trigger can't help with those. When a validation fails after my change, I check the debug log to see what the trigger set just before the validation step.
points: Validation rules run after before triggers
Trigger can correct data to pass validation
Layout-required checks from the UI run before the trigger
Use debug logs to see the values at validation time
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Where do duplicate rules run in the order of execution?
alt: Do duplicate rules run before triggers?
If a duplicate rule blocks a record, do after triggers still run?
duplicate rule order of execution
When are duplicate rules evaluated on save?
a: Duplicate rules run after before triggers and custom validation rules, but before the record is saved to the database. If a duplicate rule with a block action finds a match, the save stops there, so after triggers, workflow and after-save flows never run for that record. If the rule allows the save with an alert, the save continues normally. This also means a before trigger can clean data before duplicate matching happens. For example, someone pastes in an email with extra spaces around it. My before trigger trims and standardises it first, so the duplicate rule compares the clean value against existing contacts.
points: After before triggers and validation rules
Before the record is written to the database
Block action stops the save: no after triggers
Before trigger can normalise data before matching
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Your update trigger runs twice for the same record in one transaction, and the org still has a workflow rule with a field update. Why?
alt: Does a workflow field update fire triggers again?
Why does Trigger.old show the original value on the second trigger run?
workflow field update trigger fires twice
Trigger executed again after workflow rule
a: A workflow field update re-saves the record, and Salesforce runs the before update and after update triggers one more time. Custom validation rules, duplicate rules and flows don't re-run for that pass. An important detail is that Trigger.old in the second run still holds the values from before the original update, not from the first run. Since workflow rules are past end of support, the clean fix is to move that field update into a before-save flow or the before trigger, and make the trigger safe to run twice by checking real changes.
points: Workflow field update re-runs before and after update triggers once
Validation rules, duplicate rules and flows don't re-run
Trigger.old keeps the values from before the original update
Migrate workflow field updates to before-save flow or trigger
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: Why does the Account trigger fire when you only update an Opportunity?
alt: Child record update fires parent trigger, why?
Roll-up summary causing parent trigger to run
opportunity update account trigger executing
Does a roll-up summary recalculation run the parent's automation?
a: Usually because of roll-up summary fields. Account can have roll-up summaries on Opportunity, so after the Opportunity saves, Salesforce recalculates the roll-up on the parent Account, and the parent goes through its own save procedure, which runs Account triggers and other automation. If that changes the Account and the grandparent has a roll-up, it happens again one level up. Cross-object workflow field updates have the same effect. So the parent trigger should only act when its own relevant fields actually change.
points: Roll-up recalculation saves the parent record
Parent triggers and automation run
Can cascade to the grandparent
Parent trigger should check real field changes
area: Apex Triggers and Order of Execution

q: You enqueue a Queueable from a trigger and the transaction fails later in the save. Does the job still run?
alt: Are async jobs started before or after commit?
If the transaction rolls back is the future method still called?
post commit logic order of execution emails queueable
Will an email sent from a trigger go out if the save fails?
a: No. Async jobs like Queueables and future methods only start after the transaction commits, which is the last step in the order of execution. If anything later in the save fails, like an after-save flow error or an exception during the parent roll-up update, the whole transaction rolls back and the enqueued job is discarded. The same applies to emails sent from Apex. Say my trigger enqueues a job to send a new Order to the warehouse system, and then an after-save flow throws an error. The Order isn't saved, and the warehouse never hears about it. That's actually the benefit: an external system only hears about committed data. If I need something to happen even when the save fails, like error logging, I'd publish a platform event configured to publish immediately.
points: Async jobs and emails run post-commit
Rollback discards enqueued jobs and emails
Integrations only see committed data
Publish-immediately platform events survive rollback
