q: How do you make sure a scheduled batch does not start if the previous run is still running?
alt: Prevent overlapping batch runs
Check if a batch is already running before starting
Two instances of the same batch running at once
avoid duplicate batch execution
a: I'd guard it in two places, the scheduler and the data. In the scheduler's execute method, before calling executeBatch, I query AsyncApexJob for my batch class with a status of Holding, Queued, Preparing or Processing. If one exists, I skip this run, or log it, instead of starting a second copy. I filter by ApexClass.Name and JobType BatchApex. Why it matters: say the hourly sync batch normally takes 20 minutes, but one day it takes 90. Without this check, the next run starts while the first one is still going, and two copies of the same batch can process the same records twice and cause lock errors. As an extra safety net, the batch itself only picks records with a Pending status and marks them Processed. So even an accidental double run doesn't repeat work.
points: Query AsyncApexJob for active runs of the class
Skip or log if one is active
Status field makes the job idempotent

q: Your stateful batch fails with a heap size error near the end. What is going on?
alt: Heap limit in stateful batch
Database.Stateful too much data
Batch with stateful map runs out of memory
apex heap size too large batch
a: That's almost always state growing chunk after chunk. With Database.Stateful, instance variables are carried between chunks and serialized every time. So if I keep adding records to a list or map, the state keeps growing, and eventually it goes past the 12 MB async heap, usually late in the job. That's why it fails near the end and not at the start. Say I'm saving every processed Account into a stateful list so I can report on them in finish. It's fine at chunk 10, but by chunk 400 that list is huge. The fix is to keep only what's really needed, like counters, totals or a capped number of error messages, not whole sObjects. If I need detailed results, I write them to a custom log object inside execute instead of holding them in memory. And if the totals can be worked out later with an aggregate query, removing Stateful entirely also speeds the job up. In review, any Stateful batch that collects sObjects gets a question from me.
points: Stateful variables grow and are serialized each chunk
Async heap limit is 12 MB
Keep counters, not record lists
Write details to a log object in execute

q: A user needs to start a batch job from a button on a Lightning page and see its progress. How would you build it?
alt: How do you start a batch job from a button in an LWC?
Run batch apex from lightning web component
Call Database.executeBatch from a controller
Show batch progress in LWC
user clicks button to start batch
a: I'd build it as start-and-poll. I create an AuraEnabled Apex method that calls Database.executeBatch and returns the job Id. The LWC calls it imperatively when the user clicks the button. To show progress, a second AuraEnabled method queries AsyncApexJob by that Id and returns the status, JobItemsProcessed and TotalJobItems. The component polls it every few seconds until the status is Completed, Failed or Aborted. So the user sees something like "12 of 40 batches done" and a progress bar filling up. I also check permissions in the Apex method, for example with a custom permission, because starting a heavy batch shouldn't be available to everyone. And I can block a second run if one is already active. I'd also agree a sensible polling interval with the team, so a page left open all day isn't calling Apex nonstop.
points: AuraEnabled method returns the job Id
Poll AsyncApexJob for progress
Protect with a custom permission
Block duplicate runs

q: What is the difference between SOQL and SOSL?
alt: SOQL vs SOSL, when to use which?
When would you use SOSL instead of SOQL?
Explain sosl with an example
difference between so ql and sosl
a: I use SOQL when I know where the data lives, and SOSL when I'm searching for text. SOQL queries one object at a time, plus its related objects, with precise filters, like a SQL SELECT. I use it when I know which object the data is in, for example all open Opportunities for an Account. SOSL is a text search across multiple objects at once using the search index, like a global search. I use it when I have a search term and do not know which object or field it is in, for example searching a name across Accounts, Contacts and Leads. SOQL returns a list of records; SOSL returns a list of lists, one per object. SOSL has a limit of 20 searches per transaction and returns at most 2,000 results. In review, the thing I watch for is SOSL being used where a filtered SOQL would be more precise.
points: SOQL: one object and related objects, exact filters
SOSL: text search across many objects
SOQL returns List<sObject>, SOSL returns List<List<sObject>>
20 SOSL per transaction, max 2,000 results

q: How do you write a parent-to-child relationship query?
alt: Query accounts with their contacts in one SOQL
What is a subquery in SOQL?
How to get child records using inner query?
parent to child soql
a: I'd use a subquery, so I get parents and children in one go. A parent-to-child query uses a nested SELECT inside the field list. Inside it, I use the child relationship name, which is plural, like Contacts for standard objects, or the name ending in __r for custom ones, like Invoices__r. Each parent record then comes back with a list of its children that I can loop over. For example, SELECT Name, (SELECT LastName FROM Contacts) FROM Account gives me each Account with its Contacts attached. That saves queries, because I get parents and children in one SOQL instead of querying in a loop. If you're not sure of the child relationship name, it's shown on the lookup field definition. And the subquery can have its own WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Querying children in a loop is something I always flag in code review.
points: Nested SELECT using the child relationship name
Standard: plural name like Contacts; custom: __r
One query instead of queries in a loop
Subquery supports WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT

q: How do you query parent fields from a child record?
alt: Child to parent relationship query
What is dot notation in SOQL?
Get account name from contact query
how many levels can you go up in soql
a: I use dot notation from the child to reach the parent's fields. with the relationship name to reach the parent's fields. For a standard lookup like Contact to Account, it's Account.Name. For a custom lookup, I replace __c with __r, so Project__c becomes Project__r.Name. I can go up to five levels, like Contact.Account.Owner.Name. So if I'm showing a list of Contacts with their company name and the account owner's name, that's one query with no extra lookups. The gotcha is when the lookup is empty. Then the parent reference is null, so in Apex I check for null before reading its fields. Otherwise a Contact with no Account will throw a null pointer exception. That missing null check is one of the most common bugs I catch in review.
points: Dot notation: Account.Name
Custom lookups: __c becomes __r
Up to five levels upward
Null-check the parent in Apex

q: How do you write an aggregate query in SOQL?
alt: SOQL GROUP BY example
What is AggregateResult in Apex?
Count records per account using SOQL
sum of opportunity amount by stage
a: When I need totals, I let the database do the maths instead of looping in Apex. Aggregate queries use functions like COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, usually with GROUP BY. In Apex they return a list of AggregateResult, and I read the values with get, using the field name for grouped fields and an alias for the calculated values. For example, I can sum Opportunity Amount by StageName in one query instead of looping over thousands of records. One thing to remember: aggregate functions other than COUNT still count each aggregated row toward the 50,000 query rows limit. So on large objects I still keep the WHERE clause tight, and I remind the team that an aggregate isn't free.
points: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX with GROUP BY
Returns List<AggregateResult>
Use aliases and ar.get('alias')
Aggregated rows still count toward query row limits

q: What is the HAVING clause and how is it different from WHERE?
alt: SOQL HAVING example
Find accounts with more than 5 contacts
WHERE vs HAVING in SOQL
filter on count in soql
a: Simply put, WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped, while HAVING filters the groups after aggregation. So if I want accounts that have more than five contacts, I group contacts by AccountId and use HAVING COUNT(Id) greater than 5. I cannot put an aggregate function in a WHERE clause, that is exactly what HAVING is for. I can still use WHERE in the same query to narrow the rows first, which also helps performance. HAVING can only be used together with GROUP BY. My guidance to the team is to filter as much as possible in WHERE first, and keep HAVING for conditions on the totals.
points: WHERE filters rows before grouping
HAVING filters groups after aggregation
Aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE
HAVING requires GROUP BY
code:
List<AggregateResult> bigAccounts = [
    SELECT AccountId, COUNT(Id) contactCount
    FROM Contact
    WHERE AccountId != null
    GROUP BY AccountId
    HAVING COUNT(Id) > 5
];

q: How do you prevent SOQL injection in dynamic SOQL?
alt: What is SOQL injection?
How to use String.escapeSingleQuotes?
Safe way to build a dynamic query from user input
dynamic soql security
a: My rule is simple: user input never goes into a query string unbound. SOQL injection happens when user input is glued straight into a dynamic query string, so a crafted value can change the query logic and expose data. Say a search box builds the WHERE clause by adding whatever the user typed inside quotes. If they type a quote followed by an OR condition, they can pull back records they shouldn't see. The best defence is bind variables. In Database.query I reference a local variable with a colon, and the value is treated as data, never as query syntax. Where I can't bind, like a field name or sort direction, I check against an allowlist, for example confirming the field exists in the object's describe. String.escapeSingleQuotes is a fallback for string values. And I run the query in user mode so it respects the user's access. Any string concatenation in dynamic SOQL gets flagged in review, and I'd have a static code scan check for it too.
points: Never concatenate raw user input
Use bind variables in Database.query
Allowlist field names and sort order
escapeSingleQuotes as a fallback

q: What is Database.queryWithBinds?
alt: How do you pass bind variables as a map in dynamic SOQL?
Dynamic SOQL with a bind map
Bind variables that are not in local scope
a: It's my preferred way to run dynamic SOQL in a shared selector layer. Database.queryWithBinds runs a dynamic SOQL string where the bind values come from a Map of String to Object, instead of local variables. That's useful when the query is built in one method and run in another, like in a query builder or selector class, because normal bind variables have to be in scope where Database.query is called. The map keys match the names after the colon in the query. For example, the query says WHERE Industry = :industry, and I pass a map with the key "industry" set to "Banking". The third parameter is an AccessLevel, and I usually pass USER_MODE. It keeps the safety of bind variables, so it's a clean way to avoid injection.
points: Binds supplied as Map<String, Object>
Keys match the :names in the query
Useful in selector or query builder classes
Third parameter is AccessLevel

q: How do you use bind variables in SOQL?
alt: What is a colon variable in SOQL?
Use an Apex variable inside a SOQL query
Query records where Id is in a set
bind variable soql example
a: Bind variables are the default on my teams for any value in a query. A bind variable lets me use an Apex variable inside a SOQL query by putting a colon before its name. It works in static SOQL in square brackets and in dynamic SOQL with Database.query, as long as the variable is in scope. The most common use is binding a Set or List of Ids with IN, which is the core of bulkified code. Say a trigger fires on 200 Opportunities. I loop once to collect their AccountIds into a Set, then run one query, WHERE Id IN :accountIds, outside the loop. One query instead of 200. Bind variables are also safe from injection, because the value is never treated as query syntax. And I can bind expressions too, like a method call or Date math.
points: Prefix the Apex variable with a colon
IN :idSet is the core of bulkification
Safe from SOQL injection
Works in static and dynamic SOQL

q: What is a selective query and which fields are indexed?
alt: What makes a SOQL query selective?
Which fields are indexed by default in Salesforce?
How do indexes work in Salesforce?
non selective query error
a: Selectivity is what keeps queries working as data grows. A selective query is one where the WHERE clause filters on an indexed field and narrows the results enough that Salesforce can use the index instead of scanning the whole table. Fields indexed by default include Id, Name, OwnerId, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp, RecordTypeId, lookup and master-detail fields, and fields marked External Id or Unique. For other fields, Salesforce Support can create a custom index. Selectivity matters most on large objects. In triggers, a non-selective query on an object with more than about 200,000 records can throw a non-selective query error. For example, a trigger filtering Cases on an unindexed custom text field might work fine in a small sandbox, then fail in production once there are a million Cases. Filters like not equals, leading wildcards, or comparing with null often stop the index from being used. That's why I ask for trigger queries to be checked against production-sized data, not just a small sandbox.
points: Filter on an indexed field that narrows results
Default indexes: Id, Name, OwnerId, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp, RecordTypeId, lookups, External Id, Unique
Custom indexes via Salesforce Support
Avoid !=, leading %, null filters on big objects

q: What are the selectivity thresholds for standard and custom indexes?
alt: When does the optimizer use an index in Salesforce?
Selectivity threshold percentages
How does the query optimizer decide between index and table scan?
a: These numbers decide whether your index helps at all. The query optimizer only uses an index if the filter returns a small enough share of the object's records. For a standard index, the threshold is 30 percent of the first million records and 15 percent of records beyond that, up to a maximum of one million. For a custom index, it's 10 percent of the first million and 5 percent beyond that, up to 333,333 records. So say an object has 500,000 records. A filter on a standard indexed field has to return under 150,000 rows, and on a custom indexed field under 50,000. If it's expected to return more, the optimizer does a full table scan. With AND conditions, the combined filter can be selective even if each field alone isn't. With OR, every condition has to be indexed and selective. And records in the Recycle Bin count too. When a stakeholder asks why a filter is slow, this is the threshold I walk them through.
points: Standard index: 30% of first 1M, 15% after, max 1M
Custom index: 10% of first 1M, 5% after, max 333,333
Above threshold means full table scan
OR needs every condition indexed

q: What is the Query Plan tool and how do you use it?
alt: How do you check if a query is using an index?
Explain the developer console query plan
What does query plan cost mean?
query plan tool salesforce
a: The Query Plan tool is my first stop for any slow query. It lives in the Developer Console and shows how Salesforce would run a SOQL query. To turn it on, I go to Help, Preferences, and switch on Enable Query Plan. Then a Query Plan button shows up in the Query Editor. It lists the possible plans with the leading operation type, like Index, TableScan or Sharing, the fields used, the estimated cardinality, and a relative cost. A cost below 1 means the plan is selective. Say a list view on Cases is slow. I paste its query in, click Query Plan, and see that the best plan is a TableScan with a cost above 1. That tells me to rewrite the filter to use indexed fields, add a more selective condition, or ask Support for a custom index. I'd like the team to run it on new queries against large objects before they reach review.
points: Enable in Developer Console preferences
Shows leading operation: Index, TableScan, Sharing
Cost below 1 means selective
Use it to tune slow or non-selective queries

q: What are skinny tables?
alt: Explain skinny tables in Salesforce
How to speed up reports on a huge object?
When should you request a skinny table?
a: Skinny tables are a late-stage option, not a first fix. A skinny table is a special table that Salesforce Support creates for a large object, holding a subset of the fields people use most. Normally Salesforce joins standard and custom field storage behind the scenes. A skinny table avoids those joins, and it leaves out soft-deleted rows, so reports, list views and queries on those fields run faster. It's kept in sync automatically. Say an Opportunity object has 20 million records and the pipeline report always uses the same eight fields. A skinny table with those eight fields is exactly the use case. The limitations: it's enabled only through Support, it can't include fields from other objects, and if you need new fields in it, you contact Support again. I only look at it after indexing and query tuning, for objects with millions of records where reporting is slow.
points: Created by Salesforce Support for large objects
Subset of fields, avoids internal joins
Excludes soft-deleted rows; auto-synced
No fields from other objects; changes need Support

q: How do you handle large data volumes in Salesforce?
alt: What are LDV best practices?
Org has hundreds of millions of records, how to keep it fast?
Large data volume strategy
ldv considerations salesforce
a: I handle large data volumes in layers, and I plan for them before go-live rather than after. First, data model and queries: selective filters on indexed fields, custom indexes from Support, and skinny tables for heavy reporting objects. Second, store less: archive old data to an external store or Big Objects, and purge logs on a schedule. Third, avoid data skew, so keep the number of children per parent and records per owner reasonable. Fourth, loading: use Bulk API, defer sharing calculations during big loads, and temporarily turn off non-essential automation. Fifth, sharing: a simpler role hierarchy and public read where possible keep the sharing tables smaller. For example, if the Case object holds years of closed Cases that nobody opens anymore, I'd archive the old ones to a Big Object and keep only recent ones live. Finally, I monitor with the query plan and test with realistic volumes in a full sandbox. The archive rules need business sign-off, so I bring that conversation in early.
points: Selective queries, custom indexes, skinny tables
Archive with Big Objects or external storage
Avoid account, ownership and lookup skew
Bulk API and deferred sharing for loads
Test with realistic volumes

q: What is data skew and what are its types?
alt: Explain account data skew
What is ownership skew and lookup skew?
Why are too many child records under one parent a problem?
data skew in salesforce
a: Data skew is a design risk I look for early. It's when too many records are tied to one parent or one owner, roughly more than 10,000. There are three types. Account data skew is one Account with a huge number of child records, like Contacts or Opportunities. Updating children locks the parent, so you get record lock errors, and sharing recalculation gets slow. A classic case is a catch-all Account, something like "Unassigned", with 50,000 Contacts parked on it. Ownership skew is when one user owns a very large number of records of an object, often an integration user. Changing that user's role or the sharing model triggers heavy sharing recalculation. Lookup skew is when a very large number of records look up to the same record, which causes lock contention on inserts and updates. The fix in each case is to spread the children or ownership across more parents or users. I'd rather catch it in the data model review than in a production lock error.
points: Roughly more than 10,000 records on one parent or owner
Account skew: lock errors, slow sharing
Ownership skew: sharing recalculation pain
Lookup skew: lock contention on one lookup target

q: An integration user owns two million records and changing its role takes hours. How do you fix it?
alt: Ownership skew problem with integration user
Sharing recalculation is very slow for one user
One user owns too many records, best practice
integration user owns all records
a: This is ownership skew, and I'd fix the design, not just the timing. When a user who owns millions of records moves in the role hierarchy, Salesforce has to recalculate sharing for all of them, and that's why it takes hours. If the integration user really has to own the records, I put it in a role at the top of the hierarchy, or give it no role at all, so its records don't roll up to a lot of managers. And I never change that user's role during business hours. Better still, I spread ownership across real users or queues based on business rules. For example, records coming in through the integration get assigned by territory or region, instead of all staying with the integration user. Also, if the object's sharing is Public Read/Write, most of the sharing cost goes away, so I check whether a private model is really needed. That's a trade-off I'd take to the business, because opening up sharing is a security decision, not just a performance one.
points: Ownership skew drives heavy sharing recalculation
Keep the owner with no role or a top-level isolated role
Distribute ownership across users or queues
Review whether a private sharing model is needed

q: What does FOR UPDATE do in SOQL?
alt: How do you lock records in Apex?
Explain record locking with SOQL
Prevent two users updating the same record at the same time
for update keyword soql
a: I use FOR UPDATE when two users could change the same value at once. Adding FOR UPDATE to a SOQL query locks the returned records for the rest of the transaction. No other transaction can update them until mine commits or rolls back. Others wait, and if the lock isn't released within about ten seconds, they get an UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW error. I use it for things like counters, invoice number generation or inventory. Say two users place orders at the same moment for the last 5 units of a product. Without a lock, both read 5, both subtract, and the stock ends up wrong. With FOR UPDATE, the second one waits until the first finishes, then reads the real value. One rule: you can't use ORDER BY with FOR UPDATE. And I keep locked transactions short and only lock the records I really need. In review, I check that nothing slow or heavy runs while the lock is held.
points: Locks returned rows until the transaction ends
Prevents lost updates in race conditions
Other transactions wait, then may get UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW
Cannot combine with ORDER BY

q: Users get UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW errors during a data load. How do you troubleshoot it?
alt: Unable to lock row error, what causes it?
Record currently unavailable error in Salesforce
How to fix lock errors when loading child records?
unable to lock row fix
a: I'd treat it as a load-design problem first, not a code problem. UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW means a transaction waited too long for a record that another one had locked. During loads, the usual cause is parallel batches updating children of the same parent, because inserting or updating a child locks its parent, or a rollup summary updating the same parent. Say I'm loading Opportunities and a few big Accounts have thousands each. If those rows are spread across parallel batches, they all fight over the same Account. So my steps are: sort the load file by the parent Id so one parent's children land in the same batch, switch the Bulk API job to serial mode if needed, reduce batch size, and check for data skew. I also look for triggers or flows that update one common record, like a single settings record, and I schedule loads outside integration and batch windows. In code, a short retry can help for transient locks. I make the sorted-by-parent rule part of the team's load checklist, so it doesn't depend on who runs the load.
points: Parallel batches lock the same parent
Sort by parent Id; use serial mode or smaller batches
Check rollups, triggers and data skew
Avoid overlapping jobs; retry transient failures

q: What is the query rows limit and how do you avoid 'Too many query rows: 50001'?
alt: Too many query rows 50001 error fix
How many records can SOQL return in Apex?
Query rows governor limit
fifty thousand rows limit
a: The fix is to fetch less, or move the work to batch. In one transaction, all SOQL queries together can retrieve at most 50,000 records, sync or async. Go over that and you get Too many query rows 50001. To avoid it, I tighten filters so I only fetch what I need, use LIMIT where it makes sense, and use aggregate queries like COUNT instead of fetching rows just to count them. For example, if a page only needs to show how many open Cases an Account has, I run a COUNT query instead of pulling back every Case record. If I really do need to process more than 50,000 records, I move the work into Batch Apex with a QueryLocator, which can handle up to 50 million. I also check that a query in a trigger isn't accidentally pulling a whole table, which is exactly the kind of thing I look for in review.
points: 50,000 rows total per transaction
Tighter filters and LIMIT
Use COUNT() instead of fetching rows to count
Batch Apex for larger volumes

q: How do you fix 'Too many SOQL queries: 101'?
alt: SOQL inside a for loop problem
System.LimitException too many SOQL queries
How to bulkify a query in a trigger?
101 soql error
a: Nine times out of ten it's a query inside a loop, and bulkifying fixes it. This error means the transaction ran more than 100 SOQL queries in synchronous context. Almost always it is a query inside a loop, for example querying the Account for every Contact in a trigger, which fails as soon as 101 records come in. The fix is to bulkify: collect the Ids in a Set first, run one query outside the loop with IN, store the results in a Map by Id, and then look up from the map inside the loop. I also check for recursion, where a trigger fires again and repeats queries, and for multiple automations on the same object adding queries. That last one is why I push for one trigger per object, so the team can see every query that fires.
points: Usually a SOQL query inside a loop
Collect Ids, query once with IN, use a Map
Check trigger recursion and other automation
Limit is 100 sync, 200 async

q: What is the difference between Database.getQueryLocator and Database.query?
alt: When to use getQueryLocator vs a normal query?
Why does batch use a QueryLocator?
Database.query vs Database.getQueryLocator
a: The difference is a loaded list versus a cursor. Database.query runs a dynamic SOQL string right away and returns a list of records, so it's bound by the normal 50,000 query rows limit. Database.getQueryLocator returns a QueryLocator, which is a cursor-like object over the result set, not a loaded list. In Batch Apex start, returning a QueryLocator lets the batch go through up to 50 million records, because records are fetched chunk by chunk. So if a batch has to process 3 million Contacts, start returns Database.getQueryLocator with the query. If I tried to load them with Database.query, it would fail at 50,001 rows. QueryLocators are also used with StandardSetController for pagination in Visualforce. So in normal code I use Database.query or static SOQL, and in batch start I use getQueryLocator.
points: Database.query: returns a list now, 50,000 row limit
getQueryLocator: cursor over results
Batch start: up to 50 million records
Also used with StandardSetController

q: What are semi-joins and anti-joins in SOQL?
alt: SOQL IN with a subquery
Find accounts that have closed won opportunities in one query
What is NOT IN subquery in SOQL?
semi join anti join soql
a: Semi-joins and anti-joins let me filter on related records without writing loops. A semi-join is a WHERE condition with IN and a subquery, used to return records that have related records matching some criteria, for example Accounts that have at least one closed won Opportunity. An anti-join uses NOT IN with a subquery to return records that do not have such related records, for example Accounts with no Contacts. The subquery must select a single Id or lookup field, and there are restrictions, like not using them inside OR conditions and a limited number per query. They are efficient because the filtering happens in the database, not in Apex loops. When I see code querying children and checking for empty lists, I suggest one of these instead.
points: Semi-join: WHERE Id IN (subquery)
Anti-join: WHERE Id NOT IN (subquery)
Subquery selects one Id or lookup field
Filtering happens in the database

q: How do you query polymorphic fields using TYPEOF?
alt: What is a polymorphic relationship in Salesforce?
Query WhatId fields on Task with TYPEOF
How to get different fields based on the related object type?
type of soql
a: TYPEOF is the clean way to handle polymorphic fields in one query. A polymorphic field can point to records of different object types. Examples are WhatId and WhoId on Task and Event, or OwnerId, which can be a User or a Queue. TYPEOF lets me pick which fields to return depending on the actual type of the related record, with a WHEN branch per object and an optional ELSE. Say I'm building an activity timeline from Tasks. If the Task's What is an Account, I want its Phone. If it's an Opportunity, I want Amount and StageName. TYPEOF What WHEN Account THEN Phone WHEN Opportunity THEN Amount, StageName END gets both in one query. In Apex, I then check the type with instanceof before casting. Without TYPEOF, I can only get the common Name fields, or I filter on What.Type.
points: Polymorphic: WhatId, WhoId, OwnerId
TYPEOF ... WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END
Check with instanceof before casting
Filter by What.Type as an alternative

q: What is the difference between WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED and WITH USER_MODE?
alt: How do you enforce field level security in SOQL?
Which is better, security enforced or user mode?
Explain USER_MODE in SOQL
FLS in apex queries
a: I'd go with WITH USER_MODE. Both make a SOQL query respect the running user's permissions, because Apex runs in system mode by default. WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks object and field access only for fields in the SELECT and FROM clauses. It throws an exception on the first inaccessible field, and it has gaps, like not supporting traversal of polymorphic fields. WITH USER_MODE is newer, and it's what Salesforce now recommends. It enforces object permissions, field-level security and sharing rules, checks fields in WHERE and ORDER BY too, and can report all inaccessible fields at once. For example, if a user can't see a Salary field and the query only uses it in the WHERE clause, SECURITY_ENFORCED won't check it, but USER_MODE will. WITH USER_MODE is the standard I set for new code, and older SECURITY_ENFORCED queries get moved over when we touch them. And you can't combine both clauses in one query.
points: Apex runs in system mode by default
SECURITY_ENFORCED: SELECT/FROM only, fails on first field
USER_MODE: CRUD, FLS and sharing, all clauses
Salesforce recommends USER_MODE

q: How do you enforce security on DML and dynamic queries?
alt: What is AccessLevel.USER_MODE?
How to use Security.stripInaccessible?
Insert records in user mode in Apex
enforce crud and fls on dml
a: My default is user mode everywhere a user's data is involved. For DML, the Database methods accept an AccessLevel parameter. So Database.insert with AccessLevel.USER_MODE checks the user's object and field permissions and sharing before saving. The same works for Database.query and Database.queryWithBinds. For inline DML there's the as user keyword, like insert as user. Sometimes I'd rather quietly drop the fields a user can't see than throw an error. For example, say an LWC lists Contacts, and some users don't have access to a sensitive custom field. Before returning the data, I run Security.stripInaccessible, which gives me copies of the records without the inaccessible fields, so the component still loads for everyone. And classes should be declared with sharing, so record-level sharing applies. A class without an explicit sharing keyword doesn't get through my review.
points: Database methods take AccessLevel.USER_MODE
Inline DML: insert as user
Security.stripInaccessible removes inaccessible fields
Use with sharing for record access

q: What is the Bulk API and when do you use it?
alt: Bulk API vs REST API for data loads
What is Bulk API 2.0?
How to load millions of records into Salesforce?
serial vs parallel mode bulk api
a: Bulk API is my choice once volume goes past a few thousand records. It's built for loading or extracting large numbers of records asynchronously. Instead of sending records one request at a time, you submit a job with CSV data, and Salesforce processes it in batches in the background. Bulk API 2.0 is the simpler version. You create a job, upload the data, and Salesforce handles the batching for you. I use it for anything beyond a few thousand records, like migrations or nightly loads, and Data Loader can use it with a setting. Say a nightly job pushes 300,000 price updates from an ERP. That's one Bulk API job, not 300,000 separate calls. With Bulk API 1.0, you can choose serial mode instead of parallel to avoid record lock errors, at the cost of speed. For small, real-time updates, REST or the Composite API is a better fit. Agreeing that split with the integration team early saves a lot of rework.
points: Asynchronous, job-based, CSV data
Bulk API 2.0 handles batching automatically
Use for migrations and large loads
Serial mode in Bulk API 1.0 reduces lock errors

q: What is the difference between Data Loader and Data Import Wizard?
alt: When to use data loader vs import wizard?
Which tool to import 100,000 records?
Can Data Import Wizard delete records?
data loader versus data import wizard
a: It comes down to who's loading and how much. The Data Import Wizard is a browser-based tool in Setup for simple imports of up to 50,000 records at a time. It supports Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Solutions, Campaign Members and custom objects. It has built-in duplicate matching, but it only does insert and update. Data Loader is a client application that handles all objects and up to millions of records. It supports insert, update, upsert, delete, hard delete and export, can use the Bulk API, and can run from the command line for scheduled jobs. For example, if a marketing manager wants to upload 3,000 Leads from an event spreadsheet, I point them to the Wizard. If I need to delete 400,000 old records, or export data every night, that's Data Loader.
points: Wizard: browser, up to 50,000 records, limited objects
Wizard: insert/update with duplicate matching
Data Loader: all objects, millions of records
Data Loader: upsert, delete, export, CLI automation

q: What is an External ID and how does upsert work?
alt: Explain upsert in Salesforce
Why do we use external Id fields?
How to avoid duplicates when loading data from another system?
upsert using external id apex
a: Every integrated object on my teams gets an External ID, because it's what makes upsert safe. An External ID is a custom field marked as an external identifier, holding the record's Id from another system, like an ERP. It's indexed automatically. Upsert uses a key field to decide, per record, whether to insert or update. If a record with that External ID value exists, it's updated. If not, a new one is created. If more than one matches, that record fails. Say the ERP sends customer C-1001 every night. The first night it gets created in Salesforce. Every night after that, the same record just gets updated, with no duplicates, and I never need to know its Salesforce Id. That's what makes integrations and repeat loads safe. In Apex I use Database.upsert with the field token, and in Data Loader I pick the External ID field as the match key.
points: Custom field holding the other system's key
Indexed automatically
Upsert: match then update, else insert
Multiple matches cause an error

q: You receive Contacts from an ERP that only know the parent's ERP Id. How do you link them to Accounts?
alt: Relate child to parent using external id
Set lookup using external Id instead of Salesforce Id
Load contacts with account external id in data loader
parent reference by external id apex
a: I'd link them through the External ID, so I do not need to query Account Ids first. In Apex, I can set the relationship field with an Account instance that only has the External ID populated, and Salesforce resolves the parent during DML. So contact.Account is set to new Account with ERP_Id__c equal to the value from the ERP. In Data Loader I map the column to the Account relationship using its External ID field, and in a Bulk API CSV the header is Account dot ERP_Id__c. This saves a query, keeps the integration simple, and fails clearly if the parent does not exist. I make sure those failures land in an error log the integration team actually checks.
points: Set the relationship with a parent reference holding only the External ID
Salesforce resolves the parent during DML
Data Loader: map to the relationship using the External ID
No extra query for parent Ids

q: What is a SOQL for loop and when should you use it?
alt: How to avoid heap size errors when querying many records?
SOQL for loop vs normal list query
Iterate over large query results in Apex
for loop on soql query
a: I use a SOQL for loop when a query can return a lot of rows and heap is the worry. It runs the query right inside the for statement, and Salesforce fetches the records in batches of 200 behind the scenes, instead of loading everything into memory at once. That keeps heap usage low when a query returns a lot of records. I can go one record at a time, or use the list form to get 200 records per iteration. The list form is better when I'm doing DML, because I can update each chunk. Say a query returns 20,000 Contacts. A normal list holds all 20,000 in heap. With the list form of the for loop, I hold 200 at a time and update each group. It doesn't raise the 50,000 query rows limit, though, it only helps with heap. And I still never put a query or DML inside the inner per-record loop.
points: Fetches records in chunks of 200
Reduces heap usage
List form gives 200 records per iteration
Does not raise the 50,000 row limit

q: A trigger query fails with 'Non-selective query against large object type'. How do you fix it?
alt: Non selective query error in trigger
System.QueryException non-selective query
Query works in sandbox but fails in production with large data
how to make my query selective
a: I'd fix the filter so it can use an index. This error is thrown in triggers when a query on an object with a large number of records, roughly over 200,000, can't use an index and would need a full table scan. It often works in sandbox and fails in production, just because of the data size. To fix it, I add a filter on an indexed field, like an Id set, a lookup, CreatedDate, or an External ID field, and make sure that filter is selective. I remove patterns that block indexes, like not equals, leading wildcards, or null checks on custom fields. For example, a trigger that queries Cases where a custom Region field is not null will scan the table. Filtering by the AccountIds from the trigger records instead uses the lookup index. If the business filter has to be on a custom field, I ask Salesforce Support for a custom index, and I check the result with the Query Plan tool. Because it only shows up at production volume, I ask the team to think about selectivity whenever a trigger query touches a big object.
points: Triggered by table scans on large objects in triggers
Filter on indexed fields with selective values
Avoid !=, leading %, null on custom fields
Request a custom index; verify with Query Plan

q: What are date literals in SOQL?
alt: SOQL query for records created this month
How to filter by last 30 days in SOQL?
What is LAST_N_DAYS in SOQL?
date functions in soql
a: I prefer date literals over date maths in Apex wherever they fit. They're keywords for relative date ranges, so I don't have to calculate dates in Apex. Common ones are TODAY, YESTERDAY, THIS_WEEK, LAST_MONTH, THIS_QUARTER, THIS_YEAR, LAST_N_DAYS with a number, and NEXT_N_DAYS. For example, WHERE CloseDate = NEXT_N_DAYS:30 gives me Opportunities closing in the next 30 days, and the same query keeps working tomorrow without any change. They're evaluated in the running user's time zone. For datetime fields like CreatedDate, the literal covers the full day range, so CreatedDate = TODAY catches everything from midnight to midnight. There are also date functions like CALENDAR_YEAR or CALENDAR_MONTH that I use with GROUP BY for reports, for example counting records per month. The time zone point is the one I remind people about, because it explains a lot of "missing record" complaints.
points: TODAY, LAST_MONTH, THIS_QUARTER, LAST_N_DAYS:n
Evaluated in the user's time zone
Date functions like CALENDAR_MONTH with GROUP BY

q: You need a list of Accounts that have no open Cases. How would you query it?
alt: Find parent records with no child records matching a condition
Accounts without open cases SOQL
Query records not related to another object
anti join example scenario
a: I'd use an anti-join, which filters in the database instead of looping in Apex. The query selects Accounts where Id is NOT IN a subquery of AccountId from Case where IsClosed is false. That returns only Accounts that have no open Cases, in one query. The alternative of querying all Accounts with a Cases subquery and checking for empty lists in Apex uses many more query rows and heap. If the Account table is very large, I also add a selective filter, like a record type or an owner, so the outer query stays efficient. In review, this is a pattern I steer people towards whenever I see empty-list checks on subquery results.
points: Anti-join: Id NOT IN (subquery)
Filtering happens in the database
Avoids looping and extra query rows
Add a selective outer filter on large objects

q: How do you query deleted or archived records with ALL ROWS?
alt: How to get records from the recycle bin in SOQL?
What is ALL ROWS in Apex?
Query IsDeleted records
undelete records using apex
a: ALL ROWS is how I reach records in the Recycle Bin, because by default SOQL doesn't return them. In Apex, adding ALL ROWS at the end of the query includes deleted records, and I can filter with IsDeleted equals true to get only those. It also returns archived Activities. Say a user deletes 30 Contacts by mistake. I can query them with ALL ROWS and IsDeleted = true, then run the undelete DML statement on that list to bring them back. It's also handy for auditing. A couple of rules: ALL ROWS can't be combined with FOR UPDATE, and through the API the equivalent is the queryAll operation. And once records are purged from the Recycle Bin, you can't get them back this way. So when someone reports an accidental delete, I tell them to raise it fast, before the bin is emptied.
points: ALL ROWS includes Recycle Bin and archived activities
Filter with IsDeleted = true
Use with undelete to restore
Not allowed with FOR UPDATE

q: How do you paginate SOQL results?
alt: What is OFFSET in SOQL?
How to implement pagination in an LWC data table?
LIMIT and OFFSET in SOQL
server side pagination salesforce
a: For small lists, OFFSET is fine, but for anything large I'd go with keyset pagination. The simple way is LIMIT with OFFSET. LIMIT sets the page size, OFFSET skips the earlier rows, and ORDER BY keeps the order stable. The catch is that OFFSET maxes out at 2,000 rows, so it doesn't work for deep pages, and large offsets get slower. For bigger data sets I use keyset pagination. I remember the last record's sort value and Id, and the next page's query filters for values greater than that. Say I show 50 Accounts per page, sorted by Name. Page 41 needs an OFFSET of 2,000, which is the maximum, so page 42 breaks. With keyset, I just ask for Accounts that sort after the last one I showed, which works at any depth and uses the index. For a total count to show page numbers, I run a separate COUNT query.
points: LIMIT plus OFFSET with ORDER BY
OFFSET maximum is 2,000
Keyset pagination for large data
Separate COUNT() for totals

q: You need to migrate ten million records from a legacy system into Salesforce. How would you plan it?
alt: Plan a large data migration to Salesforce
Data migration strategy for millions of records
Steps for migrating data with relationships
how to load 10 million records
a: I'd plan it in phases, and I'd agree the cutover and rollback plan with the business before any data moves. First, mapping and cleansing. I map legacy fields to Salesforce, deduplicate, and add an External ID field on each object for the legacy key. Second, load order. Users and reference data first, then parents like Accounts, then children like Contacts and Opportunities, linking them through External IDs with upsert. So a Contact row just carries its legacy account key, and upsert finds the right Account. Third, performance. Use Bulk API 2.0 through Data Loader or an ETL tool, temporarily disable or bypass non-essential triggers, flows and validation rules, defer sharing calculations, and sort children by parent to avoid lock errors. Fourth, testing. I do a full-size run in a full sandbox first. Then, after the production load, I reconcile record counts and check sample data, so I know ten million in the source really landed as ten million in Salesforce. I want that reconciliation signed off by the data owners, not just by the team that ran the load.
points: Cleanse data and add External IDs
Load parents before children, upsert by External ID
Bulk API, bypass automation, defer sharing
Sort by parent to reduce lock errors
Rehearse in full sandbox, reconcile after

q: What is Lightning Web Components and why is it built on web standards?
alt: What is LWC?
Explain Lightning Web Components in simple words
Why did Salesforce move from Aura to LWC?
what is l w c framework
a: LWC is what I'd use for all new UI work. Lightning Web Components is Salesforce's modern UI framework, where you build components with standard HTML, modern JavaScript and CSS. Instead of a proprietary framework layer like Aura, LWC uses what the browser already gives us: custom elements, shadow DOM, ES modules, templates and events. Because the browser does most of the heavy lifting natively, components load and render faster, and the code looks like normal web development, so skills carry over. For example, a JavaScript developer who has never touched Salesforce can read an LWC class on day one, because it's just an ES module exporting a class. Salesforce only adds a thin layer on top for things like security, base Lightning components, Lightning Data Service and the wire service. And LWC and Aura can live on the same page, and an LWC can sit inside an Aura component, but not the other way round. That's also why hiring and onboarding are easier, since general web skills carry straight over.
points: Built on web standards: custom elements, shadow DOM, ES modules
Faster than Aura because the browser does most of the work
Thin Salesforce layer: base components, LDS, wire service, security
LWC can be nested inside Aura, not the other way round

q: What files make up a Lightning Web Component bundle?
alt: What is inside an LWC folder?
Which files are mandatory in an LWC?
What is the js-meta.xml file used for?
lwc bundle structure
a: Simply put, an LWC bundle is a folder named after the component, and normally it has an HTML template, a JavaScript file and a js-meta.xml configuration file. The JavaScript file is required, because it defines the class that extends LightningElement. The HTML file is needed for any component that renders UI, but a service-style module can skip it. The js-meta.xml holds the API version, whether the component is exposed, and its targets, like record page, app page, flow screen or Experience Builder, plus design properties. So for a component called accountCard, I'd have accountCard.js, accountCard.html and accountCard.js-meta.xml inside an accountCard folder. Optional files are a CSS file for scoped styles, an SVG icon for App Builder, and a __tests__ folder for Jest tests. On my teams, that __tests__ folder isn't optional for anything with real logic.
points: componentName.js is required and extends LightningElement
componentName.html for UI components
componentName.js-meta.xml: apiVersion, isExposed, targets
Optional: .css, .svg icon, __tests__ folder

q: Explain the LWC lifecycle hooks and the order in which they run.
alt: What are lifecycle hooks in LWC?
Order of constructor, connectedCallback and renderedCallback in parent and child
Tell me the life cycle of a lightning web component
what runs first connected callback or rendered callback
a: There are five hooks, and the order matters most when parents and children depend on each other. LWC gives us five lifecycle hooks: constructor, connectedCallback, renderedCallback, disconnectedCallback and errorCallback. The constructor runs when the component is created. I have to call super() first, and I don't touch child elements or public properties there. connectedCallback runs when the component is inserted into the DOM, so that's where I load data or subscribe to message channels. renderedCallback runs after every render. disconnectedCallback runs when the component is removed, so I clean up listeners and subscriptions there. errorCallback catches errors from child components. The flow is top-down for creation and bottom-up for rendering. So with a parent accountList and a child accountRow, it goes: parent constructor, parent connectedCallback, child constructor, child connectedCallback, child renderedCallback, and only then the parent renderedCallback.
points: constructor: call super() first, no DOM or public property access
connectedCallback: init, load data, subscribe
renderedCallback: after every render, child before parent
disconnectedCallback: cleanup; errorCallback: catches descendant errors

q: What is the difference between connectedCallback and renderedCallback, and when would you use each?
alt: connectedCallback vs renderedCallback
Where should I make my Apex call, connected or rendered callback?
Can I access DOM elements in connectedCallback?
when to use rendered callback in lwc
a: connectedCallback is for setup, renderedCallback is for DOM work, and I keep the second one rare. connectedCallback fires once each time the component is inserted into the DOM, before it renders. So I use it for initialization: reading public properties, calling Apex imperatively, or subscribing to Lightning Message Service. The template elements aren't available there yet. renderedCallback fires after every render, including re-renders caused by reactive changes, so the DOM is available. I use it rarely. A typical case is a third-party chart library that needs a real DOM node to draw into. I initialize it in renderedCallback, and I guard it with a flag like chartInitialized so it only runs once, not on every re-render. One more gotcha: connectedCallback can run more than once if the component is removed and re-inserted, so I don't assume it only ever fires one time. Any renderedCallback without a guard flag gets a question from me in code review.
points: connectedCallback: before render, DOM not ready, good for data loading
renderedCallback: after each render, DOM ready
Guard renderedCallback with a flag to avoid repeated work

q: My component goes into an infinite rendering loop. What could cause that and how do you fix it?
alt: Why does renderedCallback keep firing again and again?
LWC infinite loop in renderedCallback
Component keeps re-rendering, how to debug
maximum call stack in lwc rendered callback
a: Almost always, someone is updating a reactive property inside renderedCallback. Changing a field the template uses triggers another render, which calls renderedCallback again, and it loops. Say renderedCallback does this.columns = buildColumns(), and buildColumns returns a new array every time. Each render assigns a new value, which causes another render, forever. A similar loop happens when a getter used in the template changes state, or when a setter on an @api property dispatches an event that makes the parent push a new value back. To fix it, I move data changes out of renderedCallback into connectedCallback, wire handlers or event handlers. If I really need renderedCallback, I use a non-rendered flag so the logic runs only once, and I compare old and new values before assigning, so I never assign a value that hasn't actually changed. This is one pattern I specifically scan for when I review LWC changes.
points: Never set template-bound fields unconditionally in renderedCallback
Use a hasRendered flag or compare values before assigning
Getters should be pure, no side effects

q: How does errorCallback work in LWC?
alt: What is an error boundary in Lightning Web Components?
How do I catch errors from child components in LWC?
Explain errorCallback with an example
error call back lwc
a: I use errorCallback to build error boundaries, so one bad widget can't take down a page. It's a lifecycle hook that lets a parent act as an error boundary. It gets two arguments, the error and the component stack. It catches errors thrown in descendant components, in their lifecycle hooks, or in event handlers declared in their templates. It doesn't catch errors from the component itself. And it doesn't catch errors in asynchronous code, like a promise rejection from an Apex call, which I still handle with try/catch or .catch. What I usually do is wrap risky children in a small boundary component. Say a page has five child widgets and one of them throws in its connectedCallback. The boundary's errorCallback catches it, logs it, and shows a friendly "this section couldn't load" message, so one broken child doesn't blank out the whole page. I'd rather the team share one boundary component than each person writing their own.
points: Signature: errorCallback(error, stack)
Catches errors from descendants, not from itself
Async errors still need try/catch or .catch

q: What are the decorators in LWC and what does each one do?
alt: Explain @api, @track and @wire
What decorators are available in Lightning Web Components?
Difference between api track and wire decorator
at the rate api track wire
a: LWC has three decorators: @api, @track and @wire. @api makes a property or method public, so a parent component, App Builder or a flow can set it. It's reactive, so changes from the parent re-render the child. Common examples are recordId and objectApiName on record pages. @track makes the framework watch changes inside a plain object or array, not just reassignment. Since Spring '20, all class fields are reactive by default, so @track is only needed for deep mutation. @wire connects a property or function to a wire adapter, like an Apex method or getRecord. The framework provisions data and error to it automatically and re-fetches when a reactive parameter changes. So on a record page, I mark recordId with @api, wire getRecord with '$recordId', and the component loads the record by itself whenever that Id changes. In review, I also ask whether each @api property really needs to be public, because every one is a contract other components depend on.
points: @api: public, set by parent or builder, reactive
@track: deep observation of objects and arrays only
@wire: declarative data from Apex or LDS adapters
All fields are reactive on reassignment without any decorator

q: Is @track still needed in LWC? Explain the reactivity rules.
alt: When do I still need the track decorator?
How does reactivity work in Lightning Web Components?
Are all fields reactive in LWC?
do we need at track anymore
a: Mostly no, and on my teams we prefer reassignment over @track. All fields are reactive, so if I reassign a field that's used in the template, or in a getter the template uses, the component re-renders. What the framework doesn't see by default is a mutation inside an object or array, like pushing to an array or changing one property of an object. Say I have this.filters = { status: 'Open' } and then I do this.filters.status = 'Closed'. Without @track, the UI won't update. So I either decorate the field with @track, or, which I prefer, I assign a new copy with the spread operator: this.filters = { ...this.filters, status: 'Closed' }. Even @track doesn't watch Date, Set or Map internals, so for those I always reassign. And wired data is read-only, so I clone it before changing it.
points: Reassignment of any field triggers re-render
Mutation of object/array props needs @track or a new copy
@track ignores Date, Set and Map internals
Prefer immutable updates with spread

q: I updated a property on wired data and got an error, or the UI did not refresh. Why?
alt: Cannot assign to read only property in LWC wire data
Why can't I modify data returned from @wire?
UI not updating after I change an array element in LWC
proxy read only error lwc
a: That's the read-only rule on wired data, and the fix is to copy before you change. Data provisioned by @wire is frozen, so any attempt to change it, such as adding a computed field for a datatable, throws a read-only error. The fix is to make a shallow copy first and work on the copy. The second common reason the UI does not refresh is mutating an array or object in place, for example this.rows[0].Name = 'X', or this.rows.push(row). The framework only reacts to reassignment, so I build a new array with map or spread and assign it back. I also check that the field is actually referenced in the template or in a getter, because changes to unused fields never cause a re-render. These two mistakes are common enough that I cover them when new developers join the team.
points: Wired data is read-only: clone before modifying
In-place mutation does not re-render without @track
Reassign with map/spread instead

q: Can a child component change the value of an @api property passed from its parent?
alt: Should I modify a public property inside the child?
Is @api property read-only in child component?
Child wants to change data that parent passed down, what to do?
can child update api variable
a: No, and that's a rule I hold the team to: a child should treat @api properties as owned by the parent. If the parent passes an object or array, it's read-only in the child, and trying to mutate it throws an error. Even for primitives, changing it in the child creates a mismatch, because the parent will overwrite it the next time it re-renders. The clean pattern is one-way data flow: data goes down through @api properties, and changes go up through custom events. Say a parent passes a quantity of 5 to a child quantity picker. When the user clicks plus, the child doesn't set quantity to 6 itself. It dispatches an event with 6, the parent updates its own field, and 6 flows back down. If the child only needs a local editable version, it copies the value into a private field.
points: Data down via @api, changes up via events
Objects passed from parent are read-only in child
Copy into a private field for local edits

q: How do you call a method on a child component from the parent?
alt: Parent to child method call in LWC
How to expose a public method in LWC?
How do I invoke a child function from parent component?
call child component function from parent lwc
a: I'd expose the method with @api and call it through a reference. I decorate the method in the child with @api, which makes it public. Then in the parent I get a reference to the child element, using lwc:ref or this.template.querySelector, and call the method directly. This is useful for actions like reset, refresh or validate, where the parent tells the child to do something. For example, a search page has a Clear button. The child filter panel has an @api reset method, and the parent's click handler calls this.refs.filters.reset(). The gotcha is timing. I only call it after the child has rendered, so from an event handler or renderedCallback, not from the constructor or connectedCallback. Public methods can also return values or promises. I keep these for commands like reset or validate, and send data down through properties, so the parent-child contract stays easy to follow.
points: @api on the child method makes it public
Get the child with lwc:ref or template.querySelector
Call only after render, e.g. in a click handler

q: How does the wire service work in LWC? Give an example.
alt: Explain @wire with an Apex method
What is wire adapter?
How does wire get data reactively?
how to use wire with record id
a: The wire service is my default for reading data. It's a reactive, declarative way to get data. I decorate a property or function with @wire and give it an adapter, like an Apex method marked cacheable=true or an LDS adapter like getRecord, plus a config object. When a parameter is prefixed with a dollar sign, like '$recordId', it becomes reactive, so when that value changes, the wire calls the adapter again. The framework provisions an object with data and error. For example, I wire a getContacts Apex method with accountId set to '$recordId'. On an Account page it loads that Account's Contacts, and if the recordId changes, it reloads by itself. Wiring to a property is simplest. Wiring to a function lets me process the result, like cloning it or handling errors. And wire runs when the component loads, it doesn't wait for a user action.
points: Adapter + config; '$param' makes it reactive
Provisions { data, error }
Wire to a property or a function
Apex must be @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)

q: When do you use @wire versus calling Apex imperatively?
alt: Wire vs imperative Apex call
Difference between wire method and imperative method in LWC
Why would you call Apex imperatively?
wire or imperative which is better
a: My rule of thumb is wire for reads, imperative for actions. I use @wire for reading data that should load automatically and stay reactive to parameters, like records related to the current recordId. It's declarative, uses the client cache, and needs the Apex method to be cacheable=true, which means no DML. I use imperative calls when I need control over timing, like on a button click, when the method does DML or isn't cacheable, when I need to chain calls in order, or when I want to call it conditionally. For example, showing an Account's open Cases is a wire. A "Close all Cases" button that updates them is an imperative call. Imperative calls return a promise, so I use async/await with try/catch. One trade-off: refreshApex only works with wired results, so with imperative calls I simply call the method again.
points: Wire: automatic, reactive, cached, read-only
Imperative: on demand, DML allowed, ordering control
Imperative returns a promise; refreshApex only for wire

q: What does @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) do and what are its restrictions?
alt: Why does wire need cacheable true?
Can a cacheable method do DML?
Explain client-side caching of Apex in LWC
cacheable equals true meaning
a: I mark a method cacheable when it's a pure read, but I plan the refresh story at the same time. cacheable=true tells the framework the method is a read-only query, so its response can be stored in the Lightning client cache and reused for identical calls with the same parameters. It's required for @wire, and it helps performance because repeat calls can be served from the cache. The restriction is that the method can't do DML. If it tries, it throws an error. The flip side of caching is stale data. Say a component wires a cacheable getOpenTasks method, and then the user completes a task through another Apex call. The wired list still shows the old task, because the cached result isn't updated automatically. So I call refreshApex on the wired result, or notifyRecordUpdateAvailable for record data cached by LDS. Cacheable methods can still be called imperatively, too.
points: Required for @wire
No DML allowed inside
Responses cached on the client per parameters
Use refreshApex to bust stale wired data

q: How do you call an Apex method imperatively with parameters from LWC?
alt: Pass parameters from LWC to Apex
Imperative Apex call example with async await
How do I send values to an Apex method from JavaScript?
call apex on button click lwc
a: It's a simple import-and-call. I import the method from @salesforce/apex and call it like a function, passing one object whose keys match the Apex parameter names exactly. Say the Apex method is getCases(Id accountId, String status). In JavaScript I call getCases({ accountId: this.recordId, status: 'Open' }). If I write accId instead of accountId, Apex won't get that value. It returns a promise, so I use async and await with try/catch, show a spinner while it runs, and turn the spinner off in finally. The Apex method must be static, public or global, and annotated with @AuraEnabled. Parameters can be primitives, lists, maps, sObjects, or a custom wrapper class whose fields are marked @AuraEnabled. Mismatched parameter names are a quiet bug, so I check them in review.

q: What is refreshApex and how do you use it correctly?
alt: How do I refresh wired Apex data after an update?
refreshApex not working, what am I doing wrong?
How to refresh data in LWC after DML
refresh apex example
a: refreshApex is how I fix stale wired data after a change. It re-runs a wired Apex call and bypasses the client cache, so the component shows fresh data after a change. The important detail is that I have to pass the exact provisioned value the wire gave me, not the data I copied from it. When I wire to a function, I store the whole response object in a field, say this.wiredContacts, and later call refreshApex(this.wiredContacts). For example, after a user saves a new Contact in a modal, I call refreshApex on that stored value and the list updates. It returns a promise. A common mistake, and one I look for in review, is calling refreshApex on imperatively fetched data, which does nothing. For imperative calls I just call the method again. And if other components show the same record through LDS, I also call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable.
points: Pass the original wired value, not a copy of data
Store the response when wiring to a function
Does not work for imperative calls
Returns a promise

q: What is Lightning Data Service and why should you use it?
alt: What is LDS in LWC?
Benefits of Lightning Data Service
Why use LDS instead of Apex?
lightning data service explained
a: I'd use LDS before writing any Apex for single-record work. Lightning Data Service is the shared data layer for Lightning components. It lets me create, read, update and delete records without writing Apex, using base components like lightning-record-form or the uiRecordApi wire adapters and functions. The big advantages: it respects CRUD, field-level security and sharing automatically, it caches records on the client, and it keeps every component on the page in sync. Say a record page has my custom component and a standard component, both showing the same Account. If my component updates the Phone through LDS, the standard one refreshes too, with no extra code. I prefer LDS for single-record operations, and I use Apex when I need complex queries, many records, aggregations, or business logic that has to run on the server. Less Apex also means less code to test and maintain, which is a trade-off I'm happy to make.

Respects CRUD, FLS and sharing
Shared client cache keeps components in sync
Use Apex for complex queries or bulk logic

q: What is the difference between lightning-record-form, lightning-record-edit-form and lightning-record-view-form?
alt: record form vs record edit form vs record view form
Which LDS form component should I use?
When would you choose lightning-record-edit-form over lightning-record-form?
difference between three record form components
a: I pick the simplest one that meets the requirement. All three use Lightning Data Service, so no Apex is needed. lightning-record-form is the quickest. You give it an object, a record Id, and fields or a layout type, and it builds a view or edit form with modes view, edit and readonly. But customization is limited. lightning-record-edit-form gives me control over the layout, because I place each lightning-input-field myself, I can add custom buttons, and I can intercept the submit to change values or validate before saving. lightning-record-view-form is the read-only version, where I place lightning-output-field components. For example, a quick Contact edit panel with standard fields is a record-form. But if the business wants a custom two-column layout, a custom button, and a status set before saving, that's record-edit-form.

record-edit-form: custom layout with lightning-input-field, onsubmit hook
record-view-form: custom read-only layout with lightning-output-field

a: I'd intercept the submit. I handle the onsubmit event and call event.preventDefault() to stop the default save. Then I read event.detail.fields, add or change values, and call submit on the form with the updated fields. This is useful for values the user shouldn't type, like a parent Id or a status, or for running custom validation first. Say a component creates a Case from an Account page. The user fills in Subject and Description, and in onsubmit I add the AccountId from the page and set Status to New, then submit. After a successful save, the onsuccess event gives me the record Id, and onerror gives me the error. The form also shows errors through lightning-messages. If the rule must always hold, I also back it with a validation rule or server logic, because client-side defaults alone can be bypassed.

onsuccess returns event.detail.id
Add lightning-messages to show errors

q: You update a record through Apex, but the standard record page and LDS components still show old values. How do you fix it?
alt: Record page not refreshing after Apex update
How do I tell LDS that a record changed on the server?
What is notifyRecordUpdateAvailable?
getRecordNotifyChange replacement
a: I'd tell LDS the record changed. LDS doesn't know about changes made in Apex, so its cache stays stale. After the Apex call succeeds, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable from lightning/uiRecordApi with the list of changed record Ids. LDS then re-fetches those records, and every wired getRecord and standard component using them updates. For example, a button calls Apex to recalculate a discount on an Opportunity. Right after it returns, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable with that Opportunity Id, and the standard record details show the new value without a page reload. It replaced the older getRecordNotifyChange. If my own component got its data from a wired Apex method, I also call refreshApex on that wired result, because notifyRecordUpdateAvailable only refreshes LDS record data, not custom Apex results. Any component that saves through Apex needs this step, so it's on my review checklist.

q: What are the ways components can communicate with each other in LWC?

Parent to child, child to parent and unrelated components communication
how to pass data between components lwc
a: I choose the mechanism based on how the components are related. Parent to child, I pass data through @api properties or call @api methods on the child. Child to parent, the child dispatches a custom event and the parent listens with an on-handler in its template. For components that aren't in the same hierarchy, like two separate components on a Lightning page, I use Lightning Message Service with a message channel, which also works across LWC, Aura and Visualforce. For example, a list component in the left column and a details component in the right column: when a user clicks a row, the list publishes the record Id on a channel and the details component picks it up. Older projects used a pub-sub module, but LMS is the supported approach now. And for record data, LDS keeps components in sync automatically. Picking the simplest option that fits keeps the codebase easy for the next developer to follow.

The event name should be lowercase, with no 'on' prefix and no spaces, for example 'select'. In the parent template I add an attribute named on plus the event name, like onselect, pointing to a handler, and the handler reads event.detail. I keep detail to primitives or a fresh copy of data, so the parent cannot accidentally mutate the child's internal state. By default the event does not bubble, which is what I want for direct child-to-parent communication. Event naming is one of the conventions I agree with the team up front, so handlers are predictable across components.

q: What do bubbles and composed mean on a custom event?
alt: Explain bubbles true composed true in LWC
Why is my event not reaching the grandparent?
Event propagation across shadow DOM
bubbles and composed flags
a: My default is both false, and anything wider needs a reason. These two flags control how far an event travels. bubbles: true lets the event move up through the DOM tree from the element that fired it. composed: true lets it cross shadow DOM boundaries, so it can escape the component's shadow root and reach ancestors in other components. With both false, the default, only the direct parent that declared the handler on the child element hears it, and that's the cleanest option. With bubbles true and composed false, it bubbles only inside the parent's template. Both true makes the event part of the component's public API to every ancestor, so I use it sparingly, because any component up the tree can start depending on it. For example, if a row inside a table needs the page to know about a click, I usually have the table catch it and re-dispatch its own event, instead of letting the row's event travel all the way up. In review, a composed event is something I always ask about, because it quietly widens the component's API.
points: Default (false/false): only the direct owner hears it
bubbles: travels up the DOM
composed: crosses shadow boundaries
Prefer re-dispatching over bubbles+composed

q: What is Lightning Message Service and how do you use it?
alt: Explain LMS with an example
How to communicate between components on different parts of a page?
What is a message channel?
lightning message service publish subscribe
a: Lightning Message Service is my answer for components that aren't related in the DOM. It lets them exchange messages, across LWC, Aura and Visualforce on the same Lightning page, including components in the utility bar. I create a message channel as metadata, a LightningMessageChannel file, with the fields it carries. A publisher imports the channel and MessageContext and calls publish with a payload. A subscriber calls subscribe in connectedCallback and unsubscribe in disconnectedCallback. Say an app page has a filter component on the left and a chart component on the right, with no parent-child link. When the user picks a region, the filter publishes it, and the chart reloads for that region. One gotcha: by default, subscribers only get messages in the active area. Passing APPLICATION_SCOPE makes them receive messages from anywhere in the app. I also keep a short list of the org's message channels and what each carries, so teams reuse them instead of creating near-duplicates.

publish(context, channel, payload)
subscribe in connectedCallback, unsubscribe on disconnect
APPLICATION_SCOPE to receive across the whole app

<!-- messageChannels/RecordSelected.messageChannel-meta.xml -->
<LightningMessageChannel xmlns="http://soap.sforce.com/2006/04/metadata">
    <masterLabel>RecordSelected</masterLabel>
    <isExposed>true</isExposed>
    <lightningMessageFields><fieldName>recordId</fieldName></lightningMessageFields>
</LightningMessageChannel>

// publisher.js
import { publish, MessageContext } from 'lightning/messageService';
import CHANNEL from '@salesforce/messageChannel/RecordSelected__c';
@wire(MessageContext) messageContext;
handleSelect(e) { publish(this.messageContext, CHANNEL, { recordId: e.detail.id }); }

q: What is the difference between Lightning Message Service and the pub-sub module?
alt: LMS vs pubsub in LWC
Why should I replace pubsub with LMS?
Is pubsub still recommended?
pub sub versus message service
a: I'd use LMS. The pub-sub module was a small JavaScript utility from the sample recipes, not a platform feature. It only works between LWCs in the same page context, it relies on the page reference to scope events, and it doesn't work with Aura or Visualforce. Lightning Message Service is the supported platform feature. Channels are metadata you can deploy and package, it works across LWC, Aura and Visualforce, and it has proper scoping options. Say an org still has an old Visualforce page on a Lightning page, and it needs to know when an LWC filter changes. Pub-sub can't do that, LMS can. So for any new work I use LMS, and when I find pub-sub in an older org, I plan to migrate it as part of normal refactoring, which is easier to get approved than a separate clean-up project.

LMS: platform feature, metadata channels

q: What are slots in LWC and how do you use named slots?
alt: Explain slot in Lightning Web Components
How to pass markup from parent into a child component?
Default slot vs named slot
what is slot tag lwc
a: Slots are how I build reusable containers. A slot is a placeholder in a child component's template where the parent can inject its own markup. That makes components reusable as containers, like a card or modal shell where the parent decides what goes inside. An unnamed slot receives any content without a slot attribute, and named slots receive content with a matching slot attribute, like slot equals footer. Say I build one modal component for the whole app. One page puts a form in the default slot and Save and Cancel buttons in the footer slot. Another page puts a simple confirmation message in it. Same modal, different content. The injected content belongs to the parent, so the parent's CSS styles it and the parent handles its events. The child can listen to the slotchange event to know when slotted content changes. A shared modal or card shell like this is the kind of component I'd want the team to build once and reuse.
