q: How does conditional rendering work in LWC templates?
alt: lwc:if vs if:true
How to show and hide sections in LWC?
Can I write an expression in lwc:if?
lwc if else if else example
a: I use lwc:if, lwc:elseif and lwc:else, the directives on template tags. They replaced the older if:true and if:false directives, which still work but aren't recommended anymore. The directive takes a property or getter, not an expression. So I can't check something like "count greater than zero" in the template. I write a getter called hasRecords in JavaScript and use lwc:if={hasRecords}. A false branch isn't just hidden, it isn't created at all, so its child components aren't constructed. That helps performance too, because heavy sections only load when they're needed, like a big related-records table that only appears after the user clicks Show More. The branches must be siblings, in that order. For new code, I ask the team to use lwc:if rather than the old directives.

Unrendered branches are not created at all

render list in lwc template
a: I'd use for:each with for:item for normal loops, and the iterator directive when I need to know the position. Iterator gives me value, index, first and last. That's handy for separators or special styling on the first or last row, like a divider under every row except the last one. In both cases, every top-level element inside the loop needs a unique key attribute, ideally the record Id, so the engine can update only the rows that change. I avoid using the array index as the key. Say I delete the second Contact in a list of five. With index keys, the rows shift and the wrong elements get re-used. With the Contact Id as the key, only that one row is removed. Index-as-key is a small thing I still flag in review, because the bugs it causes are confusing.

q: How does shadow DOM affect styling in LWC, and how do you style base components?
alt: Why can't my parent CSS style the child component?
How to override the style of a lightning-button?
What are styling hooks in LWC?
css not applying in lwc child
a: Styling hooks are the supported answer, and I don't let the team target internal SLDS classes. Every LWC has its own shadow tree, so its CSS is scoped. Styles in a component only apply to its own template, and a parent's styles don't leak into the child. That's why a parent can't style the inside of a child, or of a base component like lightning-button. Targeting internal SLDS classes is unsupported, because they can change, which is why it's off-limits for us. Say the design wants a lightning-button with a brand-colored background. Writing CSS against the button's inner SLDS classes isn't the way, and it can break after a release. The supported way is styling hooks, which are CSS custom properties that base components expose, and they do pass through the shadow boundary. Inside my own components, I use :host to style the component's outer element. And if a design really needs global styling, light DOM is an option for my own components.
points: CSS is scoped to the component's shadow tree
Parent styles don't reach into children
Use styling hooks (CSS custom properties) for base components
:host styles the component itself

q: What is light DOM in LWC and when would you use it?
alt: Shadow DOM vs light DOM in Lightning Web Components
How do I render an LWC without shadow DOM?
When is light DOM a good idea?
lwc render mode light
a: I treat light DOM as an exception. By default an LWC renders inside a shadow tree, which isolates its markup and CSS. Light DOM renders the component's markup directly into the parent's DOM instead. I enable it by setting static renderMode = 'light' in the class and lwc:render-mode='light' on the template. It helps when global styles or a theme need to reach inside the component, when third-party libraries need normal DOM access, or for better SEO and accessibility tooling in Experience Cloud sites. For example, on an Experience Cloud site with a site-wide theme, a light DOM header component can pick up the site's fonts and colors directly. The trade-off is no encapsulation. Other code can reach in and restyle the markup, and I use this.querySelector instead of this.template.querySelector. So shadow DOM stays my default, and I use light DOM only for the components that need it. When someone wants it, I ask them to explain the reason in the pull request.
points: static renderMode = 'light' plus lwc:render-mode='light'

q: How do you implement infinite loading in lightning-datatable?

a: I'd combine the datatable's infinite loading with keyset paging in Apex. I set enable-infinite-loading on the datatable and handle the onloadmore event, which fires when the user scrolls near the bottom. In the handler I set event.target.isLoading to true, call Apex imperatively for the next batch, append the results as a new array, and set isLoading back to false. For paging on the server I prefer keyset paging, filtering by Id or a sort field greater than the last loaded value, because OFFSET is capped at 2,000 rows. Say I load 50 Accounts at a time. Each loadmore asks Apex for the next 50 after the last Id I have. When Apex returns fewer than 50, I know I've reached the end and turn infinite loading off. One gotcha: the table needs a fixed-height container, or scrolling won't work.

With querySelector, I search the component's shadow tree using a CSS selector, like this.template.querySelector('lightning-input'). With lwc:ref, I tag an element, like lwc:ref equals emailInput, and then read this.refs.emailInput directly. That's cleaner, faster, and doesn't break if I change CSS classes. Either way, the elements only exist after rendering, so I use them in event handlers or renderedCallback. lwc:ref isn't supported inside for:each or iterator loops, so for repeated elements I still use querySelectorAll, often with a data attribute.

q: How do you handle errors from Apex in LWC and show a meaningful message?
alt: Error handling in Lightning Web Components
Why does my LWC show 'internal server error' instead of my message?
What is AuraHandledException?
how to show apex error message in lwc
a: I'd handle it on both sides. On the Apex side, I catch exceptions and throw an AuraHandledException with a message that's safe for users. Otherwise the client may only get a generic internal error. On the client, imperative calls go in try/catch, and wired results are checked for the error property. The error shape varies. Apex errors usually have body.message, while LDS errors can have body as an array, or contain output.errors and fieldErrors. So if I only read error.body.message everywhere, an LDS save that fails a validation rule may show just a generic message, and the real field-level error gets lost. That's why I use a small reduceErrors helper that flattens all these shapes into readable strings, then show them in a toast or inline. And I log the technical details on the server, not in the UI. I'd keep one shared reduceErrors utility for the whole team, rather than every component parsing errors its own way.

q: How do you improve the performance of Lightning Web Components?
alt: LWC performance best practices
My Lightning page with custom components is slow, what would you optimize?
How to make LWC load faster?
performance tuning lwc
a: I'd measure first, and then start with data, because most slowness is server calls. I prefer LDS and cacheable wired Apex, so repeated calls hit the client cache. I select only the fields I need, and I combine several small Apex calls into one. For example, if a component makes four Apex calls on load for Account details, Contacts, Cases and counts, I'd merge them into one call that returns a wrapper. For big lists, I paginate or use infinite loading instead of loading thousands of rows. On the client, I debounce search inputs, use lwc:if so heavy child components aren't created until needed, load third-party libraries once, and keep getters and renderedCallback cheap, since they run on every render. I use stable keys in loops. And I check with browser dev tools and Apex logs rather than guess. Before a big release, I ask the team to test pages with realistic data volumes, not five sample records.
points: Fewer, leaner server calls; cacheable and LDS
Paginate large data sets

Keep getters and renderedCallback cheap
Measure before optimizing

q: What is the difference between Lightning Locker and Lightning Web Security?
alt: Locker Service vs LWS
What is Lightning Web Security?
Why did Salesforce introduce LWS?
locker vs lightning web security
a: LWS is the direction I'd take for any org that can switch. Both are security layers that isolate components from different namespaces, so one package can't attack another. Lightning Locker does it by wrapping global objects like window, document and DOM elements in secure proxy versions. That blocks access to other namespaces' DOM, but it also breaks a lot of third-party libraries and adds overhead. Lightning Web Security takes a newer approach. Each namespace runs in its own JavaScript sandbox, and risky APIs are modified through distortions instead of wrapped. That gives better performance, better compatibility with libraries, and lets components import modules from other namespaces. For example, if a third-party charting library keeps failing under Locker, switching the org to LWS is one of the first things I'd look at. It's turned on in Session Settings with one setting for both Lightning web components and Aura components, and new orgs have it on by default. In an older org, I'd test the switch in a sandbox first, because it affects every component at once.
points: Locker: secure wrappers around globals, strict namespace isolation
LWS: per-namespace sandboxes with API distortions
LWS: faster, more library friendly, cross-namespace imports
Enabled in Session Settings; default in new orgs

In each test, I create the component with createElement from lwc, set public properties, and append it to document.body. Apex imports are mocked with jest.mock using the virtual option. After changing state or resolving promises, I wait for the DOM to update with a resolved promise, then query the shadow root and assert. For example, to test a counter component, I create it, click its plus button, await a resolved promise, then check that the displayed number went from 0 to 1. In afterEach, I remove the elements from the body and clear mocks, so tests don't affect each other. On my teams, Jest tests run in the pipeline, so a broken component fails the build, not the user.

q: How do you make sure an LWC respects security, like CRUD, field-level security and sharing?
alt: Security best practices for LWC with Apex
Does Apex called from LWC enforce FLS?
How to prevent users seeing fields they shouldn't in LWC?
with sharing user mode lwc apex
a: LDS-based components and base components enforce CRUD, FLS and sharing automatically, so that's my first choice. Apex is different, because it runs in system mode by default. So in classes called from LWC, I declare with sharing, run queries WITH USER_MODE and DML as user, or use Security.stripInaccessible when I need to remove fields gracefully. Users also need access to the Apex class through a profile or permission set. On the client, I never trust input, because anyone can call an AuraEnabled method directly. For example, hiding a Delete button for some users isn't security on its own. Someone could still call that Apex method from the browser, so the server validates everything. I avoid inserting raw HTML with lwc:dom manual and innerHTML to prevent XSS, and I never put secrets in JavaScript.

a: There are two levels. Say a quick action recalculates an Opportunity through Apex. notifyRecordUpdateAvailable takes care of the Opportunity's own fields, and a RefreshEvent lets the other components that registered for refresh reload too. What I avoid is a full page reload with window.location, because it loses state and feels slow.

How to display an error message when the call fails?
spinner lwc example
a: I keep a few clear states: loading, error, empty and data. Before an imperative call, I set isLoading to true, and in a finally block I set it back to false, so the spinner always goes away, even when the call fails. In the catch, I store a readable error message. For a wired call, the state is loading until either data or error is provisioned. In the template, I use lwc:if and lwc:elseif to show exactly one of these: the spinner, the error, an empty message, or the data. So if an Account has no Contacts, the user sees "No contacts found" instead of a blank box, and if the call fails, they see the reason instead of a spinner that never stops.
points: Set isLoading before, reset in finally
Store a readable error in catch
Template shows one state at a time with lwc:if

q: The business wants to see and work with tens of thousands of records in one LWC. How would you design it?
alt: Showing a very large data set in a datatable
Datatable is slow with thousands of rows
Design an LWC for big data volume
how to handle 50000 records in lwc
a: I would push back on loading everything into the browser, because a single transaction can only retrieve 50,000 rows and large payloads make the page slow. Instead I design around server-side filtering and paging: users filter first, then I load in batches with infinite loading or pagination using keyset paging. I select only the columns needed, and I show counts or summaries using aggregate queries rather than raw rows. For bulk actions on all matching records, the component sends the filter criteria to Apex and a Batch Apex or Queueable job processes them asynchronously, and the UI shows progress. If they mainly need analysis, I suggest a report or dashboard instead.
points: Filter first, then page or infinite-load in batches
Keyset paging, lean field lists
Aggregates for summaries
Bulk actions via async Apex with progress
Reports may fit better

q: Users edit a field in the standard record detail, but your custom component on the same page keeps showing the old value. How do you fix it?
alt: Custom LWC not updating when the record is edited
Keep LWC in sync with the standard record detail
Component shows stale field after inline edit on record page
lwc not refreshing on record update
a: This happens when the component reads the record through Apex, because Apex results are cached separately and do not know the record changed. The best fix is to read record fields through Lightning Data Service, using getRecord or lightning-record-view-form, since LDS shares one cache with the standard components and updates automatically when the record is saved. If I really need Apex, for example for a calculated query, I wire getRecord on the fields that matter, and when its data changes I call refreshApex on my Apex wire. That way any edit on the page triggers a refresh.
points: Apex results don't see record edits
Prefer getRecord / record-view-form: shared LDS cache
Or watch getRecord and call refreshApex on change

q: You need one component that works on a Lightning record page and also in an Experience Cloud site. What do you consider?
alt: Reusing an LWC in Experience Cloud and internal org
LWC for both Lightning Experience and community site
What changes when an LWC runs in Experience Cloud?
lwc in experience site and lightning page
a: I add both sets of targets: the record page target, and lightningCommunity__Page plus lightningCommunity__Default, and expose the properties each one needs. Then I check context differences. External and guest users have different licenses, sharing and object access, so the Apex must be secure, with sharing and user mode. For guest users I'm extra careful, because they're unauthenticated. Say the component shows open Cases. Internally, an agent sees the Cases their sharing allows, but on the site, a customer user should only see what their own access allows, and the same Apex has to respect both. Navigation should use page references, not hard-coded URLs, since site URLs differ. Some modules behave differently in LWR sites. For example, ShowToastEvent isn't supported there, so I use lightning/toast. I also check styling against the site theme and test on mobile.
points: Targets for both record page and Experience Builder
Different licenses, sharing and guest access
Page references, not hard-coded URLs
Check module support in LWR sites, e.g. toasts
Test styling with site theme

quick action lwc save and close

If I used Apex, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable so the record page and related LDS components show the new values. Then I dispatch CloseActionScreenEvent to close the modal and show a success toast. On error I keep the modal open and display the message, so the user doesn't lose their input. The Cancel button just dispatches CloseActionScreenEvent.

If confirmed, I call deleteRecord from lightning/uiRecordApi with the record Id, which goes through LDS and respects permissions. On success I show a toast and navigate to the object's list view with NavigationMixin, since the record page no longer exists. If deletion fails, for example because of a validation rule or a related record, I show the error message.

q: How do you validate all inputs in a custom LWC form before saving?
alt: Form validation in Lightning Web Components
reportValidity and checkValidity example
How to check required fields in LWC before submit?
validate lightning-input fields
a: I set validation attributes on the base inputs, like required, pattern, min or type email, so each input knows its own rules. On Save I collect all inputs with querySelectorAll and reduce over them, calling reportValidity on each, which shows the error under the field and returns whether it is valid. Only if all are valid do I call Apex. For rules across fields, like end date after start date, I call setCustomValidity on the relevant input and then reportValidity. I still validate on the server too, because the client can be bypassed.

reportValidity shows messages and returns a boolean

platformResourceLoader lwc

Because the library needs a real canvas element, I load it in renderedCallback with a guard flag, then build the chart on the canvas I get through lwc:ref or querySelector. If the library manipulates DOM itself, I give it a container with lwc:dom manual. I check the library works under Lightning Web Security, and I destroy the chart in disconnectedCallback.

alt: Navigate to new record page with default values
encodeDefaultFieldValues example
Prefill fields when creating a record from LWC
open new record form with account id lwc
a: I use NavigationMixin with a standard__objectPage page reference, objectApiName Contact and actionName new. To prefill fields, I build an object of field API names and values, like AccountId set to the current recordId, encode it with encodeDefaultFieldValues from lightning/pageReferenceUtils, and pass it as defaultFieldValues in the state. Salesforce opens the standard new record modal with those values, so validation rules, layouts and record types still apply.

encodeDefaultFieldValues from lightning/pageReferenceUtils
Pass in state.defaultFieldValues
Standard form keeps layouts and validation

q: What is the difference between Aura components and Lightning Web Components?
alt: Aura vs LWC
Why is LWC faster than Aura?
Compare Aura framework and Lightning Web Components
difference between aura and lwc
a: Aura is Salesforce's older, proprietary component framework. A bundle has markup, a controller, a helper, a renderer, and events defined in its own syntax. LWC is built on modern web standards, so the browser handles things like custom elements and shadow DOM natively. That makes it lighter and faster, and the code is standard JavaScript classes and modules. LWC also has better tooling, Jest unit testing, and a cleaner event model based on DOM events. For example, a simple counter in Aura means a component markup file, a controller and often a helper. In LWC it's an HTML template and one JavaScript class, plus the meta file. Both can live on the same page and share Lightning Data Service. An LWC can be placed inside an Aura component, but an Aura component can't be placed inside an LWC. For new work, Salesforce recommends LWC.
points: Aura: proprietary syntax, controller/helper/renderer
LWC: web standards, faster, standard JS
LWC can be nested in Aura, not the reverse
Both share LDS and coexist on a page

q: Can you use an LWC inside an Aura component, and an Aura component inside an LWC?
alt: Nest LWC in Aura
Can LWC contain Aura components?
How do Aura and LWC work together?
lwc inside aura wrapper
a: Yes, one way only. An LWC can be used inside an Aura component, and in Aura markup I reference it with the c colon camelCase name, pass values as attributes, and handle its custom events with on-handlers. An Aura component cannot be used inside an LWC, because LWC only understands web components. That is why, when migrating, we usually start with leaf components and build upward, and sometimes keep a thin Aura wrapper around an LWC when we need a capability that is only available to Aura. Both kinds of components can still communicate through Lightning Message Service and share data through LDS.
points: LWC inside Aura: yes
Aura inside LWC: no
Aura passes attributes and listens to LWC events
Migrate bottom-up, leaf components first

q: When would you still use Aura instead of LWC today?
alt: Is Aura still needed?
What can Aura do that LWC cannot?
Should we build anything new in Aura?
use cases for aura components now
a: For new development I choose LWC by default, and Aura only when a specific feature has no LWC equivalent yet. Salesforce has been closing these gaps over the years, for example modals, console workspace tab APIs, URL-addressable components and page refresh now have LWC modules. Areas where teams have traditionally kept Aura include custom Lightning page templates for App Builder and some older integration points, like Flow local actions or the original Lightning Out beta, which needed an Aura app; Lightning Out 2.0 now runs LWCs directly. In those cases I keep the Aura part as a thin wrapper and put the real logic in an LWC inside it, so moving fully later is easy. I always confirm against current docs before deciding.
points: Default to LWC for new work
Gaps keep closing: modal, workspace API, URL addressable, refresh
Keep Aura as a thin wrapper when truly needed
Verify against current documentation

q: What is the difference between component events and application events in Aura?
alt: Aura component event vs application event
When to use application events?
How do Aura events propagate?
aura events types
a: A component event is fired by a component and handled by components in its containment hierarchy, usually the parent, so it's like a child-to-parent notification. It's registered with aura:registerEvent and fired with component.getEvent, and it goes through capture and bubble phases. An application event is a broadcast. Any component with a handler for it receives it, no matter where it is on the page, and it's fired with $A.get('e.c:EventName'). Application events also have a default phase. For example, a row telling its own table "I was selected" is a component event. A message like "the selected region changed, everyone refresh" would traditionally be an application event. But because broadcasts are hard to trace and can cause performance issues, the guidance is to use component events where possible, and Lightning Message Service for cross-component communication.
points: Component event: hierarchy-based, capture and bubble
Application event: broadcast to all handlers, plus default phase
Prefer component events; LMS for unrelated components

q: How does an LWC send data to an enclosing Aura component?
alt: LWC event handled in Aura
Communicate from LWC to Aura parent
How to read event detail in Aura from LWC?
aura wrapper listen to lwc event
a: The LWC dispatches a normal CustomEvent with the data in detail. In the Aura markup, I add an attribute with on plus the event name on the LWC tag, pointing to a controller action. In the Aura controller, I read each property of detail with event.getParam and the property name. Say the LWC fires a select event with detail containing contactId. In Aura, the tag has onselect pointing to c.handleSelect, and in that handler, event.getParam('contactId') gives me the Id. Going the other way, Aura passes data to the LWC through its public @api properties as attributes, and it can call @api methods by getting the component with aura:id and component.find.
points: LWC: dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('name', { detail }))
Aura markup: onname="{!c.handler}"
Aura controller: event.getParam('property')
Aura to LWC via attributes and @api methods

q: How do you call an Apex method from an Aura component?
alt: Aura server-side controller call
$A.enqueueAction example
How to get data from Apex in Aura?
aura apex call set callback
a: I get the action with component.get('c.methodName'), set parameters with setParams using names that match the Apex parameters, and register a callback with setCallback. Inside the callback, I check response.getState(). On SUCCESS, I read getReturnValue and set it on an attribute. On ERROR, I read getError. Then I queue it with $A.enqueueAction, because Aura batches server calls. For example, to load Contacts, I get c.getContacts, set accountId with setParams, and in the callback I set the result on a contacts attribute. If I forget the enqueueAction line, the call is never sent. The Apex method must be static and @AuraEnabled, and the same method can be reused from LWC, which helps during migration.
points: component.get('c.method'), setParams, setCallback
Check getState(): SUCCESS / ERROR
$A.enqueueAction to send
Apex must be static @AuraEnabled

q: What is the difference between a standard controller, a custom controller and a controller extension in Visualforce?
alt: Visualforce controller types
Standard controller vs custom controller vs extension
When do you use an extension in Visualforce?
vf page controllers explained
a: A standard controller is provided by Salesforce for an object, like standardController equals Account. It gives me the record plus actions like save, edit and delete without code, and it respects the user's permissions. A custom controller is an Apex class that completely replaces the standard one. I write all the logic myself, and it runs in system mode, so I have to handle sharing and security. An extension is an Apex class that adds to or overrides a standard or custom controller. Its constructor receives the controller, so I keep the standard save behavior and only add what's missing. For example, an Account page that needs the normal save plus a list of the Account's open Cases is a standard controller with one extension. A page can have several extensions, and if methods clash, the leftmost one wins.
points: Standard: built-in actions, respects permissions
Custom: full Apex control, system mode
Extension: adds or overrides, constructor takes the controller
Multiple extensions, leftmost wins

q: Write a simple Visualforce controller extension for the Account standard controller.
alt: Visualforce extension example
How do you get the record in a controller extension?
ApexPages.StandardController constructor example
vf extension code
a: The extension's constructor takes ApexPages.StandardController, and from it I get the current record with getRecord or the Id with getId. I can then add properties and action methods the page calls, while the page still has the standard save and cancel actions. Here the extension loads open cases for the account and adds a custom action that returns a PageReference to redirect. I declare the class with sharing so it respects record access, and query with user mode for field security.
points: Constructor(ApexPages.StandardController ctrl)
ctrl.getId() / ctrl.getRecord()
Action methods return PageReference
with sharing + user mode for security

q: What is view state in Visualforce and how do you fix a 'maximum view state size exceeded' error?
alt: Visualforce view state limit
How to reduce view state?
What is the transient keyword used for?
view state too large error vf
a: View state is the encrypted, hidden data Visualforce sends with a page that has an apex:form. It holds the controller's non-transient state, so it survives postbacks. The limit is 170 KB, and big lists, wrapper objects or blobs go past it quickly. Say a controller keeps a list of 2,000 wrapper rows with checkboxes. All of that travels with every postback, and you can easily hit the limit. To reduce it, I mark variables that can be rebuilt as transient so they aren't stored, query only the fields I need, avoid keeping large collections in controller state, paginate with StandardSetController, and use only one apex:form where possible. For read-heavy pages, JavaScript remoting avoids view state entirely. The View State tab in the development mode footer shows what's using the space.
points: View state holds controller state between postbacks
Limit 170 KB
transient variables are not saved
Paginate, fewer fields, remoting to avoid it

q: What is JavaScript remoting in Visualforce and how do you use it?
alt: @RemoteAction example
Visualforce remoting vs actionFunction
How to call Apex from JavaScript in Visualforce?
vf remoting invokeAction
a: JavaScript remoting lets JavaScript in a Visualforce page call a static Apex method annotated with @RemoteAction directly, and get the result asynchronously. It doesn't send or rebuild view state, so it's fast and good for responsive, JavaScript-heavy pages. But I have to update the page myself in the callback. I call it with Visualforce.remoting.Manager.invokeAction, passing the remote action reference, parameters, and a callback that checks event.status. For example, a type-ahead search box on a Visualforce page can call a searchAccounts remote action when the user pauses typing, and the callback draws the results list. I keep the escape option on to protect against script injection. And since the method runs in system mode, I enforce security in Apex.
points: @RemoteAction static method
No view state: fast, but manual DOM updates
Visualforce.remoting.Manager.invokeAction
Check event.status; keep escape: true

q: What is the difference between actionFunction, actionSupport and JavaScript remoting in Visualforce?
alt: apex:actionFunction vs apex:actionSupport
When do you use remoting instead of actionFunction?
AJAX options in Visualforce
action function action support difference
a: actionSupport attaches AJAX behavior to an event on another component, like onchange on an input. It calls a controller action and rerenders part of the page. actionFunction defines a JavaScript function that calls a controller action, so I can trigger it from my own scripts, and it also supports rerender. Both submit the form and view state, run in the controller's context, and Visualforce handles the partial page refresh for me. JavaScript remoting calls a static @RemoteAction method without view state, which is faster and lighter. But the method has no access to controller instance state, and I update the page in JavaScript myself. For example, if picking a Country should refresh a State list, actionSupport on onchange is simplest. If my own script needs to call the controller after some custom logic, that's actionFunction. And for a fast search with no form state, remoting.
points: actionSupport: AJAX on a component event + rerender
actionFunction: callable JS function + rerender
Both carry view state
Remoting: static method, no view state, manual UI update

q: How would you approach migrating a set of Aura components to LWC?
alt: Aura to LWC migration strategy
Steps to convert Aura components into LWC
How do you plan a migration from Aura to Lightning Web Components?
aura migration best practices
a: I start with an inventory: which components exist, where they are used, how complex they are and what Aura-only features they rely on. Then I migrate bottom-up, beginning with leaf components, because an LWC can sit inside an Aura parent but not the reverse, so the app keeps working during the migration. I map concepts as I go: attributes to @api properties or fields, aura:if and aura:iteration to lwc:if and for:each, component events to custom events, application events to Lightning Message Service, $A.enqueueAction to wire or imperative Apex, and force events like showToast and navigateToSObject to their LWC modules. I reuse existing Apex, add Jest tests, and release in small batches with regression testing rather than a big-bang rewrite.
points: Inventory and prioritize
Bottom-up: leaf components first
Map attributes, directives, events, server calls
Reuse Apex, add Jest tests, ship incrementally

q: A business still uses several Visualforce pages. How would you modernize them, and can you use LWC inside Visualforce?
alt: Migrating Visualforce to LWC
Use LWC in a Visualforce page
Lightning Out in Visualforce
should we rewrite visualforce pages
a: I first decide per page whether it needs to change at all. Pages used for PDF generation with renderAs pdf or certain email templates are still a good fit for Visualforce. Interactive pages I usually rebuild as LWCs on Lightning pages, reusing the Apex logic where it is clean and moving business rules out of controllers. If a page must stay in Visualforce for a while, I can embed an LWC in it with Lightning Out, using an Aura dependency app and $Lightning.use and createComponent, which lets me modernize piece by piece. For running LWCs on external, non-Salesforce sites, Lightning Out 2.0 is the newer generally available option. Lightning Message Service can also connect Visualforce and LWC on the same Lightning page during the transition.
points: Keep VF where it fits, e.g. PDF rendering
Rebuild interactive pages as LWC on Lightning pages
Lightning Out to embed LWC in VF during transition
Lightning Out 2.0 for external sites; LMS bridges VF and LWC

q: What is the difference between standard objects and custom objects?
alt: Standard object vs custom object in Salesforce
How do you identify a custom object by its API name?
what are standard and custom objects
When would you create a custom object instead of using a standard one?
a: Standard objects come with Salesforce out of the box, like Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity and Case. They already carry built-in behaviour, such as lead conversion or the opportunity sales path. Custom objects are the ones we create for data that's specific to the business, and their API names end with __c, like Project__c. Say a company does site inspections. There's no standard object for that, so I'd create Inspection__c. But if they just want to track their customers, I wouldn't build a Customer__c, I'd use Account. What I always do is check first whether a standard object fits, because it gives you standard features, reports and integrations for free. I only create a custom object when the data really is different, like inspections or enrollments.
points: Standard: provided by Salesforce, built-in features and processes
Custom: created by admins, API name ends in __c
Both support custom fields, relationships, page layouts and automation
Prefer standard objects when they fit the requirement

q: What is the difference between a lookup relationship and a master-detail relationship?
alt: Lookup vs master-detail, explain
When would you use master detail instead of lookup?
what happens to child records when the parent is deleted in master detail
Difference between loosely coupled and tightly coupled relationships in Salesforce
a: Master-detail is tightly coupled, lookup is loosely coupled. In master-detail the parent field is required, the child has no owner of its own, and its sharing and security come from the parent. Delete the parent and the children are deleted too. You also get roll-up summary fields on the parent. A lookup is optional by default, the child keeps its own owner and sharing, and deleting the parent just clears the field, or you can block the delete. Take an invoice and its invoice lines. A line makes no sense without its invoice, so I'd use master-detail, and I could roll up the total amount onto the invoice. But a contact's 'referred by' partner would be a lookup, because the contact should survive if that partner is removed. That's my rule: master-detail when the child can't exist without the parent.
points: Master-detail: required, cascade delete, sharing inherited, roll-up summary
Lookup: optional, independent owner and sharing, no native roll-up
An object can have at most two master-detail relationships
Standard objects cannot be on the detail side of a master-detail

q: How do you create a many-to-many relationship in Salesforce?
alt: What is a junction object?
How do you link students and courses where each can have many of the other?
Explain junction object with an example
many to many relationship salesforce how
a: You create a many-to-many relationship with a junction object, which is a custom object that has two master-detail relationships, one to each of the objects you want to connect. For example, Student and Course are linked through an Enrollment object: each Enrollment record points to one student and one course, so a student can have many courses and a course can have many students. The first master-detail field you create becomes the primary master, which controls the junction record's look and feel and some ownership behaviour. You can also build roll-up summaries on both parents from the junction.
points: Junction object = custom object with two master-detail fields
First master-detail created is the primary relationship
Roll-up summaries possible on both masters
Lookups can be used instead when you need independent ownership

q: What are hierarchical, external lookup and indirect lookup relationships?
alt: Explain hierarchical relationship in Salesforce
What is an external lookup relationship?
Difference between external lookup and indirect lookup
special relationship types in salesforce
a: These are three special relationship types. A hierarchical relationship exists only on the User object and links one user to another. The usual example is the Manager field, which approval processes use to find the approver chain. External lookup and indirect lookup are for external objects from Salesforce Connect. An external lookup links a child record, standard, custom or external, to a parent that is an external object, and it matches on the external object's External ID. An indirect lookup goes the other way. It links a child external object to a standard or custom parent in Salesforce, matching on a custom field on the parent that's marked unique and External ID. For example, say orders live in an ERP and show up as an external object. To hang those orders off Account, I'd put a unique External ID field like ERP_Customer_No on Account and use an indirect lookup.
points: Hierarchical: User object only, e.g. Manager
External lookup: parent is an external object, matched on External ID
Indirect lookup: external child, Salesforce parent, matched on a unique External ID field
Both external types come with Salesforce Connect

q: What is a roll-up summary field and what are its limitations?
alt: Explain roll-up summary fields
Can you create a roll-up summary on a lookup relationship?
What functions does roll up summary support
roll up summary field limitations
a: A roll-up summary field sits on the parent and calculates a value from the related child records. It supports COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX, and you can add filter criteria. For example, on Account I could sum only the Closed Won opportunity amounts to show total won business, and it recalculates by itself whenever an opportunity changes. The big limitation is where you can use it. It only works on the master side of a master-detail relationship, plus a few standard relationships like Account to Opportunity and Opportunity to Opportunity Product. You can't build it over a normal lookup. There's also a per-object limit on how many you can create, and some field types, like certain formula fields, can't be summarised. So if someone asks me for a roll-up over a lookup, I already know it needs a different approach.
points: Functions: COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX with optional filters
Only on master-detail and a few standard relationships
Not available on lookup relationships
Recalculates automatically when children change

q: The business needs a roll-up summary on a lookup relationship. How would you handle it?
alt: How do you do roll up on lookup relationship?
Roll-up summary is not available because the relationship is lookup, what are your options?
count child records on parent with lookup relationship
Alternatives to roll-up summary fields for lookups
a: First I'd check if the relationship can just be converted to master-detail, because then I get a native roll-up that I don't have to maintain. If the child needs its own owner or sharing, I keep the lookup and pick between a record-triggered flow, an Apex trigger, or a scheduled recalculation. For simple counts or sums at moderate volume, an after-save flow on the child that recalculates the parent with an aggregate is enough. For high volume or complex logic, I write a bulkified trigger that handles insert, update, delete and undelete. Reparenting is the case people forget. Say a ticket moves from Project A to Project B. Both projects need recalculating, the old one and the new one. I also watch for row-lock contention when lots of children update the same parent at once.
points: Prefer converting to master-detail if ownership allows
Flow for simple, low-volume roll-ups
Apex trigger for scale: cover insert, update, delete, undelete and reparenting
Watch for parent record locking and data skew

q: What is a formula field and what are its limitations?
alt: Explain formula fields in Salesforce
Can a formula field reference a parent object?
Are formula fields stored in the database?
what can't you do with a formula field
a: A formula field is a read-only field that's calculated from other fields, functions and expressions every time the record is viewed or queried. It isn't physically stored like a normal field. It can return text, number, currency, percent, date, date-time or checkbox. It can also reach up to parent records with cross-object formulas. For example, on Contact I can show Account.Industry without copying the value. The limitations: it can't reference child records, so for that you need a roll-up. It's never directly editable, and there are size limits on the formula. The one that catches people in interviews is automation. Because it's calculated at runtime, a change in its value doesn't fire triggers or flows on its own. So if the account's industry changes, a flow watching the contact's formula field won't run.
points: Read-only, calculated at runtime
Cross-object formulas can reach parent records
Cannot reference child records; use roll-ups for that
Value changes do not fire triggers or flows by themselves

q: Can you give some examples of validation rules you have written?
alt: Write a validation rule example
How does a validation rule work?
validation rule to make a field required when stage is closed won
Give me a practical validation rule
a: A validation rule is a formula that returns true when the data is wrong. When it's true, the save is blocked and the user sees an error message, either at the top of the page or on a specific field. One I've written many times: require Amount when an opportunity moves to Closed Won. I use ISCHANGED on StageName and ISPICKVAL to check for Closed Won, plus ISBLANK on Amount, and I show the error on the Amount field. Others are blocking a close date in the past for new records, or enforcing a 10-digit phone format with REGEX. Two habits I follow. I write the error message in plain business language, like 'Please enter the deal amount before closing'. And I test with data loads too, not just UI edits, because validation rules fire for API updates, imports and automation as well.
points: Formula must evaluate to TRUE to block the save
Use ISPICKVAL for picklists, ISCHANGED/PRIORVALUE for changes
Fires for UI, API, imports and automation
Show the error on the relevant field where possible

q: How would you bypass a validation rule for an integration user or a data migration?
alt: Validation rules are blocking our data load, how do you skip them?
How do you make a validation rule not apply to certain users?
bypass validation rule for admin profile
Best way to disable validation for integration user
a: I use a custom permission rather than hard-coding a profile name or a user Id. I create a custom permission, say Bypass Validation, assign it through a permission set to the integration user or the migration user, and add NOT($Permission.Bypass_Validation) as the first condition in each rule. Say we're migrating 100,000 old cases that don't have the fields our new rules require. I give the migration user that permission set, run the load, and the rules simply skip that user. Everyone else is still checked. It's clean because I can grant or remove the bypass without touching the rules, and it works the same in every sandbox. The same pattern works for bypassing flows and triggers too. Some teams use a hierarchy custom setting checkbox for one-off migrations, but the custom permission is easier to audit. And I always remove the permission once the load is done.
points: Use a custom permission referenced as $Permission
Assign through a permission set, not by profile name
Same pattern can bypass flows and triggers
Remove the bypass after the migration
code:
AND(
  NOT($Permission.Bypass_Validation),
  ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Won"),
  ISBLANK(Amount)
)

q: What is the difference between record types and page layouts?
alt: Record type vs page layout
Why do we need record types?
Can you have different picklist values for different users?
what does a record type control
a: Record types let you have different business processes and picklist values on the same object. Page layouts control how the record page looks. For example, a Case object might have Hardware and Software record types. Each one has its own Type picklist values and its own support process. Then the page layout decides which fields, sections, related lists and buttons show up, and which fields are required or read-only on screen. So the Hardware layout might show Serial Number, and the Software layout shows Version instead. The two connect through page layout assignment, where you pick a layout for each combination of profile and record type. One gotcha: users need the record type assigned to their profile or permission set, otherwise they can't create records of that type at all.
points: Record type: picklist values, business process, layout assignment
Page layout: fields, sections, related lists, buttons
Layout assignment = profile x record type
Users need the record type assigned to create those records

q: How are page layouts, Lightning record pages and Dynamic Forms different?
alt: What is Dynamic Forms and why use it?
Lightning record page vs page layout
How can you show a field only when another field has a value?
difference between page layout lightning page and dynamic forms
a: A page layout controls fields, related lists and buttons on a record in a fairly fixed way. A Lightning record page, built in Lightning App Builder, controls the whole page: which components appear, tabs, and component visibility rules. You can assign it by app, record type and profile. Dynamic Forms takes the fields out of the page layout and places them as individual fields and sections on the Lightning page, each with its own visibility rule. For example, I can show Discount Reason only when Discount is above a threshold, without a second layout. It works on custom objects and most standard objects, and it cuts down the number of page layouts you need. One caution I always mention: visibility rules are UI only. Hiding a field doesn't secure it. If the data must be protected, use field-level security.
points: Page layout: fields, related lists, actions
Lightning record page: components and visibility, assigned by app/record type/profile
Dynamic Forms: field-level placement and conditional visibility
Visibility is UI only; use FLS to secure data

q: What is a global value set and when do you use it?
alt: Global picklist vs local picklist
How do you share picklist values across multiple fields?
What is a restricted picklist?
global value set salesforce
a: A global value set is one shared list of picklist values that many picklist fields can use, on one object or many. Say Region appears on Account, Opportunity and a custom Project object. I define North, South, East and West once in a global value set. When the business adds a new region, I add it once and all three fields get it, so the data stays consistent. Fields based on a global value set are always restricted. That means users and integrations can't save a value that isn't on the list, which is good for data quality. Record types can still limit which of those values are available on each record type. If a picklist is only used in one place, a local value set is fine, and I still usually mark it restricted.
points: One list of values reused by many picklist fields
Changes apply to every field using it
Global value set picklists are always restricted
Record types can still limit which values each user sees

q: The business wants Sub-Category values to change based on the selected Category. How would you do it?
alt: What is a field dependency?
Controlling and dependent picklist explained
Can a checkbox be a controlling field?
how to filter picklist values based on another picklist
a: I'd set up a field dependency, with Category as the controlling field and Sub-Category as the dependent picklist. In Setup, on the object's Fields and Relationships, I open Field Dependencies, choose the two fields, and in the matrix tick which Sub-Category values are valid for each Category. So if Category is Hardware, the user only sees Laptop, Printer and Monitor. If it's Software, they see Install, Licence and Bug. The rules on field types: the controlling field can be a standard or custom picklist or a checkbox. The dependent field must be a custom picklist or multi-select picklist. A multi-select picklist can't be a controlling field. And record types still filter values on top of the dependency, so when a value is missing I check both places.
points: Controlling: picklist or checkbox
Dependent: custom picklist or multi-select picklist
Multi-select picklists cannot be controlling
Record type value filtering still applies

q: What is the difference between a matching rule and a duplicate rule?
alt: How does duplicate management work in Salesforce?
Matching rule vs duplicate rule
How do you stop users creating duplicate accounts?
explain duplicate and matching rules
a: A matching rule defines how two records are compared to decide they're duplicates. A duplicate rule defines what happens when a match is found. The matching rule lists the fields and the method for each, exact or fuzzy. For example, fuzzy on company name plus exact on email domain, so 'Acme Corp' and 'Acme Corporation' with the same domain count as a match. The duplicate rule uses one or more matching rules and decides whether to allow the save with an alert, or block it, on create and on edit, and whether to report the duplicates. It can also compare across objects, like a new lead against existing contacts, and found duplicates can be tracked in duplicate record sets. Salesforce ships standard rules for accounts, contacts and leads, and you can build your own for custom objects.
points: Matching rule: which fields and exact or fuzzy logic
Duplicate rule: allow with alert, report, or block
Can compare across objects, e.g. lead against contact
Duplicates found can be tracked in duplicate record sets

q: Sales says duplicate leads keep coming in from web forms and imports. How would you stop that?
alt: How do you prevent duplicate leads?
Duplicate records are being created from Web-to-Lead, what will you do?
duplicate leads from imports how to fix
How would you clean up existing duplicates and prevent new ones?
a: I'd handle prevention and clean-up separately. For prevention, I turn on a lead matching rule on email plus normalised company or phone, and a duplicate rule that alerts users in the UI. The catch is that Web-to-Lead and API inserts can't respond to an alert. So for those channels I either block or let them through and report them, depending on whether losing a lead is worse than a duplicate. Usually sales would rather have the duplicate. I also match leads against existing contacts so known customers get flagged. For imports, the Data Import Wizard can match on email to update instead of insert. So if marketing uploads 5,000 event leads and 800 already exist, those 800 get updated, not duplicated. For existing data, I run duplicate jobs or reports and merge in batches with the business.
points: Matching rule on email plus normalised fields
Duplicate rule: alert in UI, block or report for API/web
Cross-object matching against contacts
Import with match-on-email to update instead of insert
Separate one-time clean-up and merge

q: What is an approval process and what are its main components?
alt: Explain approval process in Salesforce
What happens to a record when it is submitted for approval?
What are initial submission actions?
approval process steps and actions
a: An approval process routes a record to one or more people for sign-off before it can move forward. A typical case is a discount above a limit. The main parts are: entry criteria, which decide which records can be submitted. Then approval steps, each with its own approver, like the submitter's manager, a specific user or a queue. Then actions at each stage: initial submission, final approval, final rejection and recall. Usual actions are field updates, email alerts and tasks. Say a rep submits a quote with 25 percent discount. It goes to their manager, the status becomes Pending, and on approval an email goes back to the rep. By default the record is locked when submitted, so only admins and the approver can edit it until it's done. You can also set delegated approvers and choose unanimous or first-response approval.
points: Entry criteria and who can submit
One or more steps, each with approvers
Initial submission, approval, rejection and recall actions
Record locking during approval
Delegated approvers and unanimous or first-response options

q: Design a two-level approval where discounts above 20% need the manager, and above 40% also need a VP.
alt: How would you build a multi-step approval process?
Discount approval with different levels based on amount, how?
multi level approval manager then vp
Would you use a classic approval process or Flow approvals today?
a: I'd create one approval process on Opportunity or Quote with entry criteria of discount above 20 percent. Step one goes to the submitter's manager using the Manager field on User. Step two has its own criteria, discount above 40 percent, and goes to a VP. I'd use a named user, a queue or a custom user lookup so the approver isn't hard-coded. So a 30 percent deal only needs the manager and is approved after step one. A 45 percent deal goes to the manager first, then the VP. Initial submission locks the record and sets status to Pending, final approval sets Approved, and rejection resets the discount or status. For newer builds I'd also look at Flow Approval Processes, built on Flow Orchestration, which handle more complex routing.
points: Entry criteria at the lowest threshold
Step 1: manager; Step 2: criteria-based VP step
Avoid hard-coded approvers; use user fields or queues
Status field updated by submission, approval and rejection actions
Consider Flow Approval Processes for complex routing

q: What is the difference between a queue and a public group?
alt: Queue vs public group
Can a public group own a record?
When do you use a queue?
what are public groups used for in salesforce
a: A queue can own records. A public group is just a collection of users used for access and sharing. Queues work for objects like Leads, Cases and supported custom objects. Records sit in the queue until a member takes ownership. For example, all new support cases from the website land in a Tier 1 Support queue, and whichever agent is free picks the next one. Queues are often the target of assignment rules. A public group can't own records. It's used in sharing rules, manual sharing, and list view and folder access. Say the finance team needs to see all closed opportunities. I'd make a Finance public group and share to it. A group can contain users, roles, roles with subordinates, and other groups. Queue members can also be users, roles or public groups.
points: Queue: owns records, members pick work from it
Public group: used for sharing and visibility, not ownership
Groups can contain users, roles, roles and subordinates, other groups
Queues are often the target of assignment rules

q: What are report types, and when would you create a custom report type?
alt: Standard report type vs custom report type
Why can't I see a field in the report builder?
What does with or without related records mean in a report type?
custom report type salesforce explain
a: A report type is the template that says which objects and fields a report can use and how those objects are joined. Salesforce creates standard report types automatically for standard objects and for custom objects with reporting enabled. I create a custom report type when I need a specific combination. For example, Accounts with or without Cases, adding fields from lookups with the Add Fields Related via Lookup option, or a primary object with up to three related child levels. The with or without setting really matters. Say the business wants every account and its cases. If I pick 'with Cases', accounts that never raised a case disappear from the report, which is an inner join. If I pick 'with or without Cases', those accounts show too, which is an outer join. That one choice is behind a lot of 'my report is missing records' questions.
points: Defines objects, relationships and available fields
Standard report types are auto-generated
Custom report type: primary object plus related objects
With = inner join, with or without = outer join

q: What are the report formats, and when would you use a joined report?
alt: Tabular vs summary vs matrix vs joined report
What is a joined report?
how do you show data from two report types in one report
Explain report formats in Salesforce
a: There are four report formats. Tabular is a simple list, good for exports. Summary groups rows and adds subtotals, and you need it for most dashboard charts. Matrix groups by rows and columns, like opportunity amount by owner and by quarter. A joined report shows several report blocks side by side. Each block can use a different report type, and they're linked by a common grouping field. Here's where I use joined. Say an account manager wants, for each of her accounts, the open opportunities and the open cases in one view. A single report type can't give both, because opportunities and cases are separate children of Account. So I build a joined report with an Opportunities block and a Cases block, both grouped by Account Name.
points: Tabular: flat list
Summary: row groupings with subtotals
Matrix: row and column groupings
Joined: multiple blocks, can use different report types, grouped by a common field

q: Each sales manager should see a dashboard with only their own team's numbers. How would you do it?
alt: What is a dynamic dashboard?
How can one dashboard show different data to different users?
dashboard running user vs logged in user
Managers should see only their team data on dashboard, what is the solution?
a: I'd use a dynamic dashboard. It runs as the logged-in viewer instead of a fixed running user, so each manager sees only the data their sharing access allows. With a private sharing model and a proper role hierarchy, a manager automatically sees their team's records. So if there are ten regional managers, I build one dashboard instead of ten. The North manager opens it and sees North numbers, the South manager sees South. The catch is that dynamic dashboards are limited in number per org depending on edition. So for a simpler need I might use one dashboard with a dashboard filter on role or owner, or report filters like My Team's records. Whichever way, I make sure the source report and dashboard folders are shared with the managers, otherwise they get an access error.
points: Dynamic dashboard runs as the logged-in user
Relies on sharing and the role hierarchy
Limited number per org by edition
Alternatives: dashboard filters or 'my team' report filters
Share the report and dashboard folders

q: What are the different types of sandboxes?
alt: Developer vs Developer Pro vs Partial Copy vs Full sandbox
Which sandbox copies production data?
sandbox refresh interval
Explain sandbox types in Salesforce
a: There are four sandbox types. A Developer sandbox copies only metadata, with a small data storage allowance, and can be refreshed daily. That suits individual development. Developer Pro is the same but with more storage, useful for bigger test data sets. A Partial Copy sandbox copies all metadata plus a sample of production data defined by a sandbox template, and you can refresh it every five days. That's good for QA and integration testing. A Full sandbox copies all metadata and all data, can be refreshed every 29 days, and is the right place for UAT, performance testing and staging. A quick example: if a tester needs a few thousand real-looking accounts with their opportunities, I'd use Partial Copy with a template. If business users need to test against the full production data set, that needs a Full sandbox.
points: Developer: metadata only, refresh 1 day
Developer Pro: metadata only, more storage, refresh 1 day
Partial Copy: metadata plus sampled data via template, refresh 5 days
Full: complete copy, refresh 29 days

q: You are setting up environments for a new project. Which sandbox would you use for what?
alt: How do you plan sandboxes for development, QA and UAT?
Which sandbox for UAT and which for performance testing?
environment strategy salesforce project
What sandbox would you give developers?
a: I'd give each developer, or each small feature team, a Developer sandbox, because they refresh daily and keep work isolated. Then a Developer Pro or Partial Copy sandbox as the integration and QA environment where everyone's changes come together, with a sandbox template to bring in realistic sample data. UAT and staging go into a Full sandbox, because business users need real data volumes and the final deployment should be rehearsed against a production-like copy. Performance and load testing also belong in Full. So on a typical project of four developers, that's four Developer sandboxes, one QA sandbox, and one Full sandbox for UAT. What holds it together is source control and a clear promotion path, dev to QA to UAT to production, so the environments don't drift apart.
points: Developer sandboxes for individual build
Partial Copy or Developer Pro for integration/QA
Full sandbox for UAT, staging and performance tests
Use version control and a clear promotion path

q: What are change sets, their limitations, and what would you use instead?
alt: Change sets vs Salesforce CLI deployment
What are the drawbacks of change sets?
How do you deploy metadata between orgs?
outbound and inbound change sets explained
Change sets vs DevOps Center
a: Change sets move metadata from one org to a related org, like sandbox to production. You build an outbound change set in the source and accept it as an inbound change set in the target, over an authorised deployment connection. The limitations are real. They only work between orgs connected to the same production. You can't delete components with them. There's no version control or rollback. You have to add dependencies by hand, and moving profile settings is awkward. For example, if I rename a field and remove an old one, a change set can't delete the old field, so someone does it manually in production. Best practice if you do use them: validate first, then quick deploy when tests pass. For anything beyond a small team, I'd use the Salesforce CLI with Git, through DevOps Center or a CI/CD pipeline, which gives history, review and repeatable deployments.
points: Only between orgs tied to the same production
No deletions, no version control, manual dependency selection
Validate first, then quick deploy when tests pass
Alternatives: Salesforce CLI, DevOps Center, CI/CD tools

q: Your change set deployment to production failed. How do you troubleshoot it?
alt: Change set validation failed, what do you check?
Deployment failed due to code coverage, what now?
missing dependency error in change set
Why would an inbound change set fail in production?
a: I start with the Deployment Status page in the target org. It lists every component error and failing test. The most common cause is a missing dependency. For example, a flow references a new field, but the field wasn't added to the change set. So I use View/Add Dependencies, add it, and redeploy. Next are Apex test failures, or code coverage below 75 percent org-wide. Often that's because production data or validation rules differ from the sandbox. Say a test inserts an account without a phone, and production has a rule requiring phone. It passes in the sandbox and fails in production. I also check for components someone changed directly in production, and API version mismatches. My habit is to always validate the change set first, fix issues in the sandbox, and then quick deploy once validation passes.
points: Read component and test errors on Deployment Status
Add missing dependencies
Fix failing tests and coverage (75% org-wide minimum)
Watch for production-only changes and data differences
Validate first, then quick deploy

q: How does multi-currency work in Salesforce, and what should you consider before enabling it?
alt: Explain multi currency in Salesforce
What is advanced currency management?
Can you disable multi-currency after enabling?
dated exchange rates salesforce
a: Once you enable it, every record gets a CurrencyIsoCode field, each user has a personal currency, and amounts are converted to the corporate currency for reporting using exchange rates that admins maintain. Advanced Currency Management adds dated exchange rates. So an opportunity that closed in March uses the March rate, not today's rate. Before enabling, I make sure the business understands a few things. First, multi-currency can't be turned off once enabled. Second, integrations must send the currency code. If an ERP sends 10,000 without saying EUR or USD, the record just takes a default currency and the number could be wrong. Third, roll-ups, reports and Apex need to handle conversion. In SOQL, convertCurrency() returns values in the user's currency. And I always try it in a sandbox first.
points: Cannot be disabled once enabled
Corporate currency plus maintained exchange rates
Advanced Currency Management adds dated rates
Integrations and code must handle CurrencyIsoCode
convertCurrency() in SOQL

q: What are person accounts and what should you know before enabling them?
alt: Explain person accounts
B2C model in Salesforce, how is it handled?
Can you disable person accounts?
person account vs business account
a: Person accounts are for B2C businesses where the customer is an individual, not a company. A person account combines account and contact into one record, so you see fields from both on one page. Behind the scenes there's still an account and a contact linked together. Think of a bank selling to individual customers. There's no company, so having a separate account called 'Ravi Kumar' with a contact 'Ravi Kumar' makes no sense. Person accounts fix that. Before enabling, I make sure the business really needs it, because it can't be disabled once it's on. It needs at least one person account record type, and the Contact sharing setting must be Controlled by Parent. I also review existing code, reports and integrations, because queries may now return person accounts alongside business accounts, so code often needs to check IsPersonAccount.
points: Account and contact merged into one record for individuals
Cannot be disabled once enabled
Requires person account record type and contact OWD Controlled by Parent
Review code using IsPersonAccount and reports

q: You need to load 200,000 contacts. Which tool would you use, Data Import Wizard or Data Loader?
alt: Data Import Wizard vs Data Loader
Which tool for bulk delete of records?
how many records can data import wizard handle
What tools do you use for data migration in Salesforce?
a: For 200,000 records I'd use Data Loader, because the Data Import Wizard handles up to 50,000 records at a time. Data Loader supports all standard and custom objects, and insert, update, upsert, delete, hard delete and export. It handles millions of records, can use the Bulk API, and can be scripted from the command line. The Import Wizard is browser-based and simpler. It supports accounts, contacts, leads, solutions, campaign members and custom objects, has no delete, and has built-in duplicate matching, so it suits smaller imports by business users. For this load, I'd upsert using an External ID field. Say each contact has a Legacy_Id from the old CRM, and each account does too. Then contacts link to the right accounts without me looking up Salesforce Ids. For a big load I'd also consider turning off heavy automation first.
points: Import Wizard: up to 50,000 records, limited objects, no delete
Data Loader: millions of records, all objects, all operations
Use External IDs for upsert and relationships
Consider Bulk API and turning off heavy automation for big loads

q: What is the difference between custom metadata types and custom settings?
alt: Custom metadata vs custom settings, when to use which?
Why are custom metadata records deployable?
hierarchy custom setting use case
Where would you store configuration values in Salesforce?
a: Both store configuration. The difference is that custom metadata type records are metadata, so they move with change sets, packages and source deployments. Custom setting records are data, so you load them separately in each org. Say I keep discount thresholds per region. With custom metadata, I deploy the rows with the code and every sandbox and production get them. With a list custom setting, the rows are data, so they don't go out with the deployment, and someone has to load them into each org separately. Custom metadata can also be used in flows, formulas and validation rules, and getInstance and getAll read it from cache without using SOQL. Custom settings come in list and hierarchy types. The hierarchy type is still useful because values can vary by org, profile and user, which is handy for a per-user trigger bypass. For most new configuration, I go with custom metadata.
points: Custom metadata: deployable records, usable in flows and formulas
Custom settings: data, list or hierarchy
Hierarchy settings vary by org, profile and user
Both cached; CMDT getInstance/getAll need no SOQL

q: What is Lightning App Builder and what can you build with it?
alt: Explain Lightning App Builder
What is a Lightning app?
Standard navigation vs console navigation
How do you create a custom home page in Lightning?
a: Lightning App Builder is the point-and-click tool for building Lightning pages: record pages, home pages and app pages. You drag standard, custom LWC or AppExchange components onto a template, set visibility rules, and activate the page as the org default, or for an app, a record type or a profile. A Lightning app is the container users switch between in the App Launcher. It defines the navigation items, branding, utility bar, and whether it uses standard or console navigation. Here's a practical example. For a support team I'd build a console app, because console navigation opens records in tabs and subtabs. An agent can have three cases open, each with its contact in a subtab, and switch between them without losing their place. For a sales team, standard navigation is usually enough.
points: Builds record, home and app pages
Drag-and-drop components with visibility rules
Activation by org, app, record type and profile
Lightning app: navigation, utility bar, standard or console

q: You need to convert an existing lookup relationship to master-detail. What do you check first?
alt: Can you change a lookup to a master-detail?
Steps to convert lookup into master detail relationship
Why can't I convert my lookup field to master-detail?
What changes when a lookup becomes master-detail?
a: It can be done, but every existing child record must already have a value in the lookup. So first I run a report or query for blanks and fix them. Say there are 40,000 Site Visit records under Project and 300 have no project. The conversion won't go through until those 300 are filled in or cleaned up. I also check the child doesn't already have two master-detail relationships. Then I explain the side effects to the business. The child loses its own owner, so its sharing becomes Controlled by Parent, and any sharing rules, queues or owner-based automation on the child stop making sense. Deleting a parent will now delete its children. So I check integrations, flows and reports that use the child's owner. And converting back to lookup later only works if no roll-up summary fields depend on it.
points: All child records must have the parent populated
Max two master-detail relationships per object
Child sharing becomes Controlled by Parent; owner field goes away
Cascade delete now applies
Reverse needs no dependent roll-ups

q: You are asked to design the data model for a new business requirement. How do you approach it?
alt: Walk me through how you design objects and relationships
What do you consider when choosing between lookup and master-detail in a design?
data model design best practices salesforce
How do you avoid data skew in your data model?
a: I start from the business process and the reports people need. Then I map entities to standard objects wherever they fit before adding custom ones. For each relationship, I pick lookup or master-detail based on ownership, sharing and delete behaviour, and I add junction objects for many-to-many. I plan record volumes early. Very large child counts under one parent, or one user owning huge numbers of records, cause data skew and locking. For example, I wouldn't park 200,000 unmatched contacts under one 'Unknown' account, and I wouldn't make one integration user own every record. I spread ownership and avoid giant catch-all parents. I also define External IDs for integration keys, keep picklists restricted, and decide what belongs in custom metadata as configuration. Finally I walk the business through a simple ERD before anyone builds anything.
points: Start from process and reporting needs
Reuse standard objects first
Choose relationship type by ownership, sharing and delete behaviour
Plan for volume and avoid ownership or parent skew
External IDs for integration keys

q: Can you explain the Salesforce security model?
alt: What are the layers of security in Salesforce?
Org level, object level, field level and record level security, explain
How is data access controlled in Salesforce?
salesforce security model overview
a: Salesforce security works in layers, and a user needs access at every layer to work with a value. At the org level, you control who can log in and from where, with login hours, IP ranges, MFA and password policies. At the object level, profiles and permission sets decide if a user can create, read, edit or delete records of an object. At the field level, field-level security controls which fields they can see or edit. At the record level, sharing decides which individual records they get, starting with org-wide defaults and then opened up with the role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, manual sharing and Apex sharing. So say a rep can log in and has Read on Opportunity. She still won't see a colleague's deal if the OWD is Private and nothing shares it with her. And even on her own deal, she won't see Margin if FLS hides it.
points: Org level: login access, MFA, IP and hours
Object level: CRUD via profiles and permission sets
Field level: FLS
Record level: OWD, roles, sharing rules, teams, manual and Apex sharing

q: What are org-wide defaults and what options do they have?
alt: Explain OWD in Salesforce
What does Private OWD mean?
What is Controlled by Parent?
internal vs external org wide defaults
a: Org-wide defaults set the baseline access for each object, meaning what users can see on records they don't own. Private means only the owner and people above them in the role hierarchy can access the record. Public Read Only means everyone can view but only the owner can edit. Public Read/Write means everyone can view and edit. Detail objects and contacts can also be Controlled by Parent. There are separate internal and external defaults, so Experience Cloud users can be more restricted than employees, and the external default can't be more open than the internal one. For example, I might set Case to Public Read Only internally so all agents can look up any case, but Private externally so a customer portal user only sees their own cases. The rule is: set OWD to the most restrictive level, then open access with sharing.
points: Private, Public Read Only, Public Read/Write, Controlled by Parent
Separate internal and external defaults
External default cannot be more open than internal
Set the most restrictive baseline, then open up

q: How does the role hierarchy affect record access?
alt: What is the role hierarchy used for?
Does a manager see their subordinates' records?
What is Grant Access Using Hierarchies?
role hierarchy vs profile
a: The role hierarchy opens up access vertically. Users in a role can see, and generally edit, records owned by users in roles below them. So a sales manager sees the opportunities owned by her reps, even when the OWD is Private. If her rep Arjun owns a deal, she can open it without any sharing rule. This is controlled by the Grant Access Using Hierarchies setting. It's always on for standard objects and can only be turned off for custom objects. One thing I always say: the role hierarchy doesn't have to match the HR org chart. It should reflect who needs to see whose data. And keep the distinction clear. Roles are about which records you can access, while profiles are about what a user can do.
points: Managers inherit access to subordinates' records
Grant Access Using Hierarchies can be disabled only for custom objects
Should reflect data visibility needs, not just the org chart
Roles control records; profiles control permissions

q: What is the difference between owner-based and criteria-based sharing rules?
alt: Explain sharing rules
Owner based vs criteria based sharing rule
Can sharing rules restrict access?
how do you share records with users in another role
a: Sharing rules give extra access to groups of users beyond the org-wide default and role hierarchy. An owner-based rule shares records based on who owns them. For example, all opportunities owned by the East Sales role are shared read-only with the West Sales role. A criteria-based rule shares records based on field values.
