For example, all cases where Region equals APAC are shared with the APAC support group, no matter who owns them. The difference shows up when owners change. If an APAC case gets reassigned to someone in Europe, the criteria-based rule still shares it with APAC support, because it looks at the field. You can share with public groups, roles, roles and subordinates, or territories, and give read-only or read/write. And remember, sharing rules only widen access, never restrict it.
points: Owner-based: by record owner's role or group
Criteria-based: by field values on the record
Targets: public groups, roles, roles and subordinates, territories
Only grant access; cannot take it away

q: What is manual sharing and who can do it?
alt: How do you share a single record with another user?
What happens to manual shares when the owner changes?
Sharing button in Salesforce
manual sharing limitations
a: Manual sharing lets someone share one specific record with a user, group or role when the org-wide default is Private or Public Read Only. You do it from the Sharing button or Sharing action on the record. Who can do it: the record owner, users above the owner in the role hierarchy, and users with full access or admin permissions. Say a rep owns a big account and needs a pre-sales engineer to see it for a week. She can just share it with him manually. The gotcha is that manual shares are removed when the record owner changes. So if the account moves to another rep, the engineer loses access. That's why I use manual sharing for occasional, ad-hoc access, and for repeatable needs I use sharing rules, teams or Apex sharing.
points: One record shared with users, groups or roles
Available when OWD is Private or Public Read Only
Owner, owner's managers and admins can share
Removed when ownership changes

q: How do you share records using Apex managed sharing? Can you write an example?
alt: Write Apex code to share a record with a user
What is a share object, like Project__Share?
apex managed sharing example code
How do you programmatically share a custom object record?
a: Apex managed sharing means inserting rows into the object's share table from code. For a custom object Project__c, the share object is Project__Share, with ParentId for the record, UserOrGroupId for the user or group, AccessLevel as Read or Edit, and RowCause. I create an Apex sharing reason on the custom object, like Reviewer_Access, and use it as the row cause. Shares with a custom reason survive an owner change, unlike manual shares. Say each project has a Reviewer lookup. When a reviewer is set, my trigger gives that user Read on the project. I collect all the shares in a list and insert once with Database.insert and allOrNone false, because sharing with the owner or with a user who already has more access fails. When the reviewer changes, I delete the old shares with that row cause so the previous reviewer loses access.
points: Share object: ParentId, UserOrGroupId, AccessLevel, RowCause
Use an Apex sharing reason for a custom row cause
Custom-reason shares survive owner changes
Bulkify and use Database.insert with allOrNone false
Remove stale shares when the driving field changes

q: What is a row cause in sharing, and how does it behave for standard versus custom objects?
alt: Explain RowCause on share records
Can you create Apex sharing reasons on Account?
Why did my Apex shares disappear after owner change?
manual vs apex sharing reason row cause
a: RowCause records why a share row exists. Values include Owner, Manual, Rule for sharing rules, Team, Territory, or a custom Apex sharing reason. On custom objects you can define Apex sharing reasons. Shares created with them are kept when the owner changes, and only code or admins with the right access can remove them. On standard objects like Account or Opportunity, you can't define custom sharing reasons. So Apex shares there use the Manual row cause, which means they're deleted when the owner changes, just like manual shares a user creates. Here's where it bites. Say my code shares opportunities with a finance user. A rep reassigns a deal to a colleague, and finance silently loses access. On standard objects, I either re-create those shares in the owner-change logic, or use teams or criteria-based sharing rules instead.
points: RowCause values: Owner, Manual, Rule, Team, Territory, custom reasons
Custom Apex sharing reasons only on custom objects
Custom reasons survive owner change
Standard-object Apex shares use Manual and are lost on owner change

q: What are account teams and opportunity teams?
alt: Explain account team and opportunity team
How do team members get access to records?
What is team selling?
default account team salesforce
a: Teams give a group of people working together access to a specific account or opportunity, with a defined role on it. An account team lists users like the account manager, technical consultant and support lead. For each member you set access to the account and to its related opportunities, cases and contacts. For example, the technical consultant might get Read/Write on the account but only Read on its opportunities. Opportunity teams, enabled through Team Selling, do the same for a deal, and they work with opportunity splits for revenue credit. So if two reps work a deal, they can split the credit 60/40. Users can set a default team that's added to their new records automatically. Teams create share records with a Team row cause, so they work fine with a Private sharing model.
points: Account team: per-member access to account and related records
Opportunity team requires Team Selling to be enabled
Default teams can be added automatically
Opportunity splits work with opportunity teams

q: How does territory management affect sharing?
alt: How do Sales Territories give access to accounts?
Enterprise Territory Management sharing explained
Role hierarchy vs territory hierarchy
territory based access to opportunities
a: Sales Territories, formerly Enterprise Territory Management, gives record access based on territories instead of the role hierarchy. Accounts are assigned to territories manually or with assignment rules, users are assigned to territories, and each territory or model defines the access level its users get to those accounts and to related opportunities, cases and contacts. Users higher in the territory hierarchy inherit access to territories below them. Where it really helps is when one account needs several reps. Say a large customer in Mumbai is covered by a West India rep for geography and also by a separate rep for the cloud product line. A single role hierarchy can't express that, but with territories the account simply sits in both territories and both reps get access. Territories can also be used as targets in sharing rules.
points: Access follows account-to-territory and user-to-territory assignment
Access levels for accounts, opportunities, cases, contacts
Territory hierarchy rolls access upwards
Supports multiple reps per account across dimensions

q: What is the difference between profiles, permission sets and permission set groups?
alt: Profile vs permission set
Why use permission set groups?
Can a user have more than one profile?
profiles permission sets and permission set groups explained
a: A profile is the base set of permissions and settings every user must have, and each user has exactly one. A permission set adds permissions on top of the profile, and a user can have many. So it's the flexible way to give extra access, like object permissions, field access or system permissions, to specific people. A permission set group bundles several permission sets into one unit that matches a job role. For example, a Sales Operations group might bundle three permission sets: one for opportunity access, one for reporting and one for price books. I assign one group instead of three sets. Permissions in Salesforce are additive. A permission set can grant access but not remove it. The one exception is a muting permission set inside a group, which can switch off permissions that group would otherwise give.
points: Profile: one per user, baseline settings
Permission set: many per user, extra access
Permission set group: bundles sets by job role
Access is additive; muting sets remove within a group

q: What is Salesforce's direction on profiles versus permission sets, and how would you design user access today?
alt: Is Salesforce retiring permissions on profiles?
Why should we move to permission sets?
permission set led security model
What should go on a profile now?
a: Salesforce recommends a permission-set-led model. They had announced retiring object and field permissions on profiles, but later stopped enforcing that date, and in 2026 the retirement was cancelled. So profiles still work. But the best practice hasn't changed. I keep profiles minimal, often based on the Minimum Access profile, holding things like default record types, page layout assignments, login hours, IP ranges and default apps. Object permissions, field-level security and system permissions go into small, focused permission sets, bundled into permission set groups per job role. User Access Policies can automate the assignments. For example, instead of a Sales Rep profile and a nearly identical Senior Sales Rep profile, I'd have one minimal profile, a Sales Rep group, and one extra permission set for the senior folks. That gives fewer profiles, clearer auditing and easier changes.
points: Profile permission retirement was cancelled; permission sets are still the recommended model
Minimal profiles for defaults, layouts, login settings
Object, field and system permissions in permission sets
Group sets by persona with permission set groups
Automate assignments with User Access Policies

q: A permission set group gives one team a permission they should not have. How do you remove it without breaking the group for others?
alt: What is a muting permission set?
How do you take away a permission in a permission set group?
muting permission set use case
Can you restrict access with permission sets?
a: I'd use a muting permission set, but it only works inside a permission set group. A muting set removes permissions from the group it belongs to. So I'd create a separate group for that team, say Sales Ops Limited, with the same permission sets, and add a muting permission set that mutes Delete on Opportunity or whichever permission is the problem. Everyone else keeps the original group, untouched. The gotcha is that muting only affects permissions granted through that group. If the same permission comes from the user's profile or from another directly assigned permission set, they still have it. So if a user still can delete opportunities after this, I go looking for that other source. I verify the result on the group's summary of combined permissions.
points: Muting permission sets exist only inside a permission set group
Muting removes permissions granted by that group only
Access from profiles or other sets is not muted
Check the group's combined permissions summary

q: What is field-level security?
alt: Explain FLS
How do you control who can see or edit a field?
Field level security vs page layout read only
where do you set field level security
a: Field-level security controls whether a user can see a field and whether they can edit it. It's set through profiles and permission sets. If FLS hides a field, it's hidden everywhere: record pages, list views, reports, search results and the API. That's different from making a field read-only or taking it off a page layout. That only changes that one screen, and the user can still get to the field through reports or the API. For example, if I just remove Salary from the Employee layout, a user can still build a report, add the Salary column and export it. So for anything sensitive, like salary or a credit score, I always secure it with FLS, and I treat page layouts as user experience only.
points: Visible and read-only settings per field
Set in profiles and permission sets
Applies to UI, reports, search and API
Page layouts only change the screen, not security

q: How would you hide a sensitive field from users of a particular profile?
alt: Hide a field from one profile, how?
A field should not be visible to support users, what will you do?
how to make a field invisible for some users
Remove field access for a profile
a: I'd remove access through field-level security, not just the page layout. If the field is currently granted on that profile, I uncheck Visible for it in the profile's field-level security. In a permission-set-led setup, I also make sure no permission set or group assigned to those users grants the field, and I give it only to the users who need it through a permission set. Say it's a Credit Score field and only the finance team should see it. I'd remove it from the profile, check that no other set gives it to sales, and create a Finance Credit permission set. Then I verify with the user access summary, or by logging in as a test user, that the field is gone from the record page, reports, list views and the API. Removing it from the layout alone would still leave it reachable in reports.
points: Use FLS, not just the page layout
Remove from the profile and any assigned permission sets
Grant to required users through a permission set
Verify with login-as or the user access summary

q: What are restriction rules and scoping rules, and how are they different from sharing?
alt: Restriction rules vs scoping rules
How can you restrict access below the OWD?
Can restriction rules take away access granted by sharing rules?
what are scoping rules in salesforce
a: Sharing in Salesforce only adds access, so restriction rules exist to narrow it. A restriction rule filters which records a set of users can see on supported objects, even if sharing would give them more. For example, contractors only see tasks they own. They're supported on custom objects, contracts, events, tasks, quotes, time sheets and some external objects, with a small number of active rules per object. Users with View All or Modify All bypass them and still see everything. A scoping rule is different. It doesn't remove access. It only sets the default set of records users see in list views, reports and lookups. Say a rep has access to all accounts, but a scoping rule shows only her region's accounts by default. She can still switch the scope and see everything she has access to.
points: Restriction rules reduce visible records for matched users
Scoping rules change the default view only, not access
Users with View All / Modify All bypass restriction rules
Limited supported objects and active rules per object

q: Users should only see tasks related to their own region, even though tasks are broadly visible. How would you do it?
alt: How do you restrict activity visibility by region?
Task sharing is controlled by parent, how do you limit it further?
Contractors should only see their own events, solution?
use case for restriction rules on tasks
a: Tasks and events don't have regular sharing rules. They follow the related record or the owner. So this is a good fit for restriction rules. I'd add a Region field on Task, set by a flow from the related record or the owner, and a matching Region field on User. Then I create a restriction rule on Task, with user criteria for the affected users and record criteria where Region equals the user's region. So a rep with Region = South only sees tasks stamped South, even if sharing would show more. Restriction rules only support the equals operator and one level of dot notation, so I keep the criteria simple. That's why I stamp Region directly on the task. I make sure those users don't have View All on activities, and I test list views, search and reports, because results can differ.
points: Restriction rules support tasks and events
Stamp a Region field on the task to filter on
Record criteria support only equals
View All / Modify All bypasses the rule
Test list views, search and reports

q: What is implicit sharing?
alt: Explain parent implicit and child implicit sharing
Why can a user see an account when they only own its opportunity?
implicit sharing account contact opportunity case
built-in sharing behaviour in Salesforce
a: Implicit sharing is built-in access that Salesforce grants automatically between accounts and their child records. You can't configure it or turn it off. Parent implicit sharing means if a user has access to a contact, opportunity or case, they get read-only access to its parent account. So a rep who owns an opportunity can always open the account, even if the account belongs to someone else and the OWD is Private. Child implicit sharing goes the other way. The account owner gets access to the account's child contacts, opportunities and cases, with the level defined in the owner's role settings. There's also implicit sharing for Experience Cloud users on their own account. And it only applies to accounts and these standard children, not to your custom objects.
points: Parent implicit: access to child gives read on the parent account
Child implicit: account owner gets access to child records
Child access level comes from role settings
Automatic, not configurable, account-related objects only

q: What is the difference between View All and Modify All on an object versus View All Data and Modify All Data?
alt: View All vs View All Data
What does Modify All permission do?
Does View All bypass field level security?
object level view all modify all explained
a: View All and Modify All are object-level permissions. They let a user see, or see and edit, delete and transfer, every record of one object regardless of sharing. View All Data and Modify All Data are system permissions that do the same across every object in the org, which is basically admin-level access. Both kinds override sharing, so org-wide defaults, roles and sharing rules no longer limit those users. But neither overrides field-level security. For example, a data steward who cleans up accounts might get Modify All on Account only. She can fix any account, but she can't touch opportunities, and she still won't see a field that FLS hides from her. View All Data and Modify All Data I keep for admins and carefully reviewed integration users.
points: Object level: View All / Modify All for one object
System level: View All Data / Modify All Data for every object
Both bypass sharing
Neither bypasses field-level security

q: Contractors should only log in during office hours and from the office network. How would you set that up?
alt: What are login hours and login IP ranges?
How do you restrict login by IP address?
Trusted IP ranges vs login IP ranges
restrict user login time salesforce
a: I'd set login hours and login IP ranges on the contractors' profile. Login hours define the days and times they can log in. If they're logged in when the window ends, the session is ended. Say the window is 9 to 6, Monday to Friday. A contractor working at 6:05 gets logged out. Login IP ranges on the profile block any login attempt from outside the allowed addresses, so from home they can't get in at all. This is different from Trusted IP Ranges under Network Access. Those apply org-wide and only skip the identity verification challenge for users on those networks. They don't block anyone. Since these are profile settings, I'd give contractors their own profile. And I'd check whether the restriction should apply to API access too.
points: Profile login hours limit when users can log in
Profile login IP ranges block logins from other addresses
Trusted IP Ranges only skip identity verification
Use a dedicated profile for contractors

q: What is MFA in Salesforce and which verification methods are allowed?
alt: Explain multi-factor authentication in Salesforce
Is MFA mandatory for Salesforce?
Does SMS count as MFA in Salesforce?
what verification methods can be used for MFA
a: Multi-factor authentication means users prove who they are with something they know, their password, plus something they have, like a phone app or a security key. Salesforce requires MFA for user interface logins to its products. Accepted methods are the Salesforce Authenticator app, third-party authenticator apps that generate time-based codes, physical security keys, and built-in authenticators like Touch ID or Windows Hello. Email, SMS and phone calls don't qualify as MFA methods. That's a common interview trap. A code sent by SMS might feel like a second factor, but it doesn't count. If users log in through single sign-on, MFA can be enforced at the identity provider instead. So if the company already uses Okta with MFA, that covers it. API logins for integrations are handled by the integration's own authentication, not MFA.
points: Password plus a verification method
Required for UI logins
Authenticator apps, TOTP apps, security keys, built-in authenticators
Email and SMS don't qualify
With SSO, MFA can be enforced at the identity provider

q: How does single sign-on with SAML work in Salesforce?
alt: Explain SAML SSO basics
What is the identity provider and service provider?
SP-initiated vs IdP-initiated SSO
What is Federation ID used for?
How do you set up SSO with Okta or Azure AD?
a: With SAML single sign-on, a trusted identity provider, like Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, authenticates the user, and Salesforce is the service provider that accepts the result. In SP-initiated flow, the user goes to the My Domain login page, Salesforce redirects them to the identity provider, and after login the provider posts back a signed SAML assertion. Salesforce checks the signature with the provider's certificate and finds the user, usually by Federation ID. So if Priya's Federation ID in Salesforce is her company email, the assertion carries that email and she lands in her account. IdP-initiated flow starts from the provider's portal instead. Just-in-time provisioning can create or update users from assertion attributes. My Domain is required. And I always keep one non-SSO admin login for emergencies, in case the identity provider goes down.
points: Identity provider authenticates; Salesforce is the service provider
Signed SAML assertion verified with the IdP certificate
User matched by Federation ID or username
SP-initiated vs IdP-initiated
JIT provisioning and My Domain

q: What is Salesforce Shield and what does it include?
alt: Explain Shield Platform Encryption, Event Monitoring and Field Audit Trail
What is Salesforce Shield used for?
Which tools help with compliance and auditing in Salesforce?
salesforce shield components
a: Shield is a paid add-on for organisations with strict security and compliance needs, so mostly regulated industries. Its main parts are Platform Encryption, Event Monitoring and Field Audit Trail. Platform Encryption encrypts sensitive data at rest, like fields, files and attachments, while keeping most platform features working, and it supports customer-controlled keys. Event Monitoring records detailed user activity, like logins, report exports, API calls and page views, so you can spot risky behaviour. Transaction security policies can block or alert on it in real time. Field Audit Trail extends field history tracking, with many more tracked fields per object and history kept far longer than standard field history. For example, a bank might need to prove years later who changed a customer's credit limit. Standard field history won't keep it that long, but Field Audit Trail will.
points: Platform Encryption: data at rest, key management options
Event Monitoring: detailed activity logs, transaction security policies
Field Audit Trail: more tracked fields, long-term history retention
Used for regulated industries and compliance

q: What is the difference between Shield Platform Encryption and Classic Encryption, and between deterministic and probabilistic encryption?
alt: Classic encrypted field vs Platform Encryption
Can you filter on an encrypted field?
deterministic vs probabilistic encryption scheme
What are limitations of Platform Encryption?
a: Classic Encryption is the free option. It's a special Encrypted Text field type with masking, a limited length, and access controlled by the View Encrypted Data permission. Shield Platform Encryption encrypts existing standard and custom fields, files and attachments at rest without changing field types, and it has key management options. It has two schemes. Probabilistic is the default and the strongest, because the same value encrypts differently each time, but you can't filter or match on it. Deterministic gives the same ciphertext for the same value, so exact-match filtering, some reports and duplicate matching keep working, with slightly weaker protection. For example, if I encrypt Email and the business still wants duplicate rules on email, it has to be deterministic. Before encrypting anything, I check the impact on formulas, sorting, search and integrations.
points: Classic: Encrypted Text field type, masking, View Encrypted Data
Platform Encryption: existing fields, files, at rest
Probabilistic: strongest, no filtering
Deterministic: exact-match filtering possible
Review impact on formulas, sorting and search

q: What is Event Monitoring and how have you seen it used?
alt: How can you track who exported a report?
Explain event log files and transaction security
How do you detect suspicious user activity in Salesforce?
event monitoring use cases
a: Event Monitoring captures detailed records of what users do in the org, like logins, report runs and exports, API calls, Apex executions, page views and file downloads. The data comes as event log files, typically hourly or daily, and some events can be streamed in near real time. The common uses are security, adoption and performance. For security, say a salesperson resigns and the business wants to know if they exported the customer list on their last week. The report export logs show that. For adoption, you can see which pages people actually use. And for performance, you can find slow pages or Apex. With real-time events you can build transaction security policies that block an action, require MFA, or notify admins, for example when someone exports more than a set number of records.
points: Event log files for logins, exports, API, Apex, page views
Real-time event monitoring for selected events
Transaction security policies can block, require MFA or notify
Used for security, adoption and performance analysis

q: A user says they cannot see a record. How do you troubleshoot it?
alt: User can't access a record, what will you check?
Insufficient privileges error, how to debug?
How do you find out why a user doesn't see an opportunity?
record not visible to user troubleshooting steps
a: I go through the layers in order. First, does the user have Read on the object through their profile or permission sets? Second, record access. I open the record's Sharing Hierarchy or Sharing button to see who has access and why. Then I check the org-wide default, the owner's place in the role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, territories and manual shares. Third, I check restriction rules or scoping rules, and whether a list view or report filter is just hiding it. For example, a user once said she couldn't see a case, and it turned out her list view was filtered to My Open Cases and the case was closed. If it's a specific field, I check field-level security. Finally, I log in as the user to confirm, and fix the gap with the right sharing mechanism.
points: Object permission via profile or permission sets
Sharing: OWD, role, rules, teams, territories, manual
Use the record's Sharing Hierarchy / access explanation
Check restriction and scoping rules, filters, FLS
Confirm with login-as

q: Sales reps in India need read access to opportunities owned by the US team. How would you give it?
alt: Give read access to records in another region
How do you share records across roles that are not in the same branch?
Users in one region need to view another region's accounts
cross region access sharing rule
a: The two teams sit in different branches of the role hierarchy, so I'd create a sharing rule. If ownership defines the region, an owner-based rule on Opportunity shares records owned by US Sales and subordinates with India Sales and subordinates, read-only. If region is a field on the record, a criteria-based rule on Region equals US is more precise, because it still works when a record's owner changes teams. Say a US deal gets reassigned to a rep who sits under the Canada role. The owner-based rule would stop sharing it, but the criteria-based one still does. For a cleaner design, I share with public groups instead of roles directly, so membership can change without editing the rules. I give Read Only, not Read/Write, and I keep the OWD Private so only this access is added.
points: Owner-based rule when region follows the owner's role
Criteria-based rule when region is a field
Grant Read Only, not Read/Write
Prefer public groups as sharing targets
Keep OWD restrictive

q: A user can view a record but cannot edit it. What do you check?
alt: User has read access but edit is failing, why?
Edit button missing on record, troubleshooting
Why is a record read-only for a user?
user cannot edit a field even though they can see it
a: I check four things. First, the object permission. The user needs Edit on the object, not just Read. Second, record access. Sharing might only give Read, for example a read-only sharing rule, or a Public Read Only OWD while they're not the owner. Third, whether the record is locked, usually by a pending approval process, or made read-only by validation or record-type-specific logic. The approval one is very common. Say a rep submits a discount for approval and then tries to fix a typo. The record is locked until the approver acts. Fourth, for a single field, field-level security may mark it read-only, or the page layout may show it as read-only. And if the Edit button is missing entirely, I check the page layout or the Lightning page actions.
points: Object permission Edit
Record-level access level Read vs Read/Write
Record locked by approval process
Field-level security or layout marking the field read-only
Edit action missing from layout or Lightning page

q: How would you design the sharing model for a large organisation with regional sales and support teams?
alt: Walk me through designing a sharing model
What are best practices for a scalable sharing model?
How do you avoid sharing recalculation issues with large data volumes?
sharing architecture design salesforce
a: I start with the most restrictive org-wide defaults the business can accept, usually Private for accounts, opportunities and cases, and Controlled by Parent for detail objects. I design a role hierarchy based on data visibility, not the HR chart, and keep it fairly shallow. Cross-team access goes through criteria-based sharing rules targeted at public groups, account or opportunity teams for collaboration, and territories if one account needs coverage on several dimensions. Apex sharing is a last resort, only when declarative tools can't do it. For scale, I avoid ownership skew, so one user doesn't own huge numbers of records. Say a reorg moves 300 reps to new roles. That triggers a lot of sharing recalculation, so I plan it outside business hours and use deferred sharing calculation for big changes like that.
points: Restrictive OWD baseline
Role hierarchy for visibility, kept shallow
Criteria-based rules to public groups; teams; territories
Apex sharing only when declarative cannot do it
Avoid ownership skew; defer sharing calculations for big changes

q: How do you enforce sharing, CRUD and field-level security in Apex?
alt: with sharing vs without sharing vs inherited sharing
What is WITH USER_MODE?
How do you use Security.stripInaccessible?
Apex runs in system mode, how do you respect user permissions?
a: Apex runs in system mode by default, so I enforce security explicitly. The sharing keywords control record access. with sharing respects the user's sharing, without sharing ignores it, and inherited sharing takes the caller's mode, which I use for reusable classes. But sharing keywords don't check object or field permissions. For those I use WITH USER_MODE on SOQL, or AccessLevel.USER_MODE on Database DML methods, which enforce sharing, CRUD and field-level security together. Security.stripInaccessible removes fields the user can't access instead of throwing an error. Here's a real case. Say an LWC shows account details and the controller queries AnnualRevenue. If the user doesn't have FLS on that field, a user-mode query throws an error, while stripInaccessible just drops the field and the page still loads. In LWC controllers, I default to with sharing and user mode.
points: with / without / inherited sharing control record access only
WITH USER_MODE enforces CRUD, FLS and sharing in SOQL
Database methods accept AccessLevel.USER_MODE
stripInaccessible removes inaccessible fields

q: An integration needs access to only a few objects. How would you set up the integration user's security?
alt: How do you secure an integration user?
What profile should an integration user have?
Salesforce Integration user license, explain
least privilege for API user
a: I follow least privilege. I create a dedicated integration user, not a named employee's account, ideally with the Salesforce Integration user license and the Minimum Access - API Only Integrations profile. Then I grant only the object and field permissions it needs through a permission set. For example, if an ERP only updates orders, it gets Read and Edit on Order and a few Account fields, not View All Data or Modify All Data. I restrict where it can log in from if the source IPs are fixed, and use OAuth instead of stored passwords. I only add a custom permission to bypass validation if it's truly needed. And every integration gets its own user. So if the ERP and the marketing tool each have their own user, I can trace exactly who changed what, and I can revoke one without breaking the other.
points: Dedicated API-only user per integration
Minimal profile plus a focused permission set
Avoid View All Data / Modify All Data
OAuth, IP restrictions where possible
Separate users make auditing and revoking easy

q: What are the different types of flows in Salesforce?
alt: Explain flow types
Screen flow vs record-triggered flow vs scheduled flow
What kinds of flows can you build in Flow Builder?
types of flow in salesforce
a: The main flow types are screen flows, record-triggered flows, schedule-triggered flows, platform event-triggered flows, autolaunched flows and orchestrations. A screen flow has screens and guides a user through a process, like a case intake wizard. A record-triggered flow runs when a record is created, updated or deleted, like setting a default value when a lead comes in. A schedule-triggered flow runs at a set time and frequency, optionally for a batch of records, like checking overdue invoices every morning. A platform event-triggered flow runs when a platform event message arrives. An autolaunched flow has no trigger and is started from Apex, a REST call, a button, or another flow as a subflow. And orchestrations coordinate multi-step, multi-user processes, like onboarding that passes through HR, IT and the manager.
points: Screen flow: user interaction
Record-triggered: create, update, delete
Schedule-triggered and platform event-triggered
Autolaunched (no trigger): called from Apex, API or other flows
Orchestration: multi-stage, multi-user processes

q: What is the difference between a before-save and an after-save record-triggered flow?
alt: Fast field updates vs actions and related records
When do you use a before-save flow?
before save vs after save flow
Why is a before-save flow faster?
a: A before-save flow, labelled Fast Field Updates, runs before the record is saved. So it can change fields on the triggering record by assigning values to $Record, with no extra DML. That makes it the fastest option for same-record updates. For example, when a case comes in with Priority High, set the SLA Due field. An after-save flow, labelled Actions and Related Records, runs after the record is saved. The record now has an Id, so you can create or update other records, send emails, call Apex actions, post to Chatter, and use scheduled paths and the asynchronous path. For example, when the case is created, also create a follow-up task for the account owner. That needs after-save, because before-save can't create or update other records. My rule is simple: same-record field updates go before-save, everything else goes after-save.
points: Before-save: update $Record fields, no DML, very fast
After-save: related records, emails, actions, subflows
Scheduled and async paths only in after-save
Before-save cannot create or update other records

q: What are $Record and $Record__Prior in a record-triggered flow?
alt: How do you get the old value of a field in a flow?
Explain $Record global variable
record prior value in flow
How do you check if a field changed in flow?
a: $Record holds the triggering record with its current values. It's the same idea as Trigger.new for one record. In a before-save flow, you update the record by assigning values to $Record fields. $Record__Prior holds the values before the update, like Trigger.oldMap. So I compare the two to detect changes. For example, a Decision that checks $Record.StageName does not equal $Record__Prior.StageName tells me the stage just moved, say from Proposal to Negotiation, and not that someone only edited the description. One gotcha: $Record__Prior is only populated for updates. On a new record it's empty, so don't rely on it in a create path. In entry condition formulas you can also use ISCHANGED, ISNEW and PRIORVALUE to do the same checks.
points: $Record: current triggering record
$Record__Prior: values before the update
Prior is empty on create
Compare the two, or use ISCHANGED / PRIORVALUE in formulas

q: How do entry conditions work in a record-triggered flow, and how do you stop it running on every edit?
alt: What does 'Only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements' do?
How do you prevent a flow from running on every update?
entry criteria in record triggered flow
Flow keeps firing every time the record is saved, how do you fix it?
a: Entry conditions decide whether the flow runs at all. Checking them upfront is much cheaper than letting the flow start and then exit through a Decision. You can use field conditions or a formula. The key option for updates is when to run. Either every time a record is updated and meets the conditions, or only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements. The second one runs once, when the record goes from not meeting to meeting the criteria. That stops repeated firing and recursion. Say the condition is Status equals Closed. With the first option, every later edit on a closed case, even fixing a typo, runs the flow again. With the second, it runs only at the moment the case becomes Closed. In formula conditions, I use ISCHANGED or PRIORVALUE for the same effect.
points: Filter in entry conditions, not in a first Decision
Field conditions or formula
'Only when updated to meet' runs on the transition only
ISCHANGED / PRIORVALUE in entry formulas

q: What are scheduled paths and the run asynchronously path in a record-triggered flow?
alt: What is the Run Asynchronously path?
How do you run part of a flow later?
scheduled path vs async path
Can a record-triggered flow do a callout?
a: Both are only available in after-save record-triggered flows. A scheduled path runs actions at a time relative to an event, like one hour after creation, or seven days before a date field like Contract End Date. It replaces time-based workflow actions. The run asynchronously path runs as soon as possible after the original transaction commits, in its own transaction with its own governor limits. I use the async path for callouts, through the HTTP Callout action, External Services or Apex actions, and for heavier processing that shouldn't slow down the user's save. For example, when an order is created, the user's save finishes straight away, and the async path then sends it to the ERP. The gotcha: neither path can roll back the original save if it fails. So if the ERP call fails, the order still exists, and I add fault handling for that.
points: After-save only
Scheduled path: time offset from trigger or date field
Async path: runs after commit, separate transaction and limits
Use async path for callouts and non-urgent work
Failures don't roll back the original save

q: What is the difference between a schedule-triggered flow and a scheduled path?
alt: Scheduled flow vs scheduled path
How do you run a flow every night?
When would you use a schedule-triggered flow?
daily batch job using flow
a: A schedule-triggered flow runs on a fixed calendar schedule, once, daily or weekly at a set time. It can run for every record that matches an object and filter, a bit like a simple batch job. A scheduled path is part of a record-triggered flow, and it runs relative to something that happened to a specific record, like three days after a case was created. So, if I need to check all open opportunities every morning at 7 and flag the ones with a past close date, I use a schedule-triggered flow. If I need to follow up on each record a certain time after it changed, or before a date on it, like emailing the customer three days after their case was created, I use a scheduled path.
points: Schedule-triggered: fixed time, runs for a filtered set of records
Scheduled path: relative to a record event or date field
Scheduled flows behave like a simple batch
Scheduled paths live inside record-triggered flows

q: What is a screen flow and where can you use it?
alt: Explain screen flows
How do you launch a screen flow from a record page?
Where can you embed a flow?
screen flow use cases
a: A screen flow is a flow with screens that guides a user through steps. It collects input, shows information, and then creates or updates records. Typical uses are guided case intake, onboarding wizards or a quote request form. You can launch it from a Lightning record, home or app page using the Flow component, from a quick action or button on a record, from the utility bar, from an Experience Cloud site, or from an LWC using the lightning-flow component. Say I put a 'Log Complaint' screen flow as a quick action on Account. If I create an input variable named recordId, the flow gets the account's Id automatically, so the agent doesn't have to pick the account again. Also remember a screen flow runs in user context by default.
points: Guides users through screens
Launch from Lightning pages, actions, utility bar, Experience Cloud, LWC
recordId input variable for record context
Runs in user context by default

q: What are subflows and why would you use them?
alt: How do you call one flow from another?
Explain subflow element
reusable flow logic
How do you pass values into a subflow?
a: A subflow is a flow called from another flow using the Subflow element. It lets me build reusable logic once and call it from many places. For example, I'd build one autolaunched flow that creates the standard set of onboarding tasks. Then a screen flow, a record-triggered flow and an orchestration can all call it. If HR later adds a new task, I change one flow, not three. Values go in through variables marked available for input, and results come back through variables marked available for output. Subflows keep large flows readable and easier to test. Record-triggered flows can call autolaunched subflows. One thing to remember: it all still runs in the same transaction and shares governor limits, so splitting into subflows doesn't give you extra limits.
points: Subflow element calls another flow
Input and output variables carry data
Reusable, smaller, easier to maintain
Same transaction and shared limits

q: How do you call Apex from a flow? Write an invocable method.
alt: What is @InvocableMethod?
Write Apex that a flow can call
invocable method rules and example
How do you return values from Apex to Flow?
a: I use the @InvocableMethod annotation on a public or global static method, and it shows up in Flow Builder as an Apex action. You can have only one invocable method per class. The method takes a List as input and returns a List, because Flow bulkifies calls. So if 200 records trigger the flow, Salesforce calls the method once with all 200 inputs, and the output list must match the input list in size and order. Say the method calculates a credit score for each account Id passed in. Inside, I write it like trigger code: one query for all 200 accounts, one DML for the whole list, and results added in the same order the Ids came in. The label, description and category attributes make it easy to find in Flow Builder. It's also callable from Agentforce and the REST API.
points: Public or global static, one per class
Input and output are Lists
Output order matches input order
Bulkified: one call for many interviews
Also callable from Agentforce and the REST API

q: How do you pass multiple inputs and outputs between Flow and Apex?
alt: What is @InvocableVariable?
Invocable method with wrapper class
How do you return an error message from Apex to a flow?
invocable request and response classes
a: I use request and response wrapper classes whose public fields are marked @InvocableVariable. The invocable method takes a List of the request class and returns a List of the response class, one response per request, in the same order. That lets a flow pass several values and get several back. For example, the flow sends a record Id, an owner and a number of days, and gets back the new record Id and an error message. Setting the required and label attributes on the variables makes it nicer in Flow Builder. Inside, I use Database methods with partial success, so one bad row doesn't fail the whole batch. And instead of throwing, I return the error text. Then the flow can check it with a Decision, say 'if error message is blank, continue, otherwise email the admin', instead of hitting an unhandled fault.
points: Wrapper classes with @InvocableVariable fields
List<Request> in, List<Result> out, same order
required and label attributes improve Flow Builder
Return errors as data so the flow can branch
Partial-success DML for bulk safety

q: What is a fault path in a flow, and how do you handle errors?
alt: How do you handle errors in Flow?
What happens when a flow fails without a fault connector?
What is $Flow.FaultMessage?
flow error handling best practice
a: A fault path is an alternate connector from an element that can fail, like Create, Update or Delete Records, Get Records, or an action. It only runs when that element throws an error. Without one, the user sees a generic unhandled fault message and the admin or flow owner gets an error email. On the fault path, I usually capture $Flow.FaultMessage, log it to a custom error log object or send a notification, and in screen flows show the user a friendly message. For example, if Create Records fails because a validation rule blocks it, the user sees 'We couldn't save this request, please check the phone number' instead of a scary error. In record-triggered flows, I can use the Custom Error element to show a clear message and stop the save. I add fault paths to every data and action element.
points: Fault connector runs only when the element fails
Unhandled faults show a generic error and email the admin
$Flow.FaultMessage holds the error text
Log errors, notify, and show friendly messages

q: You want a record-triggered flow to block a save and show the user a message. How do you do it?
alt: Can a flow show an error like a validation rule?
What is the Custom Error element in flow?
How do you prevent saving a record from a flow?
validation rule vs flow custom error
a: I use the Custom Error element, which is available in both before-save and after-save record-triggered flows. When the flow reaches it, the save is rolled back and the user sees my message, either at the top of the record or under a specific field, just like a validation rule. I reach for it when the check needs logic a validation rule can't easily do, like looking at related records with Get Records. For example, blocking a case from being closed while it still has open child tasks. The flow gets the open tasks, and if it finds any, the Custom Error says 'Please complete the open tasks before closing this case'. For simple field checks on the same record, I still prefer a validation rule, because it's simpler and needs no extra queries.
points: Custom Error element in record-triggered flows
Rolls back the save and shows the message on the page or a field
Good for checks needing related-record data
Validation rules remain best for simple same-record checks

q: Your flow works when you edit one record but fails during a data load of thousands of records. What would you check?
alt: How do you bulkify a flow?
Flow failing on bulk updates with too many DML statements
Why should you avoid DML inside a loop in Flow?
flow bulkification best practices
a: The usual cause is a data element inside a loop. Salesforce automatically groups the same element across all flow interviews in a batch, so one Get Records or Update Records at the top level is bulkified. But if Get Records, Create Records or Update Records sits inside a Loop, it runs once per iteration and quickly hits the SOQL or DML limits. Say a load of 200 accounts comes in, and for each account the flow loops through its contacts and updates them one by one. That's hundreds of DML statements in one transaction, and it fails. I fix it by querying once before the loop, building a collection with Assignment elements inside the loop, and doing one Create or Update after the loop. I also tighten entry conditions, and for very large volumes I move the logic to Apex or an asynchronous path. And I always test with Data Loader-sized batches.
points: No Get, Create, Update or Delete inside loops
Use Assignment to build collections, then one DML after the loop
Top-level elements are bulkified across interviews
Tight entry conditions reduce work
Test with Data Loader-sized batches

q: How do governor limits apply to flows?
alt: Do flows have their own governor limits?
Flow and Apex share limits in the same transaction?
What happened to the 2000 element limit in Flow?
flow limits salesforce
a: Flows run inside the same transaction as everything else triggered by that save. So they share the standard per-transaction limits with Apex triggers and other automation: 100 SOQL queries and 150 DML statements in a synchronous transaction, 50,000 rows queried, 10,000 DML rows, and the CPU time limit. The old limit of 2,000 executed elements per flow interview was removed in the Spring '23 release, so the real constraints now are those transaction limits and CPU time. Each Get Records counts as a query, and each data element as a DML statement. So if an opportunity save fires a trigger that uses 60 queries and a flow that uses 45, together they break the 100 limit, even though each looks fine alone. Scheduled and asynchronous paths start new transactions with fresh limits, which is a handy way to split work.
points: Shared per-transaction limits with Apex
SOQL 100 / DML 150 synchronous
2,000 executed elements limit removed in Spring '23
Async and scheduled paths get their own limits
CPU time is often the real bottleneck

q: How do you decide between Flow and an Apex trigger?
alt: Flow vs Apex trigger, which one do you choose?
When is Apex better than Flow?
clicks vs code decision
Should all automation be in flows now?
a: I pick Flow when admins can understand the logic and the volume is moderate. That covers same-record updates in before-save flows, creating related records, notifications and guided screens. I pick Apex when the logic is complex, with nested conditions, maps or heavy calculations, when the object sees high-volume data loads, or when I need precise error handling and unit tests, complex callouts or recursion control. I also avoid mixing too many tools on one object. I keep one trigger per object through a handler, and a small, well-ordered set of flows. Often the best answer is both. For example, a record-triggered flow on Opportunity handles the simple field updates and notifications, and calls an invocable Apex method for the heavy commission calculation. The admin keeps the flow, and the developer owns the tested Apex.
points: Flow: simple to moderate logic, admin-maintainable
Apex: complex logic, high volume, precise error handling, tests
Before-save flows are excellent for same-record updates
Combine with invocable Apex for heavy steps
Keep automation per object consistent and ordered

q: Where do record-triggered flows fit in the order of execution?
alt: Do before-save flows run before or after Apex before triggers?
Order of execution with flows and triggers
When does an after-save flow run compared to after triggers?
salesforce save order flows
a: Before-save record-triggered flows run early, after system validation and before Apex before triggers. That's why they're so efficient for same-record field updates. Then come before triggers, custom validation rules, duplicate rules, the save without commit, and after triggers. After that come assignment rules, auto-response rules, workflow rules and escalation rules, then after-save record-triggered flows, then entitlement rules. Roll-up summary recalculation and criteria-based sharing evaluation follow, and the transaction commits. Post-commit work, like sending emails and running async paths, happens after commit. Here's why it matters. Say a before-save flow sets Priority to High, and a before trigger on the same object sets it to Medium. The trigger runs later, so the record saves as Medium, and people blame the flow. Knowing the order explains it.
points: Before-save flows run before Apex before triggers
Validation rules run after before triggers
After-save flows run after after triggers and assignment rules
Async paths and emails run after commit

q: Your org still has Workflow Rules and Process Builders. How would you migrate them to Flow?
alt: How do you use the Migrate to Flow tool?
Workflow rules and process builder are retired, what now?
migrate process builder to flow steps
What happened to Workflow Rules and Process Builder?
a: Workflow Rules and Process Builder reached end of support on December 31, 2025. They get no bug fixes or support now, so they should be moved to Flow. I start with an inventory per object. Then I use the Migrate to Flow tool in Setup, which converts a selected workflow rule or process into a record-triggered flow. The new flow is saved inactive, so I review it, test it in a sandbox, and then activate it and deactivate the old automation together. If both stay active, the same update or email fires twice. Some features can't be converted automatically, and those I rebuild by hand. I also use the chance to consolidate. For example, five old field-update rules on Case can usually become one before-save flow.
points: End of support Dec 31, 2025
Inventory automation per object first
Migrate to Flow converts to inactive record-triggered flows
Test, then activate the flow and deactivate the old rule together
Consolidate and use before-save for field updates

q: You're leading a large migration from Process Builder to Flow. What's your strategy?
alt: How would you plan a migration of hundreds of processes to flows?
Risks when migrating process builder to flow
one flow per object or many flows?
How do you test automation migration?
a: I start with a full inventory of processes, workflow rules and triggers per object, including what each does and whether it's still needed, because many are obsolete. Then I design the target per object: same-record updates in one before-save flow, and related-record actions in a few after-save flows split by business purpose, with explicit trigger order. For example, on Opportunity I might end up with one before-save flow, plus after-save flows for 'Closed Won onboarding' and 'Partner notifications'. Process Builder logic that relied on recursion or immediate re-evaluation needs extra care, because flows behave differently there. I migrate object by object in a sandbox, using the Migrate to Flow tool where it helps. I write regression test scripts and Apex tests, and deploy with the old automation deactivated in the same release, with a rollback plan ready.
points: Inventory and retire unused automation
Design per object: before-save plus purpose-based after-save flows
Set trigger order explicitly
Watch recursion and re-evaluation differences
Migrate object by object with regression tests and rollback

q: How do you debug a flow?
alt: How do you troubleshoot a flow that isn't working?
Flow debug options
Where can you see flow errors?
How do you test a record-triggered flow?
a: I start with the Debug button in Flow Builder. It runs the flow and shows each element's path, the decisions taken and the variable values. For record-triggered flows I can pick a test record, choose create or update, and optionally roll back the changes. So if a flow should set a discount but doesn't, I debug it against that exact opportunity and usually see the Decision went down the wrong branch. If it failed in real use, I read the flow error email, which shows the failing element and the error. I also check debug logs with the workflow category at a fine level. Flow Tests let me save repeatable test cases for record-triggered flows. For scheduled paths, I check paused and waiting interviews, and the Failed Flow Interviews list helps find issues.
points: Debug button with test record and rollback option
Flow error emails show the failing element
Debug logs with workflow logging
Flow Tests for repeatable checks
Check paused, waiting and failed interviews

q: How would you automatically assign new cases to the right team?
alt: Auto assign cases to queues, how?
Case assignment rules vs flow
Assign cases based on product or region
route cases to correct support team
a: For straightforward routing I use case assignment rules. They assign a new case to a user or queue based on criteria like Origin, Product or Region, with rule entries checked in order. They run automatically for web-to-case and email-to-case, and from the UI when the assignment checkbox is used. For example, Product equals Payments goes to the Payments queue, and anything else falls to General Support. If routing needs more logic, like checking the account's support tier or the agent's workload, I use an after-save record-triggered flow that sets the case owner to the right queue. I often read the mapping from custom metadata, so the business can change it without editing the flow. And for skills or capacity-based routing, Omni-Channel is the better tool.
points: Assignment rules for criteria-based routing to queues
Record-triggered flow for complex logic
Store routing mappings in custom metadata
Omni-Channel for capacity and skills-based routing

q: How would you send a reminder 30 days before a contract expires?
alt: Contract expiry reminder with flow
Send email X days before a date field
time based reminder in flow
notify account owner before contract end date
a: I'd use a record-triggered flow on Contract with a scheduled path set to 30 days before the End Date field. The entry condition checks that the contract is activated and has an end date. The scheduled path sends an email alert or creates a task for the account owner. Before acting, the path rechecks that the contract hasn't been renewed or cancelled, because the record may change in the meantime. Say a contract ends on 31 December. On 1 December the account owner gets the reminder, unless it was renewed in November. An alternative is a daily schedule-triggered flow that finds contracts whose end date is exactly 30 days from today. That's easier to reason about when dates change often. It also covers existing contracts that never get edited, which a record-triggered flow would never pick up.
points: Scheduled path: 30 days before EndDate
Entry conditions on status and end date
Recheck status before sending
Alternative: daily scheduled flow filtering on end date
Scheduled flow also covers records that are never edited

q: Build a multi-step screen flow that validates user input. How would you design it?
alt: How do you validate input in a screen flow?
Multi-screen flow with back and next and validation
screen flow input validation formula
reactive screen components in flow
a: I break the process into a few screens, each with one purpose. For example: customer details, product selection, then review and submit. On each input component I use the built-in required setting, plus the Validate Input formula with an error message, like checking an email format or that a date is in the future. So the user can't move to the next screen until it's valid. For checks against data, like a duplicate account, I use a Get Records and a Decision between screens. If someone types a company name that already exists, I loop back to the first screen with a message saying so. Reactive components and conditional visibility keep the screens simple. The last screen shows a review of everything entered, and then Create Records runs, with a fault path in case the save fails.
points: One purpose per screen
Required and Validate Input formulas on components
Get Records + Decision for data checks between screens
Conditional visibility and reactive components
Review screen, then DML with a fault path

q: When an opportunity is Closed Won, create an onboarding project and tasks. How would you build it?
alt: Create related records when opportunity is closed won
Flow to create child records automatically
after save flow create records example
How do you avoid creating duplicates when the flow re-runs?
a: I'd build an after-save record-triggered flow on Opportunity, set to run when a record is updated. Entry conditions: Stage equals Closed Won, with the option to run only when the record is updated to meet the conditions, so it fires once. The flow creates the Onboarding Project linked to the opportunity and the account. Then it creates the standard tasks, ideally from a task template stored in custom metadata. Say the template has five tasks, like kickoff call and data setup. I build all five in a collection and insert them with one Create Records. I add a fault path that logs errors and notifies an admin. And to be safe, I check that no project already exists for that opportunity. Otherwise, if a rep reopens the deal and closes it again, the customer gets a second project.
points: After-save flow, run once when Stage becomes Closed Won
Create project, then tasks in one collection insert
Task templates in custom metadata
Guard against duplicates
Fault path with logging

q: When an account's billing address changes, all its contacts' mailing addresses should update. How would you do it in Flow?
alt: Update child records when the parent changes
Flow to update related contacts
update records without loop flow
cascade parent field change to children
a: I'd use an after-save record-triggered flow on Account that runs only when the billing address fields change, using ISCHANGED in the entry formula. Then a single Update Records element with 'Specify conditions to identify records': object Contact, filter AccountId equals $Record.Id, and set the mailing fields from $Record. That updates all matching contacts in one DML with no Loop. Because Flow bulkifies it, it also works for bulk account updates. So if an account with 25 contacts moves office, all 25 contacts get the new address in one go. The catch is accounts with very many contacts. If an account has thousands, I'd move this to the asynchronous path or Apex, to avoid row locks and CPU limits in the user's transaction.
points: After-save on Account, only when address fields change
One Update Records with filter, no loop
Bulkified across interviews
Use async path or Apex for very large child counts

q: Users get 'Too many SOQL queries: 101' when saving a record that has flows and triggers. How do you troubleshoot?
alt: System.LimitException too many SOQL queries from flow
Flow and trigger combined hitting limits
How do you find which automation is using all the queries?
fix SOQL 101 error caused by flow
a: That error means the whole transaction, flows, triggers and other automation together, used more than 100 queries. I reproduce it with a debug log and look at the limit usage and the sequence of flow elements and trigger executions to see what repeats. The common causes are Get Records inside a loop, a trigger or flow updating records that fire other automation, and recursion where an update re-triggers the same flow or trigger. For example, an Opportunity flow updates the Account, an Account trigger then updates all its opportunities, and that fires the Opportunity flow again. I fix it by moving queries out of loops, tightening entry conditions so flows only run when relevant fields change, adding recursion guards in Apex, and moving non-urgent work to the async path or a Queueable.
points: Limit is per transaction across all automation
Debug log shows limit usage and execution sequence
Causes: queries in loops, cascading updates, recursion
Fix: tighter entry criteria, no queries in loops, async for non-urgent work

q: What is a platform event-triggered flow and when would you use it?
alt: How can a flow subscribe to a platform event?
Platform event flow use case
event driven automation in salesforce
Which user does a platform event flow run as?
a: A platform event-triggered flow starts when a message for a specific platform event is published, for example an Order_Shipped__e event sent by an external system or by Apex. It runs in its own transaction, separate from the publisher. By default it runs as the Automated Process user, which matters for record ownership and audit fields. It has no screens. I use it for event-driven, decoupled automation. Say the ERP publishes Order_Shipped__e with an order number and tracking Id. The flow reads those from $Record, updates the order to Shipped, and notifies the account owner. The ERP doesn't need to know anything about our flows. Another use is logging errors through an event, so the log survives a rollback. And because it runs as Automated Process, the Last Modified By shows that user, not a real person.
points: Starts on a published platform event message
Separate transaction from the publisher
Runs as the Automated Process user by default
Good for integrations and decoupled processing
Event fields available in $Record

q: What is Flow Orchestration and when would you use it?
alt: Explain orchestration in Flow Builder
Stages and steps in flow orchestration
How do you build a multi-user approval in Flow?
flow orchestration vs regular flow
a: Flow Orchestration coordinates a long-running business process that involves several people and systems. It's organised into stages that run in sequence, with steps inside each stage. Interactive steps assign a screen flow to a user, group or queue, who sees it as a work item. Background steps run autolaunched flows without user input. Each stage and step has entry and exit conditions, so steps can run in parallel and the process waits until conditions are met. Take employee onboarding. In stage one, HR fills in details and IT sets up a laptop in parallel. Stage two, the manager assigns a buddy, but only after both of those are done, maybe three days later. That's exactly what orchestration handles. Flow Approval Processes, Salesforce's newer approval option, are also built on orchestration.
points: Stages run in sequence; steps can run in parallel
Interactive steps assign screen flows as work items
