q: A record-triggered flow must send data to an external system when a record is created. How would you build it?
alt: Can you make a callout from a record-triggered flow?
You have uncommitted work pending error in flow
Flow integration with external API
HTTP callout from flow on record create
a: A callout can't run in the same transaction after DML has happened. That's why a direct callout from the triggering transaction gives an 'uncommitted work pending' error. So I use the run asynchronously path of an after-save flow, which runs after the record commits, in its own transaction. In that path I call the external API with the HTTP Callout action or an External Services action, using a named credential for authentication. If the payload or response needs complex handling, I use an invocable Apex method marked callout=true instead. Say a new customer account must be sent to the billing system. If billing is down, the fault path logs the failure and sets a Sync Status field to Failed. Then a scheduled flow picks up the failed records and retries them later.
points: Use the asynchronous path, not the synchronous part
HTTP Callout action, External Services or invocable Apex with callout=true
Named credentials for authentication
Fault path, sync status field and retry

q: What is integration in Salesforce and what are the main types?
alt: What do you mean by Salesforce integration?
Explain the different types of integration in Salesforce
how do you connect salesforce with other systems
What are inbound and outbound integrations?
a: Integration just means connecting Salesforce with other systems so data and processes stay in sync. I think of it in two directions. Outbound is when Salesforce calls an external system, using Apex callouts, outbound messages or events. Inbound is when an external system calls Salesforce, through the REST, SOAP, Bulk or Pub/Sub APIs, or a custom Apex REST service. Then by style there are three types. Data integration keeps records in sync, like customers matching between Salesforce and the ERP. Process integration is when a business process spans systems, like order to invoice: the order is closed in Salesforce, and the invoice gets raised in the finance system. And UI or virtualization integration is when we show external data inside Salesforce without copying it, for example showing ERP order history on the Account page with Salesforce Connect.
points: Outbound: Salesforce calls out (Apex callout, outbound message, events)
Inbound: external system calls Salesforce APIs or Apex REST/SOAP
Types: data, process, and UI/virtualization integration

q: What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
alt: REST vs SOAP API, which one would you use?
Explain REST and SOAP web services
rest versus soap difference in salesforce
Why is REST preferred over SOAP nowadays?
a: REST is an architectural style. It uses standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE on resources, and usually sends lightweight JSON, so it's simple and fast and works well for mobile and web apps. SOAP is a protocol with a strict XML envelope and a WSDL contract that defines every operation and data type. It's heavier but strongly typed, and some enterprise and legacy systems, like banks or older ERPs, still require it. In Salesforce, I consume SOAP by generating Apex classes from a WSDL, and I consume REST with HttpRequest. Say I'm connecting to a modern shipping API, that's REST, and I'll just send JSON. But if a bank's payment gateway only gives me a WSDL, I'll generate the classes and use SOAP. For new integrations I default to REST unless the other system only offers SOAP.
points: REST: HTTP verbs, resources, JSON (or XML), lightweight
SOAP: XML envelope, WSDL contract, strongly typed
Salesforce consumes SOAP via WSDL2Apex, REST via HttpRequest
Default to REST for new work

q: How do you make a REST callout from Apex?
alt: Write code for an HTTP callout in Apex
How do you call an external API from Salesforce?
explain HttpRequest Http and HttpResponse classes
Show me a GET callout using a named credential
a: I use three classes. HttpRequest holds the endpoint, method, headers, body and timeout. Http has the send method that actually makes the call. HttpResponse gives me the status code and body. For the endpoint I always use a Named Credential with the callout: prefix, so the URL and authentication aren't hard-coded and I don't need a Remote Site Setting. Say I'm fetching an exchange rate. I set the endpoint to callout:FX_API/rates?base=USD, method GET, and a timeout, because that API can be slow. After the call I check getStatusCode. If it's 200, I parse the JSON. If it's anything else, I throw a custom exception or log the error. The main thing is failures are never silent, otherwise you find out weeks later that rates haven't updated.
points: HttpRequest = what to send; Http.send = sends it; HttpResponse = result
Use callout:NamedCredential/path for endpoint and auth
Always check getStatusCode() and handle errors
Set a timeout explicitly when the API can be slow

q: What are Remote Site Settings and when do you need them?
alt: Why do we need remote site settings for a callout?
What happens if you call an endpoint without a remote site setting?
remote site setting vs named credential
Do I need remote site settings if I use named credentials?
a: Remote Site Settings is a whitelist of external URLs that Apex is allowed to call. If I make a callout to a URL that isn't registered there, I get an 'Unauthorized endpoint' error. I only need it when I put a raw URL in setEndpoint. If I use a Named Credential, the named credential itself authorizes the endpoint, so no Remote Site Setting is needed. That's one more reason I prefer named credentials. The URL and the authentication live in one place. For example, in the sandbox the named credential points to the vendor's test URL, and in production to the live URL. The Apex code is identical in both, and nobody has to edit code or add remote sites after a refresh.
points: Whitelist of URLs Apex may call
Missing entry gives 'Unauthorized endpoint' error
Not required when the callout uses a Named Credential

q: What is a Named Credential and why should you use it?
alt: Why use named credentials instead of hard-coding the URL and password?
Explain named credentials in Salesforce
what is the callout colon syntax
How do you store API credentials securely in Salesforce?
a: A Named Credential stores the endpoint URL of an external system together with how to authenticate to it. So in Apex I just write callout:My_Named_Credential/path, and Salesforce adds the authentication for me. The benefits: security, because secrets aren't in code or custom settings. Maintainability, because I can change the URL per environment without a deployment. And less code, because Salesforce can handle OAuth token refresh automatically. For example, if we call a payment API with OAuth, I don't write any code to get or refresh the token. When it expires, Salesforce gets a new one. Named credentials also work for External Services and Salesforce Connect, not just Apex. And in the current model, the authentication part lives in a separate External Credential.
points: Endpoint + authentication in one reusable setup
Apex uses 'callout:Name/path'
No secrets in code; no Remote Site Setting needed
Used by Apex, External Services and external data sources

q: What is the difference between a Named Credential and an External Credential in the current model?
alt: Explain the new named credential and external credential setup
What is a principal in an external credential?
Why does my callout fail even though the named credential is configured? permission set?
legacy named credentials vs new named credentials
a: In the current model, introduced in Winter '23, the work is split in two. The Named Credential holds the endpoint URL and callout options. The External Credential holds the authentication protocol, like OAuth 2.0, JWT, Basic, AWS Signature V4 or Custom, plus the principals. A principal is the identity used for the call. A named principal means one shared integration identity. A per-user principal means each user authenticates separately. Users only get access when a permission set or profile is mapped to that principal. That's a very common reason callouts fail right after setup. Everything looks configured, but the running user's permission set isn't mapped, so the callout has no credentials. One external credential can serve several named credentials. Legacy named credentials are deprecated, so I build new ones in this model.
points: Named Credential = URL + callout options
External Credential = auth protocol + principals
Named principal (shared) vs per-user principal
Grant principal access through a permission set
Legacy named credentials are deprecated

q: How do you pass an API key to an external system securely?
alt: How do I send an API key header without hard-coding it?
Where do you store API keys in Salesforce?
custom header in named credential with credential formula
Should I store the API key in a custom setting?
a: I don't keep API keys in code, custom labels or plain custom settings. I create an External Credential with the Custom authentication protocol, and add the key as an encrypted authentication parameter on the principal. Then I define a custom header, say X-API-Key, whose value is a $Credential formula referencing that parameter. The Named Credential points to the base URL and uses that external credential. Now the Apex just calls the named credential, and the header is added at runtime. Apex never sees or logs the key. So the key is encrypted, hidden from developers, and an admin can rotate it without a deployment. For example, if the vendor says the key leaked and issues a new one, the admin pastes it into the principal and we're done in five minutes.
points: External Credential with Custom protocol
Store key as an encrypted principal parameter
Custom header uses a $Credential formula
Apex never sees or logs the key

q: How do you parse a JSON response in Apex?
alt: How do you convert JSON into an Apex object?
Explain JSON.deserialize with a wrapper class
how to read json response from api in apex
What is a wrapper class for JSON parsing?
a: When I know the structure, I create a wrapper class whose property names match the JSON keys, and call JSON.deserialize with that class type. It's type-safe and easy to read, and nested objects or arrays just become nested classes and lists. For example, if the response is an order with a customer object and a list of items, I'd have an Order class with a Customer property and a List of Item. One thing to know: unknown keys are ignored by JSON.deserialize. JSON.deserializeStrict throws an error if the JSON has fields that aren't in the class. So if the vendor adds a new field tomorrow, deserialize keeps working, deserializeStrict breaks. For the reverse, building a request body, I use JSON.serialize. And tools that generate Apex from sample JSON can speed up creating the wrapper.
points: Wrapper class properties match JSON keys
JSON.deserialize(body, MyClass.class)
deserializeStrict fails on unknown fields
JSON.serialize for request bodies

q: When would you use JSON.deserializeUntyped, and how do you handle JSON keys that are Apex reserved words?
alt: How do you parse dynamic JSON without a wrapper class?
JSON key is a reserved keyword like currency, how to deserialize?
deserialize untyped map string object example
How do you parse JSON when the structure keeps changing?
a: I use JSON.deserializeUntyped when the structure is dynamic, or very large with only a few fields I need, or has keys I can't use as Apex property names. It returns Object, which I cast to Map<String, Object> for objects and List<Object> for arrays, then cast each value. For example, if a response has 80 fields and I only need status and id, I don't build a wrapper for all 80. For reserved words, like a key called currency or limit, one option is deserializeUntyped. Another is to replace the key in the raw string before deserializing into a wrapper, for example renaming currency to currency_x. For building JSON I use JSON.serialize, and passing true as the second argument suppresses null values.
points: deserializeUntyped returns Map<String,Object> / List<Object>
Good for dynamic or partially used payloads
Reserved keys: untyped parsing or rename key before deserialize
JSON.serialize(obj, true) drops nulls

q: What is OAuth 2.0 and how does it work at a high level?
alt: Explain OAuth in simple words
What is an access token and a refresh token?
how does oauth authentication work with salesforce
Why use OAuth instead of username and password?
a: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. It lets an application access an API on behalf of a user, or on its own behalf, without sharing the user's password with that application. The client app is registered with the authorization server. In Salesforce that's through an External Client App or Connected App, and it gets a client Id and secret, or a certificate. Through one of the OAuth flows, it gets an access token, a short-lived key sent in the Authorization Bearer header on every API call. A refresh token, when issued, lets the app get a new access token without the user logging in again. Scopes limit what the token can do. A simple example: a mobile app logs a rep in once, gets a token with just the api and refresh_token scopes, and keeps working for weeks using the refresh token, without ever seeing her password.
points: Access without sharing passwords
Access token: short-lived, sent as Bearer header
Refresh token: gets new access tokens
Scopes limit what the app can do

q: Which OAuth flows does Salesforce support and when do you use each?
alt: Explain the OAuth flows: web server, JWT, client credentials, device
Which OAuth flow would you use for server to server integration?
difference between jwt bearer flow and client credentials flow
What OAuth flow should a mobile app use?
a: I pick the flow based on who the user is and where the client runs. Web server, or authorization code with PKCE, is for apps where a real user logs in through a browser and the app can keep a secret on its server. JWT bearer is for server-to-server integration with no user interaction, signed with a certificate, acting as a pre-authorized user. Client credentials is also server-to-server, using client Id and secret with a configured run-as user. Device flow is for devices with limited input, like a TV or a CLI. User-agent was used by browser and mobile apps, but code flow with PKCE is the better choice today. Refresh token flow renews access. So, a nightly ERP sync would be JWT bearer, and a customer-facing web portal would be auth code with PKCE. I avoid username-password flow, because it's being phased out.
points: Web server (auth code + PKCE): interactive users
JWT bearer: server-to-server with certificate
Client credentials: server-to-server with run-as user
Device: limited-input devices; refresh token: renew access
Avoid username-password flow

q: How does the OAuth 2.0 JWT bearer flow work with Salesforce?
alt: Explain JWT bearer token flow step by step
How do you set up server to server integration using a certificate?
what goes in the JWT claims for salesforce
JWT flow without user login how does it work
a: The JWT bearer flow is for server-to-server integration where nobody can log in interactively. First I generate a certificate and private key, upload the certificate to the External Client App, enable JWT, and pre-authorize the integration user through admin-approved users with a permission set or profile. The external system builds a JWT. iss is the consumer key, sub is the Salesforce username, aud is the login URL, like login.salesforce.com or test.salesforce.com, and exp is short. It signs that with its private key and posts it to the token endpoint. Salesforce checks the signature with the certificate and returns an access token. No refresh token is issued, the client just creates a new JWT when needed. A common mistake: pointing a sandbox integration at login.salesforce.com in aud, when it should be test.salesforce.com.
points: Certificate uploaded to the app; private key stays with client
Claims: iss = consumer key, sub = username, aud = login URL, exp
User must be pre-authorized (admin-approved)
No refresh token; sign a new JWT each time

q: What is the OAuth client credentials flow and what is the run-as user?
alt: When would you use client credentials flow in Salesforce?
client credentials vs jwt bearer which is better
What user does the client credentials flow run as?
How do you integrate without a user context?
a: The client credentials flow lets a backend system get an access token using only the consumer key and secret, with no user login. But every Salesforce API call needs a user context. So I configure a run-as user on the External Client App, and all calls run with that user's permissions. I make it a dedicated integration user with least privilege, ideally on the Salesforce Integration license, with only the permission sets it needs. For example, if a warehouse system only updates stock levels, the run-as user only gets edit on the product inventory fields, nothing else. Compared with JWT bearer, it's simpler because there's no certificate. But the secret must be stored and rotated carefully. JWT is stronger when the client can manage a private key.
points: Consumer key + secret only, no user interaction
Run-as user defines permissions
Use a dedicated least-privilege integration user
Simpler than JWT, but secret must be protected

q: What is the difference between Connected Apps and External Client Apps?
alt: Should I create a connected app or an external client app?
Why can't I create a new connected app in my org?
What changed with connected apps in Spring 26?
external client app vs connected app
a: Both register an external application to Salesforce for OAuth access, but External Client Apps are now the recommended option. As of Spring '26, creating new connected apps is restricted by default, and you have to contact Salesforce Support if you really need one. Existing connected apps keep working. External Client Apps split developer settings, like OAuth flows, scopes and callback URL, from admin policies, like permitted users, IP relaxation and session policies. They're closed by default, so nothing exists in an org until it's installed. They can be local or packaged with second-generation packaging. They don't support the username-password flow, which is another push toward secure flows. So if a team today asks me to set up a new integration that logs in with username and password, I'd tell them to use an ECA with JWT or client credentials instead. Also note the SOAP API login() is being retired too.
points: New connected app creation restricted since Spring '26
ECA: settings (developer) vs policies (admin) separated
Closed by default; local or 2GP packaged
No username-password flow on ECAs
Existing connected apps still work; SOAP API login() is also being retired

q: How do you expose an Apex class as a REST web service?
alt: Write an Apex REST service with HttpGet
What is @RestResource and urlMapping?
how do external systems call my custom apex rest api
What is the endpoint URL for an Apex REST class?
a: I annotate a global class with @RestResource and a urlMapping, and add global static methods annotated with @HttpGet, @HttpPost, @HttpPut, @HttpPatch or @HttpDelete. The external system calls /services/apexrest/ followed by my mapping, with an OAuth access token. For example, with urlMapping '/orders/*', a GET to /services/apexrest/orders/12345 hits my @HttpGet method. I read the request from RestContext.request, like the URI or parameters, and set status codes on RestContext.response. I use with sharing and user-mode queries so the integration user's permissions are respected. And I only build custom Apex REST when the standard REST API can't do the job. A typical reason is multi-object logic in one call, like creating an account, contact and opportunity together and applying business rules.
points: @RestResource(urlMapping='/path/*') on a global class
Global static methods with @HttpGet/@HttpPost etc.
Endpoint: /services/apexrest/<mapping>
Use RestContext for request and response

q: How do you write an Apex REST POST method that reads a JSON body and returns proper status codes?
alt: HttpPost example in Apex REST with error handling
How to read request body in apex rest service
return 201 or 400 from apex rest
RestContext request requestBody example
a: For full control I make the @HttpPost method return void. I read RestContext.request.requestBody as a Blob, convert it to a string, and deserialize it into a wrapper class. Then I do the DML and write the JSON response body and status code myself: 201 for created, 400 for validation problems, 500 for unexpected errors. Say the caller posts a new order but leaves out the customer number. Instead of a raw Salesforce exception, they get a 400 with a body like code MISSING_FIELD and a clear message. Returning a consistent error structure makes life much easier for the calling team, because they can handle every error the same way. I also set the Content-Type header, and keep business logic in a separate service class so it can be reused and unit tested.

Consistent JSON error format

Create a custom SOAP service in Salesforce
how does external system get wsdl for my apex class
Apex SOAP web service example
a: I create a global class and mark the methods as webservice static. Any inner class used in the response has its fields marked with the webservice keyword so they appear in the WSDL. From the Apex class page in Setup, I generate the WSDL and share it with the other team. To authenticate, they also use the Enterprise or Partner WSDL, or an OAuth token, and pass the session in the SOAP header. The endpoint is /services/Soap/class/ followed by the class name. So for a class called InvoiceService, it's /services/Soap/class/InvoiceService. I only build this when the consumer insists on SOAP, like an older ERP that can only generate SOAP clients. Otherwise Apex REST is simpler for everyone.

How do you generate Apex from a WSDL?
calling a soap api from apex
What if the WSDL import fails in Salesforce?
a: I use Generate from WSDL on the Apex Classes page, which is WSDL2Apex. It creates a stub class with a port type and request and response element classes. So in my code, I create the port and call the operation like a normal method. For example, if the WSDL has a getCreditScore operation, I just call port.getCreditScore with the customer Id. I set the endpoint, ideally to a named credential, plus timeout and headers on the stub. The import doesn't support every WSDL feature. Some imports, complex schema constructs or multiple bindings can fail. When that happens I either simplify the WSDL, or build the XML manually with HttpRequest and the Dom or XmlStreamWriter classes. For tests I use the WebServiceMock interface.

q: What APIs does Salesforce provide and when do you use each one?
alt: Name the Salesforce APIs and their use cases
Which API should I use for loading millions of records?
REST API vs Bulk API vs SOAP API vs Streaming API
what is metadata api tooling api graphql api in salesforce
a: The REST API is my default for record CRUD and queries from web and mobile apps. The SOAP API does the same with a WSDL contract for systems that need it. Bulk API 2.0 is for large data loads or extracts, roughly anything beyond a few thousand records, processed asynchronously. Composite resources group several REST calls into one round trip. For events I use the Pub/Sub API, or the older Streaming API, to subscribe to platform events and Change Data Capture. Metadata API deploys and retrieves configuration, Tooling API works with developer artifacts like Apex classes and debug logs, and the GraphQL API lets a client fetch exactly the fields it needs across related objects in one request. For example, a nightly load of 500,000 product prices goes through Bulk API 2.0, while a mobile app updating one visit uses REST.
points: REST/SOAP: record CRUD and queries
Bulk API 2.0: large async loads and extracts
Composite: many operations in one call
Pub/Sub & Streaming: events and CDC
Metadata/Tooling: config & dev tools; GraphQL: precise queries

q: How does Bulk API 2.0 work and how is it different from Bulk API 1.0?
alt: Explain the steps of a Bulk API 2.0 ingest job
bulk api 1 vs bulk api 2
How do you upsert a large CSV using Bulk API?
When do you use Bulk API instead of REST API?
a: Bulk API 2.0 is a REST-based, asynchronous API for loading or extracting large volumes. For ingest, I create a job with the object, operation and external Id field, upload the CSV data, mark the job UploadComplete, then poll until it's complete and download the successful, failed and unprocessed results. The big difference from 1.0 is that 2.0 manages batching for me. I don't create or size batches myself, and query jobs handle chunking automatically. But 2.0 only supports CSV, while 1.0 also supports XML and JSON and lets me choose serial or parallel mode. Say I upsert 300,000 contacts and 1,200 fail. I always process the failedResults file, fix those rows and reload them. I use Bulk API when volumes are big enough that REST would waste API calls.

2.0 handles batching and chunking automatically

q: What is the Composite API and how do you create related records in one call?
alt: Explain composite request with referenceId
How can I create an account and contact in a single API call?
composite vs batch vs sobject tree vs collections
How do you reduce the number of API calls from an external system?
a: The Composite resource lets a client send up to 25 subrequests in one call. Later subrequests can reference results from earlier ones with the @{referenceId.field} syntax. Say a website signs up a new customer. In one call I create the Account with referenceId newAcc, then create a Contact with AccountId set to @{newAcc.id}. With allOrNone set to true, if the contact fails, the account rolls back too, so I don't end up with an orphan account. The whole call counts as one API request against limits. Related options: Composite Batch for independent subrequests, sObject Tree for nested record trees, and sObject Collections for up to 200 records of one type in one call. For very large related sets, Composite Graph is the next step.
points: Up to 25 subrequests in one call
@{refId.id} passes values between subrequests
allOrNone for transactional behavior

q: What is the difference between the Streaming API and the Pub/Sub API?
alt: PushTopic vs platform events vs Pub/Sub API
Should I use CometD or Pub/Sub API to subscribe to events?
what is the pub sub api in salesforce
How do external systems listen to Salesforce events?
a: Both let external clients receive events from Salesforce, but the technology is different. The Streaming API is based on CometD long polling over HTTP. It supports PushTopic events, generic events, platform events and Change Data Capture. PushTopic and generic events are legacy and aren't being enhanced. The Pub/Sub API is the newer interface, built on gRPC and HTTP/2 with Avro-encoded payloads. A client can both publish and subscribe through one API. It uses a pull model with flow control, so the client asks for as many events as it can handle, and it's more efficient for high volumes. For example, if a data warehouse needs to consume thousands of change events an hour, with Pub/Sub it can ask for 100 at a time and not get flooded. For new external subscribers, I use the Pub/Sub API.
points: Streaming API: CometD, PushTopic/generic are legacy
Pub/Sub API: gRPC, HTTP/2, Avro
Pub/Sub can publish and subscribe
Client-controlled flow, better for high volume

q: How do subscribers avoid missing events when using platform events or Change Data Capture with the Pub/Sub API?
alt: What is a replay Id and how do you use it?
What happens to events if my subscriber is down?
event retention period for platform events
How do you resume from where you left off after a subscriber crash?
a: Every event has a replay Id, and high-volume platform events and change events are retained for 72 hours. My subscriber stores the replay Id of the last event it processed successfully. If it restarts, it subscribes with that replay Id and gets everything after it, instead of only new events or everything in the window. For example, if the subscriber crashes at 2 a.m. and comes back at 6, it resumes from its saved replay Id and catches up on those four hours. But if it's down longer than the 72-hour window, those events are gone. So I need a fallback, like a reconciliation job or querying changed records. With the Pub/Sub API, managed subscriptions, still in beta, can let Salesforce track the committed replay position for me. And because replays can deliver an event again, processing must be idempotent.
points: Persist last processed replay Id
Retention: 72 hours for high-volume events and CDC
Resubscribe from stored replay Id after downtime
Have a reconciliation fallback; make handlers idempotent

q: What is the Salesforce GraphQL API and when would you use it?
alt: Explain GraphQL in Salesforce
GraphQL vs REST API in Salesforce
Can you do mutations with Salesforce GraphQL?
how to use graphql in lwc
a: The GraphQL API lets a client ask for exactly the fields it needs, including related objects, in one request. So it avoids over-fetching and multiple REST round trips. It's built on the UI API, which means it respects field-level security and sharing. In LWC I use the lightning/uiGraphQLApi wire adapter, and external apps call the graphql endpoint under the REST data path. Mutations to create, update and delete records are generally available from API version 66.0, after being in beta. Say a mobile screen needs an account's name, its five latest opportunities, and each opportunity's owner name. With REST that's several calls. With GraphQL it's one query that returns just those fields. I'd use it for UI-driven or mobile scenarios like that, and stay with REST or Bulk for heavy data movement.

Respects FLS and sharing (UI API based)
LWC: lightning/uiGraphQLApi
Mutations GA from API v66.0

q: What are Platform Events and when would you use them?
alt: Explain platform events in Salesforce
What is an event-driven architecture in Salesforce?
platform event use case example
How do you publish and subscribe to platform events?
a: Platform Events are custom event messages, defined like an object with the __e suffix, and used for event-driven integration. A publisher fires an event and doesn't know or care who listens. Subscribers react to it. So systems are loosely coupled. I can publish from Apex, Flow or an external system through the API. I can subscribe with an Apex trigger, a platform event-triggered Flow, LWC using empApi, or externally through the Pub/Sub API. For example, when an order is ready, Salesforce publishes Order_Ready__e. The ERP picks it up and starts fulfilment, and a flow in Salesforce emails the customer. Neither one knows about the other. q: How do you handle failures inside a platform event trigger, including retries?

How do you retry a failed platform event trigger?

platform event subscriber keeps failing what do you do
a: For transient errors like record locks, I throw EventBus.RetryableException. Salesforce then re-runs the trigger with the same batch of events. I check the retries count on the trigger context, so after a few attempts I stop and log the failure instead. Retries are limited, so after the last attempt the events need to be handled another way. For example, if a batch of 2,000 events hits a lock on the first try, a retry usually works. But if the problem is bad data, retrying five times won't help, so I log it. For large batches I can call setResumeCheckpoint with the replay Id of the last processed event. Then if the trigger fails at event 1,500, processing resumes after the checkpoint, not from the start. And because callouts aren't allowed directly in the trigger, I enqueue a Queueable for any outbound call.

q: What is an Outbound Message and what are its limitations?

a: An Outbound Message is a no-code way to send a SOAP XML message with selected field values of a record to an external endpoint. The receiver must send back an acknowledgement. If it doesn't, Salesforce keeps retrying, with increasing intervals, for up to 24 hours. Since Workflow Rules reached end of support at the end of 2025, I trigger outbound messages from a record-triggered Flow. The limitations: it's SOAP only, it includes fields from one object only, the receiver must implement the WSDL Salesforce generates, and messages can arrive more than once or out of order. So the receiver must be idempotent. For example, if the same order message arrives twice, the ERP should update the order, not create a second one. For anything more complex, like fields from the account and its order lines, I use an Apex callout or platform events.

q: What are the standard Salesforce integration patterns?

Which integration pattern would you use for real-time sync?
a: Salesforce describes a few core patterns. Remote Process Invocation, Request and Reply: Salesforce calls a system and waits for the answer, like a credit check. Remote Process Invocation, Fire and Forget: Salesforce sends a message and carries on, using platform events, outbound messages or an async callout. Batch Data Synchronization: bulk loads or extracts on a schedule, usually through middleware and Bulk API. Remote Call-In: an external system creates or updates Salesforce data through the APIs. UI Update Based on Data Changes: the UI refreshes when data changes, using streaming events. Data Virtualization: show external data without storing it, using Salesforce Connect. I choose by timing, volume and who starts it. For example, a nightly product catalogue load is batch sync, while an ERP pushing order status back into Salesforce is remote call-in.

q: When do you choose request-reply versus fire-and-forget?

When is a synchronous callout acceptable?

a: I use request-reply when the user or process needs the answer right now to continue. Like validating an address, checking credit before saving an order, or getting a live price. The external system has to be fast and reliable, because the user is waiting and callout timeouts apply. I use fire-and-forget when Salesforce only needs to notify another system and doesn't need the result straight away, like sending a new order to the ERP. That's done with platform events, outbound messages, or an asynchronous callout. It's more resilient, because a slow or down target doesn't block users. Say the ERP is down for an hour. With fire-and-forget, reps keep closing orders and they flow through later. With request-reply they'd all be stuck. If a result is needed later, the target can call back into Salesforce.

For authentication, I register an External Client App with JWT bearer or client credentials, and a dedicated integration user with least-privilege permission sets. I give each object an External Id field so the caller can upsert, and retries don't create duplicates. For example, if the ERP sends invoice INV-1001, times out, and sends it again, the upsert on ERP_Invoice_Id just updates the same record. I also think about the triggers and flows that will fire on incoming data, API limit consumption, error responses the caller can act on, and monitoring through login history and API usage.

q: What is Salesforce Connect and how do External Objects work?

what is the odata adapter in salesforce connect
a: Salesforce Connect lets me show and work with data that lives in another system, without copying it into Salesforce. I define an External Data Source, using an OData 2.0 or 4.0 adapter, the cross-org adapter for another Salesforce org, or a custom adapter written with the Apex Connector Framework. Then I sync to create External Objects, with the __x suffix. When a user opens a record or related list, Salesforce queries the external system in real time. For example, ten years of invoices can stay in the ERP, and reps still see them as a related list on the Account. External objects can relate to standard objects through external and indirect lookups. The limitations compared with custom objects: no standard triggers, limited reporting and automation, and performance that depends on the external system. q: When would you use middleware like MuleSoft instead of point-to-point integration?

a: Point-to-point is fine when there are one or two systems, low volume and simple mapping, like Salesforce calling a single payment API. Middleware like MuleSoft makes sense when many systems need the same data, when transformations and orchestration are complex, or when I need reliable queuing, retries, guaranteed delivery and central monitoring. It decouples systems. Say customer data goes from Salesforce to the ERP, the billing system and the data warehouse. If the ERP is replaced, only the middleware mapping changes, not three separate integrations in Salesforce. MuleSoft's API-led approach adds reusable system, process and experience APIs. It also protects Salesforce limits by handling bulk processing and throttling outside the platform. The trade-off is licensing cost and one more platform to run.

q: What are the callout limits and timeouts in Apex?
alt: How many callouts can I make in one transaction?
What is the default and maximum callout timeout?
callout governor limits salesforce
Why is my callout timing out after 10 seconds?
a: One Apex transaction can make up to 100 callouts. The default timeout for each callout is 10 seconds. I can set it with setTimeout anywhere from 1 millisecond up to 120 seconds. The cumulative timeout across all callouts in a transaction is also capped at 120 seconds. So if I make three calls that each take 50 seconds, the third one will fail, even though each call is under the per-callout max. Also, I can't make a callout after DML or other pending work in the same transaction, and callouts from triggers must be asynchronous. In Developer Edition orgs there's also a limit on concurrent callouts to external endpoints. For slow APIs I move the work to Queueable or Batch, and from the UI I can use a Continuation.

Default timeout 10 s, max 120 s per callout
120 s cumulative per transaction
No callouts after uncommitted DML

q: You get the error 'You have uncommitted work pending. Please commit or rollback before calling out'. How do you fix it?
alt: callout after DML error how to resolve
uncommitted work pending error
Why can't I make a callout after inserting a record?
how to do a callout after dml in apex
a: Salesforce doesn't allow a callout after DML in the same transaction, because the database transaction would stay open while waiting on an external system. The simplest fix is to reorder: make the callout first, then do the DML with the response. For example, call the tax API, get the tax amount, then insert the order with it. If the DML has to happen first, I move the callout into a separate transaction. That's a Queueable with Database.AllowsCallouts, a future method with callout=true, or a platform event whose subscriber enqueues the callout. In test classes, I do the setup DML before Test.startTest and the callout after it. And the same rule applies to pending async jobs and emails queued earlier in the transaction, not just DML.

Fix 1: callout first, then DML
Fix 2: move callout to Queueable/future
In tests: DML before Test.startTest()

q: How do you make a callout from a trigger?
alt: Can you make a callout directly from a trigger?
Callout from trigger is not allowed, what is the workaround?
future method callout true example
trigger to call external api on insert
a: A trigger can't make a synchronous callout, because it runs inside the database transaction. So I collect the record Ids in the trigger and hand them to an asynchronous method. Either a future method with callout=true, or, my preference, a Queueable that implements Database.AllowsCallouts, because it accepts complex types, can be monitored, and can chain or use a finalizer. I pass Ids rather than sObjects to a future method, and re-query inside the async method so I send the latest committed data. I also bulkify. Say a data load inserts 200 accounts. I enqueue one job with all 200 Ids, not 200 separate jobs, one per record.

q: Can you make a callout after rolling back DML to a savepoint?
alt: Database.releaseSavepoint callout
All active savepoints must be released before making callouts error
savepoint and callout in the same transaction
dry run DML then call external system
a: On recent API versions, yes, but only with a specific sequence. If I roll back all uncommitted DML to a savepoint and then explicitly call Database.releaseSavepoint, the transaction has no pending work, and the callout is allowed. If savepoints are still active, the callout fails with an error saying all active savepoints must be released. Before API version 60.0, any callout after creating a savepoint throws an exception, full stop. Where this helps is a dry-run pattern. Say I need to know what a quote total would be after all the pricing automation runs. I insert the quote lines temporarily, read the calculated total, roll back to the savepoint, release it, and then call the external tax API with that total. One gotcha: after releasing, I can't roll back to that savepoint anymore.

q: How do you handle errors and logging in integrations?

how do you log integration failures in salesforce

a: I classify errors first. Transient ones, like timeouts, 429 or 5xx, can be retried. Permanent ones, like a 400 validation error or bad data, need a person or a data fix. Retrying a 400 ten times just gives you ten failures. Every callout is wrapped in try-catch with status code checks, and failures go to a custom Integration Log object with the endpoint, a payload reference, status, error and the related record Id. If the transaction might roll back, I publish a logging platform event set to Publish Immediately, so the log survives. Otherwise the rollback wipes out the very log that explains it. I never log secrets or full sensitive payloads. On top, a dashboard or alert shows failures, and a retry mechanism or a reprocess button handles the transient ones.

q: What is idempotency and how do you make an integration idempotent?
alt: Explain idempotent APIs
How do you prevent duplicate records when a message is retried?
idempotency key in rest api
the same order came twice from the external system what do you do
a: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice gives the same result as doing it once. It matters because retries, redelivered events and outbound message retries all cause duplicates. Inbound, I use upsert on an External Id, so a repeated message updates the same record instead of creating a new one. Outbound, I send a unique key, like the Salesforce record Id plus a version, or an idempotency key header if the target supports it, so the receiver can ignore duplicates. For events, I store processed message or replay Ids and skip ones I've already seen. And I prefer absolute values over incremental ones. For example, 'set status to Shipped' is safe to apply twice. 'Add one to quantity' isn't, because if the message comes twice, quantity goes up by two.
points: Same request twice = same result
Inbound: upsert on external Id
Outbound: idempotency key / unique message Id
Track processed event Ids; avoid incremental updates

In Setup, System Overview and Company Information show usage, and API Usage Notifications can email admins when a threshold is crossed, say 80 percent. To find who's using the calls, I check the API usage report by user or app, and Event Monitoring logs, then look at login history for the integration users. For example, if usage suddenly doubles, the report usually shows one integration user making most of the calls, often a new sync job polling too often. In Apex, the OrgLimits class gives the same data.

q: How do certificates and mutual TLS work for Salesforce integrations?

a: For outbound mutual TLS, the external server wants Salesforce to present a client certificate. I create or import a certificate in Certificate and Key Management, share the public certificate with the other team, and reference it on the Named Credential, or with setClientCertificateName on HttpRequest. For inbound mutual TLS, the client must present a certificate when calling Salesforce. I upload the client's CA-signed certificate as a mutual authentication certificate, give the integration user the Enforce SSL/TLS Mutual Authentication permission, and the client connects on port 8443. Certificates are also used to sign JWTs. The thing I always stress is expiry. Say a certificate was set up two years ago and expires on a Sunday. On Monday every call fails, and nobody remembers who set it up. So I track expiry dates and set reminders well ahead.

a: An External ID is a custom field marked as External ID, usually also unique, that stores the record's identifier from another system, like the ERP customer number. It's indexed, so lookups are fast. Its main value is upsert. The external system sends records with its own Id, and Salesforce updates the match or inserts a new one, without knowing Salesforce Ids. I can also set relationships by External ID. For example, the ERP sends a contact with Account ERP number C-1001, and Salesforce links it to the right account without the ERP ever knowing the account's Salesforce Id. This makes integrations idempotent. If the same customer message is sent twice because of a retry, the second one just updates the existing record instead of creating a duplicate.

Then I confirm the running user has principal access through the permission set, and for OAuth, that the principal has actually authenticated. I check certificate names and expiry, IP allowlisting on the external side, and then the debug log and the raw response body for the exact error.

q: How do you make a callout from a Queueable and handle paginated responses?

a: I implement Queueable and Database.AllowsCallouts. Each execution fetches one page, upserts the records on an External Id with partial success allowed, and if the response has a next page token, it enqueues a new instance of itself with that token. That keeps each page inside its own set of governor limits, like heap, CPU and the callout timeout. Say the API returns 500 products per page and there are 20 pages. That's 20 chained jobs, each handling 500 records with fresh limits, instead of one job trying to hold 10,000 in memory. In tests I skip chaining, since chained jobs can't run in test context. For very large imports, I'd rather use middleware with the Bulk API, but this works well for moderate volumes.

q: How do you handle very large API responses or payloads without hitting heap limits?

a: First, I avoid pulling huge payloads in one call. I ask the API for pagination, filters like 'modified since last sync', or only the fields I need. Then I process page by page in async Apex, where the heap limit is 12 MB instead of 6 MB, using a chained Queueable or a Batch. When parsing, I deserialize into lean wrapper classes with only the properties I need, or use JSONParser to stream through tokens without building the full object tree. And I release references to the raw body once it's parsed, so I'm not holding the string and the objects at the same time. For example, if a customer response has 200 fields and I need six, my wrapper has six. For truly large volumes, the right answer is usually that the other system or middleware pushes data in through Bulk API 2.0 instead.

How do you call an external API when a record is updated?
trigger plus queueable callout example
a: I'd use an after update trigger that calls a handler. The handler collects only accounts where the synced fields actually changed, so unrelated edits don't cause callouts. For example, if the ERP only cares about name, address and tax number, a rep editing the account description shouldn't send anything. The handler enqueues one Queueable per trigger chunk that implements Database.AllowsCallouts, not one per record. The Queueable re-queries the accounts, sends them in one bulk request through a Named Credential, and writes a sync status back. Because the status fields aren't in the changed-field check, that update doesn't trigger another callout, so there's no recursion. I'd also attach a finalizer for retries, and store the ERP Id that comes back.
points: After update trigger, only on relevant field changes
One Queueable per chunk, not per record
Bulk payload through Named Credential
Write back sync status without recursion

q: What could go wrong with a trigger-to-Queueable real-time sync at scale, and how would you design around it?
alt: Problems with queueable callouts during data loads
What happens when someone mass updates 50,000 accounts and each fires a callout?
too many queueable jobs added to the queue error
How do you make real-time sync scale?
a: The risks show up during bulk updates. A large load runs the trigger in chunks of 200, so one transaction can try to enqueue many jobs and hit the limit of 50 Queueables per transaction. And enqueuing from a batch or another Queueable is even more limited. Many parallel jobs can also flood the ERP, causing rate limiting, ordering problems and duplicate updates. Picture a data fix that updates 100,000 accounts. That would mean hundreds of jobs hammering the ERP at once. To design around it, I'd mark records as pending and let a scheduled or chained job drain them in controlled batches. Or I'd publish platform events or use Change Data Capture and let middleware handle throttling and ordering. I'd add a bypass switch for data migrations, and make the ERP side idempotent.
points: Bulk loads can exceed enqueue limits
Parallel jobs flood the target; ordering issues
Pending flag + controlled drain job
CDC/events + middleware for throttling
Bypass switch for migrations

q: An external system needs to send orders with line items into Salesforce. How would you build the Apex REST endpoint?
alt: Receive orders from an external system using upsert on external Id
Apex REST service to create order and order lines
How do you avoid duplicate orders when the external system retries?
inbound order integration code
a: I'd build an @HttpPost Apex REST service that deserializes the payload into wrapper classes, then upserts the order on its external order Id and links the account by the account's ERP external Id, so no Salesforce Ids are needed. Line items are upserted on a composite external Id, order number plus line number, so resending the same order updates instead of duplicating. I use a savepoint so the order and lines succeed or fail together, and return a clear status code with the Salesforce Id or the error.
points: Upsert parent on external order Id
Relate account by its external Id
Lines keyed by orderId-lineNo
Savepoint for all-or-nothing; clear responses

q: Would you use a custom Apex REST service or standard APIs to receive orders from an external system?
alt: custom apex rest vs composite api for inbound data
When should I build a custom endpoint instead of using standard REST API?
design inbound order integration
Is Apex REST better than sObject collections?
a: I start with standard APIs, because Salesforce maintains them, they need no code, and they respect security automatically. sObject Collections or Composite Graph with upsert on External Ids handles an order with its lines as an all-or-nothing unit very well. I build a custom Apex REST service when the caller's contract can't change and needs mapping, when there's business logic or validation that must run before saving, when several unrelated objects must be handled in one call, or when I want to hide the internal data model. For example, if an old e-commerce platform sends one fixed JSON format and the vendor won't change it, a custom endpoint can map it. If MuleSoft sits in between, it usually does the mapping and calls the standard APIs, so custom Apex isn't needed. Either way, I upsert on External Ids.
points: Default: standard APIs (collections, composite graph)
Custom Apex REST: fixed contract, logic, hide data model
Middleware can do mapping instead
Either way: upsert on external Ids

q: How would you design a nightly sync of one million records from an external system into Salesforce?
alt: Nightly bulk sync of 1M records design
How do you load millions of records every night?
large data volume integration design
bulk data synchronization pattern example
a: I'd use the batch data synchronization pattern, with middleware or an ETL tool calling Bulk API 2.0. First, send only deltas using a last-modified watermark instead of the full million every night. Usually only a few thousand records actually change in a day, so that's a big saving. Load with upsert on an External Id, so reruns are safe. Load parents before children, and sort children by parent to reduce record lock contention. For example, load accounts first, then contacts sorted by account, so two batches aren't fighting over the same account. For heavy automation, I'd use a bypass setting for the integration user, or move logic into async processing, so triggers and flows don't slow the load. Afterwards, the middleware reads failed results, retries transient failures and reports the rest. I'd schedule it outside business hours and monitor API and Bulk usage.
points: Bulk API 2.0 via middleware/ETL
Delta loads with a watermark
Upsert on external Id; parents before children
Bypass or defer heavy automation
Process failed results; monitor limits

q: How would you send a large number of records from Salesforce to an external system every night?
alt: Batch Apex with callouts example
Database.AllowsCallouts in batch class
nightly outbound sync using batch apex
Can batch apex make callouts?
a: If Salesforce has to push the data, I'd use Batch Apex that implements Database.AllowsCallouts, scheduled at night. The start method selects records flagged as pending sync. Each execute sends its scope in one bulk request, and I set the scope size so the payload and the callout count stay within limits. Say 50,000 orders are pending and the target accepts 200 per request. A scope of 200 gives one callout per execute. I mark records synced or failed in each execute, and use Database.Stateful to count failures, so the finish method can send a summary like '49,880 sent, 120 failed'. If the target can pull instead, a middleware job using a Bulk API 2.0 query is often better for very large volumes.
points: Batchable + Database.AllowsCallouts
Query only records pending sync
One bulk request per execute; tune scope size
Stateful counters and summary in finish

q: The external system is sometimes down. How do you retry failed callouts automatically?
alt: Retry callouts using queueable and transaction finalizer
What is a transaction finalizer and how do you use it for retries?
external API is down how do you handle it in apex
exponential backoff retry in salesforce
a: I make the callout in a Queueable and attach a Transaction Finalizer with System.attachFinalizer. If the callout throws, say on a timeout, or a 5xx that I convert into an exception, the finalizer still runs and sees UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION. It then re-enqueues the job with an attempt counter and a delay, using System.enqueueJob with a delay in minutes for backoff. For example, first retry after 1 minute, then 5, then 10. A finalizer can enqueue one job, and a failing Queueable can be re-enqueued by its finalizer up to five times in a row. So after my maximum attempts, I write a failure log and alert someone, instead of retrying forever.
points: System.attachFinalizer in Queueable execute
Finalizer runs even after unhandled exceptions
Re-enqueue with delay for backoff
Max five consecutive re-enqueues; then log and alert

q: How would you design a resilient outbound integration if the target system can be down for hours?
alt: Design for guaranteed delivery when the external system has outages
external system down for a long time, how do you avoid losing data?
dead letter queue in salesforce
retry with platform events and logs
a: Short retries aren't enough for long outages, so I make every outbound change durable. When a record changes, I write it to a sync queue, either a custom staging object or a status field, or I publish a platform event that a subscriber turns into a queue record. A scheduled job picks up pending items, calls out with retries and backoff, and marks them sent, failed-retryable or failed-permanent. After a maximum number of attempts, items go to a dead-letter state with an alert and a reprocess button. Say the ERP is down for six hours overnight. All the changes just pile up in the queue, and when it comes back they go out. Because items are replayed after the outage, I process them in order per record and keep the target idempotent. With middleware, its persistent queues handle much of this.
points: Persist outbound changes in a queue/staging object
Scheduled processor with backoff retries
Dead-letter state + alert + reprocess
Ordering per record and idempotent target

q: How would you secure a callout to an external API that requires a JWT?
alt: Secure a callout using JWT bearer token
Auth.JWT and Auth.JWS example
How do you sign a JWT in Apex?
external credential with JWT bearer flow
a: My first choice is declarative. An External Credential using OAuth 2.0 with the JWT bearer flow, or the JWT protocol, with the signing certificate from Certificate and Key Management, and a Named Credential on top. Then the Apex just calls the named credential, and Salesforce mints and refreshes the tokens. If I need custom claims or the setup doesn't fit, I can do it in code. Auth.JWT builds the claims, Auth.JWS signs it with the certificate, and Auth.JWTBearerTokenExchange swaps it for an access token. That last one needs the token URL allowed as a remote site. I'd cache the token in Platform Cache until it expires. Say the token lasts an hour and we make 500 calls in that hour. That's one token exchange instead of 500. And I never hard-code keys.
points: Prefer External Credential with JWT bearer
Signing cert in Certificate and Key Management
Code option: Auth.JWT, Auth.JWS, JWTBearerTokenExchange
Cache tokens; never hard-code keys

q: How would you design an integration between Salesforce and SAP?
alt: Salesforce SAP integration approach
How do you sync customers, orders and invoices with SAP?
integrate salesforce with sap erp design
Which tools would you use to connect SAP and Salesforce?
a: I'd start by defining the system of record per object: typically SAP owns materials, pricing, credit and invoices, Salesforce owns leads, opportunities and service, and customers need a clear ownership rule. Then I'd pick the pattern per flow: order submission as fire-and-forget through middleware, credit or stock checks as request-reply, and master data as nightly or near-real-time sync. Middleware like MuleSoft or SAP Integration Suite usually sits in between, because SAP speaks IDocs, BAPIs, RFCs and OData and mapping is complex. For showing SAP data without copying, I'd expose OData services and use Salesforce Connect. SAP numbers become external Ids in Salesforce, and I'd plan error queues and reconciliation reports.
points: System of record per object
Pattern per flow: async orders, sync checks, batch master data
Middleware for IDoc/BAPI/OData mapping
Salesforce Connect over SAP OData for virtualization
SAP keys as external Ids; reconciliation

q: How do you write a test class for an Apex callout?
alt: Test HTTP callout using HttpCalloutMock
Why do callouts fail in test classes?
Test.setMock example
how to mock api response in apex test
a: Test methods can't make real callouts. So I implement the HttpCalloutMock interface, whose respond method returns a fake HttpResponse with the status code and body I want. In the test I call Test.setMock with the mock, call the code under test, and assert on the results. For example, for a weather service, one mock returns 200 with a temperature in the JSON, and I assert the record got that temperature. A second mock returns 500, and I assert that an error log was created and nothing was overwritten. That way the error handling is covered too, not just the happy path. For fixed responses, I can also use StaticResourceCalloutMock with a JSON file stored as a static resource.
points: Implement HttpCalloutMock.respond
Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mock)
Test success and failure status codes
StaticResourceCalloutMock for file-based responses

q: How do you test an Apex REST service?
alt: Write a test class for @RestResource
How do you set RestContext in a test?
test apex rest post method
unit test for inbound api
a: I don't need an HTTP call; I build a RestRequest with the URI, method and JSON body, assign it and a new RestResponse to RestContext, and then call the static method directly. Afterwards I assert on the response status code and body, and query the database to confirm the records. For an upsert endpoint I call it twice with the same payload to prove it's idempotent and doesn't create duplicates. I also add a negative test with a bad payload to cover the error branch.
points: Build RestRequest and RestResponse manually
Assign to RestContext, call method directly
Assert status code and database state
Call twice to prove idempotency

q: How do you test a SOAP callout generated from a WSDL?
alt: WebServiceMock example
test class for wsdl2apex generated class
How do you mock a SOAP response in Apex?
doInvoke method in webservicemock
a: For WSDL2Apex classes, I implement the WebServiceMock interface. Its doInvoke method receives the request object and a response map. I build the generated response element class, set its fields, and put it into the map under the key response_x. In the test I call Test.setMock with WebServiceMock.class, then call the generated port method, or my service class that uses it, and assert on the result. For example, if the stub has getCreditScore, my mock builds the generated response element with score 750, and I assert my service returns 750. A common mistake is trying HttpCalloutMock here. It doesn't work, because the generated stub uses WebServiceCallout.invoke, not Http.send.
points: Implement WebServiceMock.doInvoke
Put generated response element in map as 'response_x'
Test.setMock(WebServiceMock.class, mock)
HttpCalloutMock is for HTTP, not WSDL2Apex

q: How do you test a Queueable that makes a callout after a trigger inserts or updates records?
alt: Test class for trigger plus queueable callout
uncommitted work pending in test class
how does Test.stopTest run queueable jobs
testing async callouts in apex
a: I insert the test data before Test.startTest, so that DML belongs to the setup. Then I set the HttpCalloutMock, call Test.startTest, do the update that fires the trigger, and call Test.stopTest. stopTest forces the enqueued Queueable to run synchronously, including its mocked callout. After stopTest, I query the records and assert the sync status was written. For example, I insert an account in setup, then inside start and stop I change its billing city, and after stopTest I check the Sync Status field says Synced. Keeping the DML before startTest avoids the uncommitted work pending error in tests. And setting the mock is required, otherwise the callout throws.
points: Setup DML before Test.startTest()
Set mock, then start/stop test around the action
stopTest runs queued async jobs
Assert the written-back results

q: Sales users need to see live invoice data from the ERP on the Account page, but you don't want to store it in Salesforce. What do you do?
alt: Show ERP invoices in Salesforce without importing them
display external data on a record page in real time
We don't want to copy invoice data into Salesforce, options?
data virtualization scenario
a: This is the data virtualization pattern. If the ERP or middleware can expose invoices as an OData service, I'd use Salesforce Connect to create an Invoice external object. I relate it to Account with an indirect lookup on the account's ERP number, so invoices show up as a related list on the account without any code. So a rep opens the account and sees last month's invoices straight from the ERP, and nothing is stored in Salesforce. If OData isn't available, I'd build an LWC that calls an Apex method making a callout through a Named Credential, cached for a short time. I'd set expectations first, though. External data can't drive normal triggers, reporting on it is limited, and the page depends on the ERP being available and fast.
points: Salesforce Connect + external object
Indirect lookup on account ERP number
Alternative: LWC + Apex callout with caching
Set expectations on reporting and availability

q: An external system calls Salesforce once per record and you are running out of daily API calls. How do you fix it?
alt: We keep hitting the API request limit, what do you do?
external system makes too many api calls
reduce API consumption from integration
REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error from integration
a: First I find the consumer, using API usage reports, Event Monitoring and login history by integration user. Then I cut down the calls. I switch single-record calls to sObject Collections, which handle up to 200 records per call, or Composite for related operations. That alone can turn 10,000 calls into 50. I move large volumes to Bulk API 2.0. And I replace polling with Change Data Capture or platform events through the Pub/Sub API, so the system only hears about real changes instead of asking every minute. I'd also have them cache reference data and query only changed records. If volume is still legitimately high, buying more API capacity is an option, but only after fixing the design. And I'd set API usage notifications to catch it early next time.
points: Identify consumer via usage reports and Event Monitoring
Batch calls: sObject Collections / Composite
Bulk API 2.0 for volume
Replace polling with CDC/events
Notifications; buy capacity only if needed

q: An integration suddenly starts failing with INVALID_SESSION_ID. What do you check?
alt: invalid session id error in integration
access token expired error
integration works for a while then fails with 401
session expired invalid in api call
a: INVALID_SESSION_ID means the access token is no longer valid. Common reasons: it expired after the session timeout, an admin revoked it or the session was logged out, or the token belongs to another org or My Domain. For example, someone refreshes the sandbox and the integration is still holding a token from before the refresh. I'd check that the client handles a 401 by getting a new token, through the refresh token flow, or for JWT and client credentials just by requesting a new token, and then retrying once. I'd also check the app's session and refresh token policies, whether the integration user is frozen or deactivated, and login history for failed attempts.
points: Token expired, revoked, or wrong org
Client must refresh/request a new token and retry
Check app session and refresh token policies
Check user status and login history

q: A user clicks a button to check a customer's credit score from an external service before saving an opportunity. How would you build it?
alt: Real-time credit check from Salesforce
request reply integration example
call external API from LWC button and show result
synchronous callout from lightning component
a: This is request-reply, because the user needs the answer to carry on. I'd build an LWC button that calls an @AuraEnabled Apex method. The method makes the callout through a Named Credential with a sensible timeout and returns a simple result object, like score and status. In the component I show a spinner, then either the score or a friendly error if the service is slow or down, and only then let the user save. So the rep clicks Check Credit, waits a couple of seconds, sees 720 - Approved, and saves. If the service is often slow, I'd use a Continuation. A no-code alternative is External Services called from a screen flow. I'd log failures, and avoid storing sensitive data I don't need.
points: Request-reply: LWC calls @AuraEnabled Apex
Named Credential + sensible timeout
Spinner and friendly error handling
Continuation or External Services as options

q: Data from two systems keeps overwriting each other in a bidirectional sync. How would you solve it?
alt: bidirectional sync conflict resolution
integration loop where updates bounce back and forth
How do you prevent infinite update loops between Salesforce and an ERP?
two systems updating the same field
a: First I define ownership. Ideally each field has one system of record. So Salesforce owns some fields and the ERP owns others, and each side only sends what it owns. For example, Salesforce owns the account's phone and the ERP owns the credit limit. To stop echo loops, I skip outbound sync when the change was made by the integration user, or compare a last-synced hash or timestamp so unchanged data isn't sent back. Otherwise the ERP updates a record, Salesforce sees a change and sends it back, the ERP sees a change, and it keeps bouncing. Where both sides can edit the same field, I pick a rule like last-writer-wins using a reliable modified timestamp, or send conflicts to a review queue. I also make sure updates are idempotent and ordered per record.
points: Field-level system of record
Ignore changes made by the integration user
Compare hash or timestamp to skip echoes
Explicit conflict rule or review queue

q: The business wants the ERP to know immediately when an Opportunity is Closed Won, without writing Apex. How would you do it?
alt: no code integration when opportunity is closed won
Send data to an external system from Flow
declarative integration options in salesforce
notify erp on closed won using flow
a: There are good declarative options. If the ERP or middleware can subscribe to events, I'd have a record-triggered Flow publish a platform event, like Deal_Won__e, when the stage changes to Closed Won, carrying the fields the ERP needs, like amount, account number and products. The middleware subscribes through the Pub/Sub API. If the ERP exposes a REST API with an OpenAPI spec, I could register it with External Services and call it from an asynchronous path in the record-triggered flow. For a simple SOAP receiver, the flow can send an Outbound Message, which retries for up to 24 hours. Workflow Rules and Process Builder are end of support, so Flow is the tool. All three options mean an admin can maintain it without Apex.
points: Flow publishes a platform event
External Services action on async path
Outbound Message from Flow for SOAP receivers
Use Flow, not Workflow/Process Builder

q: You need to connect Salesforce to a new third-party REST API. What steps would you follow?
alt: Walk me through setting up a new API integration
steps to integrate salesforce with an external rest api
How do you start a new integration project?
first time api integration checklist
a: I start by understanding the API documentation: endpoints, authentication method, request and response formats, rate limits and error codes. I test it in Postman first, so I know exactly what a good and a bad response look like before writing code. Then I set up an External Credential for the auth and a Named Credential for the base URL, with permission set access for the users who'll trigger it. I write a small Apex service class with wrapper classes for the JSON, proper status code handling and logging, called asynchronously if it starts from a trigger. Say it's a shipping rates API. In Postman I'd see it returns 429 after a burst of calls, so I'd handle that in the code. Finally, I write tests with HttpCalloutMock, set separate endpoints for sandbox and production, and document the integration.
points: Study docs and test in Postman
External + Named Credential, permission set
Apex service with wrappers, errors, logging
Mock tests; separate sandbox and prod endpoints

q: An external system sends the same order event multiple times and sometimes out of order. How do you handle it in Salesforce?
alt: duplicate and out of order messages from integration
How do you make sure an older update doesn't overwrite a newer one?
message ordering in event driven integration
same webhook received twice
a: For duplicates, I upsert on the external order Id and store the message Id, so a repeated message either does nothing or produces the same result. For ordering, I ask the source to include a version number or a source timestamp on each message and store the last applied value on the record. When a message arrives, I only apply it if its version is newer than the stored one; older messages are logged and skipped. Status transitions can also be validated, so a shipped order can't go back to pending. If ordering is critical across many messages, middleware with ordered queues per key is a better place to enforce it.
points: Upsert on external Id + store message Id
Version or source timestamp per message
Apply only if newer than stored version
Validate state transitions; middleware for strict ordering

q: How would you design logging and monitoring for all integrations in an org?
alt: Integration monitoring framework design
how do you know when an integration fails in production
central error logging for integrations
integration observability in salesforce
a: I'd create one reusable logging service that every integration uses. It writes to an Integration Log object with integration name, direction, endpoint, status, duration, correlation Id, related record and error details. Payloads are trimmed and sensitive data is masked. Logging goes through a platform event with Publish Immediately, so it survives rollbacks. I'd pass a correlation Id in a header so we can trace one transaction across Salesforce and middleware. For example, when a customer says their order never reached the warehouse, support searches that one correlation Id and sees Salesforce sent it, MuleSoft received it, and the warehouse API returned an error. On top, I'd build dashboards and alerts for error rates and stuck items, monitor API usage and certificate expiry, and set a retention policy to purge old logs.
points: Shared logging service + log object
Log via Publish Immediately platform event
Correlation Id across systems
Dashboards, alerts, cert and API monitoring
Mask data; purge old logs

q: What is a Lead in Salesforce and how does the lead process work?
alt: Explain the lead lifecycle in Sales Cloud
What is a lead and what is a lead process?
how do leads work in salesforce
What are lead statuses used for?
a: A Lead is a person or company that has shown interest but isn't qualified yet as a real sales opportunity. The lead process is just the set of Lead Status picklist values it moves through, like Open, Contacted, Working, Qualified and Unqualified. Say a laptop seller gets a web form from an office manager asking about fifty laptops. That comes in as a lead, an assignment rule routes it to a rep or a queue, and the rep calls and moves it to Contacted, then Working. Once budget and timing check out, it's Qualified, and the rep converts it into an Account, a Contact and, if there's a real deal, an Opportunity. Leads can also come in from imports, campaigns or integrations. One thing to remember: if business units qualify leads differently, you can have separate lead processes and attach each one through a record type. Before building any of it, I get sales and marketing to agree in writing what Qualified actually means, because that definition drives every conversion and pipeline report after it.
points: Lead = unqualified prospect, separate object from Contact
Lead process = set of Lead Status values, tied to record types
At least one status must be marked Converted
End of the lifecycle is conversion or disqualification

q: What happens when you convert a lead?
alt: Explain lead conversion in Salesforce
Which records get created on lead conversion?
what happens to the lead after you convert it
Lead convert kya karta hai, which objects are created?
a: Conversion is a one-way step, so I treat it carefully. When I convert a lead, Salesforce creates an Account, a Contact and, optionally, an Opportunity from the lead data. Say a rep converts a lead for Priya from a small accounting firm. If that firm already exists as an account, I'd link the lead to it instead of creating a new one, and the same for an existing contact. That's how you avoid duplicates. The lead itself isn't deleted. It's marked IsConverted true, becomes read-only for normal users, and keeps the new record Ids in ConvertedAccountId, ConvertedContactId and ConvertedOpportunityId. Priya's campaign memberships and open activities move over to her contact. The gotcha is fields: standard fields map automatically, but custom fields only carry over if you map them in the lead field mapping setup. On my teams, any new custom Lead field has to come with a mapping decision in the same story, otherwise data quietly gets lost at conversion.
points: Creates Account, Contact and optional Opportunity
Can merge into existing Account or Contact
Lead stays in the system, flagged IsConverted, read-only
Custom fields need Map Lead Fields setup

q: A custom field on Lead is not carrying over to the Contact after conversion. Why, and how do you fix it?
alt: How does lead field mapping work for custom fields?
Custom lead field data lost after converting lead
Where do you map lead fields to account contact opportunity?
lead custom field not copying on convert
a: Almost always this is a missing field mapping. Standard lead fields map on their own, but a custom field only carries over if you map it. I'd go to the Lead object's Fields and Relationships, open Map Lead Fields, and map it to a matching custom field on Account, Contact or Opportunity. Say the lead has a custom Preferred Laptop Model text field, 100 characters long. The contact field has to be a compatible type, like text to text, or picklist to picklist or text, and at least as long, so 100 or more. Each lead field can map to only one target field, so you can't send that one field to both the contact and the opportunity. If the mapping is already there, I check field-level security on the target field, and then whether a trigger or flow on the contact is overwriting the value right after conversion. To stop it recurring, I add Map Lead Fields to the definition of done for any new Lead field, and I check it in review.
points: Map Lead Fields is under Lead object setup
Target must be a compatible data type and length
One lead field maps to one target field
Also check FLS and automation overwriting the value

q: What are lead assignment rules?
alt: How do you auto assign leads to reps or queues?
Explain assignment rules for leads
how many lead assignment rules can be active
How does Salesforce decide who owns a new lead?
a: Lead assignment rules set the owner of a lead automatically, either a user or a queue, based on criteria like country, industry or lead source. Only one lead assignment rule can be active at a time, but it can have many entries, and Salesforce checks them in order and stops at the first match. For example, entry one says country is India, send to the India queue. Entry two says industry is Education, send to Ravi. A lead from a school in India hits entry one first, so it goes to the India queue, not to Ravi.
