q: After conversion, the business wants the opportunity to get the right record type and some values that are not on the lead. How would you handle it?
alt: Set opportunity fields during lead conversion that do not exist on the lead
How do you control the opportunity record type on lead convert?
default price book and name format for converted opportunities
lead conversion mapping is not enough, what next?
a: Lead field mapping only copies fields that exist on the lead, so anything else needs automation on the new opportunity. Example: an equipment rental company wants converted opportunities to use the New Business record type, the India price book and a name like Company - Rental - Month. The opportunity record type follows the converting user's default, so I'd set that default for the reps who convert. For the rest, I add a checkbox on Lead that defaults to true, map it to a From_Lead__c checkbox on Opportunity, and a before-save record-triggered flow on Opportunity checks it to set the name format and price book. Standard and custom values that do exist on the lead are mapped per object in Map Lead Fields, so I use that first and automation only for what mapping can't do. In review I'd check that flow only acts on create, so later edits don't rename the opportunity.

q: Sales leadership wants to realign territories mid-year. How would you do it without breaking things?
alt: How do you do territory realignment in Sales Territories?
Change territory model safely
ETM realignment steps, planning model then activate
What happens to forecasts when you activate a new territory model?
a: I'd build the new alignment in a separate territory model and switch at a quiet time, rather than editing the live one. In Sales Territories (formerly Enterprise Territory Management) only one model can be active, so I clone the active model to get a copy in Planning state. In the copy I change territories, assignment rules and user assignments; for example, a manufacturer splitting its West region into West Industrial and West Retail. I run the rules in Planning and use reports to compare old and new account assignments with sales ops and managers. Then, right after a month or quarter close, I archive the old model, activate the new one, and rerun opportunity territory assignment. I warn leadership that archiving deletes the old model's territory forecasts and quotas and clears territories on opportunities, so I export forecasts and assignments first. I'd also brief reps before the switch, since some will see accounts move overnight.

Change territories, rules, users; run rules and compare
After a period close, archive the old model, then activate the new one
Export forecasts first; rerun opportunity territory assignment

q: New leads sit untouched for hours. The business wants them reassigned if nobody acts within 2 hours. How would you build it?
alt: Lead SLA, reassign if not contacted in time
Lead escalation if the rep does not respond
how to auto reassign leads after 2 hours
Can you use escalation rules on leads?
a: I'd use a record-triggered flow on Lead with a scheduled path, since escalation rules only exist for cases, not leads. The flow runs when a lead is created with Status New, and its scheduled path fires two hours after the created date. When it runs, a decision checks the lead is still New and still owned by the same rep; if so, it reassigns the lead to the round-robin queue and notifies the manager. Example: a car dealership gets a test-drive request at 10 am; if the rep hasn't touched the status by 12, it moves to the next available salesperson. The decision at run time matters because the lead may have changed since it was created. I'd also stamp a First Response Time field so management can see the SLA by rep. Before building, I'd agree with the business whether the two hours means business hours, because that changes the design.
points: Escalation rules are only for cases
Record-triggered flow with a scheduled path
Re-check status and owner when the path runs
Track first response time for reporting

q: Leads created by an integration are not being assigned by the assignment rules. How do you fix it?
alt: Assignment rules not firing for API created leads
How do you run lead assignment rules from Apex?
leads inserted by apex all owned by integration user
DMLOptions assignment rule header example
a: The fix is in the integration code, because assignment rules don't run automatically for Apex or SOAP API inserts; the caller has to ask for them. In the UI there's the Assign using active assignment rule checkbox, Web-to-Lead uses the active rule on its own, and the Data Import Wizard has an option for it. Data Loader takes the assignment rule Id in its settings. The standard REST API is the exception: it applies the active rule by default, and the Sforce-Auto-Assign header turns that off or names a rule. In Apex I set DMLOptions with useDefaultRule = true before the insert. Example: a marketing tool pushes leads through a custom Apex service and they all end up owned by the integration user. Adding the DML options sends every lead through the same routing as web leads. I'd also make it a review checklist item for any new lead integration, because this one is easy to miss in testing.
points: Apex and SOAP API inserts must request assignment; REST applies it by default
Data Loader: rule Id in settings; REST: Sforce-Auto-Assign header controls it
Apex: Database.DMLOptions assignmentRuleHeader
Same routing for every lead source

q: Reps keep pushing close dates out every month. How would you deal with it in Salesforce?
alt: Opportunities keep slipping to next month
How do you track how many times a close date was pushed?
reps keep changing close date, manager is unhappy
Stop sandbagging close dates on opportunities
a: I'd make the pushing visible first, then add a little friction. Pipeline Inspection already shows a push count and highlights close date changes, so I'd get managers using it in weekly reviews. Then I'd add a Close Date Push Count field that a before-save flow increments whenever the close date moves into a later month, plus a Push Reason picklist and comment that a validation rule requires when the date moves out. Example: an industrial chemicals rep moves a big deal from September to October to November; each push now needs a reason like customer budget delay, and the manager sees the count on a dashboard. I wouldn't block pushes outright, because real delays happen and blocking just teaches reps to enter fake dates. I'd agree the push reasons with sales managers so they're the ones enforcing it, not the admin team.
points: Pipeline Inspection shows push count and changes
Flow increments a push counter
Validation requires a reason when the date moves out
Don't block pushes; make them visible

q: Reps are skipping stages, jumping from Prospecting straight to Negotiation. How would you stop that?
alt: Validation rule to prevent skipping opportunity stages
Force reps to move one stage at a time
opportunity stage should go in sequence
How do you enforce stage order with PRIORVALUE?
a: I'd use a validation rule that gives each stage a number and blocks a jump of more than one step forward. Moving backward is allowed, and Closed Lost is allowed from any stage, since a deal can die at any point. Example: at a construction supplies company, a rep tries to go from Prospecting straight to Negotiation and gets the message 'Please complete Qualification and Proposal first'. I'd add a custom permission so sales ops can bypass it during data fixes. Two things I check in review: keep the stage names in the formula in sync with the picklist, and if there are several sales processes with different stages, either add their stages or check the record type in the rule.
points: Number each stage with CASE
Compare with TEXT(PRIORVALUE(StageName))
Allow backward moves and Closed Lost
Bypass via custom permission
code:
AND(
  ISCHANGED(StageName),
  NOT(ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Lost")),
  NOT($Permission.Skip_Stage_Rules),
  CASE(StageName,
    "Prospecting", 1, "Qualification", 2, "Proposal", 3,
    "Negotiation", 4, "Closed Won", 5, 0)
  -
  CASE(TEXT(PRIORVALUE(StageName)),
    "Prospecting", 1, "Qualification", 2, "Proposal", 3,
    "Negotiation", 4, "Closed Won", 5, 0)
  > 1
)
area: Sales Cloud: lifecycle, features and scenarios

q: A rep says they cannot edit the Amount on an opportunity. Why?
alt: Opportunity amount field is read only
Why is amount locked on my opportunity?
cannot change opportunity amount after adding products
Rep wants to type a different amount but the field is greyed out
a: The most common reason is that the opportunity has products. Once it has opportunity line items, Amount becomes the sum of their total prices and is read-only. Example: a rep at a furniture company adds 50 chairs and 5 desks, the amount becomes 12,000, and when the customer asks for 11,000 the rep can't type it in. The right fix is to change the sales price or discount on the line items. If there are no products, I'd check field-level security on Amount for their profile and permission sets, whether the page layout makes it read-only, whether an approval process has locked the record, and whether a validation rule blocks the change. Logging in as the user is the quickest way to confirm. I'd also explain the products rule to the sales team, because it saves a lot of tickets.
points: With products, Amount = sum of line items, read-only
Change the line item price or discount instead
Otherwise: field-level security, layout, approval lock, validation
Log in as the user to confirm

q: Prices go up next year. How do you update price books without disturbing open deals?
alt: Annual price increase in Salesforce price books
How do you handle new prices from January?
changing list price affects existing opportunities?
Price book versioning for a yearly price change
a: I'd handle it with a new price book rather than editing the old one. Changing a list price on a price book entry doesn't touch products already on opportunities; they keep their sales price, so the real question is switching new deals over cleanly. For a medical supplies company raising prices on 1 January, I'd create a new price book, like 2027 Domestic, load the new entries with Data Loader using product external Ids, and activate it on the day. Then I make the old price book inactive so new deals can't choose it. Open opportunities stay on the old book unless sales wants to reprice them, and changing an opportunity's price book removes all its products, so I'd warn reps or do it with a script that re-adds the lines. I don't delete old entries; entries in use can't be removed anyway, and deactivating is enough. The decision on repricing open deals belongs to sales leadership, so I'd get that agreed before the date.
points: Existing line items keep their sales price
New price book loaded and activated on the date
Deactivate, do not delete, old entries
Changing an opportunity price book removes its products

q: The business wants branded quote PDFs with different terms for India and US customers. How would you do it?

Different quote PDF layout per region
add company logo and terms to the quote pdf
Quote template for GST details in India
a: I'd build two quote templates, one per region, and show reps which one to pick. In Setup under Quote Templates, I clone the standard template, add the logo image and a header with company details, set up the line item table with the fields they want, and add a text section for terms. The India template might show GST details and INR wording, and the US one different payment terms. Example: a rep at an electronics distributor creates a quote for a Pune customer, clicks Create PDF, picks the India template, and emails it from the quote. Standard templates don't have conditional sections, so if they need many variants or clauses that change with the deal, I'd look at a document generation tool rather than maintaining ten templates. I'd raise that option early, because template sprawl gets expensive to maintain.

q: Marketing ran a trade show and wants to know how much revenue it produced. How would you set that up?
alt: How do you measure campaign ROI for an event?
Track leads and revenue from a trade show
event leads import into campaign and report on won deals
Which report shows revenue generated by a campaign?
a: I'd make the event a Campaign, make the attendees campaign members, tie the resulting opportunities to it, and report on that. Before the show I create the Campaign with Budgeted Cost and member statuses like Registered, Visited Booth and Meeting Booked. Afterwards marketing imports badge scans with the Data Import Wizard straight into the campaign, matching on email so known people aren't duplicated. When reps convert those leads, the campaign becomes the opportunity's Primary Campaign Source, and if several campaigns touched a deal, Customizable Campaign Influence spreads the credit. The campaign's Actual Cost and Value Won Opportunities fields, plus a campaign ROI report, answer the question. Example: a tractor maker spends 20,000 on an agri expo and can see the won deals sourced from it. I'd agree the member statuses with marketing before the event, because changing them after the import is messy.

Actual Cost vs Value Won Opportunities for ROI

q: Sales leadership wants a mandatory loss reason when a deal is Closed Lost. How would you do it?
alt: Require a reason when the opportunity is lost
Validation rule for closed lost reason
how to track why deals are lost
Make loss reason required only for closed lost
a: I'd add a Loss Reason picklist on Opportunity and a validation rule that requires it when the stage is Closed Lost. Example: a software company keeps losing deals and nobody knows why. Now when a rep moves a deal to Closed Lost, they must pick Price, Competitor, No Budget, No Decision or Timing, and if it's Competitor, which competitor. I'd also add Loss Reason as a key field on the Path so the rep fills it while closing. Then a report of lost deals grouped by reason and quarter goes on the sales dashboard. Using a picklist instead of free text is the part I insist on, because you can't report on a text box where everyone writes something different.

q: Reps want a scored list of their best leads, but you do not have Einstein. How would you build lead scoring?
alt: Custom lead scoring without Einstein Lead Scoring
How do you prioritise leads with a formula or flow?
lead score field hot warm cold design
Simple points-based lead scoring in Salesforce
a: I'd build a simple points model in a before-save flow, with weights agreed by sales and marketing. For an HR software company, points might be: company size over 200 gives 20, a title with HR or People gives 15, lead source Demo Request gives 25, a target country gives 10, and a webinar attendance adds a few more. A number field Lead_Score__c holds the total, and a formula shows Hot, Warm or Cold. Reps get a list view sorted by score. I'd choose a flow over one giant formula because weights are easier to change and it can use related data like campaign membership. Later, Einstein Lead Scoring can learn from real conversions, or Marketing Cloud Account Engagement (formerly Pardot) can add engagement scoring. Whatever we build, I'd review the weights with sales and marketing every quarter.

q: An SDR team qualifies leads and hands them to account executives. How would you set up the handoff?
alt: SDR to AE lead handoff process
How do inside sales pass leads to closers?
track which SDR sourced the opportunity
Who should convert the lead, SDR or AE?
a: I'd make the handoff a clear status change with routing, and keep a record of who sourced the deal. The SDR works the lead through statuses like Working, then Sales Accepted once a discovery call is booked. That change fires a flow that assigns the lead to the right AE, by territory or round robin, and creates a task with the call notes. The AE converts after the meeting, so the AE owns the opportunity, and an SDR lookup on the lead is mapped to an SDR Sourced field on the opportunity. Example: at a cybersecurity firm, an SDR books a meeting with a bank's IT head; the AE gets it with context, and the SDR still gets credit through that field or an overlay split. Reports then show meetings booked and pipeline sourced per SDR. I'd get SDR and AE managers to agree what Sales Accepted means, because a fuzzy definition is what usually breaks the handoff.

q: A rep cannot see an account that should be in their territory. What do you check?
alt: Territory member cannot access account
Sales territories access not working
account not showing for territory user
ETM user cannot see accounts assigned to territory
a: I go down the chain: model, account assignment, user assignment, access level. First, is the territory model active, not still in Planning. Second, is the account actually assigned to the territory: I check the account's assigned territories, and for rule-based assignment, whether the criteria match the account's current values and whether rules have run since the account changed. Third, is the rep added as a user on that territory. Fourth, what access the territory grants: access levels for accounts, opportunities and cases are set per territory, so Read account access won't let them edit. Example: a pharma rep moved to the Gujarat territory, but rules weren't re-run after an account's district was corrected, so it still sat in the Rajasthan territory. Running the rules for that account fixed it. I'd also make re-running rules part of the routine whenever ops corrects account data in bulk.

Is the account assigned, and have rules run since it changed?
Is the user a member of the territory?
Check territory access levels for account, opportunity, case

q: Leadership wants a Closed Won opportunity to automatically create an order with the same products. How would you build it?
alt: Create order and order products from opportunity on closed won
Copy opportunity line items to order items
auto order creation when deal is won apex
Flow vs Apex to create an order from an opportunity
a: I'd use an after-save record-triggered flow or Apex on Opportunity that fires only when the stage changes to Closed Won. It creates an Order with the account, the opportunity's price book, an effective date and status Draft, then copies each opportunity product into an Order Product with the same price book entry, quantity and unit price. Example: a packaging supplier closes a deal for three box sizes, and operations immediately sees a Draft order with those three lines to check before activation. Things I'd check in code review: bulk-safe logic, because a data load could close 200 deals at once; a check so reopening and re-closing a deal doesn't create a second order; and if there's a synced quote, copying from the quote lines so negotiated prices win.

Bulk-safe, no duplicate orders

q: Einstein Activity Capture is on, but managers say activity reports show almost nothing. What would you check?
alt: Emails captured by EAC not showing in activity reports
Why are captured emails missing from reports?
activity dashboard empty even though EAC is enabled
EAC emails visible on timeline but not in reports
a: That usually means captured emails aren't being stored as normal activities, so standard activity reports can't see them. With Einstein Activity Capture, unless the setting to sync email as Salesforce activity is on, emails show on the timeline but live outside the records that reports and flows use. So I check that setting first, remembering that synced emails use data storage. Next I check event sync: events syncing from Outlook or Google into Salesforce become Event records and should report. Then I check who is actually connected, because a rep whose mailbox connection failed captures nothing, and I review the exclusion list. Example: a sales director at a logistics firm sees five calls logged in a week for a team of ten; after turning on email-as-activity sync and reconnecting three mailboxes, the dashboard matched reality. On a rollout I'd agree the storage trade-off with the business before turning email sync on.
points: Check the sync email as Salesforce activity setting
Synced events become Event records
Check each rep connection status
Review exclusions in the configuration

q: Reps can see each other's opportunities, but the client wants each rep to see only their own. How do you set it up?
alt: Make opportunities private to the owner
Reps should not see other reps' deals
opportunity OWD private but reps still see records
How do managers see team deals when opportunities are private?
a: I'd set the Opportunity org-wide default to Private and then open access back up on purpose. With Private, a rep sees only the opportunities they own, plus anything the role hierarchy, teams, territories or sharing rules give them. Example: at a real estate developer, reps compete for the same buyers and shouldn't see each other's deals, but managers need their team's, and they get that through the role hierarchy. If reps still see others' deals after the change, I look for what's granting it: sharing rules, territory access levels, View All on Opportunity in a permission set, or account access, since an account owner can get access to opportunities on their account depending on the account sharing settings. Checking Sharing on one record shows exactly why someone has access. I'd test with a few real users in a sandbox before switching the default, because a change like that can surprise people.

q: Marketing gives you a CSV of 5,000 webinar attendees to load as leads and add to a campaign. How would you do it?
alt: Import leads into a campaign from a spreadsheet
Data Import Wizard for webinar leads
how to add imported leads to campaign members
Load event attendees without creating duplicates
a: I'd use the Data Import Wizard, because it can create leads, match existing ones and add everyone to a campaign in one go. First I clean the file: fix email formats, standardise country names to match our picklist, and remove junk rows. I create the Campaign, say October Product Webinar, with statuses like Registered and Attended. In the wizard I pick Leads, match on email so people already in Salesforce are updated instead of duplicated, choose the campaign and member status, and decide whether to run the assignment rule so leads go to reps. Example: of 5,000 rows, a chunk match existing leads and the rest are new. One gap: the lead import matches leads, not contacts, so existing customers can come in as new leads; I'd check the file against contacts first. q: Your company is merging with another and both have Sales Cloud orgs. How would you plan consolidating the sales data?
alt: Org merge strategy for two Salesforce orgs
How do you migrate accounts and opportunities from an acquired company's org?
merging two sales clouds after an acquisition
Deduplicating accounts across two orgs
a: I'd start with decisions, not data: which org survives, whose sales process and stages win, and how roles and territories will look after the merger. Then I map the objects: users, accounts, contacts, leads, opportunities with products, price books, campaigns, activities and files. Example: a paint company buys a smaller coatings firm, and both sell to the same hardware dealers. Duplicate accounts across the two orgs are the biggest problem, so I match on tax Id, website or another shared identifier, agree survivor rules field by field, and keep the old org's record Id in a Legacy_Id__c field. Opportunity stages need a mapping table. Load order matters: users, accounts, contacts, opportunities, line items, then activities. I'd rehearse fully in a sandbox, freeze changes during cutover, and reconcile counts and pipeline totals before go-live. The biggest risk is the decisions, not the scripts, so I'd get those signed off by leadership from both sides first.

q: The lead assignment rule has grown to 300 entries and nobody can maintain it. How would you redesign it?
alt: Lead assignment rules are too big to manage
Better alternative to hundreds of assignment rule entries
metadata driven lead routing design
How do you let sales ops change lead routing without an admin?
a: I'd move the routing logic out of the rule entries into data the business can maintain, and keep the assignment rule very thin. The usual cause is one entry for every combination of country, product and segment. First I agree the real routing keys with sales ops, say region, company size and product line. Then I put the matrix in custom metadata or a custom object, one row per combination with the target queue, and a before-save flow or Apex handler looks up the row and sets the owner or a routing field. Existing customers go to the account owner or territory first. For an electronics manufacturer that might shrink 300 entries into a small table ops can edit. I'd add a fallback queue, tests for each key, and a report of leads that hit the fallback. The win is ownership: sales ops changes routing without a deployment, and we review the table, not 300 entries.

Routing matrix in custom metadata or a custom object

q: Inside sales wants every new inbound lead to get a call within an hour and three emails over a week. How would you set it up?

How do you automatically add leads to a cadence?
follow up sequence for new leads in salesforce
Cadence with call and email steps for SDRs
a: I'd use Sales Engagement with a cadence and add new leads to it automatically. The cadence steps might be: call now, email on day 1, call on day 2, email on day 3, then a final email on day 7, with branches if the call connects or the lead replies. Reps work from their Work Queue, which shows who to contact next and which template or call script to use. To add leads automatically, a record-triggered flow on new inbound leads uses the Assign Target to Cadence action, after assignment has set the owner. Example: a clinic software company gets a demo request at 3 pm, and the rep sees it at the top of the queue with a call script. Exit matters too: when the lead converts or is disqualified, remove it from the cadence so nobody emails a new customer. I'd agree the steps with the inside sales manager and review how the cadence is performing after the first few weeks.

q: Sales managers want their reps to practise negotiation before big meetings. How would you use Agentforce for this?

AI role play for sales reps in Salesforce
reps want to rehearse a pitch with AI
Setup needed for Agentforce Sales Coach
a: I'd look at Agentforce Sales Coach, which lets a rep role-play with an AI buyer using the deal's context and then get feedback. The rep opens a big opportunity in Negotiation, starts a role-play, and the agent plays the customer pushing back on price or terms. Afterwards it gives feedback based on best practice for that stage, using the CRM data on the deal. Example: a rep at an industrial automation company practises handling 'your competitor is cheaper' the day before the meeting. q: The client wants to sell product bundles but does not have CPQ. What would you do?
alt: Product bundles in standard Sales Cloud
How do you model kits without CPQ?
parent child products on opportunity without cpq
When do bundles mean you need Revenue Cloud?
a: My first move is to find out how complex the bundles really are, because standard Sales Cloud has no bundle concept. If a bundle is a fixed package, like a Starter Kit with a camera, tripod and bag at one price, I'd make it a single product and let the ERP break it into parts. If reps need to see the components on the deal, I'd add a custom Bundle Component object linking a parent product to its child products, and a flow that adds the child line items at zero price when the parent is added. Example: a solar company's Home Pack automatically adds panel, inverter and installation lines. Once they need options, rules like 'battery requires inverter X', or bundle-level discounting, that's real configuration, and I'd recommend Revenue Cloud Advanced, since Salesforce CPQ is end-of-sale for new customers. With push, Omni-Channel takes cases from a queue, or uses skills, and sends each one to an available agent who has free capacity, so nobody picks and chooses. q: What is the difference between tab-based and status-based capacity in Omni-Channel?

a: For long-running cases I'd usually pick status-based. Both decide when an agent's capacity is used and freed; the difference is what frees it. Tab-based is the default: a routed case uses capacity from the moment the agent accepts it until they close the console tab. Status-based ties capacity to a picklist field on the record, usually Case Status. In the service channel you map each value to In Progress, Completed or Paused, and only In Progress uses capacity. Example: an insurance claims team keeps cases open for days. With tab-based, an agent with five open tabs looks full even if they're waiting on documents. With status-based, moving a case to Waiting on Customer, mapped to Paused, frees capacity, so Omni-Channel sends them a new case. Status-based is meant for records like cases and leads, not for chat, messaging or voice. The risk I plan for: if agents forget to update the status, capacity stays locked, so I pair it with a report on cases sitting In Progress too long.

Case Classification predicts fields like Type, Reason or Priority from the subject and description, and Case Routing uses those predictions to send the case to the right queue. Article Recommendations suggests Knowledge articles on the case. Reply Recommendations suggests approved replies during chat and messaging, while Service Replies uses generative AI to draft a full reply that the rep edits before sending. Work Summaries drafts a summary, issue and resolution at the end of a conversation, and Knowledge Creation drafts an article from solved work. Agentforce Service Assistant can draft a step-by-step resolution plan on a case. Example: a phone company's agent opens a case about a cracked screen; the type is already predicted, a repair article is suggested, and after the chat the summary is filled in. The rep always reviews before anything goes out. That review step is the guardrail I'd hold the team to, especially early on.

q: Explain milestone actions and recurrence types in an entitlement process.

a: Each milestone can have three kinds of timed actions: warning actions fire before the target, violation actions fire when it's missed, and success actions fire when it's completed in time. Actions can send an email alert, update a field or create a task, and a field update can kick off a flow for anything more complex. Recurrence decides how often a milestone happens on one case: No Recurrence means once per case, Independent means a new milestone each time the criteria become true, and Sequential means it repeats, but each new one starts only after the previous one is completed. Example: a hospital IT desk wants a two-hour response on high-priority tickets. At 90 minutes the warning emails the owner and team lead, at 120 the violation reassigns the ticket to an urgent queue, and the success action marks the SLA as met. Something like 'respond to every customer email within four hours' fits Sequential. In design reviews I check that every violation action has a clear owner, otherwise the alert just becomes noise.

What are the limitations of macros?
a: A macro is a saved set of steps an agent runs with one click, and bulk and irreversible macros are two special kinds. A bulk macro can run on many records at once from a list view, but only if its steps can run without the agent filling something in on screen, so macros that need the agent to edit text in the publisher can't be used in bulk. The risk I'd point out to the business: Web-to-Case has a daily limit, so heavy spam can actually block real customers once it's hit.

q: Cases created by Apex or an integration are not following assignment rules. Why, and how do you fix it?
alt: Assignment rules not firing for cases inserted via apex
DMLOptions assignmentRuleHeader example
integration user owns all cases
How do you run case assignment rules from code?
a: The cause is almost always the same: assignment rules don't run automatically when you insert cases from Apex, so the case stays with the running user or integration user. The fix is to set DML options with the assignment rule header before inserting, which tells Salesforce to apply the active rule, and you can request the auto-response email the same way. The standard REST API is different: it applies the active rule by default, and the Sforce-Auto-Assign header turns that off or names a rule. Example: a smart-home company's device platform creates cases through a custom Apex REST service when a thermostat reports a fault; they were all owned by the integration user until we added DML options, and now they land in the Devices queue. If you need a specific rule instead of the active one, set assignmentRuleId instead of useDefaultRule. Also check that no trigger or flow overwrites the owner afterwards. On my teams that DML options check is part of code review for any Apex that inserts cases.

q: Email-to-Case suddenly stopped creating cases. How would you troubleshoot it?

a: I'd follow the email's path from the customer's mailbox into Salesforce. One: is forwarding still working? Check that the company mailbox, like support@, still forwards to the Salesforce Email Services address; a mail server change or a removed forwarding rule is the most common cause. Two: is the routing address still set up and verified in the Email-to-Case settings? Three: is mail bouncing? Look for bounce or error messages in the support mailbox. Four: are cases failing on save, for example because of a new validation rule, a required field, or an error in a trigger or flow on Case or EmailMessage? These usually show up as error emails or in debug logs for the automated process. Five: check recent changes, like a deactivated user set as the case owner on the routing address. Example: at a logistics company, IT moved support@ to a new mail system and dropped the forwarding rule, so nothing reached Salesforce. Afterwards I'd ask IT to tell us before mail changes and add a simple alert if no cases arrive for a few hours.

q: What is Experience Cloud and what is it used for?

What are Experience Cloud sites used for?
experience cloud kya hai, basics batao
a: Experience Cloud lets you build branded websites and portals on top of your Salesforce org, so people outside the company can work with your Salesforce data. Typical examples are customer self-service portals where customers log cases and read knowledge articles, partner portals where resellers register deals and work leads, and public sites like help centers. Say a laptop seller wants its distributors to register deals and its customers to track repair cases. Both can be sites on the same org. The big advantage is that it uses the same data, security model, flows and components as the internal org, so there's no separate database to sync. The product was formerly called Community Cloud and is now Experience Cloud, which is why people still call these sites communities. You build the site in Experience Builder, pick a template, and control access through external licenses, profiles, permission sets and sharing.

LWR sites are much faster because pages are frozen and cached at publish time and served efficiently, so they suit public and high-traffic sites. For example, a public product help site with heavy traffic and a custom design suits LWR, while a quick partner portal that needs standard deal pages out of the box might go faster on Partner Central. For new builds where performance and custom design matter, I usually lean to LWR.

q: A public Experience Cloud site is slow. How would you improve its performance?

a: First I measure, using the browser developer tools and the Experience Cloud page optimizer to find which components or server calls are slow. Then the biggest win is often moving to an LWR template, because LWR freezes pages at publish time and uses HTTP caching and a CDN, which helps guest traffic a lot. I also make sure the CDN is on and avoid personalizing public pages unnecessarily, because personalized content can't be cached as well.

q: What is Health Cloud?

a: Health Cloud, which Salesforce now markets as Agentforce Health, is its industry solution for healthcare organizations, like hospitals, clinics, home health providers and health insurers. It extends Sales and Service Cloud with a healthcare data model for patients or members, clinical data, care plans, care programs, providers, and payer objects like member plans and benefits. On top of that it gives you the patient or member 360 view, timeline, care coordination, utilization management, appointment management and FHIR-based interoperability. Think of a care coordinator at a clinic who's looking after a patient with diabetes. Instead of checking the EHR, a spreadsheet and her email, she opens one patient record and sees his conditions, his care plan, his care team and his next appointment. That's the goal: one view of the person, so care teams and service agents can coordinate care and service better.

a: The clinical data model is a set of standard objects, aligned with FHIR R4, that store a patient's medical information. The key ones are HealthCondition for diagnoses and problems, CareObservation for vitals and lab results, ClinicalEncounter for visits, MedicationStatement and MedicationRequest for medications, AllergyIntolerance, PatientImmunization and PatientMedicalProcedure. Codes like ICD-10, SNOMED or LOINC are stored through the CodeSet and CodeSetBundle objects. For example, a clinic visit where a patient is diagnosed with hypertension and has her blood pressure taken becomes a ClinicalEncounter, a HealthCondition with the ICD-10 code, and a CareObservation with the reading. These objects replaced the older EHR data model objects from the managed package, so for new projects I build on the clinical data model, which makes FHIR integrations much easier to map.

q: What HIPAA and compliance considerations do you keep in mind on a Health Cloud project?
alt: How do you protect PHI in Salesforce?
Is Salesforce HIPAA compliant?
What is a BAA and why does it matter?
security and compliance for health cloud implementation
a: Salesforce supports HIPAA compliance, but it's shared responsibility. Salesforce signs a Business Associate Agreement that covers specific services, and the customer has to configure and use the org correctly. So first I confirm which services the BAA covers before storing protected health information in them. Then least-privilege access: a Private sharing model, permission sets, and field-level security on clinical fields. Salesforce Shield adds Platform Encryption for data at rest, Event Monitoring to track who accessed what, and Field Audit Trail for longer history retention. I also keep PHI out of places like email templates, debug logs, report subscriptions and sandboxes, using data masking for non-production orgs. For example, a clinic's weekly report subscription shouldn't email out a list of patient names with diagnoses. And I capture patient consent where required.

q: A hospital wants to integrate Health Cloud with its EHR system, like Epic or Cerner. How would you design the integration?
alt: How do you bring EHR data into Salesforce?
HL7 vs FHIR integration with Health Cloud
What is the integration architecture between an EMR and Health Cloud?
ehr integration health cloud mulesoft
a: First I agree the scope: which data moves, in which direction and how fresh it needs to be, because the EHR stays the clinical system of record. Modern EHRs expose FHIR APIs, so I map FHIR resources like Patient, Condition, Observation and Encounter to the matching Health Cloud clinical objects, which are FHIR R4 aligned. Older feeds often use HL7 v2 messages like ADT for admissions, so I use an integration layer, commonly MuleSoft with the Accelerator for Healthcare, to translate and route them. For example, when a patient is admitted, the EHR sends an ADT message, MuleSoft turns it into an upsert on the patient and a ClinicalEncounter, and the care coordinator sees the admission. I use external IDs for upserts, a patient matching strategy to avoid duplicates, and bulk or event-driven loading depending on volume. Error handling, retries and audit logging are essential because this is protected health data.

q: What are HL7 and FHIR, and how do they differ?
alt: Explain FHIR in simple terms
HL7 v2 vs FHIR
What healthcare data standards should a Health Cloud developer know?
f h i r kya hota hai
a: HL7 is a family of healthcare data exchange standards. HL7 version 2 is the older, very widely used one. It sends pipe-delimited messages, like ADT messages for patient admissions and discharges, usually through interface engines. FHIR, which stands for Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, is the modern HL7 standard. It uses REST APIs with JSON or XML, and defines resources like Patient, Condition, Observation and Encounter. FHIR is much easier for web and cloud systems like Salesforce to consume, and the Health Cloud clinical data model is aligned with FHIR R4, so mapping is straightforward. For example, a hospital might still send admissions as HL7 v2 ADT messages through its interface engine, while a newer lab system offers a FHIR API for Observation. In real projects you often see both, HL7 v2 for legacy feeds and FHIR for newer APIs.

q: What are the key design decisions you make at the start of a Health Cloud implementation?
alt: What are common pitfalls in Health Cloud projects?
Health Cloud implementation best practices
What would you decide first as a Health Cloud architect?
health cloud project planning
a: The first decisions are about the data model. I confirm person accounts for patients, since that can't be undone, and I choose the standard clinical data model and the newer standard care plan objects instead of older managed-package structures, unless the org already depends on them. I decide the system of record for each data type, usually the EHR for clinical data, and how much clinical history really needs to be in Salesforce. Then the security model: Private sharing, who can see PHI, Shield encryption scope and what the BAA covers. I also plan the integration approach, FHIR or HL7 through middleware, patient matching and duplicates, and which features use OmniStudio. a: The Work Order is the job to be done, often created from a case, and it can have Work Order Line Items for individual tasks or assets. q: What is the difference between a Work Order and a Work Order Line Item?

Work Order Line Items break that job into individual tasks or assets: for example, inspect the boiler, replace the filter on the air handler, and test the alarm. Each line item can have its own work type, asset, status, products and skill requirements, and even its own service appointment if the tasks need different technicians or days. So if the alarm test needs a certified electrician on a different day, that line item gets its own appointment, while the boiler and filter are done on the first visit. q: What is the difference between a Work Order and a Service Appointment?

What gets scheduled in Field Service, the work order or the appointment?
a: The Work Order describes what needs to be done. The Service Appointment describes when and by whom it's done. Scheduling happens on the Service Appointment: it holds the earliest start and due date window, the arrival window, scheduled start and end, the assigned resource through an assigned resource record, and the appointment status. One work order can have several appointments. For example, an AC repair company gets a job to fix a unit that's leaking. The work order says replace the compressor. The first appointment on Monday is the technician diagnosing it, and a second appointment on Thursday is the visit to fit the new part, both under the same work order. q: What are Service Territories and Service Territory Members?

A Service Territory Member links a service resource to a territory for a period of time, and the member type matters. Primary is the resource's main territory. Secondary is an extra territory they can also work in. Relocation is a temporary move to another territory for a set period, and it replaces the primary during that time. Say a technician normally covers Pune as Primary and helps out in Mumbai as Secondary. If he's sent to Nagpur for two weeks of installs, that's a Relocation, and for those two weeks Nagpur takes the place of Pune. The scheduling engine uses territories to decide which resources are candidates, and the member's address can be the home base for travel calculations.

They also define the arrival window slots offered to customers when they book. The technician only uses one, so he logs one Product Consumed linked to the product item on his van, and his van stock drops from ten filters to nine. q: What are scheduling policies, work rules and service objectives in Field Service?
alt: How does the FSL scheduling engine decide who gets the job?
Work rules vs service objectives
Explain Customer First, High Intensity and Emergency policies
scheduling policy in field service lightning
a: A scheduling policy is a set of work rules and service objectives that tells the engine how to schedule. Work rules are hard filters: a resource that breaks one isn't a candidate. Examples are Match Skills, Match Territory, Service Resource Availability, Maximum Travel from Home, Excluded Resources and Visiting Hours. Service objectives are weighted goals for ranking the valid options, like ASAP, Minimize Travel, Minimize Overtime, Preferred Service Resource and Skill Level. Say five technicians are available. Match Skills filters out the two without the right skill. Then objectives rank the other three, so if Minimize Travel has the highest weight, the closest one wins. Out of the box there are policies like Customer First, High Intensity, Soft Boundaries and Emergency, and you can clone and tune them. Different teams or situations can use different policies, like an emergency policy for urgent jobs.

q: What is the difference between global optimization, in-day optimization and resource schedule optimization?
alt: Explain the types of optimization in Field Service
When would you run in-day optimization vs global?
What is resource schedule optimization in FSL?
global vs in day vs RSO optimization
a: Global optimization looks at one or more territories over a longer horizon, usually days ahead, and rebuilds the schedule to best meet the policy's objectives. It typically runs as a scheduled overnight job. In-day optimization focuses on today or a short window, re-optimizing after the day has started to handle cancellations, emergencies and jobs that run long, while respecting appointments already in progress. Resource schedule optimization works on a single technician's day, for example after one job runs over, so it fixes that resource without disturbing everyone else. There's also reshuffle, which moves lower-priority work to fit in an important appointment. For example, global runs at 2 am for the next five days. At 11 am two customers cancel, so in-day fills the gaps. And when Ravi's first job runs two hours over, resource schedule optimization redoes just his afternoon.
points: Global: territories over days, often overnight
In-day: short window, handles same-day changes
Resource schedule: one resource's day
Reshuffle: make room for a priority job

q: What is Enhanced Scheduling and Optimization in Field Service?

What changed with the new Field Service scheduling engine?
Enhanced optimization vs legacy optimization
e s o field service lightning
a: Enhanced Scheduling and Optimization, often called ESO, is the newer Field Service scheduling engine. It replaces the older optimization and the related manual and semi-automatic scheduling services. It runs as a service on Hyperforce and is designed for better scalability, performance and schedule quality. It adds things like travel time calculated from routing setup, travel modes, flexible breaks and improved availability work rules. Newer orgs may already have it on. Otherwise you enable it in settings and turn it on per service territory, so you can move territories over gradually. For example, I'd switch one smaller city territory first, compare a week of its schedules against the old engine, and only then move the bigger ones. Some legacy work rules and features behave differently or aren't supported, so I always review the considerations and limitations list before switching a territory.

q: What is the lifecycle of a service appointment and its statuses?
alt: What are the default service appointment statuses?
How do status transitions work in Field Service?
Explain status categories for service appointments
service appointment status flow
a: The default statuses are None, Scheduled, Dispatched, In Progress, Cannot Complete, Completed and Canceled. A new appointment starts as None, becomes Scheduled when a time and resource are assigned, Dispatched when it's sent to the technician, In Progress when they start work, and then Completed or Cannot Complete. Canceled is for when the visit isn't needed any more. Each status maps to a status category, which the managed package relies on, so you can add custom statuses like Travelling as long as they map to a category. Admins also define allowed status transitions and which profiles can make them. So a technician can't jump from Scheduled straight to Completed if the business doesn't allow it. For example, the business can require Dispatched, then Travelling, then In Progress, in that order.

q: How does the Field Service mobile app work offline?

How is data primed for offline in the Field Service app?
What is a briefcase in Field Service mobile?
offline mode field service mobile
a: The Field Service mobile app is offline-first. When a technician syncs, the app primes data to the device: their service appointments for the scheduling window and the related work orders, accounts, assets and other related records, and a Briefcase can define extra records to download. While offline, the technician can view records, update statuses, log products consumed, capture photos and signatures, and run supported flows and offline-capable LWCs. Changes are queued and uploaded when the device is back online, and conflicts are surfaced if the same record changed on the server. For example, a technician in a hospital basement with no signal can still finish the job, log the part he used and get the customer's signature, and it all uploads when he's back in the car park. I always test offline with the real data volume, because priming too many records slows sync.

a: Deep linking lets another app, an email or a text message open a specific screen in the Field Service mobile app. The URI uses the com.salesforce.fieldservice scheme with a version, then the object record Id and an optional action, like opening details, launching a flow or launching a quick action, with URL-encoded parameters to pass values. q: A service appointment is not getting scheduled and the engine says no candidates were found. How do you troubleshoot it?

a: I start with the appointment itself. It needs a service territory, a valid address with geolocation, a duration, and an earliest start and due date window that's in the future and wide enough. Then the resources: are there active service resources who are territory members for that date, with the right capacity, and operating hours or shifts that overlap the window? Next, the scheduling policy's work rules. Missing skills, expired skill dates, excluded resources, maximum travel from home or visiting hours often filter everyone out, and resource absences can block the time too. Using Get Candidates with a looser policy, or removing one rule at a time, quickly shows which rule is knocking everyone out. For example, if a job's window is only one hour but its duration is two hours, no slot can ever fit, so no candidates come back.

q: A company operates Field Service in many regions with separate dispatch teams. How would you design the setup?
alt: Multi-region Field Service architecture
How do dispatchers see only their own territory?
Territory based sharing in FSL
large scale field service implementation design
a: I'd model a territory hierarchy that matches the operational regions, keeping each optimized territory a reasonable size so optimization runs stay fast. For visibility, I'd use Field Service territory-based sharing, so dispatchers and technicians see appointments, work orders and resources for the territories they belong to, on top of a Private sharing model. Each region can get its own scheduling policy and optimization jobs at local off-peak times, and operating hours must use the correct time zones. For example, the India team's overnight optimization runs at 2 am India time, and the UK team's at 2 am UK time, and neither dispatcher sees the other's technicians. I'd standardize work types, skills and statuses globally to keep reporting consistent. For mobile, briefcase and priming rules should be sized for the busiest technicians. I'd also check Enhanced Scheduling and Optimization limits for the expected volumes.
points: Territory hierarchy sized for optimization
Territory-based sharing on a Private model
Regional policies, time zones, off-peak jobs
Global standards for work types, skills, statuses
area: Experience Cloud, Health Cloud and Field Service

q: A dispatcher cannot see some service appointments or technicians on the Dispatcher Console Gantt. What would you check?
alt: Service appointments missing from the Gantt
Technician not showing in dispatcher console
Why don't I see resources on the FSL Gantt?
appointment list empty in dispatcher console
a: First I check the territory filter in the console, because the Gantt only shows resources who are members of the selected territories for the visible dates, and appointments in those territories. Then I check the resource is active and the territory member record covers the date range. For example, a new technician starts on the 1st, but his territory member record starts on the 15th, so he doesn't show up for the first two weeks. For appointments, the list filter and date horizon matter, and unscheduled appointments only show in the list, not on the Gantt. Next is access: the dispatcher needs the Field Service Dispatcher permission set and record access to the appointments and resources, especially with territory-based sharing. Finally, a missing geolocation can affect the map view, so I check addresses were geocoded.
points: Territory filter and member dates
Active resource, list filters, date horizon
Dispatcher permission set and record sharing
Geolocation for map issues
area: Experience Cloud, Health Cloud and Field Service

q: Walk me through the full lifecycle of an Experience Cloud site, from planning to go-live and beyond.
alt: What are the stages of building a portal in Salesforce?
Explain the Experience Cloud site lifecycle end to end
How do you take a community from idea to production?
experience cloud site life cycle steps
a: I think of it in eight stages. First, planning: who the users are, what they need to do, and how many there will be. Second, I pick a template, usually Build Your Own (LWR) for custom work or an Aura template like Customer Service or Partner Central for ready-made features. Third, licenses, based on whether users need roles, reports or sales objects. Fourth, I create the site and set up members, profiles and permission sets. Fifth, sharing: external OWD, sharing sets for Customer Community users, roles and sharing rules for Plus and partners. Sixth, branding, pages, navigation and CMS content in Experience Builder. Seventh, guest access and security review, then publish and activate. Last, I deploy through sandboxes with ExperienceBundle or DigitalExperienceBundle, and after launch I run moderation and analytics. For example, for a laptop seller's support portal: Customer Service template, Customer Community licenses, a sharing set on Case, knowledge for deflection.
points: Plan users and use cases, then template and licenses
Members, profiles, permission sets, then sharing
Builder: branding, pages, navigation, CMS
Security review, publish, activate, deploy, monitor
area: Experience Cloud: site lifecycle, features and scenarios

q: What do you decide in the planning phase before building an Experience Cloud site?
alt: What questions do you ask the business before creating a portal?
How do you plan an Experience Cloud implementation?
Requirements gathering for a community site
planning a customer portal what to consider
a: Before I open Experience Builder, I answer a few questions with the business. Who are the users: customers, partners, or anonymous visitors? Roughly how many, and how often will they log in, because that drives member-based versus login-based licenses. What must they do: view cases, register deals, read articles, pay invoices? Which records should each user see, so I can plan the sharing model early. How will they log in: username and password, social sign-on, or company SSO? And what branding, languages and devices are needed. Say a clinic wants patients to book appointments and see their invoices. I would note individual users, high volume, read-mostly access, so Customer Community licenses with sharing sets and probably person accounts. Getting this right early avoids a painful license or sharing redesign later.
points: Audience, volume and login frequency
Use cases decide objects and template
Sharing model planned early
Login method, branding, languages
area: Experience Cloud: site lifecycle, features and scenarios

q: How do you choose the right Experience Cloud template for a project?
alt: Customer Service vs Partner Central vs Build Your Own LWR, which do you pick?
Which template would you use for a partner portal?
How do you decide between Help Center and Customer Account Portal templates?
choosing community template
a: I match the template to the main job of the site and to how much custom development we plan. Customer Service is an Aura template with cases, knowledge and questions ready to go, good for a support portal. Help Center is lighter and focused on public self-service articles. Customer Account Portal suits customers checking their account, orders and invoices. Partner Central is built for channel sales, with lead inbox, deal registration and partner dashboards. Build Your Own (LWR) is a fast, mostly blank site for teams who will build with Lightning web components. For example, a manufacturer with dealers who register deals would start on Partner Central, while a brand that wants a fast, custom-designed product site would go with Build Your Own (LWR). I also check that every standard component we rely on exists in that template, because LWR does not have all the Aura components.
points: Customer Service: cases, knowledge, Q&A
Partner Central: leads, deals, channel sales
Build Your Own (LWR): fast, custom LWC builds
Check component availability before choosing

q: A manufacturer has about 200 dealers and 50,000 end customers who need portal access. Which licenses would you recommend?
alt: How do you pick the right external license for different user groups?
Dealers and consumers on one portal, which licenses?
Customer Community vs Partner license for a dealer network
license selection for experience cloud project
a: I would split them by what each group needs to do. The dealer staff work leads and opportunities and need reports, so they get Partner Community licenses, or the Channel Account license if pricing per partner account works out better. The 50,000 end customers mostly log cases, read articles and check their products, so Customer Community licenses fit, and since many will log in only a few times a month, login-based licenses are usually cheaper than member-based ones. If some business customers need to see each other's records through roles or need reports, those few get Customer Community Plus. I also avoid giving everyone a bigger license than needed, because Customer Community users skip the role hierarchy, which keeps sharing recalculation light at high volume. I always confirm final pricing and object limits with the Salesforce account team.
points: Partner Community or Channel Account for dealers
Customer Community for high-volume consumers
Login-based for infrequent users
Plus only where roles or reports are needed

q: What are the steps to set up a new Experience Cloud site?
alt: How do you create a community in Salesforce?
Steps to enable digital experiences and create a site
How do I get started with Experience Cloud setup?
create experience site steps
a: First I enable Digital Experiences in Setup and confirm the domain, which with enhanced domains looks like yourcompany.my.site.com. Then in All Sites I click New, pick a template, and give the site a name and URL path. That opens Experience Workspaces, where under Administration I add members by profile or permission set, choose the login and registration options, and set up email templates. Next I go to Experience Builder to design pages, theme and navigation. Then I set up access: object permissions on the external profiles, sharing sets or sharing rules, and the guest user profile if any page is public. Finally I publish from Builder and activate from Administration. For example, for a solar installer's customer portal I would create the site from the Customer Service template at the path /support, add the Customer Community User profile as a member, and add a sharing set on Case before activating.

All Sites > New > template, name, URL

q: How does a contact become an Experience Cloud user, and how do you give them access to the site?
alt: How do you create a portal user from a contact?
What is Enable Customer User?
How do you add members to an Experience Cloud site?
steps to create community user
a: An external user is always tied to a contact on an account. On the contact I click Enable Customer User, or Enable Partner User for a partner account, pick an external license and profile, and save. For partner and Customer Community Plus users, the account owner must have a role, because their portal roles sit under that owner in the hierarchy. The user then needs to be a member of the site: in Administration, Members, I add their profile or a permission set. Without that, the user exists but cannot log in to the site. For example, when a new contact at a dealer joins, I enable them as a partner user with the Partner Community User profile, and since that profile is already a site member, they get a welcome email if that option is on and can log in right away.

q: How do you handle branding, pages and navigation in Experience Builder?
alt: How do you change the look and feel of an Experience Cloud site?
What are theme, branding sets and navigation menus?
How do you add a new page and menu item in a community?
branding in experience builder
a: Branding lives in the Theme panel, where I set colors, fonts, logo and header images; I can save these as branding sets and switch between them. Pages come from the Pages menu, where I create a standard page, an object page, or a record detail page, then drag components onto it. Each page uses a theme layout that controls the header and footer. Navigation is a navigation menu component where I add menu items that point to site pages, Salesforce objects, external URLs or menu labels with sub-items, and I can mark items as public or private. For example, for a bike shop's owner portal I would set the brand colors, add a "My Bikes" object page for a custom object, and add it to the navigation menu under "My Account". Remember that nothing goes live until I publish.
points: Theme panel and branding sets for colors and fonts
Pages: standard, object and record pages
Theme layout controls header and footer
Navigation menu items point to pages, objects or URLs

q: What is the difference between previewing, publishing and activating an Experience Cloud site?
alt: Publish vs activate in Experience Cloud
What are the site statuses Preview, Active and Inactive?
Why can users not see the site after I published it?
difference publish and activate community
a: Publishing pushes the changes from Experience Builder to the live version of the site. Activating changes the site status so that members can actually reach it. A new site starts in Preview, where only admins with the right access can view it. When I activate it, the status becomes Active, members can log in, and welcome emails go out if that setting is on. I can also deactivate it, which makes it Inactive and shows a maintenance message. Preview inside Builder just shows my unsaved draft so I can check it on desktop, tablet and phone sizes. For example, on a new clinic portal I publish many times during build while it stays in Preview status, and only on go-live day do I activate it so patients start getting their welcome emails.
points: Publish: pushes Builder changes live
Activate: makes site reachable to members
Statuses: Preview, Active, Inactive
Welcome emails go out on activation if enabled

q: Which metadata types do you need to deploy an Experience Cloud site from sandbox to production?
alt: How do you move a community with change sets or SFDX?
What is ExperienceBundle and DigitalExperienceBundle?
package.xml for Experience Cloud deployment
deploy experience site metadata
a: A site is made of a few metadata types that travel together. Network holds the site settings like members and login options, CustomSite holds the underlying site and URL, and the Builder content is either ExperienceBundle for Aura and older LWR sites, or DigitalExperienceBundle with DigitalExperienceConfig for enhanced LWR sites. For Aura sites I first turn on the ExperienceBundle Metadata API setting in Digital Experiences settings. I also include the pieces the site depends on: NavigationMenu, Audience, profiles, permission sets, Apex classes and LWCs. For example, if I deploy a partner site, I retrieve these with a package.xml, commit them to Git, and deploy them in one go. CMS content in a separate workspace and some settings, like which users are members, may still need manual steps after deployment.
points: Network + CustomSite + bundle type travel together
ExperienceBundle: Aura and non-enhanced LWR
DigitalExperienceBundle + DigitalExperienceConfig: enhanced LWR
Include menus, audiences, profiles, code

q: How would you manage releases and change management for an Experience Cloud site that several teams work on?
alt: What is your deployment strategy for a portal with many developers?
How do you avoid overwriting site changes during deployment?
Source control and CI/CD for Experience Cloud
change management for community builder changes
a: The main risk is that Builder changes are made by clicking, so two teams can overwrite each other. My rule is one source of truth in Git: admins make Builder changes in a dev sandbox, retrieve the site bundle, and commit it like code. For enhanced LWR sites, DigitalExperienceBundle splits the site into smaller pieces like routes and views, which makes merges and reviews easier than one big ExperienceBundle. Each release goes dev to QA to UAT to production through the pipeline, never by editing production Builder directly. I keep a post-deploy checklist: publish the site, check members and login settings, move CMS content, and smoke-test as a real external user. For example, if the marketing team edits the home page while developers ship a new LWC, both changes merge in Git first, and only the merged bundle is deployed.
points: Git is the source of truth, no direct prod edits
Retrieve Builder changes and commit them
Enhanced LWR bundle splits into smaller files
Post-deploy: publish, members, CMS, test as user
area: Experience Cloud: site lifecycle, features and scenarios

q: After a site goes live, how do you manage moderation, engagement and analytics?
alt: How do you monitor an Experience Cloud site after launch?
What are moderation rules in Experience Cloud?
How do you track adoption of a community?
site analytics and moderation
a: After launch the work moves into Experience Workspaces. For moderation I set up moderation rules with keyword lists, so a post with banned words can be blocked, replaced, sent for review or flagged, and rate limit rules to slow down spam posting. I give trusted members or staff moderation permissions so they can review flagged content. For engagement I can turn on reputation points and recognition badges. For analytics I use the dashboards in Workspaces, Salesforce's free analytics package for ready-made reports on logins and activity, and a Google Analytics tracking ID set in the site settings for page views. For example, on a gadget company's Q&A forum I would block posts containing competitor coupon links, review first posts from new members, and watch weekly how many questions got a best answer without a case being logged.
points: Moderation rules: block, replace, review, flag
Rate limit rules against spam
Reputation and badges for engagement
Workspace dashboards and Google Analytics

q: What is Market Development Funds (MDF) in a partner portal and how does it work?
alt: How do partners request marketing funds in Salesforce?
Explain fund allocation, fund request and fund claim
What are the channel marketing objects in PRM?
MDF partner relationship management
a: MDF is money a vendor sets aside for partners to spend on marketing, and Salesforce tracks it with a small set of channel marketing objects. A partner marketing budget holds the total amount for a period. From that budget I create fund allocations for individual partner accounts. The partner then submits a fund request through the portal, describing the campaign and amount, and it goes through an approval process. After the activity happens, the partner submits a fund claim with proof, like invoices, and once it is approved the claim is paid. For example, a network-equipment maker gives a reseller a 10,000 dollar allocation for the quarter; the reseller requests 3,000 for a trade-show booth, gets it approved, runs the event, then claims the money back with receipts. I expose these objects on Partner Central pages and use approvals and reports to track spend.
points: Budget > allocation > request > claim
Requests and claims go through approvals
Partners submit through the portal
Reports show spend per partner

q: How do you make Knowledge articles visible on an Experience Cloud site?
alt: What are Knowledge channels for customers and partners?
Why is my knowledge article not showing in the portal?
How to publish articles to a customer community
knowledge in experience cloud setup
a: Three things must line up: the article channel, data category visibility, and user access. When an article is published, it has channel checkboxes: Internal App, Customer, Partner, and Public Knowledge Base. Customer users only see articles marked for Customer, partner users need Partner, and guest users need Public Knowledge Base. Then, if articles use data categories, the external profile or the guest profile needs visibility to those categories. Finally the users need Read on the Knowledge object and the fields shown. For example, a printer company publishes a "Paper jam fix" article for Customer and Public Knowledge Base, so anyone on the help site can read it, while a "Warranty override process" article stays Internal App only. On the site I use the standard search and article components so people find answers before logging a case.

Data category visibility per profile

q: Write a registration handler for social sign-on that creates a portal user the first time someone logs in with Google.
alt: How does Auth.RegistrationHandler work for Experience Cloud?
Social login creating community users automatically
What do createUser and updateUser do in a registration handler?
registration handler apex code
a: When someone signs in through an auth provider like Google, Salesforce calls the registration handler class. createUser runs the first time: for a site login the portalId is set, so I create a contact on a default account and return a new external user linked to that contact. updateUser runs on later logins, where I usually just sync the name or email. For example, a fitness brand lets members sign in with Google; the first login creates a contact under a "Self-Registered Members" account and a Customer Community user. I avoid hard-coded Ids by querying the account and profile by name or from custom metadata, I keep usernames unique, and I make sure the default account owner has a role if the license needs one.

q: What login options can you configure for an Experience Cloud site?
alt: How do you customize the login page of a community?
What are the Login and Registration settings in Experience Cloud?
Can portal users log in without a password?
experience cloud login page options
a: In Administration, under Login and Registration, I choose the login page type: the default page, a page I build in Experience Builder, or a Visualforce page. On that page I can show username and password, buttons for social sign-on through auth providers like Google or Facebook, and buttons for SAML single sign-on with a corporate identity provider. I can also turn on self-registration, and use passwordless login where users sign in with a one-time code sent by email or SMS. A login discovery page can ask for the email first and then send the user to the right method. I also brand the page, set the logout URL and pick the password and forgot-password pages. For example, a hotel chain's guest portal might offer email code login and Google, while its partner travel agents see an Okta SSO button.

q: How do you get the current site and user information inside an LWC on an Experience Cloud site?
alt: Which @salesforce/community modules are there?
How do I know if the user is a guest in LWC?
Get community base path and site Id in LWC
current user id in experience cloud lwc
a: Salesforce gives scoped modules for this. @salesforce/user/Id gives the current user Id, @salesforce/user/isGuest tells me if the visitor is not logged in, @salesforce/community/Id gives the site Id, and @salesforce/community/basePath gives the site path prefix, which helps when building links. For example, on a pet insurance portal I show a "Log in to see your policies" message to guests and the policy list to logged-in users, all in one component. If I need the user's account, I pass the user Id to Apex and query the user's ContactId and Contact.AccountId there. In Apex, Network.getNetworkId() tells me which site the request came from.

q: What is the difference between a guest user and an authenticated external user?
alt: Guest user vs logged in community user
Who is the guest user in Experience Cloud?
Does a guest user need a license?
difference between public user and portal user
a: A guest user is the single shared user that represents every anonymous visitor to the site's public pages. It has no license cost, it uses the site's guest user profile, and it can only get read access to records through guest user sharing rules. An authenticated external user is a real person tied to a contact, with a Customer Community, Plus, Partner or other license, their own profile, and access through sharing sets, roles or sharing rules. For example, on a car dealer's site, anyone can browse the public "Book a test drive" page as the guest user, but only a logged-in owner can see their own service history. The key point is that whatever the guest user can see, the whole internet can see, so I keep its access to the minimum.
points: Guest: one shared user per site, no license
Guest access: read-only via guest sharing rules
Authenticated: real contact, license, profile
Guest access is public to everyone

q: What guest user restrictions does Salesforce enforce today after the guest security changes?
alt: What changed with secure guest user record access?
Can a guest user update or delete records?
Who owns records created by a guest user?
guest user security policy rules
a: Salesforce locked down guest users a few years ago, and these rules cannot be turned off. The org-wide default for guest users is Private on every object. The only way to give them record access is a guest user sharing rule, and that is read-only. Their object permissions are limited to Read and Create, never Edit, Delete, View All or Modify All. Records a guest creates are assigned to a default internal owner, because guests cannot own records. Guests cannot be added to queues or public groups, cannot get manual or Apex managed sharing, and lost the View All Users permission. For example, if a pizza chain's public site lets visitors post a feedback form, the guest can create the feedback record, but it is owned by the site's default owner and the guest cannot read it back afterwards.
points: Guest OWD is Private, cannot change
Read-only access via guest sharing rules only
Object perms: Read and Create only
Guest records go to a default owner

q: What is the difference between an Experience Cloud site, Salesforce Sites and a Visualforce portal?
alt: Experience Cloud vs Force.com Sites
When would you use Salesforce Sites instead of Experience Cloud?
Are Salesforce Sites the same as communities?
experience cloud vs salesforce sites
a: Salesforce Sites, formerly Force.com Sites, gives you public Visualforce pages on your org's domain for anonymous visitors, but there is no login for external members, no Experience Builder and no ready-made portal features. Experience Cloud is the full external portal product: logged-in customers and partners with licenses, sharing sets and roles, Experience Builder with drag-and-drop pages, templates, knowledge, CMS, moderation and analytics. A Visualforce page can still run inside an Experience Cloud site if you have legacy pages. For example, if a museum only needs a simple public event list pulled from Salesforce, Salesforce Sites with one Visualforce page could do it. If members must log in to see their tickets and update their profile, that is an Experience Cloud site. For anything new, I go with Experience Cloud and LWC.
points: Salesforce Sites: public Visualforce pages, no member login
Experience Cloud: licensed members, Builder, templates
Visualforce can run inside Experience sites
New builds: Experience Cloud with LWC

q: How do you add an Agentforce service agent to an Experience Cloud site?
alt: Can Agentforce answer customer questions on our portal?
How do you embed an AI agent in a community?
Agentforce on Experience Cloud with handoff to a human
deploy agentforce agent on help center site
a: I deploy the agent through Messaging, the same way as live chat. First I build and test the service agent in Agentforce Builder, with subagents (formerly topics) and actions for things like order status or case creation. Then I create an Enhanced Chat messaging channel for web, route it with an Omni-Channel flow that sends conversations to the agent, and set a fallback queue so it can escalate to a human. Next I set up an Embedded Service deployment, publish it, and in Experience Builder drag the Embedded Messaging component onto the page or footer and publish the site. I add the site domain to the CORS allowed list, or the chat window will not load. For example, an electronics shop's help center lets the agent answer "where is my order" at night and hand complex warranty claims to a human agent in the morning.
