q: What are the main differences between Salesforce CPQ and Revenue Cloud Advanced?
alt: CPQ vs Revenue Cloud Advanced
How is RCA different from Steelbrick CPQ?
cpq versus rca architecture differences
Why is Revenue Cloud Advanced better than CPQ?
a: The biggest difference is architecture. CPQ is a managed package with its own SBQQ objects, while RCA is native and uses standard objects like Quote, Quote Line Item, Order and Asset. For configuration, CPQ uses product rules and option constraints. RCA uses Product Catalog Management with attributes and classifications, plus a Product Configurator that supports Constraint Modeling Language. For pricing, CPQ uses price rules, the waterfall and the calculator plugin, while RCA uses pricing procedures driven by context definitions. CPQ amends and renews through contracts and subscriptions, and RCA is asset-based. So if a packaging customer adds more pallet storage mid-year, in CPQ you amend the contract, and in RCA you amend the asset. RCA also adds Dynamic Revenue Orchestrator for fulfillment, native billing and an API-first design, and that's where new innovation lands.
points: Managed package (SBQQ) vs native standard objects
Product rules vs configurator rules and CML
Price rules/QCP vs pricing procedures
Contract/subscription-based vs asset-based lifecycle
Quote Line Editor vs Transaction Line Editor

q: What is Product Catalog Management in Revenue Cloud?
alt: What is PCM in Revenue Cloud Advanced?
How are products modelled in Revenue Cloud?
what are attributes and product classifications
Explain product catalog in agentforce revenue management
a: Product Catalog Management, or PCM, is where you model what you sell in Revenue Cloud Advanced. Instead of creating a separate product for every variation, you define attributes and group them into product classifications that act as templates, so products inherit consistent attributes. Say a packaging manufacturer sells custom boxes. Rather than a SKU for every size, board grade and print colour, I'd make those attributes on one custom box product that uses a box classification. Products are linked to product selling models that say whether they're one-time, evergreen or term-defined. You build bundles through product relationships and component groups, organise products into catalogs and categories for browsing, and use qualification rules to decide which products a customer is eligible for. And because it's built on standard objects and exposed through APIs, the same catalog serves reps, portals and agents.
points: Attributes and product classifications reduce SKU explosion
Product selling models define how products are sold over time
Bundles, catalogs, categories, qualification rules

q: What is a product selling model in Revenue Cloud Advanced?
alt: Explain one time, evergreen and term defined selling models
How are subscriptions defined in Revenue Cloud?
what is product selling model option
How do you sell the same product monthly and annually in RCA?
a: A product selling model defines how a product is sold over time. There are three types. One Time is for things like hardware or setup fees. Term Defined is for subscriptions with a fixed term, like 12 months. Evergreen is for subscriptions that keep going until cancelled. A product can have more than one selling model option. So a packaging company could sell box tooling as One Time, and offer its managed kitting service either as a 12-month Term Defined plan or as Evergreen. Price book entries are created per product and selling model combination, so each of those options gets its own price. This replaces a lot of the CPQ subscription fields like subscription type and term, and it drives how quotes, assets, amendments and billing behave downstream.
points: Types: One Time, Term Defined, Evergreen
Products can have several selling model options
Price book entries are per product + selling model

q: What is a pricing procedure in Revenue Cloud Advanced?
alt: How does Salesforce Pricing work?
Explain pricing procedures and pricing elements
what replaces price rules in revenue cloud
What is Sync Pricing Data?
a: Salesforce Pricing is the pricing engine in Revenue Cloud Advanced, and a pricing procedure is the ordered recipe it follows to calculate prices. Each step is called a pricing element. It reads input from the context definition, calculates something, and passes its output to the next element. For a packaging quote, a typical procedure gets the carton list price from the price book, applies the volume discount from a price adjustment schedule, adds any attribute-based adjustment like extra print colours, takes off the rep's manual discount, and then totals it. The data behind it lives in decision tables, which are refreshed by running Sync Pricing Data after changes. So if you change a price and skip the sync, the procedure still works off the old data. You can also simulate a procedure and see the price waterfall step by step. It replaces CPQ price rules and much of what we used the calculator plugin for.

Reads/writes through the context definition
Decision tables refreshed by Sync Pricing Data

q: What is a context definition in Revenue Cloud and why does it matter?
alt: Explain SalesTransactionContext
How does pricing know which fields to read in Revenue Cloud?
what is context service in rlm
How do you make a custom field affect pricing in RCA?
a: A context definition is a data contract. It tells Revenue Cloud services what data they work on, without hard-coding object queries. It defines nodes and attributes, like a sales transaction and its line items, and maps them to real objects and fields such as Quote, Quote Line Item, Order and Order Item. Pricing procedures, configurator rules and Dynamic Revenue Orchestrator all read and write through these contexts, for example the standard SalesTransactionContext for quotes and orders. Here's a practical case. Say a packaging business adds a custom delivery region field and wants it to affect the price. I extend the standard context definition, add the attribute, map it to that field, and then the pricing procedure can use it. Skip that mapping and pricing has no way to see the field.
points: Abstract data model mapped to real objects and fields
Used by pricing, configurator and DRO
Standard contexts such as SalesTransactionContext

q: What is the Product Configurator and Constraint Modeling Language in Revenue Cloud?
alt: What is CML in Revenue Cloud Advanced?
How are configuration rules done in RCA?
constraint modeling language salesforce
What replaces product rules in Revenue Cloud?
a: Product Configurator is the RCA engine that lets reps configure bundles and attributes, and it enforces which combinations are valid. For simpler needs you use standard configuration rules, like require or exclude a component. For complex products there's Constraint Modeling Language, or CML. It's a domain-specific language where you describe the product as a model with types, attributes, relationships and constraints. A constraint engine then solves the model, so it can auto-select values, prevent invalid combinations and surface conflicts, instead of running rules one by one in a fixed order like CPQ product rules. Think of a packaging line where box size, board strength, pallet type and stacking height all depend on each other. That's where combinations explode and CML is worth it. It needs a modelling mindset though, so I keep simple logic in standard rules.
points: Configurator enforces valid bundles and attributes
Simple rules for basic require/exclude logic
CML: declarative constraint models solved by an engine
Use CML for highly combinatorial products

q: How do quotes and orders work in Revenue Cloud Advanced?

What is the Transaction Line Editor?
quote and order capture revenue cloud
How does a quote become an order in RCA?
a: In RCA, quotes and orders are handled by Transaction Management, which used to be called Quote and Order Capture. The rep creates a quote on the standard Quote object from an opportunity or account, adds products through the Transaction Line Editor, configures them, and the pricing procedure prices every line. The quote can go through approvals and document generation, and then gets converted into an order. Because quotes and orders share the same sales-transaction model, that conversion is clean. So say a packaging customer signs a quote for printed cartons plus a kitting service. When the order is activated, it can start fulfillment through Dynamic Revenue Orchestrator and it creates assets. Those assets are the basis for later amendments, renewals and billing. The same steps are available as APIs for headless or partner channels.

API-first for headless channels

q: How do amendments, renewals and cancellations work in Revenue Cloud Advanced compared with CPQ?
alt: What does asset-based ordering mean in Revenue Cloud?
Asset based vs contract based amendments
how to amend a subscription in rca
What are asset state periods?
a: RCA is asset-based. When an order is fulfilled, the products become assets with a timeline of state periods that record quantity, price and dates over time. To change something mid-term you start an amendment from the asset. A new quote or order captures just the change, prorated for the remaining period, and the asset timeline is updated. Renewals and cancellations work the same way, from the assets. For example, if a packaging customer goes from 50 to 80 pallet spaces in month seven, the asset shows 50 for the first period and 80 from then on. In CPQ, the same processes start from the contract and create subscription records. So the way I put it: CPQ is contract and subscription centric, RCA is asset centric, and that gives a clearer single view of what the customer owns right now.
points: Orders create assets with state periods over time
Amend, renew, cancel from the asset
CPQ: contract and subscription records instead

q: What is Dynamic Revenue Orchestrator in Revenue Cloud?
alt: What is DRO?
How is order fulfillment handled in Revenue Cloud Advanced?
explain decomposition and orchestration in dro
What fulfillment step types does DRO support?
a: Dynamic Revenue Orchestrator, or DRO, manages fulfillment after an order is placed, and it works in two stages. Decomposition converts the commercial products the customer bought into the technical products fulfillment teams care about, based on decomposition rules. Orchestration then builds a plan of steps with dependencies, like procure equipment, dispatch, install and activate. Say a packaging manufacturer sells an automated packing line bundle. Decomposition might split it into the machine, the installation and the operator training, and orchestration puts those in the right order. Step types include manual tasks for people, callouts to external systems, auto tasks that run a flow, milestones to track checkpoints, and pauses that wait for something to finish. Once an order is submitted, DRO decomposes it and generates the orchestration plan automatically, and simple orders can skip decomposition. It replaces custom order-processing code and gives operations a visible plan per order.
points: Decomposition: commercial -> technical products
Orchestration plan with dependent steps
Steps: manual task, callout, auto task (flow), milestone, pause

q: How does Revenue Cloud handle contracts?

how are contract documents generated in revenue cloud
Where do contracts fit in quote to cash?
a: Revenue Cloud covers the contract stage through Salesforce Contracts, often described as contract lifecycle management. After a quote is accepted, you create a contract from it and generate the contract document from templates that pull in quote and account data. Legal language stays standard because you use approved clauses. Teams can collaborate and negotiate on the document, and then send it for e-signature. Once it's signed, the contract is activated and its terms flow into orders, assets and billing. For example, say a packaging customer accepts a two-year supply quote. The contract is generated with the agreed prices and the approved clauses, legal negotiates one change, the customer e-signs, and the activated terms carry straight through to the order and the invoices. The real benefit is that commercial terms and the legal document stay connected in one platform, instead of living in a separate tool someone has to update by hand.

Terms flow into orders, assets and billing

q: What does Revenue Cloud Billing do?
alt: How does billing work in Revenue Cloud Advanced?
What are billing schedules and invoice runs?
revenue cloud billing invoices payments credit memos
How are invoices generated from orders in Revenue Cloud?
a: Revenue Cloud Billing handles everything after the order: turning what was sold into invoices and collecting the money. When an order is activated, billing schedules are created from the order lines, based on billing settings like frequency and whether you bill in advance or in arrears. Invoice batch runs pick up what's due, daily, weekly or monthly, and generate invoices that can be posted, rendered as PDFs and emailed. a: Usage-based selling is for products charged by consumption, like API calls, storage or minutes. In Revenue Cloud Advanced, Usage Management defines the usage resources a product consumes, the allowances or grants included with a purchase, how usage is summarised, and when overages apply. Rate Management defines the rates, like a price per thousand API calls, possibly tiered, and rates the usage records. Billing then invoices the rated usage, usually in arrears alongside the recurring fee. So one product can have a fixed monthly fee, an included allowance and a per-unit overage. In a packaging business, picture a fulfilment service where the customer pays a monthly fee that includes a set number of packed orders, then pays per order above that. In practice, getting reliable, timely usage data into Salesforce is the hardest part, so I plan that integration early.

q: What is OmniStudio?

What are the main OmniStudio tools?
a: OmniStudio is a suite of low-code tools for building guided, industry-style digital experiences on Salesforce. It came from Salesforce's acquisition of Vlocity and was first used in the Industry Clouds like Communications, Insurance and Health. It has four main building blocks. FlexCards show contextual information and actions. OmniScripts are guided multi-step processes. Integration Procedures do server-side orchestration in a single call. And Data Mappers, formerly DataRaptors, read, transform and write data. Business rules can be handled with Decision Matrices and Expression Sets. To picture them together: an insurance agent sees a FlexCard with the customer's policies, clicks File a Claim, which launches an OmniScript, and behind the scenes an Integration Procedure uses Data Mappers to pull and save the data. Salesforce now styles the name as Omnistudio, and it runs either on the standard runtime built into the core platform or on the original managed package.

a: An OmniScript is a guided, step-by-step process you build declaratively. Think of a wizard for onboarding a customer, filing a claim or creating a quote. You drag elements onto a canvas: Steps that act as pages, inputs like text, radio, select and date, display elements, and actions such as Data Mapper, Integration Procedure, Remote Action, HTTP and Navigate actions. Everything the user enters is held in a single data JSON that flows through the script, and you can add conditional views, formulas and validation. Say it's a claim journey. Step one captures the incident date, step two only shows vehicle questions if the claim type is Auto, and the last step calls an Integration Procedure to save it. OmniScripts are versioned, can embed other OmniScripts, and run as Lightning Web Components. Compared with a Screen Flow, I'd say they're better suited to complex, branded, customer-facing journeys.

Why use an Integration Procedure instead of multiple Data Mapper calls?
a: An Integration Procedure is a server-side, declarative process that runs several actions in a single server call and returns one combined response. Inside it you chain elements like Data Mapper Extract and Load actions, HTTP actions for REST callouts, Remote Actions for Apex, Set Values, conditional blocks, loop blocks, try-catch blocks and a response action. For example, a portal page might need the account details, the open orders and a credit check from an external system. Instead of the OmniScript or a FlexCard making three separate calls from the browser, one IP does all of it on the server and sends back a single JSON. That's why it's much faster. IPs can be called from OmniScripts, FlexCards, Apex and REST, and they support caching and versioning. I think of them as the back-end orchestration layer of OmniStudio.

q: What are Data Mappers (formerly DataRaptors) and what types are there?
alt: What is a DataRaptor in OmniStudio?
Explain Extract, Turbo Extract, Transform and Load
data raptor types
What is the difference between a DataRaptor and a Data Mapper?
a: Data Mappers, formerly called DataRaptors, are the OmniStudio tools for reading, transforming and writing Salesforce data without code. The new name is the one used in the standard designers. There are four types. Extract reads data from one or more objects, with filters, and maps the output into whatever JSON shape you design. Turbo Extract is a faster, simpler read from a single object, optionally with parent fields, but without formulas or custom output mapping. Transform reshapes data in memory, like renaming keys, flattening lists or converting formats, with no database access. Load writes data, inserting, updating or upserting one or more related objects in one call. In a typical claim journey I'd use a Turbo Extract to prefill the policy, a Transform to reshape an external response, and a Load to save the claim. OmniScripts, FlexCards and Integration Procedures all use them.
points: Same tool, new name: Data Mapper (formerly DataRaptor)
Extract: multi-object read with mapping

Transform: in-memory reshape; Load: write

q: What is the difference between an Extract and a Turbo Extract Data Mapper?
alt: Turbo Extract vs Extract
When should I use Turbo Extract?
dataraptor turbo extract limitations
Which Data Mapper is faster for reading data?
a: Both read data, but they trade flexibility for speed. An Extract can query multiple objects, follow relationships, apply formulas and map the output into any JSON shape, so it's ideal when the consumer needs a specific structure. A Turbo Extract reads from a single object, can include parent fields through relationship notation, and returns the fields without custom output mapping or formulas, which makes it faster and quicker to build. For example, a FlexCard showing a contact's name, email and account name is a Turbo Extract job. But if an OmniScript needs the account, its open cases and a calculated total in one nested structure, that's a regular Extract. My rule: Turbo Extract by default for simple reads in FlexCards and OmniScripts, and a regular Extract, or an Extract plus a Transform inside an Integration Procedure, when I need several objects, calculated values or a reshaped response.
points: Extract: multi-object, formulas, custom output mapping
Turbo Extract: single object (+ parent fields), no formulas or mapping
Default to Turbo for simple reads

How do you reshape an API response in OmniStudio?

Convert JSON structure between steps in an Integration Procedure
a: A Transform Data Mapper reshapes data that's already in memory; it never queries or writes to the database. I use it when the shape coming from one system doesn't match what the next one expects, for example converting an external API response into the structure an OmniScript or a Load expects, renaming nodes, flattening nested lists, merging values, applying formulas or defaults, or converting between JSON and XML. In an Integration Procedure a very common pattern is HTTP action, then Transform, then Load. Because it's declarative and has a preview tab, it's easier to maintain than writing Apex just to map fields.

q: How does a Load Data Mapper save related records, like an account and its contacts?

a: A Load Data Mapper writes data, and one Load can save several related objects in a single call. On the Objects tab you list them in order, for example Account first and Contact second, and link Contact to Account so the new Account Id flows into the contact's AccountId automatically. On the Fields tab you map JSON paths from the input to object fields, and a list node in the JSON creates multiple child records. For updates you set an upsert key, like a record Id or an external Id, so existing records are matched instead of duplicated. I check the object order and required fields, and test in the Preview tab before wiring it into an OmniScript.

q: What are Decision Matrices and Expression Sets in OmniStudio?
alt: Explain the Business Rules Engine
Decision Matrix vs Expression Set
what replaced calculation procedures and calculation matrices
How do you store business rules outside code in OmniStudio?
a: Both are part of the Business Rules Engine, and both keep business rules out of code. A Decision Matrix is a lookup table. You define input and output columns, load rows, often from a spreadsheet, and the matrix returns the outputs for a matching combination. For example, an insurer could look up a rate by age band and region. An Expression Set is a sequence of steps that can call decision matrices, calculate, apply conditions and branch, and it returns results like an eligibility flag or a calculated discount. So the Expression Set might take that rate from the matrix, check a condition, and work out the final figure. Both are versioned with effective dates, so business users can update rules without a deployment. OmniScripts and Integration Procedures call them through actions, and they replace the older calculation procedures and calculation matrices.
points: Decision Matrix = lookup table of inputs to outputs

Replace calculation procedures/matrices

q: When would you use an Integration Procedure instead of Apex?
alt: Integration Procedure vs Apex
Should this logic be in an IP or an Apex class?
low code vs code in omnistudio
Do Integration Procedures avoid governor limits?
a: I start with an Integration Procedure when the job is orchestration: fetch data, call a REST API, transform it and save it, with modest logic. IPs are declarative, versioned, quick to change, support caching, and admins can read them. I choose Apex when the logic is complex or computational, needs heavy loops or recursion, needs precise transaction control and error handling, processes large data volumes, or needs strong unit testing. Often the answer is both. Say an onboarding journey has to fetch the customer, call a credit API and save the result, but also run a complicated scoring calculation. The IP handles the fetch, the callout and the save, and calls an Apex class through a Remote Action just for the scoring. One thing people miss: an IP still runs under Apex governor limits in the same transaction, so it's not a way around limits.
points: IP: declarative orchestration, caching, versioning
Apex: complex logic, volume, transaction control, testing
Combine via Remote Action
IPs still count against governor limits

q: How does caching work in Integration Procedures?
alt: What is a Cache Block in an Integration Procedure?
Session cache vs org cache in OmniStudio
how to cache external api responses in omnistudio
Does OmniStudio use platform cache?
a: Integration Procedures can store results in Salesforce Platform Cache, so repeat calls skip the expensive work. There are two levels. You can cache the whole IP response in the procedure's configuration, choosing session cache for user-specific data or org cache for data shared by everyone, with a time to live in minutes. Or you wrap specific steps in a Cache Block, so only that part is cached and the other steps still run fresh. For example, if an IP calls an external product catalogue that rarely changes and then reads the user's own cart, I'd put a Cache Block around just the catalogue HTTP call. Cached entries depend on the inputs, so different inputs get different entries. You need a platform cache partition with capacity allocated, and I never put user-specific or sensitive data in org cache. I pick TTLs based on how stale the data can safely be.
points: Uses Platform Cache: session or org
Whole-IP response caching or a Cache Block around steps
TTL in minutes; entries vary by input
Needs allocated cache partition; no sensitive data in org cache

a: You use a Remote Action element. It calls an Apex class and method by name, passes data from the data JSON as input, and merges the output back. On the standard runtime the class implements the Callable interface, so it receives an action name and an args map containing the input, output and options maps. In older managed-package orgs you'll see the namespaced VlocityOpenInterface2 interface instead, where the invokeMethod method takes the method name and the same input, output and options maps. Say an OmniScript needs a delivery date worked out by some tricky logic. The Remote Action passes the postcode and order size, my class reads them from input, puts the date into output, and the script picks it up. Inside, I keep the logic bulk-safe, run queries in user mode, and return clean keys the OmniScript can use. I usually call it from an Integration Procedure, so it's combined with other steps in one server trip.

a: OmniScript elements fall into a few groups. Group elements organise the screen: a Step is a page, a Block groups fields, an Edit Block lets users add and edit a list of records, and there are Radio Group and Type Ahead Block. Input elements capture data, like Text, Email, Date, Number, Checkbox, Radio, Select and Multi-select. Display elements show content, like Text Block and Line Break. Function elements include Formula, Aggregate and Messaging. Any element can be shown or hidden with conditional view. Action elements do the work: Data Mapper actions, Integration Procedure Action, Remote Action, HTTP Action, Set Values, Set Errors, Navigate Action and DocuSign. So in a simple address change journey, I'd have a Step with a Block of Text inputs, a Formula to build the full address, an Integration Procedure Action to save it, and a Navigate Action at the end. And when standard elements aren't enough, you can embed a custom Lightning Web Component.

Each step creates a node named after the step, and each element writes its value under it, so the structure mirrors the script. To use a value elsewhere, I reference it with merge field syntax: percent signs around the path, with colons for nesting, like %CustomerInfo:FirstName% or %ContextId%. Actions send part or all of this JSON as input and merge responses back in. Keeping it small with the send and response JSON path settings helps performance, and in preview I can watch it change live.

q: What are the performance best practices for OmniStudio?

how to reduce server calls in omnistudio

a: My main rule is fewer server trips and smaller payloads. Instead of an OmniScript calling three Data Mappers and an Apex class separately, I combine them into one Integration Procedure. I use Turbo Extract where possible, only return fields the UI needs, and trim the data JSON with response paths or transforms. I cache stable data in IPs with session or org cache. For actions the user doesn't need to wait on, I use non-blocking or fire-and-forget invoke modes. I avoid loading everything on the first step and fetch data when a step needs it. For heavy processing, I use the chainable or queueable settings in IPs to stay within limits. And on the managed package, I convert Angular OmniScripts to LWC.

The standard runtime runs OmniStudio natively on the core platform, with standard designers and the standard object model, so components are real metadata deployed with Salesforce CLI. Salesforce positions the standard runtime as faster, both in the designer and at runtime, and it gives access to newer features like Integration Procedure actions for Agentforce and better support for LWR sites in Experience Cloud. So if a team wants an Agentforce agent to reuse an existing Integration Procedure, that's a strong reason to be on the standard runtime. To move across, Salesforce provides the Omnistudio Migration Assistant, a Salesforce CLI plugin, to assess and convert components.

States are alternative layouts with conditions, and the card shows the state whose conditions match. q: You need to show data from a slow, rate-limited external API in an OmniScript. How would you design it?

q: An OmniScript takes several seconds to load each step and users are complaining. How would you troubleshoot and fix it?

How to speed up a slow OmniScript
omniscript performance issue each step loading
Users complain OmniScript steps take too long
a: I'd open the OmniScript in preview with the browser network tab and the action debugger to see how many server calls each step makes and how long each one takes. Common causes are several separate Data Mapper or Remote actions on one step, large payloads because the whole data JSON is sent with every action, slow external callouts, and heavy Extracts returning fields nobody uses. The fixes are to combine calls into one Integration Procedure, use Turbo Extract, send and return only the nodes needed with the JSON path settings, cache stable data, and use non-blocking invoke modes where the user doesn't need to wait. a: That's the standard Apex rule showing up inside OmniStudio: an Integration Procedure runs in one transaction, and you can't make a callout after DML in the same transaction. Here the Load step runs before the HTTP action, so the callout fails. The simplest fix is to reorder: make the callout first, then save the record with its result. If the order really must stay, I move the callout into a separate transaction, for example with the IP's queueable or chainable options, or with Queueable Apex or a platform event fired after the save. I also wrap the callout in a try-catch block, return a clear failure response, and log the error so support can retry.

What are the stages of quote-to-cash and which objects are used?
a: Quote-to-cash is the path from an opportunity to money collected, and each stage has its own object. Say a software company sells 100 licenses plus onboarding. The rep creates an opportunity, then a CPQ quote, and marks it primary. In the Quote Line Editor they configure the bundle, picking features and options while product rules block bad combinations. CPQ prices every line through the waterfall: list price, contracted or special price, discount schedules, the rep's additional discount, then partner and distributor discounts, with price rules adjusting values along the way. If the discount is too high, Advanced Approvals sends it to a manager. The rep generates the PDF from a quote template and the customer signs. The quote is ordered, which creates an Order with order products. The order is activated and contracted, creating a Contract with subscriptions and assets. From there the contract drives amendments, renewals and the hand-off to billing.

What does the Contract Co-Termination setting do?
a: Co-termination means lining up end dates so subscriptions finish together and renew together. Inside one contract CPQ does this automatically on amendments. Say a contract runs January to December and the customer adds ten licenses in July: the new licenses run July to December and are prorated for that half year, so everything renews on the same day. Across contracts on one account, the account's Contract Co-Termination field, with Never, Prompt or Always, together with Co-Termination Event, decides whether a new add-on quote picks up an existing contract's end date: Prompt lets the rep choose the contract, Always uses the earliest end date. You can also renew several contracts into one renewal quote using a master contract. The business value is one renewal conversation and one invoice date instead of a dozen.

In the asset-based model, the rep works from what the account owns, using Amend Assets or Renew Assets from the account or opportunity, and picks the assets and subscriptions to change. Picture an IT reseller whose customer bought firewalls across five separate deals: asset-based lets the rep see and renew everything the customer has in one place. a: An amendment changes the existing contract instead of creating a new one. q: What are partner and distributor discounts in CPQ?
alt: Where do partner discount and distributor discount sit in the price waterfall?

How does CPQ handle reseller pricing?
What is partner price vs net price?
a: Partner and distributor discounts are the last two steps of the price waterfall, used when you sell through a channel. After the customer price is set, the partner discount gives the partner price, and the distributor discount on top of that gives the net price, which is what syncs to the opportunity. Say a networking vendor sells a switch with a customer price of 1,000 through a reseller: a 15% partner discount makes the partner price 850, and a 5% distributor discount makes the net price 807.50. You can set them on the quote so they apply to all lines, or per line, by hand or automatically through a price rule or flow. Keeping them separate from the rep's additional discount makes margin reporting much clearer.
points: Customer price -> partner discount -> partner price
Partner price -> distributor discount -> net price
Set on quote or line, manually or via automation

The quote process is linked to the quote, and Guided Only forces reps to add products only this way. how to add a custom field to the qle

Can different quotes show different QLE columns?

q: In the Quote Line Editor, what is the difference between Calculate, Quick Save and Save?
alt: Does Calculate save the quote in CPQ?
quick save vs save qle
Why is my net amount not updated after I clicked Calculate?
What do the buttons on the line editor do?
a: Calculate runs the pricing calculation so the rep can see the numbers, but it doesn't save anything. Quick Save calculates and saves the quote while keeping the rep in the editor. Save calculates, saves and closes the editor, taking the rep back to the quote record. A common support call: a rep changes the discount on a 30-line hardware quote, clicks Calculate, closes the tab, and wonders why the quote record still shows the old total. The answer is that nothing was saved. I tell reps to use Quick Save while they're iterating and Save when they're done, and on big quotes to wait until the calculation finishes before trusting the totals.

Save: recalc + save + exit

What does the Add Group button do?
a: Quote line groups let the rep organise lines into sections, each with its own subtotal, and groups can carry their own start date, term and discount. A typical case is a hospital chain buying equipment for three sites: the rep creates groups for North, Central and South, puts the right lines in each, and the PDF shows each site with its own subtotal. Groups also help with ordering, because Order By Quote Line Group creates one order per group, so each site gets its own order. You add groups in the Quote Line Editor with Add Group, and the Groups tab in package settings covers options like solution groups and requiring a group name. The trade-off is that grouping makes big quotes heavier, so I use it when there's a real business reason.

q: What is percent-of-total pricing in CPQ?
alt: How do you price support as a percentage of hardware?
percent of total pricing method cpq
Warranty priced at 20 percent of the quote, how?
What is a percent of total product?
a: Percent-of-total pricing makes one product's price a percentage of other lines, instead of a fixed price. The classic example is support: a premium support product priced at 20% of the hardware on the quote. If the rep adds 50,000 of servers, support becomes 10,000, and if they add more servers, support goes up automatically on the next calculation. You set the product's pricing method or subscription pricing to Percent Of Total and give it the percentage. Then you control which lines count toward the base, for example excluding services and other percent-of-total products, so support isn't charged on itself. It's cleaner than a price rule for this kind of rule and reps can't forget to update it.

show price changes while configuring a bundle

price rule not updating option price in configuration page

Say a bike shop's custom bike bundle gives the frame upgrade a lower price when the carbon wheels option is also selected: a configurator-scoped rule shows the rep the right option price before they click Save. Configurator rules can only see the bundle being configured, not the rest of the quote, and you choose the configurator event they fire on. q: How do you read, calculate and save a CPQ quote from Apex using the CPQ API?

cpq api quote reader quote calculator quote saver
How do you recalculate a CPQ quote from code?
Why not just update quote lines with DML in CPQ?
a: I use the CPQ API through SBQQ.ServiceRouter, because plain DML on quote lines skips CPQ's pricing logic. First you add the CPQ API model classes, like QuoteModel and QuoteLineModel, to the org. Then QuoteReader returns the quote as JSON, which I deserialize, change, and pass to QuoteCalculator. The calculator runs in the background and calls a callback class that implements SBQQ.CalculateCallback, and that callback saves with QuoteSaver. For example, when a partner portal changes quantity on a quote, my service reads the quote, sets quantity to 25, calculates and saves, so price rules and discount schedules apply as if the rep did it. The context property names quote and callbackClass must stay exactly as shown, and the API isn't meant for instant results.

q: You are asked to migrate a company from a legacy quoting tool into Salesforce CPQ. How do you approach the data migration?
alt: CPQ data migration best practices
what order do you load cpq data in
How do you migrate active contracts and subscriptions into CPQ?
cpq config is data not metadata how do you deploy it
a: I treat it as two migrations: configuration and transactions. CPQ configuration, like products, options, rules and templates, is data, not metadata, so I move it with a data deployment tool and external Ids, loading parents first: products and price book entries, features, options, constraints, then rules with their conditions and actions. For transactions I load accounts and opportunities, then quotes and quote lines, then orders, contracts and subscriptions, with bundle parents before children so the required-by links resolve. Active contracts matter most, because renewals and amendments read them. Say a telecom has 3,000 live contracts: I'd migrate them with correct start and end dates, quantities and net prices, then test renewals on a sample. During loads I disable CPQ triggers, reactivate them afterwards, and reconcile totals against the legacy system.
points: Config is data: use external Ids and parent-first order
Transactions: quotes, lines (parents first), orders, contracts, subscriptions
Disable CPQ triggers during loads, re-enable after
Validate with renewal and amendment tests

q: When would you use MDQ, and when would you just add separate quote lines instead?
alt: MDQ vs multiple lines with different dates
downsides of multi dimensional quoting
Is MDQ always the right answer for ramp deals?
segmented quote lines vs normal lines cpq
a: I use MDQ when the same product changes quantity or price over time inside one contract and the customer wants to see it year by year. Say a call-centre software deal ramps from 100 to 300 agents over three years: MDQ gives one line with Year 1, 2 and 3 columns, and each segment becomes its own subscription. If the change is a one-off, like adding a product halfway through, separate lines or an amendment are simpler. MDQ has real costs: more quote lines behind the scenes, price rules that must handle segments, templates that need segmented tables, and renewals that must be tested carefully. So I ask whether the ramp is standard for the business before turning it on.

Each segment is its own line and subscription
Cost: more lines, rules, templates, renewal behaviour
One-off changes: separate lines or amendments

How do you limit the product catalog for certain reps?
filter rules in product selection

Search filters and the search results columns are driven by product field sets, so you choose what reps can search on and see. Guided selling narrows the list through questions. Filter product rules can narrow dynamic searches and option lookups, like only showing EU-certified chargers for European accounts. And separate price books per region or channel control the catalog at a higher level. javascript in cpq to default the discount before price rules
how to set quote line fields in the calculator plugin

Every field I use must be listed in the Custom Script's quote and line field lists, otherwise it comes through undefined. The function returns a Promise. q: You need to write a test class for Apex that works with CPQ quotes. How do you keep the CPQ package from getting in the way?
alt: test class for code on SBQQ quote lines
cpq triggers make my test class slow
How do you create CPQ test data?
Can I rely on CPQ calculation in Apex tests?
a: I test my own logic and keep CPQ's package logic out of the data setup. In @TestSetup I wrap inserts of the quote and quote lines in SBQQ.TriggerControl.disable() and enable() inside try/finally, so CPQ's triggers don't fire calculations while I build data. I set the price and discount fields I need directly, rather than waiting for CPQ to calculate them, because tests shouldn't depend on the background calculator. Then I test my class with startTest and stopTest and assert on my fields. For example, a class that flags quotes with any line above 20% discount for VP approval gets one quote with a 25% line and one with 10%, and I assert only the first is flagged.

Test positive and negative cases

q: How do Salesforce CPQ concepts map to Revenue Cloud Advanced?
alt: If I know CPQ, what is the equivalent in RCA?
cpq vs revenue cloud advanced terminology
What replaces price rules and product rules in Revenue Cloud?
mapping sbqq objects to revenue cloud objects
a: Most CPQ ideas carry over, but they live in different places. CPQ's SBQQ quote and quote line become the standard Quote and Quote Line Item. Bundles, features and options become product structures in Product Catalog Management, with attributes and classifications. Product rules and option constraints map to configurator rules and Constraint Modeling Language. Price rules, discount schedules, summary variables and calculator plugin logic map to pricing procedures driven by context definitions. CPQ subscriptions on a contract become assets in an asset-based lifecycle, which amendments and renewals start from. For example, a CPQ volume discount schedule on a laptop becomes a tiered price adjustment in a pricing procedure. I tell interviewers my CPQ knowledge of the business problems transfers fully; the tooling is what's new.
points: SBQQ Quote/Line -> standard Quote/Quote Line Item
Bundles -> Product Catalog Management structures
Product rules -> configurator rules / CML
Price rules, schedules, QCP -> pricing procedures
Subscriptions -> asset-based lifecycle

q: The business says any quote with a discount over 20% must be approved by the VP of Sales. How would you build it in CPQ?
alt: Discount above 20 percent needs VP approval in CPQ
set up advanced approvals for high discount
how to route cpq quotes to vp when discount is high
Approval rule based on max line discount
a: I'd build it in Advanced Approvals. First I decide what '20%' means: usually the biggest total discount on any line, so I add a formula field on the quote line that combines additional discount and schedule discount into one percentage. Then I create an Approver record for the VP, or point to a user field so it follows org changes. I add an approval variable on the quote that takes the MAX of that line field, and an approval rule targeting the quote with a condition 'variable greater than 20'. I add Submit and Recall buttons, lock editing while the quote is pending, and stop document generation until it's approved. For example, a 25% discount on a server line goes to the VP, while 15% goes straight through. Without the Advanced Approvals package, a roll-up MAX on the quote plus a standard approval process also works.

Lock the quote while pending

q: Discounts between 10 and 20% need the sales manager, above 20% also the VP, and non-standard payment terms need Finance at the same time. How would you design the approvals?
alt: multi level approvals in cpq with parallel finance approval
serial and parallel approvals advanced approvals
How do approval steps and chains work for tiered discounts?
design approval matrix in salesforce cpq
a: I'd use Advanced Approvals with separate rules and step numbers. Rule one: discount over 10%, approver is the rep's manager from a user field, step 1. Rule two: discount over 20%, approver is the VP, step 2, so it only starts after the manager approves. Rule three: payment terms not equal to Net 30, approver is a Finance group, also at step 1, so Finance and the manager review in parallel. If the same manager-then-VP sequence repeats across rules, I put it in an approval chain and reuse it. For a quote with 25% off and Net 90 terms, the manager and Finance get emails together, then the VP. I'd also enable smart approvals on the rule conditions so a resubmission doesn't re-ask approvers whose condition didn't change, and test with Preview Approval.
points: One rule per condition; step numbers set order
Same step = parallel; dynamic approver from a field

q: The price of a product must change by region and by quantity tier. How would you implement it without creating dozens of price rules?

price matrix by country and volume
use a lookup table for region pricing in salesforce cpq
Different unit price for EMEA and APAC with volume breaks
a: I'd use one price rule with a lookup table. I create a custom object, say Regional Price, with Region, Product Code, Min Qty, Max Qty and Unit Price, and the pricing team maintains rows like 'EMEA, LAP-01, 1 to 49, 950' and 'EMEA, LAP-01, 50 to 199, 900'. The price rule uses that object as its lookup object, with lookup queries matching region, product code and quantity between min and max, and a price action that writes the matched unit price to the line's special price On Calculate. New regions or tiers are just new rows, no admin change. If it were only quantity, a discount schedule would be simpler; the lookup table wins when there are two or more dimensions.

q: A customer six months into a 12-month contract wants to add 20 more licenses. What do you do in CPQ?
alt: customer wants to add licenses mid contract
how to upsell on an existing cpq contract
add users halfway through subscription term
Mid-term add-on licenses in Salesforce CPQ
a: This is an amendment, not a new quote. I open the customer's contract and click Amend. CPQ creates an amendment opportunity and quote showing the current 100 licenses. I change the quantity on that line to 120, or add a new line, and CPQ prices only the extra 20, prorated to the contract end date, so they pay for six months, not twelve. The existing licenses keep their original price. After approval and signature, I order the amendment quote; the order holds just the 20, and when it's contracted, CPQ adds those subscriptions to the same contract. At renewal, all 120 come through together. The key point for interviewers: never create a separate new contract for add-ons, or you lose co-termination and get two renewal dates.

Only the delta is priced, prorated to end date

Keeps one renewal date

q: A renewal quote is showing the wrong prices. How do you troubleshoot it?
alt: cpq renewal quote pricing incorrect
renewal price is list price but should be same as last year
uplift not applied on renewal quote
Why is my renewal quote price different from the contract?
a: I start with the renewal pricing method, because it decides the source of the price. Same keeps the previous price, List reprices from the current price book, and Uplift adds the renewal uplift rate. I check the Renewal Pricing Method on the account, and the uplift rate on the contract and subscriptions. Then I check the subscriptions themselves: if lines were combined because Combine Subscription Quantities is on, lines with different prices can merge into one price. Next I look at price rules or the calculator plugin, because they also run on renewal quotes and can overwrite the price unless they check the quote type. Finally I check contracted prices and discount schedules on the account. Say a gym chain expected last year's price plus 3% but got list price: usually the method was List on the account.
points: Check Renewal Pricing Method on the account

Combined subscription lines with different prices
Price rules/QCP running on renewal quotes

q: An integration creates CPQ quotes with around 500 lines, and the totals come out wrong or the calculation times out. What do you do?
alt: quote lines inserted by integration not calculated
cpq large quote via api times out
how to recalculate a 500 line quote created by data load
Quote totals are zero after lines inserted through API
a: First I check how the lines are being created. If the integration inserts SBQQ__QuoteLine__c records with plain DML, CPQ's pricing doesn't run properly, so totals are blank or stale. I'd switch it to the CPQ API: read the quote, add products, then call the calculator with a callback that saves the quote, so price rules and schedules apply. Since that calculation runs in the background, the integration must not read totals right away; I have it check back later or wait for a platform event raised after the save. For 500 lines I also review the Large Quote Threshold and Quote Batch Size settings, custom triggers and flows on quote lines, and the plugin, because they all multiply with line count. Where possible, bundles or MDQ reduce the number of lines. For example, an equipment rental site sending nightly quotes had to move from DML to the API.

Calculation is async: do not read totals immediately

Reduce line count with bundles or MDQ

q: Every server bundle must include a support product, and support must be priced at 18% of the bundle. How do you configure it?
alt: force support in a bundle cpq
required option with percent of total pricing
bundle must always have maintenance at a percentage
How do you stop reps removing support from a bundle?
a: Two pieces: make support mandatory inside the bundle, then price it as a percentage. In the server bundle I add a Support feature with a minimum option count of 1, and options for Standard and Premium Support, so the rep must pick one; if there's only one support product, I mark that option Required so it can't be removed. Then I set the support product to percent-of-total pricing at 18%, so its price is 18% of the lines in its base. I make sure the base only includes the server bundle's hardware, not services or other support lines. For example, a 40,000 server configuration gives 7,200 of support, and if the rep adds two more disks, support recalculates. I'd also add a quote-level validation if support sold outside the bundle must follow the same rule.

Support product priced Percent Of Total at 18%
Control which lines form the base
Optional validation rule at quote level

q: The quote PDF must show a different layout for each region. How would you handle it?
alt: different quote template per country
quote document layout based on region cpq
How do you choose the quote template automatically?
EMEA and US quotes need different terms and logo
a: If the layouts are really different, I create one quote template per region and pick it automatically. Each template gets its own logo, sections, line columns and terms. Then a before-save flow sets the quote's template lookup based on the region, so when the rep clicks Preview Document, the right template is already chosen. If the differences are small, I keep one template and use conditions instead: template sections or quote terms that only print when a quote field matches, such as VAT wording only for EU quotes. For example, an industrial equipment vendor might show prices in EUR with VAT notes and a German address for Europe, and USD with sales tax wording for North America. I prefer fewer templates with conditions, because every extra template is another thing to maintain.

q: A custom trigger on quote lines changes prices, and CPQ keeps overwriting the values or recalculating in a loop. How do you fix it?
alt: trigger on sbqq quote line conflicts with cpq calculation
cpq overwrites the field my trigger sets
quote keeps recalculating after my trigger update
Should I update CPQ price fields from a trigger?
a: The root problem is that the trigger is fighting the calculator. CPQ owns fields like list, regular, customer and net price, and it recalculates them on every calculate, so anything a trigger writes there gets overwritten, and trigger updates can make CPQ calculate again. My steps: move the price logic into a price rule or the calculator plugin, where it runs inside the calculation sequence. Keep triggers for non-price work, like stamping a margin band or syncing to another object, and only run when a relevant field actually changed. Use a static guard so the logic runs once per transaction. And check SBQQ.TriggerControl.isEnabled(), so the trigger stays quiet during data fixes where CPQ triggers are switched off. For example, a 'Gold customer extra 3%' trigger becomes a one-condition price rule.
points: Do not write CPQ-calculated price fields from triggers
Move price logic to price rules or QCP
Changed-field checks and a static guard
Respect SBQQ.TriggerControl.isEnabled()

q: A rep says a product does not show up when they click Add Products. What do you check?
alt: product missing from cpq product selection
cannot find product in add products cpq
Why is my new product not visible on the quote?
product not appearing in quote line editor search
a: I walk the checklist in order. Is the product active? Does it have an active price book entry in the quote's price book, and in the quote's currency? That's the most common miss: someone adds a product in USD but the quote is in EUR. Is the quote using the price book I think it is? Then I check filters: a guided selling process, a filter product rule, or a search filter can hide it. I check whether the product is set up as a component only meant to be sold inside a bundle, and whether the rep has access to the product and price book. For example, a new SSD upgrade for a laptop seller didn't appear because the price book entry existed only in the standard price book, not in the regional one the quotes use.
points: Product active + active entry in quote price book and currency
Quote price book is the expected one
Guided selling, filter rules, search filters
Component-only products and user access

q: A product gets added to the quote with a zero or blank price. Why might that happen?
alt: quote line list price is zero in cpq
price not populating on cpq quote line
why is the unit price empty after adding a product
cpq option price shows 0 in bundle
a: Usually the price is coming from a different place than expected. I check the price book entry for the quote's price book and currency first. If the product is an option inside a bundle, I check whether the option is marked Bundled, which makes its price zero because it's included in the parent, or whether there's an option-level unit price override. Then I check the pricing method: Cost needs a cost record, Block needs block price tiers, and Percent Of Total needs other lines to calculate from. Finally I look for a price rule that writes a zero, for example a rule built for promotions with conditions that are too broad. For example, a printer bundle showed a 0 toner cartridge because the option was marked Bundled, which was correct behaviour; the business just hadn't realised it.

WHERE SBQQ__Discount__c > 20
  AND SBQQ__Quote__r.SBQQ__Primary__c = true

a: A Data Lake Object, or DLO, stores data as it arrives from a source, in that source's own shape and field names. A Data Model Object, or DMO, is the harmonized, standard view of the data, based on the Customer 360 Data Model, like Individual, Contact Point Email or Sales Order. You map DLO fields to DMO fields. So say the CRM calls it Email, the online store calls it customer_email and the loyalty system calls it mail_id. Each one lands in its own DLO as is, and all three map to the same field on the Contact Point Email DMO. Identity resolution, calculated insights, segments, activation and agent grounding all work on DMOs, not on raw DLOs. So the DLO is the storage layer and the DMO is the business-friendly, unified layer. Quick way to spot them: DMOs end with __dlm in their API names, and DLOs end with __dll.

q: What is identity resolution in Data 360?

what is a unified profile and how is it built

a: Identity resolution takes records about the same person from different sources and links them into one unified profile. I configure a ruleset with match rules, which decide when two records are the same person, for example exact email, or fuzzy first name plus exact last name plus normalized phone. Then reconciliation rules decide which value wins for each attribute when sources disagree, like most recent or a source priority order. Say Priya Sharma exists in CRM, and P. Sharma signed up on the website with the same email. The email rule links them, and if their addresses differ, reconciliation picks one, for example the most recent. The result is the Unified Individual DMO plus link objects that connect each unified profile back to its source records. Segments, insights and agents then work on that unified profile instead of on duplicates.

q: What is the difference between match rules and reconciliation rules?

How do reconciliation rules decide which value wins?
what are the match methods in data 360

a: Match rules decide whether two source records belong to the same person. Reconciliation rules decide which attribute values the unified profile shows. A match rule is a set of criteria that must all be true, like exact normalized email, or fuzzy first name plus exact last name plus exact phone. You can have several match rules, and any one of them can link records. Reconciliation rules work at the field level: last updated, most frequent, or source priority, where I rank sources, say CRM above web forms. So if a web form has one phone number and CRM has another, source priority means the profile shows the CRM number. In practice I start strict, check the consolidation rate and sample unified profiles, and only loosen rules when I can prove they're not merging different people.

q: What is the difference between calculated insights and streaming insights?

a: Calculated insights run in batch over the full historical data, so they are perfect for long-term metrics like lifetime value, loyalty tier or purchase frequency, and they can join across unified profiles. Streaming insights are computed on events as they arrive, inside a time window, like counting product views in the last fifteen minutes, so latency is seconds to minutes. Streaming insights cannot look at lifetime history the way a calculated insight can, but they pair well with data actions to react immediately, for example triggering a cart-abandonment follow-up. My rule is: use calculated insights to understand and segment customers, and streaming insights to trigger something right now. Streaming also tends to consume more credits, so I only use it when timing really matters.

a: Zero copy lets Data 360 use data that lives in an external platform like Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery or Amazon Redshift, without copying it into Data 360. Inbound is called federation. I ingest when the data is used constantly in identity resolution, frequent segments or real-time use cases, because querying the same external tables over and over can cost more credits and warehouse compute than ingesting once. q: How does Data 360 handle unstructured data, and what is the difference between vector and hybrid search indexes?

a: Data 360 can ingest unstructured content like PDFs, knowledge articles, transcripts and web pages. It maps that to unstructured data model objects, splits it into chunks and creates vector embeddings, all stored in a search index. A vector index does semantic search. It finds chunks that mean the same thing as the question even if the words differ, so it works well for longer natural questions. A hybrid index combines vector search with keyword search and merges the results, which helps when questions include exact terms like product codes or error numbers. So 'my printer keeps jamming' suits vector search, but 'what does error E-204 mean' needs the keyword side of hybrid. There's also an enriched option that adds summaries, keywords and likely questions to chunks for better retrieval, at extra credit cost. Retrievers then query these indexes to ground prompts and agents.

q: Identity resolution is merging different people into one unified profile. How do you fix it?

q: What is Agentforce?

What is the difference between Agentforce and a chatbot?

a: Agentforce is Salesforce's platform for building autonomous AI agents. An agent can understand a request, reason about it, and take action using your Salesforce data and automation. Einstein Copilot was renamed Agentforce, and today Agentforce is the center of the Agentforce 360 platform. The big difference from a traditional rule-based chatbot is that there's no fixed dialog tree. An agent uses a large language model with the Atlas Reasoning Engine to choose which subagent and actions to use. So if a customer types 'my order hasn't arrived, what can you do?', the agent can look up the order and create a case, without anyone scripting that exact path. Agents can work for customers, like a service agent on a website, or for employees, like an assistant inside Salesforce or Slack. And everything runs through the Einstein Trust Layer for security.

q: What are the main building blocks of an Agentforce agent?

Explain topics, instructions and actions
components of an agentforce agent
how is an agent structured
a: An agent has a role and description, which tell it what job it does and for whom. It has subagents, which used to be called topics, and each subagent covers one area of work. Each subagent has a description used for routing, instructions that guide how it behaves, and actions it can call. Actions are the things it can actually do, like running a flow, an Apex invocable method, a prompt template or an external API. Take a retail service agent. Its role is helping online shoppers. It might have an Order Status subagent with a flow action that looks up the order, and a Returns subagent with an instruction like 'always confirm the order number first'. Around that sit system messages like the welcome and error messages, variables to hold context, the channel where it's deployed, and the agent user and permissions that control what data it can touch. Guardrails come from the Trust Layer, instructions and permissions together.

q: What is a topic, or subagent, in Agentforce?
alt: What are topics in Agentforce?
topics vs subagents, what is the difference
why are topics now called subagents
explain subagent in agentforce
a: A subagent, which Salesforce previously called a topic, is a focused job within an agent, like order management, returns or account questions. Salesforce started calling topics subagents in 2026. The functionality is the same, so you'll see both words in the docs. Each subagent has a description that the reasoning engine uses to decide whether a user's message belongs to it, instructions that tell it how to behave, and a set of actions it's allowed to use. Say a customer asks 'where's my parcel?'. The reasoning engine matches that to the order management description, and that subagent's actions are the ones in play. That's why well-scoped subagents matter. They keep routing accurate and stop the model choosing between too many actions at once. In the new builder, a parent agent can also orchestrate subagents, and each subagent can even use its own model.

q: What is the difference between a topic's classification description, scope and instructions?

a: The classification description is what the reasoning engine reads to decide which topic, now called a subagent, a message belongs to, so I write it in terms of what users ask, like questions about where an order is or when it will arrive. The scope describes the job and its boundaries, what the subagent can and cannot do, which helps keep it from overreaching. Instructions are the behavioral guidance once the subagent is chosen, such as always confirm the order number first, or never promise a refund date. In the new builder with Agent Script, the same ideas map to the subagent description and the reasoning instructions. If routing is wrong, I fix descriptions; if behavior is wrong, I fix instructions or add deterministic logic.

a: Actions are the tools an agent uses to get work done. There are standard actions that Salesforce provides, like querying records, summarizing a record, drafting an email or answering questions with knowledge. Then there are custom actions I build: an autolaunched Flow, an Apex class with an @InvocableMethod, a prompt template from Prompt Builder, and external API actions, for example through External Services or MuleSoft APIs. Each action has a name, a description, and input and output descriptions. The reasoning engine reads those to decide when to call it and what to pass. Here's why that matters. If I describe a flow as 'Process records', the agent has no idea when to use it. If I describe it as 'Gets the delivery status for an order number', it picks it at the right time and knows to pass the order number. So good descriptions are as important as good code.

q: What is the Atlas Reasoning Engine?
alt: How does Agentforce decide what to do?
Explain Atlas reasoning engine
what is the brain of agentforce
how does the agent plan and choose actions
a: The Atlas Reasoning Engine is the brain behind Agentforce. When a user sends a message, it understands the intent, picks the right subagent, plans which actions to run, runs them, looks at the results, and decides whether it has enough to answer or needs another step. Then it writes the response. For example, a customer asks to change the delivery address on their last order. Atlas routes to the order subagent, runs a lookup action, looks at what comes back, decides it needs one more step, runs the update action, and then confirms. It uses large language models along with the agent's descriptions, instructions, variables and grounding data. In the new Agentforce Builder, Atlas runs on an enhanced graph-based engine that supports hybrid reasoning. So some steps follow a fixed path every time, and others are left to the model's judgment. That gives more predictable behavior and lower latency than letting the model re-evaluate everything on every turn.
points: Understand, route, plan, act, observe, respond
Uses LLMs plus agent metadata and grounding

Supports hybrid reasoning

q: What is hybrid reasoning in Agentforce, and when do you use deterministic steps versus LLM reasoning?

How do you make an agent predictable?

When should the agent not decide on its own?
a: Hybrid reasoning means combining deterministic, scripted logic that runs the same way every time with flexible LLM reasoning for the conversational parts. In the new Agentforce Builder, Agent Script lets me write if-else conditions, run actions in a fixed order, set variables and transition between subagents, while still giving the model natural-language instructions where judgment is useful. I make steps deterministic when the business needs a guarantee: identity verification before sharing data, compliance checks, mandatory sequences like check eligibility then create the return, or routing rules. I leave things to the LLM when the task is understanding free text, summarizing, or choosing among a few safe actions. Deterministic steps also cut latency and token use.
points: Deterministic: verification, compliance, fixed sequences
LLM: understanding, summarizing, flexible choices
Agent Script provides if, run, set, transition

q: What is Agent Script? Can you show an example?
alt: Explain Agent Script in Agentforce

a: Agent Script is the language behind the new Agentforce Builder. It mixes natural-language prompt instructions with deterministic logic, so I control exactly which steps must happen and where the model can reason. A script has blocks like system for agent-wide messages, variables, start_agent for routing, and subagent blocks with reasoning instructions and actions. Inside instructions, an arrow starts logic and a pipe starts a prompt line for the LLM. In the logic I can use if and else, run an action, set a variable, or transition to another subagent. For example, in a returns subagent I'd write logic that says if the customer isn't verified, transition to the verification subagent, and then a prompt line telling the model to explain the return options. Variables can be mutable, set during the conversation, or linked to a source like the messaging session. And edits in Canvas view write Agent Script behind the scenes.

# simplified illustration
variables:
    is_verified: mutable boolean = False
        description: "True after the customer passes verification."

subagent Order_Status:
    description: "Answers questions about the status of an existing order."
    reasoning:
        instructions: ->
            if @variables.is_verified == False:
                transition to @subagent.Verify_Customer
            | Ask for the order number if you do not have it,
            | look up the order and explain its status briefly.

q: What is the Einstein Trust Layer?
alt: How does Salesforce keep AI secure?
Explain the Einstein Trust Layer features
trust layer data masking toxicity
Is our data used to train the LLM?
a: The Einstein Trust Layer is the set of security and governance controls that every Agentforce and Prompt Builder request passes through. On the way in, it grounds prompts with data the user is allowed to see, masks sensitive data like personal information before it reaches the model (for prompt templates and features like Service Replies; Salesforce turned masking off for Agentforce agents because it slowed them down and hurt accuracy, and relies on zero data retention and access controls there), and adds prompt defense to reduce injection and misuse. Salesforce has zero data retention agreements with its model providers, so prompts and responses aren't stored or used to train their models. On the way back, it scans responses for toxicity, unmasks the data, and records an audit trail, including prompts, responses and feedback, in Data 360. So say a rep asks for a summary of a customer's case. The model doesn't see the customer's personal details in clear text, the reply is checked before the rep sees it, and there's a record of what was asked. That's the reason companies can use generative AI with their CRM data safely.
points: Secure grounding with user permissions
Data masking and prompt defense
Zero data retention with LLM providers
Toxicity detection and audit trail

q: How do data masking and zero data retention work in the Einstein Trust Layer?
alt: What does zero data retention mean for Agentforce?
How is PII protected when calling the LLM?
trust layer masking explained
does the llm provider keep our prompts
a: Data masking detects sensitive values in the prompt, like names, emails, phone numbers or card numbers, plus fields classified as sensitive, and replaces them with placeholder tokens before the prompt leaves Salesforce. The model works with the placeholders. When the response comes back, the Trust Layer puts the real values back in before showing it to the user. So if a case mentions a customer's name and email, the model only sees placeholders, and the user still sees the real name and email in the reply. Admins can configure which entity types are masked. Big gotcha in interviews: this masking applies to prompt templates and features like Service Replies, but Salesforce turned it off for Agentforce agents, because it added latency and hurt the planner's accuracy. For agents, protection comes from zero data retention, guardrails and what the agent user can access. Zero data retention means the external model providers Salesforce uses have agreed not to store the prompts or responses, and not to use them for training, once the response is returned. That trade-off is why I tune masking with the security team rather than masking everything.
points: Mask before the LLM, demask on return

q: How do you ground a prompt template with data?

a: Grounding means adding real, trusted data to the prompt, so the model answers about our business instead of guessing. In Prompt Builder there are several options. Merge fields pull fields from the input record and related records, and I can include related lists. A template-triggered prompt flow lets me run logic, query several objects and return text into the prompt. An Apex class with an invocable method tagged for the template type can return computed text, which is great for complex queries or callouts. Retrievers bring in chunks from Data 360 search indexes for knowledge-style content, and Data 360 objects can be used too. Say I'm building a sales email template. q: What is RAG and how does Agentforce use it?
alt: Explain retrieval augmented generation
How does an agent answer from our documents?
what is r a g in salesforce
grounding vs fine tuning
a: RAG stands for retrieval augmented generation. Instead of relying only on what the model learned in training, the system first retrieves relevant pieces of our own content, like knowledge articles, PDFs or policies, and adds them to the prompt, so the model answers from that content. Say a customer asks how long they have to return a sale item. On its own the model might just guess. With RAG, the retriever finds the chunk of our returns policy that covers sale items, that goes into the prompt, and the answer matches our actual policy. In Agentforce, content is chunked and indexed in a Data 360 search index, a retriever finds the most relevant chunks for the user's question, and the agent's knowledge action or a prompt template includes them. This reduces hallucination, keeps answers current without retraining, and lets you cite sources. The Agentforce Data Library makes this much simpler to set up by creating the index and retriever for you.
points: Retrieve relevant content, then generate
Data 360 search index + retriever
Reduces hallucination, no retraining
Data Library simplifies setup

q: What is the Agentforce Data Library?

a: The Agentforce Data Library is a simple way to ground agents and prompts in your own content without configuring Data 360 by hand. You create a library and point it at a source, like Salesforce Knowledge articles or uploaded files. It then sets up the pieces behind the scenes automatically: the data stream, the data lake and data model objects, chunking, the search index, and a retriever dedicated to that library. At runtime, the agent's Answer Questions with Knowledge action, or a prompt template, uses that retriever to find relevant content. For example, if a support team uploads its product manuals into a library, the service agent can answer 'how do I reset my router?' from those manuals, without anyone building an index by hand. It's the quickest path to a knowledge-grounded service agent. You can even generate test cases from a data library to check answer quality.

q: Your agent gives a wrong answer to a customer. How do you debug it?

the agent hallucinated, how do you fix it

a: I reproduce the exact conversation in Preview, or find the session in the traces, and look at what happened step by step. First, routing: did it pick the right subagent? If not, I fix the descriptions. Second, actions: did it call the right action with the right inputs, and did the action return correct data? If the data was wrong, it is a Flow, Apex, permission or data problem, not an AI problem. Third, grounding: for knowledge answers, I check which chunks were retrieved; missing or outdated content means fixing the article or index. q: How do you prevent an agent from answering out-of-scope questions?

off topic handling in agentforce
how to keep agent on topic
agent guardrails for scope
a: I use several layers. The agent's role, description and each subagent's description clearly say what it does, so unrelated requests do not match a business subagent. Templates include an Off Topic subagent that politely declines and steers the user back, and an Ambiguous Question subagent that asks for clarification, and I tune their descriptions and instructions. Inside business subagents I add instructions like only answer using retrieved knowledge or action results, and never give legal or financial advice. Where it must be guaranteed, I use Agent Script logic or limit which actions are available. The Trust Layer adds prompt defense and toxicity checks. Then I test with out-of-scope and jailbreak-style utterances in Testing Center.

q: How would you design guardrails and security for a customer-facing agent?
alt: Security design for an Agentforce service agent
What controls would you put on an agent before go live?
agent guardrails best practices
how to make a customer facing agent safe
a: I think in layers. Identity: verify the customer before any personal data is shared, using deterministic logic, and tie actions to the verified contact so one customer can never query another's records. Access: a least-privilege agent user, with sharing Apex, user mode queries, and actions that return only needed fields. Scope: clear subagent descriptions, off-topic handling and instructions to answer only from trusted sources. Actions: confirmation steps before anything irreversible, and limits like refunds only under a threshold, otherwise escalate. Platform: Trust Layer prompt defense, toxicity detection, zero data retention and audit (data masking is off for agents, so access control matters even more). Operations: adversarial testing in Testing Center, monitoring sessions after launch, and a clear human escalation path.

q: How do you monitor Agentforce agents after go-live?
