Say a developer is used to deterministic code. The biggest shift is accepting that the same input can give slightly different outputs, so we test with many variations and review transcripts. I'd also run short sessions to share what worked and what didn't after each sprint.
points: Learn by building a small real agent together
Core concepts: reasoning, descriptions, grounding, trust
Clear roles across developers, admins, testers, architect
Mindset shift to testing non-deterministic behaviour
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: When would you advise a client NOT to use an AI agent?
alt: Is Agentforce always the right answer?
When is a Flow or a simple form better than an agent?
A client wants an agent for everything. When would you push back?
when should you not use agentforce
a: I'd advise against an agent when the process is fixed and predictable, when a mistake is very costly, or when the data isn't ready. If every case follows the same steps, a Flow, a screen form or a simple automation is cheaper, faster and fully predictable. Say a company wants an agent so employees can submit expense claims. If the claim is always the same fields and rules, a well-designed form does it better than a conversation. I'd also push back where wrong answers carry serious legal, financial or safety risk with no human check, like giving medical advice or approving large credit decisions. And if the knowledge base is outdated or the data is spread across systems with no access, the agent will give confident wrong answers, so we fix the data first. Low-volume processes may not justify the build and credit costs either. Saying no to the wrong use case protects trust in the right ones.
points: Fixed, predictable processes suit Flow or forms
High-risk decisions need human control
Poor or inaccessible data must be fixed first
Low volume may not justify cost
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: A business leader wants the agent live for all customers next week, but testing shows it isn't ready. What do you do?
alt: How do you handle pressure to launch an agent too early?
The agent still gives wrong answers sometimes but the business wants to go live. What would you say?
How do you negotiate a safer Agentforce launch?
agent not ready but business wants to launch
a: I'd show the evidence, offer a safer launch option that still gives them a date, and let them make an informed decision. First I'd share the test results in plain terms: which kinds of questions it handles well and where it fails. For example, 'it answers order status correctly almost every time, but it confuses return and warranty rules.' Then I'd suggest a staged launch: go live next week with only the parts that pass, like order status, and route returns and warranty to humans for now. Or launch to a limited audience, like logged-in customers or one region, with close monitoring and the kill switch ready. Meanwhile, we fix the failing area and add those cases to the test set. Say the leader has announced the launch publicly. A narrower launch on that date still lets them keep the promise without risking a bad customer experience. If they still want everything live, I document the risk and who accepted it.
points: Share test results in plain language
Launch only what passes, route the rest to humans
Limited audience with monitoring and kill switch
Document the risk if overruled
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: How do you manage changes to an agent's instructions and actions once it's in production?
alt: What change control do you need for a live AI agent?
Someone wants to tweak the agent's prompt in production. What's your process?
How do you release agent changes safely as a lead?
agentforce release governance after go live
a: I treat any change to instructions, subagent descriptions or actions as a real release, because a small wording change can shift how the agent behaves across many conversations. The process: the change is made in a sandbox, tracked in source control, and run against our regression test set in Testing Center before it goes anywhere. The test set includes normal questions, edge cases and attempts to misuse the agent, and it grows every time we find a problem in production. A business owner reviews results and signs off, then it's deployed and activated through the pipeline, with the previous version ready to reactivate if needed. Say marketing wants the agent to mention a new promotion. That sounds harmless, but it might make the agent push the promotion in unrelated conversations. The tests would catch that before customers see it. After release, we watch the key measures closely for a few days. Small, frequent, tested changes are safer than big rewrites.
points: Instruction changes are releases, not quick edits
Sandbox, source control, regression tests before deploy
Test set grows from production issues
Business sign-off, monitored rollout, quick rollback
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with an architect.
alt: Describe a situation where you challenged a senior person's technical decision
Have you ever disagreed with your solution architect? What happened?
Tell me about a technical disagreement with someone more senior
time you disagreed with architect behavioural question
a: I'd answer in four parts: the disagreement, how I raised it, how it was decided, and what I learned. The interviewer wants to see that I disagree with evidence, respect the decision process, and don't hold grudges. A story with this shape works: the architect proposed a synchronous callout from a trigger to an external system, and I was worried about timeouts and record locks under load. Rather than arguing in a meeting, I asked for a short session, explained the risk, and brought evidence, like a quick proof of concept showing the failure under bulk updates, plus an alternative using a queueable with retry. Then the ending: either they agreed and we changed it, or they kept their design for a good reason I hadn't known, and I committed fully. I close with the lesson, for example that bringing an alternative and data turns a disagreement into a joint decision. I'd fit my own real example into this shape.
points: Structure: disagreement, how raised, decision, lesson
Raise it privately with evidence and an alternative
Respect the decision and commit either way
Use your own real story in this shape
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Tell me about a time you missed a deadline.
alt: Describe a time your team didn't deliver on time. What did you do?
Have you ever missed a project deadline?
Tell me about a delivery that slipped and how you handled it
missed deadline interview question for lead
a: I'd own it, show that I raised it early, explain what I did to limit the impact, and what I changed afterwards. The structure: what the deadline was and why it mattered, when and why I realised it would slip, how I told stakeholders and what options I gave them, and the lesson. A story with this shape works well: an integration with an external system turned out to need an authentication method nobody had flagged, and getting access from the other team took longer than planned. As soon as I knew, I told the product owner, explained the cause, and offered options: release the rest of the feature on time with the integration behind a switch, or move the whole date. We agreed a new date, and I kept them updated until it landed. The lesson I'd give is something concrete, like now confirming integration access and credentials during refinement, before committing to a date. I'd use my own real example here.
points: Own it, no blaming
Show you flagged it early with options
Explain how you limited impact
End with a concrete process change
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: What was your biggest technical mistake, and what did you learn?
alt: Tell me about a time you broke something in production
Describe a technical decision you got wrong
What's a mistake you made as a developer or lead?
biggest mistake in your career interview question
a: I'd pick a real mistake with real impact, but one I caught, fixed and learned from, and I'd spend most of the time on the fix and the lesson. The structure: what I did, what went wrong, how I found out, what I did immediately, and what I changed so it can't happen again. A story with this shape works: I deployed a change that included a validation rule which blocked an integration user from updating records, so overnight syncs started failing. I spotted it from error logs in the morning, told the stakeholders, deactivated the rule to restore the sync, then fixed it properly by excluding the integration user with a custom permission. The lesson: we added integration user scenarios to our test checklist and started reviewing failed sync logs after every release. Interviewers want to hear ownership and a system fix, not a tiny mistake dressed up. I'd use my own real example in this structure.
points: Pick a real mistake with real impact
Own it clearly, no blaming others
Focus on the immediate fix and the lasting change
Use your own true story in this shape
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Tell me about a time you influenced a decision without having authority.
alt: How have you convinced people who don't report to you?
Describe a time you got another team to change their approach
Give an example of leading without a formal title
influence without authority example
a: I'd show that I understood what the other side cared about, and used evidence and a low-risk first step to win them over. The structure: the decision, why I couldn't just decide it, what the other side cared about, how I made the case, and the result. A story with this shape works: another team owned an integration that sent duplicate records into our org, and they didn't see it as their problem. I collected a few real examples showing the duplicates and how much clean-up time our users spent, then framed it in terms they cared about, such as failed loads in their own logs. I proposed a small change on their side, like sending an external Id so we could upsert, and offered to help test it. Once they saw it was small and helped them too, they agreed. The lesson is that people move faster when the change is small and clearly helps them. I'd plug in my own real example.
points: Understand what the other side cares about
Bring real examples and evidence
Propose a small, low-risk first step
Show how it helps them too
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a stakeholder.
alt: How do you tell a client their project is going to be late or over budget?
Describe a difficult conversation with a business stakeholder
Have you ever had to tell a manager something they didn't want to hear?
giving bad news to stakeholders example
a: I'd show that I delivered it early, directly and with a plan, not buried in a status report. The structure: what the bad news was, how quickly I raised it, how I framed it, the options I offered, and how the relationship held up. A story with this shape works: during testing we found that a requested feature, like real-time sync with an external system, couldn't meet the response time they expected without a bigger middleware change. I set up a short call instead of sending an email, stated the problem in the first minute, explained why in plain language, and gave two or three options with cost and timing, for example near-real-time sync now and true real-time in a later phase. I told them what I recommended and why. Ending: they picked an option, and they trusted my updates more afterwards because I'd been straight with them. The lesson is that surprises damage trust far more than bad news itself. I'd use my own real story here.
points: Raise it early, in a conversation not a buried email
State the news in the first minute
Give options with cost and timing, plus a recommendation
Surprises hurt trust more than bad news
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Tell me about a time you gave difficult feedback to a team member.
alt: Describe how you handled a hard conversation with someone on your team
Have you had to tell a colleague their work wasn't good enough?
Give an example of giving constructive feedback as a lead
difficult feedback example behavioural
a: I'd show that I gave it privately, specifically and soon, and that I helped the person improve afterwards. The structure: the situation, why it needed addressing, how I prepared, what I actually said, how they reacted, and what changed. A story with this shape works: a capable developer kept merging changes without waiting for review, which caused a couple of broken builds and frustrated others. I asked for a one-to-one, described the specific instances and their effect on the team, without labels like 'careless', and then asked for their side. It turned out they felt reviews were too slow and were blocking them. We agreed they'd follow the review process, and I'd fix the slow-review problem by setting a same-day review expectation. Ending: the behaviour stopped, and the team's review speed improved for everyone. The lesson is that difficult feedback often uncovers a process problem too. I'd fit my own real example into this shape.
points: Private, specific and soon
Describe behaviour and impact, not personality
Ask for their side; there may be a real cause
Agree actions on both sides
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Tell me about a time you turned around a struggling project or team.
alt: Have you ever taken over a project that was failing?
Describe a time you rescued a project that was off track
What did you do when you joined a team that was behind schedule?
turning around a failing salesforce project example
a: I'd show a clear sequence: understand, stabilise, then improve, with steps rather than heroics. The structure: what state the project was in, what I found when I dug in, the first few changes I made, how I brought stakeholders along, and the outcome. A story with this shape works: a project was missing sprint goals, UAT kept failing and the business had lost confidence. I spent the first days talking to the team and the product owner, and found the main causes, for example vague stories, no shared test data and frequent environment conflicts. I made a few focused changes: a definition of ready so stories were clear before the sprint, a basic pipeline so environments stayed in sync, and a reset of the plan with the business, with a smaller, realistic scope. I sent short weekly updates so trust came back. Ending: delivery became predictable. The lesson is that struggling projects usually need fewer, clearer priorities, not more effort. I'd use my own real story here.
points: Understand, stabilise, improve
Find root causes by talking to the team
A few focused process changes and a re-planned scope
Rebuild trust with regular honest updates
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Tell me about a time you had to make a technical decision with incomplete information.
alt: Describe a decision you made under uncertainty
How do you decide when you don't have all the facts?
Give an example of a call you made without enough time to research it fully
making decisions with incomplete information example
a: I'd show that I separated what I knew from what I didn't, made the decision reversible where I could, and set a point to review it. The structure: the decision and why it couldn't wait, what was unknown, how I reduced the risk, what I chose, and how it turned out. A story with this shape works: we had to choose how to integrate with a partner system before their API documentation was final. Waiting would have blocked the sprint. I picked an approach that kept our side flexible, like putting the callout behind an interface with a mock implementation, so we could build and test our logic now and plug in the real API later. I told the team and stakeholders what assumptions we were making and agreed when we'd revisit them. Ending: when the final API arrived, only the adapter needed changing. The lesson is that a reversible decision made on time usually beats a perfect decision made too late. I'd use my own real example.
points: Separate known from unknown
Prefer reversible decisions; isolate the risky part
State assumptions and set a review point
On time and reversible beats perfect and late
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural

q: Why do you think you're ready for a lead role?
alt: What makes you a good fit for a technical lead position?
You've been a developer. Why move into a lead role now?
What leadership experience do you have?
why should we hire you as a salesforce lead
a: I'd answer with the lead behaviours I'm already doing, backed by short real examples, rather than claiming a title. The structure: say what I believe a lead does, give two or three examples of me doing those things, and say what I'm still growing in. For a Salesforce technical lead, I'd say the job is making the team effective: good technical decisions, reviews that teach, clear communication with the business, and protecting quality under pressure. Then the examples, from my own work, for instance reviewing others' code and setting up patterns the team reused, mentoring or training newer developers, leading a technical discussion with business stakeholders, or handling a production issue calmly. Say I'm the person colleagues already come to when a deployment fails. That's leadership without the title. I'd finish honestly with one area I'm developing, like running architecture reviews across several teams, and how I'm working on it. Self-awareness is part of being ready.
points: Define what a lead does
Two or three real examples of already doing it
Name one honest growth area and how you're working on it
Show leadership without the title
area: Lead roles: leadership, governance and behavioural
